docs.title: Detailed Breakdown of Scale Architectures:
docs.text:
1. PAN (Personal Area Network):

  2. Operates over short ranges (around 1 m to 10 m).

  3. Uses technologies like Bluetooth (IEEE 802.15.1) or Zigbee (802.15.4) in master-slave configurations. [Faculty — Slide 17]

  4. LAN (Local Area Network):

  5. Privately owned networks operating within a single building or campus.

  6. Wired LANs: Use point-to-point links connected via a central Switch (Switched Ethernet, IEEE 802.3).

  7. Wireless LANs (WLANs): Use radio signals broadcast from an Access Point (AP) (IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi). [Faculty — Slide 18]

  8. MAN (Metropolitan Area Network):

  9. Covers an entire city.

  10. Classic example: Cable Television networks upgraded to convey two-way Internet data (DOCSIS standards). [Faculty — Slide 19]

  11. WAN (Wide Area Network):

  12. Spans large geographical areas (countries/continents).

  13. Consists of two distinct elements:

  14. Hosts: Customer machines executing user applications.

  15. Subnet / Network Core: Connects hosts. Consists of Transmission Lines (copper/fiber/radios) and Routers (switching elements that connect two or more transmission lines). [Faculty — Slide 20 / General — Slide 20-22]

+-------------------------------------------------------+
| WAN Subnet                                            |
|     [Router R1] ------------ [Router R2]              |
|          |                        |                   |
|     [Router R3] ------------ [Router R4]              |
+----------+------------------------+-------------------+
           |                        |
      +----+----+              +----+----+
      | Host H1 |              | Host H2 |
      +---------+              +---------+

[Diagram: WAN Structure with Subnet & Routers — Faculty Slide 20]

docs.title: 3.3 Key Hardware & Switching Terms
docs.text:
• Packet: A discrete block of data containing a header (control info, addresses) and payload (actual data). [General — Slide 23]

  • Packet Switching: Transmission technique where data stream is divided into packets that are routed independently across shared network links. [General — Slide 23]

  • Circuit Switching: A dedicated physical path (circuit) is established between sender and receiver for the entire duration of the call (e.g., traditional telephone network). [Faculty — Slide 43]

  • Datagram: A connectionless packet transfer mechanism where each packet carries full source and destination addresses and is routed independently. [General — Slide 23]

  • Virtual Circuit: A connection-oriented packet switching technique where a pre-planned logical path is established through routers before data packets are sent. [General — Slide 23]

docs.title: 4.1 Protocol Hierarchies
docs.text:
To reduce design complexity, most networks are organized as a stack of layers or levels, each built upon the one below

it.

  • Layer: A module designed to perform a specific abstraction or task. [Faculty + General — Slide 24]

  • Protocol: An agreement/set of rules between the communicating parties (peer entities) on how communication is to take place across a layer. [Faculty + General — Slide 24-25]

  • Interface: Defines which primitive operations and services the lower layer offers to the layer directly above it. [Faculty + General — Slide 25]

  • Network Architecture: A set of layers and protocols. The specification of the architecture must contain enough information to allow an implementer to write the software or build the hardware for each layer. [Faculty + General — Slide 25]

  • Protocol Stack: The specific list of protocols used by a system, one protocol per layer. [Faculty + General — Slide 25]

docs.title: 4.2 The Philosopher-Translator-Secretary Analogy
docs.text:
To visualize layered communication:

  • Two philosophers (Layer 3 entities) in different countries want to communicate. Philosopher 1 speaks Swahili; Philosopher 2 speaks French.

  • Philosopher 1 passes his message to a Translator (Layer 2 entity), who translates it to English (an agreed protocol).

  • The Translator passes the English message to a Secretary (Layer 1 entity), who sends it via Fax/Email (Physical medium).

  • At the destination, the Secretary receives the raw fax, hands it to the Translator (who translates English to French), who hands the French message to Philosopher 2.

+------------------+                          +------------------+
| Philosopher (L3) | <--- Virtual Protocol--> | Philosopher (L3) |
+--------+---------+                          +--------+---------+
         | Interface                                   | Interface
+--------v---------+                          +--------v---------+
| Translator  (L2) | <--- Virtual Protocol--> | Translator  (L2) |
+--------+---------+                          +--------+---------+
         | Interface                                   | Interface
+--------v---------+                          +--------v---------+
| Secretary   (L1) | <--- Virtual Protocol--> | Secretary   (L1) |
+--------+---------+                          +--------+---------+
         | Physical Medium                             | Physical Medium
+--------v---------------------------------------------v---------+
|                    Physical Communication Path                  |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+

[Diagram: Virtual vs Actual Layered Communication — Faculty Slide 26]

docs.title: 4.3 Encapsulation and Decapsulation
docs.text:
• As message data passes down the protocol stack on the sending host:

  • Layer N receives a Service Data Unit (SDU) from Layer N + 1.

  • Layer N prepends its own Header ( H N ) (and sometimes appends a Trailer) containing control information (addresses, sequence numbers, checksums).

  • The resulting unit is the Protocol Data Unit (PDU) of Layer N, which is passed down as the SDU of Layer N - 1.

  • This process is called Encapsulation.

  • At the receiving host, as data moves up the stack, headers are stripped off layer-by-layer ( Decapsulation). [Faculty — Slide 27 / General — Slide 27] Layer 5: [ Application Message ]

                 |

             v

Layer 4: [ H4 | Application Message ]                  (Segment / Transport PDU)
               |
               v
Layer 3: [ H3 | H4 | Application Message ]            (Packet / Network PDU)
               |
               v
Layer 2: [ H2 | H3 | H4 | Application Message | T2 ]   (Frame / Data Link PDU)
               |
               v
Layer 1:  101101001011001010110010101101010010101      (Physical Bits)

[Diagram: Data Encapsulation Information Flow — Faculty Slide 27]

docs.title: 4.4 Major Layer Design Issues
docs.text:
1. Addressing: Identifying senders and receivers across layers.

  2. Error Control: Detecting and correcting bit errors introduced by physical links.

  3. Flow Control: Preventing a fast sender from swamping a slow receiver.

  4. Multiplexing & Demultiplexing: Combining multiple upper-layer conversations onto a single lower-layer channel, and separating them at the destination.

  5. Routing: Choosing optimal paths through a mesh of intermediate routers.

  6. Scalability & Security: Ensuring performance holds as network grows, and preventing tampering/eavesdropping. [Faculty — Slide 24 / General — Slide 24]

docs.title: 5.1 Detailed Breakdown
docs.text:
Services
                              |
      +-----------------------+-----------------------+
      |                                               |
Connection-Oriented                             Connectionless
(Telephone Model)                               (Postal Mail Model)
  1. Setup Connection                             1. Packets sent independently
  2. Use Connection                               2. No setup / teardown
  3. Release Connection                           3. Packets may arrive out-of-order

  1. Connection-Oriented Service:

  2. Patterned after the telephone system.

  3. Requires establishing a connection prior to sending data, using it for data transfer, and tearing it down afterwards.

  4. Acts like a pipe: sender pushes bits in at one end, receiver extracts them in the exact same order at the other end. [Faculty + General — Slide 28]

  5. Connectionless Service:

  6. Patterned after the postal system.

  7. Each message (datagram) carries the full destination address and is routed independently through the intermediate nodes.

  8. Later-sent packets may arrive before earlier-sent packets (out-of-order delivery). [Faculty + General — Slide 28]

docs.title: 5.2 Classification Grid of Services
docs.text:
Service Category Service Type Standard Example / Analogy Connection-Oriented Reliable Message Stream Sequence of discrete pages/documents Reliable Byte Stream Movie streaming, file transfer (TCP) Unreliable Connection Digitized voice / IP Telephony Connectionless Unreliable Datagram Electronic junk mail, UDP Acknowledged Datagram Registered mail with return receipt Request-Reply Client-server database query

[Faculty — Slide 28 / General — Slide 28]

docs.title: 6.1 Service vs. Protocol (Crucial Distinction)
docs.text:
• Service: A set of primitive operations that a lower layer provides to the layer above it. The service defines what operations the layer is prepared to perform, but says nothing about how these operations are implemented (Vertical Interface abstraction). [Faculty + General — Slide 31]

  • Protocol: A set of rules governing the format and meaning of frames, packets, or messages that are exchanged between peer entities within the same layer across different machines (Horizontal Interaction). [Faculty + General — Slide 31]

    ```text Host A (Layer N+1) Host B (Layer N+1) | ^ | Service Primitive | Service Primitive v (Vertical) | (Vertical) Host A (Layer N) <===== Layer N Protocol =====> Host B (Layer N) (Horizontal) 

    ---





### 6.2 The Six Core Service Primitives





For a simple connection-oriented service:





| Primitive  | Type    | Meaning / Action                                   |
|------------|---------|----------------------------------------------------|
| LISTEN     | Passive | Block waiting for an incoming connection request   |
| CONNECT    | Active  | Establish a connection by sending a request packet |
| ACCEPT     | Active  | Accept an incoming connection request              |
| RECEIVE    | Passive | Block waiting for an incoming data packet          |
| SEND       | Active  | Send a data packet to the peer entity              |
| DISCONNECT | Active  | Terminate / release the connection                 |





[Faculty — Slide 29 / General — Slide 29]


---





### 6.3 Sequence of Primitives in Client-Server Communication





```text
   Client Host                                   Server Host
+---------------+                             +---------------+
|               |                             | Exec `LISTEN` |
|               |                             | (Blocks)      |
| Exec `CONNECT`| -- (1) Connect Request -->  |               |
| (Blocks)      |                             | Unblocks      |
|               | <- (2) Connect Ack/Accept-- | Exec `ACCEPT` |
| Unblocks      |                             | Exec `RECEIVE`|
| Exec `SEND`   | -- (3) Data Request ------> | (Blocks)      |
| Exec `RECEIVE`|                             | Process Data  |
| (Blocks)      | <- (4) Data Reply -------- | Exec `SEND`   |
| Exec `DISCONN`| -- (5) Disconnect Req --->  | Exec `DISCONN`|
+---------------+                             +---------------+

[Diagram: Client-Server Interaction via Primitives — General Slide 30]

docs.title: 7.1 The OSI Reference Model (7 Layers)
docs.text: Developed by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO). [Faculty + General — Slide 32-35]

docs.title: ISO OSI Principles for Layering:
docs.text:
1. A layer should be created where a different abstraction is needed.

  2. Each layer should perform a well-defined function.

  3. The function of each layer should be chosen with an eye toward defining internationally standardized protocols.

  4. Layer boundaries should be chosen to minimize information flow across interfaces. [General — Slide 33]

+-----------------------------------+


| 7. Application Layer              |


+-----------------------------------+


| 6. Presentation Layer             |


+-----------------------------------+


| 5. Session Layer                  |


+-----------------------------------+


| 4. Transport Layer                |  <-- End-to-End Control


+-----------------------------------+


| 3. Network Layer                  |  <-- Subnet Routing


+-----------------------------------+

docs.title: Functions of the 7 OSI Layers:
docs.text:
1. Physical Layer (Layer 1): Transmits raw bits over a communication channel. Defines voltage levels, bit timing, pin counts, and transmission media specs. [Faculty — Slide 35]

  2. Data Link Layer (Layer 2): Takes raw transmission facility and transforms it into a line that appears free of undetected transmission errors. Groups bits into frames, handles frame synchronization, error detection/correction, and flow control. [Faculty — Slide 35]

  3. Network Layer (Layer 3): Controls the operation of the subnet. Handles packet routing, congestion control, and internetworking between heterogeneous networks. [Faculty — Slide 35]

  4. Transport Layer (Layer 4): Accepts data from Session layer, splits it up into smaller units, passes these to Network layer, and ensures that all pieces arrive correctly at the other end. True end-to-end layer. [Faculty — Slide 35]

  5. Session Layer (Layer 5): Allows users on different machines to establish sessions between them. Provides dialog control (keeping track of whose turn it is to transmit) and synchronization (inserting checkpoints into long transfers). [Faculty — Slide 35 / General — Slide 57]

  6. Presentation Layer (Layer 6): Concerned with the syntax and semantics of the information transmitted. Handles data format conversions, encoding, data compression, and encryption. [Faculty — Slide 35 / General — Slide 57]

  7. Application Layer (Layer 7): Contains a variety of protocols that users commonly need (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS). [Faculty — Slide 35]

docs.title: Functions of the TCP/IP Layers:
docs.text:
1. Link Layer (Host-to-Network): Describes what links (such as serial lines or Ethernet) must do to meet the needs of the connectionless Internet layer. It is not really a layer in the strict sense, but an interface between hosts and transmission links. [General — Slide 36]
  2. Internet Layer: The linchpin of the architecture. Defines an official packet format and protocol called IP (Internet Protocol). Routes IP packets to their destinations independently. Handles packet delivery across network boundaries. [General — Slide 36]
  3. Transport Layer: Allows peer entities on the source and destination hosts to carry on a conversation.
  4. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): Reliable connection-oriented, byte-stream protocol. Provides flow control and congestion control.
  5. UDP (User Datagram Protocol): Unreliable connectionless datagram protocol for applications that prefer low latency over reliability. [General — Slide 36]
  6. Application Layer: Contains all higher-level protocols (HTTP, Telnet, FTP, SMTP, DNS). [General — Slide 36]

docs.title: 7.3 The Hybrid 5-Layer Model (Used in Textbook & Course)
docs.text: Combines the features of OSI and TCP/IP for pedagogical clarity: [Faculty — Slide 39 / General — Slide 39] text 5-Layer Hybrid Model +------------------------+ | 5. Application Layer | +------------------------+ | 4. Transport Layer | +------------------------+ | 3. Network Layer | +------------------------+ | 2. Data Link Layer | +------------------------+ | 1. Physical Layer | +------------------------+

docs.title: 7.4 Detailed Comparison: OSI vs. TCP/IP Models
docs.text:
Feature / Property OSI Model TCP/IP Model Number of Layers 7 Layers 4 Layers Service vs Protocol Distinction Explicitly distinguished. Services, Interfaces, and Protocols are clear. Implicitly merged. Distinctions are blurry; protocols fit loosely. Development Approach Model was devised before protocols were written (Theoretical). Protocols were written first; model was a description of existing protocols (Practical). Network Layer Communication Supports both Connection-Oriented and Connectionless communication. Supports only Connectionless communication (IP). Transport Layer Communication Supports only Connection-Oriented communication. Supports both Connection-Oriented (TCP) and Connectionless (UDP). Session & Presentation Layers Present as separate, explicit layers (5 & 6). Omitted entirely / integrated into Application layer. Physical & Data Link Layers Explicitly separated into Layers 1 and 2. Combined into a single "Link" or "Host-to-Network" layer.

[Faculty — Slide 40 / General — Slide 40]

docs.title: A. Critique of the OSI Model ("The Four Bads") [Faculty + General — Slide 41]
docs.text:
1. Bad Timing: The OSI standards were published after TCP/IP was already heavily deployed in universities and industry ( The "Elephant Problem": TCP/IP took over the market before OSI was finalized).

  2. Bad Technology: Session and Presentation layers are virtually empty; Data Link and Physical layers are heavily redundant; complex and inefficient implementation.

  3. Bad Implementation: Initial OSI implementations were slow, bulky, and buggy compared to TCP/IP.

  4. Bad Politics: OSI was seen as government/telecom bureaucrat-driven, while TCP/IP was seen as open-source academic hacker- driven.

docs.title: B. Critique of the TCP/IP Model
docs.text:
1. Does not clearly distinguish between concepts of service, interface, and protocol.

  2. Not general; hard to adapt to describe protocol stacks other than TCP/IP.

  3. The Link layer is not really a layer in the architectural sense, but an interface.

  4. Completely omits physical and data link layer specifications. [General — Slide 41]

docs.title: 8.1 ARPANET History & Paul Baran's Innovation
docs.text:
• In the 1960s, the US Defense Department wanted a command-and-control network that could survive a nuclear strike.

  • Centralized / Hierarchical Networks (Telephone System): Vulnerable because destruction of a single central switch breaks communication for all connected nodes.

  • Paul Baran's Distributed Packet Switching: Proposed a mesh network of interconnected switching nodes (IMPs - Interface Message Processors). Packets dynamically route around destroyed nodes. [Faculty — Slide 42-43 / General — Slide 43-46]

    ```text (a) Centralized (b) Distributed Mesh (Baran) [Switch] (O)-----(O)-----(O) / | \ | \ / | / | (O) (O) (O) | (O)----(O)---- | (O)------------- (O) 

    [Diagram: Centralized Telephone System vs Baran's Distributed Network — General Slide 43]

docs.text:
• Infrastructure Mode: Wireless hosts connect to a wired network via a central Access Point ( AP). [Faculty — Slide 48 / General — Slide 49]

docs.text:
1. Network Metric Conversion (Bandwidth vs Storage):

  2. Transmission Speed: 1 Mbps = 10⁶ bits/sec

docs.title: 11.2 Important Definitions
docs.text:
• Computer Network: A collection of autonomous computers interconnected by communication links to exchange information.

  • Protocol: Rules governing the format and meaning of messages exchanged between peer entities at the same layer.

  • Service: Operations a lower layer provides to the layer directly above it via an interface.

  • Encapsulation: Adding layer headers/trailers to higher-layer SDUs as data moves down the stack.

  • Network Neutrality: Treating all Internet data traffic equally without discrimination by source, content, or application.

docs.title: 11.3 Important Comparisons
docs.text:
• Computer Network vs Distributed System: Explicit node visibility vs transparent unified system.

  • OSI vs TCP/IP: 7 layers vs 4 layers; theory-driven vs practical-driven; strict service/protocol separation vs merged concept.

  • Connection-Oriented vs Connectionless: Dedicated setup phase / in-order delivery vs independent datagram routing / possible reordering.

docs.title: 11.4 Exam Revision Notes
docs.text:
• Must-Know Diagrams: OSI 7-layer model, TCP/IP 4-layer model, Client-Server architecture, Encapsulation flow down stack.

  • Must-Know Concepts: Distinction between Service (vertical interface) and Protocol (horizontal peer rule).

  • Commonly Confused Prefixes: 1 Mbps in transmission bandwidth is 10⁶ bits/s, NOT 2²⁰.

Chapter 3 — Data Link Layer

docs.title: 1.1 Role and Core Objectives of Data Link Layer
docs.text:
• The Physical Layer delivers raw bits over a physical medium. However, physical channels suffer from:

  • Limited bandwidth

  • Signal distortions and bit errors

  • Propagation delays [Faculty — Slide 3]

  • Primary Objective of Data Link Layer: To transform a raw transmission facility into a line that appears free of undetected transmission errors to the Network Layer above it. [Faculty — Slide 4]

docs.title: 1.2 Functions of Data Link Layer
docs.text:
1. Providing a well-defined service interface to the Network Layer.

  2. Framing: Grouping physical bit streams into discrete units called frames.

  3. Error Handling: Detecting and correcting errors (corrupted, lost, or duplicate frames).

  4. Flow Control: Regulating data transmission rate so fast senders do not overwhelm slow receivers. [Faculty — Slide 4]

docs.title: 1.3 Layer Relationship & Implementation Architecture
docs.text:
• Virtual vs. Actual Communication: The Data Link Layer entities communicate virtually via a Data Link Protocol, but actual data flows down to the Physical Layer, across the physical medium, and back up. [Faculty — Slide 6 / General — Slide 9]

    ```text Host A (Network Layer) Host B (Network Layer) | ^ v Virtual Data Link Protocol Path | Host A (Data Link Layer) =====================> Host B (Data Link Layer) | ^ v Actual Physical Transmission Path | Host A (Physical Layer) ---------------------> Host B (Physical Layer) 

    - Hardware vs. Software Implementation:


- NIC (Network Interface Card): Handles Physical Layer processes and time-critical Data Link Layer functions (framing, CRC hardware check, bit stuffing).


- OS Kernel Device Driver: Handles higher link-layer logic, software timers, and Network Layer interactions on the main CPU. [Faculty — Slide 34 / General — Slide 32]





---





### 1.4 Services Offered to Network Layer





1. Unacknowledged Connectionless Service:


   - Source sends independent frames without destination acknowledging them.


   - No connection setup or release.


   - Lost frames are not recovered by the link layer.


   - Use Cases: Low error rate channels (copper LANs) or real-time voice traffic where delay is worse than lost frames. [Faculty — Slide 8 / General — Slide 11]


2. Acknowledged Connectionless Service:


   - Source sends independent frames, but each frame is individually acknowledged by the receiver.


   - If a frame does not arrive within a timeout period, it is retransmitted.


   - Use Cases: Highly unreliable wireless links (e.g., IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi). [Faculty — Slide 9 / General — Slide 12]


3. Acknowledged Connection-Oriented Service:


   - Connection is established before any data is sent.


   - Frames are numbered, acknowledged, and guaranteed to arrive exactly once and in the correct order.


   - Three Phases: Connection Establishment → Data Transfer → Connection Release.


   - Use Cases: Long-distance point-to-point satellite channels. [Faculty — Slide 10 / General — Slide 13]





---





## 2. Framing





### 2.1 Why Framing is Necessary





Physical Layer delivers a continuous stream of raw bits. To detect and recover from errors, the stream must be broken


down into


discrete Frames, so checksums can be computed for each frame. [Faculty — Slide 11 / General — Slide 14]


---





### 2.2 Framing Methods





#### Method 1: Character Count / Byte Count





- Uses a field in the frame header to specify the total number of characters/bytes in the frame.


- Mechanism: Receiver reads the count field to know where the frame ends. [Faculty — Slide 12 / General — Slide 15]





      ```text
Frame 1 (5 bytes)     Frame 2 (5 bytes)     Frame 3 (8 bytes)
+---+---+---+---+---+ +---+---+---+---+---+ +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+
| 5 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | | 5 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | | 8 | 9 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
+---+---+---+---+---+ +---+---+---+---+---+ +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+

    | 5 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | | 5 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | | 8 | 9 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |

    +---+---+---+---+---+ +---+---+---+---+---+ +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+

  • Fatal Flaw / Disadvantage: If a single bit error corrupts the count field (e.g., a 5 becomes a 7), the receiver loses frame synchronization completely and cannot locate the start of subsequent frames. [Faculty — Slide 12 / General — Slide 16]

docs.title: Method 2: Flag Bytes with Byte Stuffing (Character Stuffing)
docs.text:
• Delimits frames with special control bytes called FLAG bytes (e.g., ASCII DLE STX / DLE ETX or 0x7E).

  • Problem: What if the binary payload data itself contains the byte value matching FLAG?

  • Byte Stuffing Rule:

  • Sender inserts a special Escape byte (ESC) (e.g., 0x7D) immediately before any instance of FLAG or ESC occurring within the payload.

  • Receiver strips off the ESC byte upon reception. [Faculty — Slide 13-16 / General — Slide 17-19] Original Payload: [ A ] [ FLAG ] [ B ] Transmitted (Stuffed): [ FLAG ] [ A ] [ ESC ] [ FLAG ] [ B ] [ FLAG ] Original Payload: [ A ] [ ESC ] [ B ] Transmitted (Stuffed): [ FLAG ] [ A ] [ ESC ] [ ESC ] [ B ] [ FLAG ]

docs.title: Method 3: Flag Bits with Bit Stuffing
docs.text:
• Allows frames to contain an arbitrary number of bits (bit-oriented framing).

  • Frame start and end are marked by the special flag bit pattern: 01111110 (six consecutive 1s).

  • Bit Stuffing Rule (Sender):

  • Whenever sender's data link layer encounters FIVE consecutive 1s in the payload, it automatically stuffs a 0 bit immediately after them into the outgoing bit stream.

  • Destuffing Rule (Receiver):

  • When receiver sees five consecutive 1s followed by a 0 bit, it automatically strips out the 0 bit.

  • If followed by a 1 bit and a 0 bit, it is a valid end-of-frame FLAG (01111110).

  • If followed by two 1 bits, an error has occurred (01111111). [Faculty — Slide 17-20 / General — Slide 20-22] Original Data: 01101111111001111101 Stuffed Stream: 0110111110110011111001 ^ ^ (Stuffed 0s inserted)

docs.title: Method 4: Physical Layer Coding Violations
docs.text:
• Used in networks where Physical Layer encoding has inherent redundancy (e.g., Manchester encoding where every bit period has a signal transition).

  • High-High or Low-Low signals are invalid data transitions; they are used as delimiters to mark frame boundaries. [Faculty — Slide 21 / General — Slide 24]

docs.title: 3.1 Error Types
docs.text:
• Single-Bit Error: Only 1 bit of a data unit is inverted.

  • Burst Error: 2 or more bits in a data unit are corrupted. Length of burst k is measured from the first corrupted bit to the last corrupted bit. [Faculty — Slide 22]

docs.title: 3.2 Error Control Strategies
docs.text:
• Forward Error Correction (FEC): Sender includes enough redundant bits for receiver to detect AND correct errors without retransmission. Used on noisy/high-delay channels (wireless, satellite). [Faculty — Slide 22 / General — Slide 25]

  • Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ): Sender includes just enough redundancy to detect errors. Receiver requests retransmission upon detecting error. Used on low-noise channels (optical fiber). [Faculty — Slide 22 / General — Slide 25]

docs.title: Definition: Hamming Distance
docs.text:
The number of bit positions in which two binary codewords differ. Calculated by performing an XOR operation between two

codewords and counting the number of 1s in the result. [Faculty — Slide 24 / General — Slide 26]

docs.title: Formula: Error Detection Requirement
docs.text:
\[ d_{\text{min}} \ge d + 1 \]

To detect d single-bit errors, the minimum Hamming distance \(d_{\text{min}}\) of the code must be at least d + 1.

[Faculty — Slide 25]

docs.title: Formula: Error Correction Requirement
docs.text:
\[ d_{\text{min}} \ge 2p + 1 \]

To correct p single-bit errors, the minimum Hamming distance \(d_{\text{min}}\) must be at least 2p + 1.

[Faculty — Slide 25]

docs.title: 3.4 The Hamming Code (Single-Bit Error Correcting Code)
Rules of Hamming Code Construction:
docs.text:
1. Bit positions are numbered starting at 1 (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7...).

  2. Check bits (Parity bits \(P_k\)) are placed at positions that are powers of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16…(\(2^k\)).

  3. Data bits (\(D_j\)) fill all remaining positions (3, 5, 6, 7, 9…). [Faculty — Slide 27 / General — Slide 27]

docs.title: Formula: Relationship Between Data Bits and Redundant Check Bits
docs.text:
For m data bits and r redundant check bits:

\[ (m + r + 1) \le 2^r \]

[Faculty — Slide 27]

docs.title: Step-by-Step Worked Numerical Example 1: Hamming Code Encoding
docs.text:
Problem: Encode the 4-bit data message \(D = 1101_2\)

(\(D_4=1,D_3=1,D_2=0,D_1=1\)) into a (7,4) Hamming code using EVEN parity.

  • Given: Data \(m = 4\) bits (1101).

\(r = 3\) check bits are required because:

\[ (m+r+1) \le 2^r \] \[ (4+3+1) \le 2^3 \] \[ 8 \le 8 \]

docs.title: Bit Positioning:
docs.text:
Bit Position:  1   2   3   4   5   6   7


Bit Type:     P1  P2  D1  P4  D2  D3  D4


Bit Value:    ?   ?   1   ?   0   1   1

docs.title: Parity Computation Groups:
docs.text:
• \(P_1\) checks positions (1,3,5,7):
\[ P_1,D_1,D_2,D_4 = P_1,1,0,1 \]

For EVEN parity:

\[ P_1 = 0 \]
  • \(P_2\) checks positions (2,3,6,7):
\[ P_2,D_1,D_3,D_4 = P_2,1,1,1 \]

For EVEN parity:

\[ P_2 = 1 \]
  • \(P_4\) checks positions (4,5,6,7):
\[ P_4,D_2,D_3,D_4 = P_4,0,1,1 \]

For EVEN parity:

\[ P_4 = 0 \]

docs.title: Final Transmitted Codeword:
docs.text:
\[ \text{Codeword} = \mathbf{0110011} \]

[Faculty — Slide 29]

docs.title: 3.6 Internet Checksum (UDP Worked Numerical Example) [Faculty — Slide 33]
docs.text:
• Data is treated as a sequence of 16-bit integers.

  • Integers are added together using 1's complement arithmetic.

  • The final sum is bitwise inverted (NOT operation).

docs.title: 4.1 Definition
docs.text:
Mechanisms to prevent a fast transmitting node from swamping a slower receiving node with more data than its buffers can

store.

[Faculty — Slide 27 / General — Slide 27]

docs.title: 4.2 Three Flow Control Strategies
docs.text:
Flow Control Strategies
                                  |
        +-------------------------+-------------------------+
        |                         |                         |
  Feedback-Based             Rate-Based               Credit-Based
(Receiver sends ACKs)    (Built-in Rate Limit)   (Receiver grants credits)

  1. Feedback-Based Flow Control: Receiver sends feedback messages back to the sender giving explicit permission to transmit more data (e.g., Stop-and-Wait, Sliding Window ACKs). [Faculty — Slide 28 / General — Slide 28]

  2. Rate-Based Flow Control: Protocol mechanism limits transmission to a fixed data rate built-in, without explicit feedback frames. [Faculty — Slide 29 / General — Slide 29]

  3. Credit-Based Flow Control: Receiver grants sender explicit window credits (in bytes or frames). Sender deducts credits for each byte sent and stops when credits reach zero. [Faculty — Slide 30 / General — Slide 30]

docs.title: 5.1 Protocol Environment Architecture
docs.text:
In Tanenbaum framework, protocol code interacts with lower (Physical) and upper (Network) layers via interface

primitives:

  • to_network_layer(p) / from_network_layer(&p)

  • to_physical_layer(&f) / from_physical_layer(&f)

  • start_timer(k) / stop_timer(k)

  • wait_for_event(&event) [Faculty — Slide 35-36 / General — Slide 34-36]

docs.title: Key Assumptions:
docs.text:
1. Communication is strictly unidirectional (Simplex).

  2. Physical channel is completely error-free.

  3. Receiver's network layer has infinite processing speed and buffer space (No flow control needed). [Faculty — Slide 37 / General — Slide 37]

docs.title: Mechanism:
docs.text:
Sender loops infinitely fetching packets from network layer and sending frames. Receiver loops infinitely waiting for

frames and

handing packets up.

// Sender (Utopian)


void sender1(void) {


    frame s; packet buffer;


    while (true) {


        from_network_layer(&buffer);


        s.info = buffer;


        to_physical_layer(&s);


    }


}

docs.title: 5.3 Protocol 2: Simplex Stop-and-Wait Protocol for Error-Free Channel
Key Assumptions:
docs.text:
1. Communication is unidirectional.

  2. Physical channel is error-free.

  3. Receiver has finite buffer capacity and limited processing speed. [Faculty — Slide 39 / General — Slide 39]

docs.title: Mechanism:
docs.text:
Sender sends 1 frame, then stops and waits until receiver sends back an explicit ACK dummy frame signaling it is ready

for the

next frame.

   Sender Machine                                Receiver Machine
+------------------+                          +-------------------+
| Send Frame 0     | -----------------------> | Receive Frame 0   |
| (Wait for ACK)   |                          | Pass to Network L |
|                  | <----------------------- | Send Dummy ACK    |
| Receive ACK      |                          | (Wait for Frame)  |
| Send Frame 1     | -----------------------> |                   |
+------------------+                          +-------------------+

docs.title: 5.4 Protocol 3: Simplex Stop-and-Wait for Noisy Channel (PAR)
Key Assumptions:
docs.text:
1. Channel is noisy: frames can be corrupted or lost completely.

  2. ACKs can also be corrupted or lost. [Faculty — Slide 42 / General — Slide 42]

docs.title: Key Mechanisms added:
docs.text:
1. Timer & Retransmission: Sender sets a timer upon transmitting a frame. If ACK does not arrive before timer expires, sender retransmits.

  2. 1-Bit Sequence Numbers (0 and 1): Prevents duplicate frame acceptance when an ACK is delayed/lost. [Faculty — Slide 44 / General — Slide 44] Normal Sequence: Sender --(Frame 0)--> Receiver --(ACK 0)--> Sender --(Frame 1)--> Receiver Lost ACK Scenario: Sender --(Frame 0)--> Receiver (Gets Frame 0, Sends ACK 0 [LOST!]) Sender Timer Expires! Sender --(Retransmit Frame 0)--> Receiver (Sees Seq 0 duplicate, discards payload, re-sends ACK 0!)

docs.title: 6.1 Bidirectional Transmission & Piggybacking
docs.text:
• Piggybacking: Temporarily delaying an outgoing ACK so it can be hooked onto the header of the next outgoing data frame.

  • Timer for Piggybacking: If no outgoing data frame is generated within a short timeout, a separate ACK frame must be sent to avoid sender timeout. [Faculty — Slide 48 / General — Slide 48]

docs.title: 6.2 Sequence Number Space & Window Concept
docs.text:
• Sequence numbers range from 0 to MAX_SEQ = 2ⁿ - 1 (for n-bit sequence numbers).

  • Sender Window (Wₛ): Contains sequence numbers of frames sent but not yet acknowledged.

  • Receiver Window (Wᵣ): Contains sequence numbers of frames receiver is willing to accept. [Faculty — Slide 49 / General — Slide 49]

docs.title: 6.3 Protocol 4: One-Bit Sliding Window (\(W_s = 1, W_r = 1\))
docs.text:
• Stop-and-Wait protocol implemented using a 1-bit sequence number (0 or 1).

  • Simultaneous Start Anomaly: If both sender and receiver initiate transmission at the exact same moment, duplicate frames are transmitted back and forth, wasting half the link bandwidth. [Faculty — Slide 52 / General — Slide 52]

docs.title: Formula: Frame Transmission Time
docs.text:
\[ T_{\text{frame}} = \frac{L}{B} \]

  • L = Frame length in bits.

  • B = Link bandwidth in bits per second (bps).

docs.title: Formula: Round-Trip Time (RTT)
docs.text:
\[ \text{RTT} = 2 \cdot T_{\text{prop}} \]

*

T

prop

= One-way propagation delay over link.

docs.title: Formula: Stop-and-Wait Efficiency (η)
docs.text:
\[ \eta = \frac{T_{\text{frame}}}{T_{\text{frame}} + \text{RTT}} = \frac{1}{1 + 2a} \]

where

\[ a = \frac{T_{\text{prop}}}{T_{\text{frame}}} \]

. [Faculty — Slide 50 / General — Slide 53]

docs.title: Step-by-Step Worked Numerical Example 4: Satellite Channel Efficiency [Faculty — Slide 50 / General — Slide 53-54]
Problem
docs.text:
• Bandwidth B = 50 kbps = 50,000 bps

  • Round-Trip Delay RTT = 500 ms = 0.5 seconds

  • Frame Size L = 1000 bits

  • Calculate the link efficiency under Stop-and-Wait (Window = 1), and find the minimum window size W needed for 100% utilization.

docs.title: Step 1: Calculate Frame Transmission Time (
docs.text:
T


 frame

)

\[ T_{\text{frame}} = \frac{1000 \text{ bits}}{50,000 \text{ bps}} = 0.020 \text{ seconds} = 20 \text{ ms} \]

docs.title: Step 2: Calculate Total Cycle Time (
docs.text:
T


 total

)

\[ T_{\text{total}} = T_{\text{frame}} + \text{RTT} = 20 \text{ ms} + 500 \text{ ms} = 520 \text{ ms} \]

docs.title: Step 3: Calculate Channel Efficiency (η)
docs.text:
\[ \eta = \frac{T_{\text{frame}}}{T_{\text{total}}} = \frac{20 \text{ ms}}{520 \text{ ms}} \approx 0.03846 = \mathbf{3.85\%} \]

(The link is idle 96.15% of the time!)

docs.title: Step 4: Calculate Window Size (W) needed for 100% Efficiency
docs.text: \[ W \ge \frac{T_{\text{total}}}{T_{\text{frame}}} = \frac{520 \text{ ms}}{20 \text{ ms}} = \mathbf{26 \text{ frames}} \quad (\text{or } 1 + 2a = 1 + 2(12.5) = 26) \]

docs.title: Key Characteristics:
docs.text:
• Sender Window \(> 1\), Receiver Window \(= 1\).

  • Receiver discards all out-of-order frames and sends cumulative ACKs for the last correctly received in-order frame.

  • On timeout, sender retransmits ALL unacknowledged outstanding frames starting from the oldest unacked frame. [Faculty — Slide 51 / General — Slide 56]

docs.title: Crucial Rule: Maximum Window Size for Go-Back-N
Formula: Maximum Sender Window Size (GBN)
docs.text:
\[ W_s \le \text{MAX_SEQ} = 2^n - 1 \]

  • Reason / Proof: If sequence numbers are 3 bits (0 to 7, size 8), and Wₛ = 8:

  • Sender transmits frames 0..7. Receiver receives all 8 frames and expects frame 0 next.

  • All ACKs are lost in transit.

  • Sender timeout occurs and retransmits frame 0.

  • Receiver cannot distinguish whether frame 0 is a retransmission or a brand new frame 0 from the next sequence cycle!

  • Setting Wₛ = 7 (2ⁿ - 1) prevents this ambiguity. [Faculty — Slide 52 / General — Slide 58]

docs.title: Key Characteristics:
docs.text:
• Sender Window \(> 1\), Receiver Window \(> 1\).

  • Receiver accepts and buffers out-of-order frames within its window.

  • Receiver sends a NAK (Negative Acknowledgement) to trigger fast retransmission of only the missing frame.

  • Sender retransmits ONLY the single corrupted/missing frame upon receiving a NAK or timer expiry. [Faculty — Slide 57 / General — Slide 68]

docs.title: Crucial Rule: Maximum Window Size for Selective Repeat
Formula: Maximum Window Size (Selective Repeat)
docs.text:
\[ W_s = W_r \le \frac{\text{MAX_SEQ} + 1}{2} = 2^{n-1} \]

  • Reason / Proof: If sequence space is 0..7 (8 numbers), max window size is 4.

  • If Wₛ = 5, sender sends 0,1,2,3,4. Receiver receives and ACKs them, advancing its window to 5,6,7,0,1.

  • If all ACKs are lost, sender retransmits frame 0.

  • Receiver's new window contains 0; it would mistakenly accept the old duplicate frame 0 as new data!

  • Restricting Wₛ ≤ 2ⁿ⁻¹ guarantees no overlap between old and new sequence windows. [Faculty — Slide 58 / General — Slide 77]

docs.text:

docs.title: 7.1 Packet over SONET (PoS)
docs.text:
• Used over wide-area optical fiber backbone links.

  • Uses SONET (Synchronous Optical Network) at the Physical layer and PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) at the Data Link layer. [Faculty — Slide 64 / General — Slide 80]

docs.title: Three Core Components of PPP:
docs.text:
1. Framing Method: HDLC-based frame format with byte stuffing.

  2. LCP (Link Control Protocol): For bringing links up, testing them, negotiating options, and bringing them down cleanly.

  3. NCP (Network Control Protocol): Negotiates network-layer options (e.g., assigning IP addresses via IPCP). [Faculty — Slide 65 / General — Slide 81]

docs.title: 7.3 ADSL (Asymmetric Digital Subscriber Loop)
docs.text:
• Provides broadband Internet over legacy copper telephone local loops.

  • Protocol Stack:

\[ \text{IP} \rightarrow \text{PPP} \rightarrow \text{AAL5} \rightarrow \text{ATM} \rightarrow \text{ADSL Physical} \]
  • AAL5 Frame: Encapsulates PPP data, pads payload to multiples of 48 bytes, and appends an 8-byte trailer containing length and CRC-32.

[Faculty — Slide 67-68 / General — Slide 84-85]

docs.text: \[ d_{\text{min}} \ge d+1 \]

docs.title: 2. Error Correction Requirement

docs.text:
\[ T_{\text{frame}}=\frac{L}{B} \]

Where:

  • \(L\) = Frame length (bits)

  • \(B\) = Bandwidth (bits/sec)

\[ \eta=\frac{T_{\text{frame}}}{T_{\text{frame}}+RTT} \]

docs.title: 8.2 Important Definitions
docs.text:
• Framing: Grouping bits from the Physical Layer into discrete frames with headers/trailers.

  • Bit Stuffing: Inserting a 0 bit after five consecutive 1s to prevent payload data from matching the 01111110 flag.

  • Hamming Distance: Number of bit positions in which two binary codewords differ.

  • Piggybacking: Delaying ACKs to attach them to outgoing data frame headers.

  • Pipelining: Transmitting multiple frames before receiving an acknowledgment for the first frame.

docs.title: 8.3 Important Comparisons
docs.text:
• Forward Error Correction (FEC) vs ARQ: Self-correcting via redundancy (high overhead, noisy links) vs detecting & retransmitting (low overhead, clean links).

  • Byte Stuffing vs Bit Stuffing: ESC byte insertion before FLAG/ESC bytes vs single 0 bit insertion after five 1s.

  • Go-Back-N vs Selective Repeat: Receiver window 1 / discards out-of-order / retransmits whole window vs Receiver window \(> 1\) / buffers out-of-order / retransmits only missing frame via NAK.

docs.title: 8.4 Exam Revision Sheet
docs.text:
• Must-Know Numerical Calculations:

  • Hamming Code encoding and syndrome-based error location.

  • CRC polynomial long division (XOR) and remainder determination.

  • UDP Checksum 1's complement addition.

  • Channel efficiency (η) and required pipelining window size (W).

  • Must-Know Proof Rules:

  • Why Go-Back-N window cannot exceed 2ⁿ - 1.

  • Why Selective Repeat window cannot exceed 2ⁿ⁻¹.

  • Must-Know Diagram Structures:

  • Bit stuffing vs character stuffing frame formats.

  • Sliding window sender/receiver state diagrams.

  • PPP frame format and state transition diagram.

docs.title: 2. Chapter Overview
docs.text:
This chapter introduces the fundamental concepts of Data Analysis and Visualisation (DAV). It covers the definitions of data, the data lifecycle, types of data, quantitative vs qualitative analysis, and the end-to-end data analysis process. It explores Big Data (5 V's), the DIKW model, process models (CRISP-DM and KDD), analytics types (descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive), visualization techniques, standard software tools/libraries, open data sources, and industry case studies.

[Source: ch1_text.txt, Slides 1-44; 1.Introduction to DAV.pdf]

docs.title: 3. Fundamental Concepts: The DIKW Hierarchy & Data Life Cycle
docs.text:
The DIKW Model describes the transformation of raw facts into strategic actions:

\[ \text{Data} \longrightarrow \text{Information} \longrightarrow \text{Knowledge} \longrightarrow \text{Wisdom} \] 
graph BT
    A["Data: Raw Facts"] --> B["Information: Contextualized Data"]
    B --> C["Knowledge: Actionable Information"]
    C --> D["Wisdom: Applied Knowledge"]
    style A fill:#e1f5fe,stroke:#01579b,color:#01579b
    style B fill:#b3e5fc,stroke:#01579b,color:#01579b
    style C fill:#81d4fa,stroke:#01579b,color:#01579b
    style D fill:#4fc3f7,stroke:#01579b,color:#01579b

docs.title: Data Life Cycle
docs.text:
The data lifecycle represents the sequence of stages that data goes through from its initial generation to its final visualization and analysis. 

flowchart LR
    A["Generation/Collection"] --> B[Storage]
    B --> C["Processing/Transformation"]
    C --> D[Analysis]
    D --> E["Visualization/Communication"]

docs.title: Definition: Data
docs.text:
Meaning: Raw, unprocessed facts, figures, and symbols without context.

Formal definition: Raw facts or figures without any context. It can be numbers, words, measurements, observations, or even just symbols.

Intuition: Before processing, data is just raw material waiting to be evaluated.

Example: Sensor readings: \(38, 39, 40\).

docs.title: Definition: Information
docs.text:
Meaning: Data that is structured and given meaning.

Formal definition: Data organized and structured to answer "who", "what", "where", and "when".

Intuition: After analysis, data becomes information or knowledge because context is added.

Example: The readings \(38^\circ\text{C}, 39^\circ\text{C}, 40^\circ\text{C}\) represent daily peak temperatures in July.

docs.title: Definition: Knowledge
docs.text:
Meaning: The synthesis of information.

Formal definition: Synthesized information revealing patterns and answering "how".

Intuition: The ability to find actionable trends within the information.

Example: Understanding that temperatures above \(35^\circ\text{C}\) trigger a \(40\%\) surge in air conditioner purchases.

docs.title: Definition: Wisdom
docs.text:
Meaning: The application of knowledge.

Formal definition: Evaluated knowledge incorporating judgment to answer "why" and guide strategy.

Intuition: Making a strategic business decision based on the generated knowledge.

Example: Pre-emptively increasing regional warehouse inventory of air conditioners in May.

docs.title: Definition: Data Analysis
docs.text:
Meaning: Asking questions of the data to find actionable insights.

Formal definition: The process of making sense of the data. Analysis means asking questions to the data and finding answers.

Intuition: Extracting useful signals from collected records to aid decision-making.

Example: For a small online shop, analyzing what products people bought, when they bought them, and how much they paid to determine if discounts should be offered on weekends.

docs.title: Definition: Data Visualisation
docs.text:
Meaning: Creating visual artifacts of data.

Formal definition: Turning numbers into visuals, like graphs, charts, and dashboards, so people can understand the story behind the data quickly and easily.

Intuition: Because human brains process images faster than raw text or tables, charts can show trends or problems at a glance without reading rows of numbers.

Example: A pie chart showing how sales are split between regions, or a line graph showing revenue changes over time.

[Source: ch1_text.txt, Slides 14, 18, 24]

  1. Ungrouped (Raw) Data: Individual raw observations listed directly.

  2. Example: \(X = \{12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 25, 25, 30\}\)

  3. Grouped (Class Table) Data: Aggregated observations into continuous class intervals with frequencies.

  4. Example:

docs.title: The 5 V's of Big Data
docs.text:
1. Volume: Scale of data (Gigabytes to Zettabytes).

  2. Velocity: Speed of generation and streaming ingestion.

  3. Variety: Structural diversity (Structured, Semi-structured, Unstructured).

  4. Veracity: Data quality, noise, and trustworthiness.

  5. Value: Actionable business utility derived from analysis.

docs.title: 8. Data Transformation & Visualisation
docs.text:
"Visualization provides a unique perspective on the dataset. Visualization is critical to data analysis. It provides a front line of attack, revealing intricate structure in data that cannot be absorbed in any other way. We discover unimagined effects, and we challenge imagined ones."

— William S. Cleveland, Visualizing Data

docs.title: Data Transformation
docs.text:
Data transformation is the process of converting data or information from one format to another, usually from the format of a source system into the required format of a new destination system.

It can be divided into two steps:

  1. Data mapping: Maps data elements from the source data system to the destination data system and captures any transformation that must occur.

  2. Code generation: Creates the actual transformation program.

docs.title: How to Visualize Data
docs.text:
Depending on the goal, different visual components are used:

  • Tables: Very powerful when dealing with a relatively small number of data points.

  • Charts: Allow mapping dimensions in data to visual properties of geometric shapes (e.g., Bar charts, Pie charts).

  • Maps: The power of maps is to re-connect the data to our physical world.

  • Graphs: Used for showing inter-connections (edges) between data points (nodes).

[Source: ch1_text.txt, Slides 24-29]

docs.title: 10. Industry Applications & Case Studies
docs.text:
Data visualization and analysis assist almost every company or sector that aims to grow by giving them the vision to increase customer satisfaction.

Industry Use Case / Benefit Healthcare Hospitals use visualizations to track patient wait times and identify bottlenecks in the emergency department, allowing for better resource allocation. Marketing Marketers visualize data from social media and website analytics to analyze campaign performance, understand consumer behavior/preferences, and identify trends. Finance Professionals interpret complex financial data quickly. Investment firms use interactive charts to visualize stock prices or compare portfolios to spot anomalies impacting decisions. Manufacturing Empowers manufacturers to optimize operations by monitoring KPIs. Visual metrics on throughput or defect rates help identify inefficiencies promptly. Technology In cybersecurity, visualizations allow analysts to detect patterns in network traffic efficiently and respond swiftly to potential threats.

[Source: ch1_text.txt, Slide 31, 43]

docs.text:
Researchers and practitioners can leverage various public datasets for learning and analysis:

  • Global Health Observatory data (Curated by WHO): E.g., Universal access to reproductive health.

  • Data.gov.sg (Curated by Singaporean government): E.g., Resident demographics.

docs.text: \[ \bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \]

docs.title: Definition Sheet
docs.text:
• Data: Raw, unprocessed facts, figures, and symbols without context.

  • Information: Data organized and structured to answer who, what, where, and when.

  • Knowledge: Synthesized information revealing patterns and answering how.

  • Wisdom: Evaluated knowledge incorporating judgment to answer why and guide strategy.

  • Data Analysis: Process of making sense of data by asking questions and finding answers.

  • Data Visualisation: Turning numbers into visual representations to clearly communicate findings.

  • Descriptive Analytics: Summarizing historical observations (What happened?).

  • Diagnostic Analytics: Determining causes of past events (Why did it happen?).

  • Predictive Analytics: Forecasting future outcomes (What will happen?).

  • Prescriptive Analytics: Optimizing actions based on predictive outcomes (What should we do?).

  • CRISP-DM: Standardized 6-phase data mining lifecycle.

  • Data Transformation: Converting data from a source format to a required destination format via mapping and code generation.

docs.title: Exam-Oriented Review
docs.text:
Q1: Contrast Descriptive Analytics and Prescriptive Analytics with examples.

A: Descriptive analytics summarizes past data (e.g., total sales revenue last month was \(\$50,000\)). Prescriptive analytics provides actionable recommendations based on optimization models (e.g., reorder 200 units of product X now to maximize profit and avoid stockout).

Q2: What is the difference between Quantitative and Qualitative data?

A: Quantitative data is numerical and can be measured directly (e.g., age, salary). Qualitative data is descriptive and categorized but not directly measured in numbers (e.g., gender, feedback).

Q3: How does raw ungrouped data differ from grouped class table data?

A: Raw ungrouped data preserves every individual measurement. Grouped class table data aggregates measurements into class intervals with frequency counts, trading individual precision for compact representation.

Q4: List the 6 phases of the CRISP-DM model.

A: 1. Business Understanding, 2. Data Understanding, 3. Data Preparation, 4. Modeling, 5. Evaluation, 6. Deployment.

Q5: Explain the two steps of Data Transformation.

A: 1. Data mapping: Mapping data elements from source to destination and capturing the required logic. 2. Code generation: Creating the actual transformation program to execute the mapping.

Q6: Name four ways to visualize data and when to use them.

A: 1. Tables: For small number of data points. 2. Charts: To map dimensions to geometric shapes like bars or pies. 3. Maps: To reconnect data to the physical world. 4. Graphs: To show interconnections/edges between data points/nodes.

Course Code: Data Analysis & Visualization (DAV)

Primary Focus: Data Types, Scales of Measurement, Ungrouped vs Grouped Representation, Frequency Distributions, and Summary Statistics

docs.title: 1. Chapter Overview
docs.text:
Data comes in many forms, each requiring specific statistical treatments and visualization methods. Understanding data types and measurement scales is essential for selecting appropriate analytical algorithms and visualization charts.

This chapter covers:

  1. Categorical vs Numerical Data: Qualitative attributes versus quantitative metrics.

  2. Discrete vs Continuous Data: Distinct countable values versus measurable real intervals.

  3. Scales of Measurement: Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, and Ratio scales.

  4. Data Representation Formats: Raw ungrouped observations versus grouped frequency distributions.

  5. Measures of Central Tendency & Dispersion: Mean, Median, Mode, Variance, and Standard Deviation.

docs.title: 2.1 Categorical (Qualitative) Data
docs.text:
Categorical data represents labels, categories, or non-numeric characteristics that describe an attribute of an observation.

  • Key Characteristics: Arithmetic operations (such as addition or averaging) are meaningless on categorical values.

  • Subtypes: Nominal and Ordinal.

  • Examples: Eye color (Blue, Brown, Green), Gender (Male, Female), Customer Feedback (Satisfied, Neutral, Dissatisfied).

docs.title: 2.2 Numerical (Quantitative) Data
docs.text:
Numerical data represents measurable or countable quantities expressed as numbers.

  • Key Characteristics: Standard mathematical and statistical operations (addition, subtraction, mean, standard deviation) are valid and meaningful.

  • Subtypes: Discrete and Continuous.

  • Examples: Height (in cm), Temperature (in °C), Account Balance (in USD), Number of Website Visits.

docs.title: 3.1 Discrete Data
docs.text:
Numerical data whose values are distinct, separate, and countable.

  • Values: Usually integers with finite or countably infinite values. No intermediate values exist between two adjacent points.

  • Examples: Number of children in a household, number of defect items in a batch, roll of a die.

docs.title: 3.2 Continuous Data
docs.text:
Numerical data that can take any real value within a given continuous interval or range.

  • Values: Uncountably infinite possible values within an interval, dependent on measurement precision.

  • Examples: Temperature (\(36.6^\circ\text{C}\)), Weight (\(70.45\text{ kg}\)), Time to complete a task (\(12.34\text{ seconds}\)).

docs.title: 4. The 4 Scales of Measurement
docs.text:
Data attributes are classified into four hierarchical levels of measurement:

Measurement Scale Ordering Equal Intervals True Absolute Zero Allowed Mathematical Operations Examples Nominal No No No Equality (\(=\)/\(\neq\)), Mode, Frequency Count Marital Status, Zip Codes, Eye Color Ordinal Yes No No Order (\(<\)/\(>\)), Median, Percentiles Star Ratings (1–5), Letter Grades (A, B, C) Interval Yes Yes No Addition, Subtraction, Mean, Variance Temperature (°C, °F), Calendar Years Ratio Yes Yes Yes Multiplication, Division, Ratios, Geometric Mean Weight, Height, Income, Age

docs.text:

    Qual --> Nom["Nominal Scale: Unordered Categories"]

docs.title: 6. Data Representation Formats: Ungrouped vs Grouped
6.1 Raw Ungrouped Data
docs.text:
• Meaning: A simple list of individual numerical observations recorded directly.

  • Formal Definition: A set of observations \(X = \{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_N\}\) where each \(x_i\) is an individual raw data point.

  • Example: Ages of 10 students:

$$ X = {14, 17, 18, 18, 22, 25, 26, 28, 30, 32} $$

  • Advantage: Retains \(100\%\) precision of original data.

  • Disadvantage: Difficult to interpret when dataset size \(N\) is large.

docs.title: 6.2 Grouped Class Table (Frequency Distribution)
docs.text:
• Meaning: Data organized into non-overlapping continuous class intervals, with counts (frequencies) for observations falling into each interval.

  • Components:

  • Class Interval \([a, b)\): Range defined by lower limit \(a\) and upper limit \(b\).

  • Class Width (\(w\)):

    \[ w = b - a \]

  • Midpoint (\(x_i\)):

    \[ x_i = \frac{a + b}{2} \]

  • Relative Frequency:

    \[ \text{Relative Frequency} = \frac{f_i}{N} \]

docs.title: 1. Sample Mean (\(\bar{x}\))
docs.text:
The arithmetic average of all observations:

\[ \bar{x} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i \]

docs.title: 2. Median
docs.text:
The middle value when data is sorted in ascending order:

\[ \text{Median} = \begin{cases} x_{\left(\frac{N+1}{2}\right)} & \text{if } N \text{ is odd} \\[6pt] \frac{x_{\left(\frac{N}{2}\right)} + x_{\left(\frac{N}{2}+1\right)}}{2} & \text{if } N \text{ is even} \end{cases} \]

docs.title: 3. Mode
docs.text: The most frequently occurring value in the dataset.

docs.title: 1. Sample Variance (\(s^2\))
docs.text:
Measures the average squared deviation from the mean:

\[ s^2 = \frac{1}{N - 1} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \]

docs.title: 2. Sample Standard Deviation (\(s\))
docs.text:
The square root of variance, expressed in original data units:

\[ s = \sqrt{s^2} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N - 1} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^2} \]

docs.title: 8. Formula Sheet
docs.text:
• Sample Mean:

$$ \bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{N} $$

  • Sample Variance:

$$ s^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{N - 1} $$

  • Class Midpoint:

$$ x_i = \frac{a + b}{2} $$

  • Relative Frequency:

$$ \text{RF}_i = \frac{f_i}{N} $$

docs.title: 9. Definition Sheet
docs.text:
1. Nominal Scale: A measurement level for unordered categorical variables where numbers act only as labels.

  2. Ordinal Scale: A measurement level where categories have a natural rank or order, but differences between ranks are not uniform.

  3. Interval Scale: A measurement level with meaningful, equal distances between values, but no absolute true zero point.

  4. Ratio Scale: The highest measurement level, featuring ordered categories, equal intervals, and a true absolute zero point.

  5. Frequency Distribution: A tabular summary showing the count of data points in each non-overlapping class interval.

docs.title: 10. Exam-Oriented Review
docs.text:
1. Compare the four measurement scales (Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio) across ordering, equal intervals, absolute zero, and allowed mathematical operations.

  2. Given a raw dataset, calculate the sample mean, median, variance, and standard deviation.

  3. Explain why temperature in Celsius is an Interval scale variable while temperature in Kelvin is a Ratio scale variable.

  4. Convert a raw dataset of \(N = 30\) observations into a grouped frequency distribution table with class width \(w = 10\).

docs.title: Chapter 3 — Dataset and Attributes
docs.text: Course: Data Analysis and Visualization Primary Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf Files Integrated: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, ch3_text.txt

docs.title: 1. Chapter Overview
docs.text:
This chapter covers datasets, attribute types, and structural properties in data mining. Key topics include attribute taxonomy (nominal, binary, ordinal, numeric), dataset structures (record, graph, ordered, time series), matrix representations (Data Matrix, Document-Term Matrix), characteristics (dimensionality, sparsity, resolution), and data representation formats.

[Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slide 1]

docs.title: Definition: Attribute
docs.text:
Meaning: An attribute is a data field representing a characteristic or feature of a data object.

Synonyms: Feature (Machine learning), Variable (Statistics), Column (Databases), Dimension (Data warehousing).

Example: Customer attributes: Customer ID, Name, Address.

[Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slide 2]

docs.title: Definition: Attribute Vector and Distribution
docs.text:
Meaning: An attribute vector is a set of attributes describing an object.

Distribution types based on attribute count:

  • Univariate: Involves one attribute.

  • Bivariate: Involves two attributes.

  • Multivariate: Involves multiple attributes.

[Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slide 3]

docs.title: 3. Qualitative vs Quantitative Data
docs.text:
graph TD
    Data[Types of Data Based on Nature]
    Data --> Qual[Qualitative Data]
    Data --> Quant[Quantitative Data]
    Qual --> Nom[Nominal]
    Qual --> Ord[Ordinal]
    Quant --> Disc[Discrete]
    Quant --> Cont[Continuous]

docs.title: Qualitative (Categorical) Data
docs.text:
Information representing characteristics that you do not measure with numbers. Observations fall within a countable number of groups. It captures subjective information or things not easily measured.

Examples: Taste, the color of a car, architectural style, marital status.

[Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slide 31, 34]

docs.title: Quantitative (Numerical) Data
docs.text:
Information recorded as numbers representing an objective measurement or a count.

Examples: Age, height, temperature, weight, count of transactions.

[Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slide 31, 37]

docs.title: 4. Attribute Taxonomy
docs.text:
graph TD
    Attr[Attribute Types]
    Attr --> Nom[Nominal: Unordered Categories]
    Attr --> Bin[Binary: Two States]
    Attr --> Ord[Ordinal: Ordered Categories]
    Attr --> Num[Numeric: Quantitative]
    Bin --> Sym[Symmetric: Equal Importance]
    Bin --> Asym[Asymmetric: Unequal Importance]
    Num --> Int[Interval-Scaled: No Absolute Zero]
    Num --> Rat[Ratio-Scaled: Absolute Zero]

docs.title: 1. Nominal Attributes
docs.text:
Meaning: Categorical values with no meaningful order (also called enumerations). They can be coded with numbers, but arithmetic operations are meaningless.

Example:

  • Hair Color: black, brown, blond, red

  • Marital Status: single, married, divorced

  • Occupation: teacher, farmer, etc.

[Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slide 5, 35]

docs.title: 2. Binary Attributes
docs.text:
Meaning: A special nominal type with only two states, typically represented as 0 (absent/false) and 1 (present/true).

Example:

  • Smoker: 0 = No, 1 = Yes

  • Medical Test: 0 = Negative, 1 = Positive

Types:

  • Symmetric: Both states equally important (e.g., gender).

  • Asymmetric: One state more important than the other (e.g., HIV test result).

[Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slide 6]

docs.title: 3. Ordinal Attributes
docs.text:
Meaning: Ordered categories where the interval or distance between them is unknown. They are treated as categorical, but the numbers have mathematical meaning purely in their ordering.

Example:

  • Size: \(\text{Small} < \text{Medium} < \text{Large}\)

  • Grades: \(\text{A+} > \text{A} > \text{B+}\)

  • Satisfaction Level: 0 = Very Dissatisfied, 1 = Dissatisfied, 2 = Neutral, 3 = Satisfied, 4 = Very Satisfied.

  • Restaurant Rating: Scale from 0 to 4 stars.

[Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slide 7, 36]

docs.title: 4. Numeric Attributes
docs.text:
Meaning: Quantitative measurable values represented in integer or real values.

Types:

  • Interval-Scaled: Equal intervals, but no true zero-point. Arithmetic difference is meaningful, but ratios are not.

  • Example: Temperature in °C or °F, Calendar dates. 20°C is 5° more than 15°C, but 20°C is NOT twice as hot as 10°C.

  • Ratio-Scaled: Has a true zero-point. Can compute ratios, differences, mean, median, mode.

  • Example: Years of Experience, Weight, Height, Income. ₹100 is exactly 10 times ₹10.

[Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slides 8-10]

docs.title: Discrete vs Continuous Attributes
docs.text:
• Discrete: Finite or countably infinite values. Cannot be meaningfully divided into smaller increments.

  • Example: Hair Color, Zip Code, Age (0-110), Smoker (0/1). A household can have 1 or 2 cars, but not 1.6 cars.

  • Continuous: Infinite real values, can take on almost any numeric value including fractional/decimal values. Usually stored as floating-point.

  • Example: Height, Weight, Temperature. The mean height in India is 5 feet 9 inches for men and 5 feet 4 inches for women.

[Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slides 11, 38-39]

docs.title: 5. Dataset Types & Matrix Formats
docs.text:
graph TD
    DS[Dataset Types]
    DS --> Rec[Record Data]
    DS --> Gr[Graph Data]
    DS --> OrdDS[Ordered Data]
    Rec --> Flat[Flat Files / Relational DB]
    Rec --> Trans[Transaction / Market Basket]
    Rec --> DM[Data Matrix]
    Rec --> DTM[Sparse / Document-Term Matrix]

    OrdDS --> Seqs[Sequence Data]
