- What it shows: The statistical inference loop connecting finite samples to unobservable population parameters. - Component Breakdown: - Population: Complete universe containing fixed, unknown Greek parameters (\(\mu, \sigma, \sigma^2\)). - Sample: Observed subset containing variable Roman statistics (\(\bar{X}, s, s^2\)). - Flow / Relationship: Arrow 1 represents physical sample selection. Arrow 2 represents inductive mathematical estimation.

docs.title: 10.3 Master Definition Sheet
docs.text:
• Data Reduction: The systematic transformation of a dataset to obtain a reduced representation that is substantially smaller in volume while preserving the integrity and analytical conclusions of the original data.
  • Dimensionality Reduction: The reduction of input feature attributes via feature extraction (e.g., PCA) or feature selection (e.g., Correlation Filter) to address the curse of dimensionality and facilitate visualization.
  • Numerosity Reduction: The replacement of raw data rows with alternative, smaller representations (e.g., cluster centroids, frequency histograms, parametric regression equations, or representative samples).
  • Lossless Compression: Data compression algorithms (e.g., ZIP, Huffman) that allow exact, bit-for-bit mathematical reconstruction of original data without information loss.
  • Lossy Compression: Data compression algorithms (e.g., JPEG, MP3) that achieve high compression ratios by permanently discarding imperceptible, high-frequency components.
  • Stratified Sampling: A probability sampling design that partitions the population into mutually exclusive, homogeneous strata and draws independent random samples from each stratum to protect minority classes.
  • Cluster Sampling: A probability sampling design that partitions the population into naturally occurring, heterogeneous clusters and evaluates all elements within a random selection of clusters to minimize logistical costs.
  • Principal Component Analysis (PCA): An unsupervised linear transformation that converts a set of correlated variables into a set of linearly uncorrelated, orthogonal variables (principal components) ranked by variance explained.
  • Eigenvalue: A scalar \(\lambda\) associated with an eigenvector indicating the total variance captured along that component's direction.
  • Eigenvector: A normalized directional vector \(v\) specifying the orientation of a principal component axis in the original feature space.

docs.title: 10.4 Exam-Oriented Review: University Questions & Model Solutions
Q1. Define data reduction and state its four primary goals.
docs.text: Model Answer: Data reduction is the process of reducing the physical volume and complexity of a dataset while preserving its analytical integrity. Its four primary goals are: 1. Efficiency: Minimizing RAM/disk storage and accelerating computation. 2. Scalability: Permitting big data processing without system crashes. 3. Noise Removal: Eliminating irrelevant and redundant collinear features. 4. Better Visualization: Projecting high-dimensional spaces to 2D/3D for human interpretation. [Source: Unit 4_Data reduction and Sampling.pdf, Slides 2, 3]

docs.title: Q2. Differentiate between SRSWOR and SRSWR.
docs.text: Model Answer: - In Simple Random Sampling Without Replacement (SRSWOR), an element is removed from the population upon selection and cannot appear again, generating \(n\) distinct elements with \(\binom{N}{n}\) possible sample configurations. - In Simple Random Sampling With Replacement (SRSWR), an element is returned to the pool after selection, allowing duplicate selections with \(N^n\) possible sample configurations and independent draws. [Source: Unit 4_Data reduction and Sampling.pdf, Slides 9, 11]

docs.title: Q3. Explain why naive row-level sampling may fail to reduce disk I/O in relational databases.
docs.text: Model Answer: Relational databases read and write data in physical disk pages (e.g., 8 KB blocks). Naive row-level sampling selects rows uniformly scattered across virtually every disk block. Because the database engine must fetch entire pages into RAM to read single records, 100% of the physical disk pages are still read, resulting in zero reduction in disk I/O operations. [Source: Unit 4_Data reduction and Sampling.pdf, Slide 6]

docs.title: Q4. Define the Explained Variance Ratio (EVR) in PCA.
docs.text:
Model Answer: The Explained Variance Ratio is the fraction of total dataset variance captured by a given principal component \(k\):

\[ \text{EVR}_k = \frac{\lambda_k}{\sum_{j=1}^d \lambda_j} \]

It quantifies the information preserved by each component and serves as the criterion for component truncation. [Source: Unit_4_PCA.pdf, Slide 37]

docs.title: Q5. Why is feature normalization mandatory prior to executing PCA?
docs.text: Model Answer: PCA is scale-sensitive. If features have vastly different measurement units or numerical magnitudes (e.g., Salary in thousands vs. Age in decades), high-magnitude variables artificially dominate the variance calculations. Normalizing (via Z-score standardization) scales all features to equal variance (\(\sigma^2 = 1\)), ensuring all attributes contribute fairly to principal component directions. [Source: DAV_Comprehensive_Lab_Manual_and_Notes.md, Practical 6]

docs.title: Q6. Classify statistical sampling techniques into a structured taxonomy and contrast probability vs. non-probability sampling.
docs.text:
Model Answer: Statistical sampling is partitioned into two major classes: 1. Probability Sampling: Every element has a known, non-zero probability of selection. Eliminates subjective bias and allows rigorous calculation of confidence intervals and margins of error: - Simple Random Sampling (SRS): Equal probability (\(P = 1/N\)) via SRSWOR or SRSWR. - Systematic Sampling: Elements selected at fixed step intervals \(k = N/n\) after a random start. - Stratified Sampling: Population split into homogeneous strata; samples drawn from each stratum. - Cluster Sampling: Population split into heterogeneous clusters; random clusters sampled entirely. 2. Non-Probability Sampling: Selection relies on subjective judgment, geographic availability, or network referrals. Margins of error cannot be calculated: - Convenience Sampling: Selecting readily accessible subjects. - Judgmental / Purposive Sampling: Deliberately selecting experts. - Quota Sampling: Filling demographic quotas via convenience methods. - Snowball Sampling: Existing participants recruit acquaintances from hidden groups.

flowchart TD
    ST["Sampling Techniques"] --> P["Probability (Known non-zero P)"]
    ST --> NP["Non-Probability (Subjective / Unknown P)"]
    P --> P_EX["SRSWOR, SRSWR, Systematic, Stratified, Cluster"]
    NP --> NP_EX["Convenience, Judgmental, Quota, Snowball"]

[Source: Unit 4_Data reduction and Sampling.pdf, Slides 18, 19, 20]

docs.title: Q7. Compare Stratified Sampling with Cluster Sampling across four structural dimensions.
docs.text:
Model Answer:

Dimension Stratified Sampling Cluster Sampling Subgroup Homogeneity Homogeneous within strata: Elements in a stratum are similar. Heterogeneous within clusters: Each cluster is a diverse mini-population. Between-Group Variation Heterogeneous between strata: Strata differ substantially from one another. Homogeneous between clusters: Different clusters have similar aggregate profiles. Selection Mechanism Random samples are drawn from every single stratum. A random selection of clusters is chosen; unchosen clusters are omitted. Primary Objective Maximizes statistical precision and guarantees representation of minority classes. Minimizes logistical data collection costs across dispersed geographic regions.

[Source: Unit 4_Data reduction and Sampling.pdf, Slide 10]

docs.title: Q8. Derive the characteristic equation for PCA eigenvalues and state the geometric role of eigenvectors.
docs.text:
Model Answer: Given a centered data matrix with sample covariance matrix \(S \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\), PCA seeks directional vectors \(x\) whose orientation remains invariant under transformation by \(S\):

\[ S x = \lambda x \]

Rearranging the linear system:

\[ \begin{aligned} S x - \lambda I x &= \mathbf{0} \\ (S - \lambda I)x &= \mathbf{0} \end{aligned} \]

For non-zero eigenvector solutions (\(x \neq \mathbf{0}\)) to exist, the matrix \((S - \lambda I)\) must be singular, requiring its determinant to vanish:

\[ \det(S - \lambda I) = 0 \]
  • Eigenvalues (\(\lambda\)): The roots of this characteristic polynomial. Each eigenvalue equals the statistical variance of the data projected along its corresponding eigenvector.
  • Eigenvectors (\(x\) / \(v\)): Orthonormal vectors (\(v_i \cdot v_j = 0\) for \(i \neq j\); \(\|v_i\| = 1\)) that define the physical directions of the new orthogonal principal component coordinate axes. [Source: Unit_4_PCA.pdf, Slides 14, 15, 16, 19]

docs.title: Section C: 10–15 Mark University Exam Numerical Problem
Q9. Complete Numerical Problem Statement:
docs.text:
A healthcare biometric study recorded Blood Pressure (\(BP\)) and Oxygen Saturation (\(Oxy\)) across six individuals (\(n = 6\)): - \(P_1(126, 78)\), \(P_2(128, 80)\), \(P_3(128, 82)\), \(P_4(130, 82)\), \(P_5(130, 84)\), \(P_6(132, 86)\).

Required: 1. Zero-mean center the dataset. 2. Compute the sample covariance matrix \(S\). 3. Calculate the eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2\) using the characteristic equation. 4. Derive the unit-normalized eigenvectors \(v_1, v_2\) and prove their orthogonality. 5. Compute the Explained Variance Ratio (EVR) for each component. 6. Calculate the transformed Principal Component Scores for all six patients. 7. Prove total variance preservation and discuss the dimensionality reduction outcome.

Model Solution: (See Section 7 of this document for the complete, step-by-step mathematical derivation, including intermediate substitutions, quadratic root calculations, dot-product orthogonality verification, and final variance conservation proofs).

docs.title: Section Narrative Spines & Pedagogical Flow
docs.text:
To prevent disconnected concept enumeration, each section of these study notes is governed by a distinct narrative spine:

  • Section 1 (Small Multiples): Explains how human visual processing circumvents working-memory bottlenecks when multi-category comparisons are partitioned across identical, aligned visual facets rather than stacked into an unreadable "spaghetti chart."
  • Section 2 (Perceptual Variables & Visual Hierarchy): Connects neuro-cognitive preattentive sensory registration (\(< 200\text{ ms}\)) to Edward Tufte's Data-Ink ratio and Cleveland & McGill's empirical psychophysical accuracy rankings, structuring the 3-tier enterprise dashboard layout.
  • Section 3 (Visual Analytics & Interaction): Transitions from static visual displays to dynamic human-in-the-loop visual analytics, formalizing Shneiderman's Mantra and the 4 fundamental interaction primitives.
  • Section 4 (Specialized Chart Topologies): Addresses non-standard geometrical coordinate systems (polar radial tables, dual-axis multi-Y graphs, and hierarchical space-filling treemaps), detailing their mathematical foundations, pitfalls, and design rules.
  • Section 5 (Master Case Study & System Synthesis): Synthesizes the entire 9-session curriculum through the forensic deconstruction of the enterprise CRSI (Concrete Reinforcing Steel Institute) Market Intelligence Dashboard.
  • Sections 6–10 (Quantitative & Exam Foundations): Provides mathematical formulations, step-by-step derivations, university-caliber worked numerical problems (10–15 marks), comparison matrices, acronym dictionaries, formula sheets, and exam review questions.

docs.title: Core Terminology Dictionary (Quick-Reference Glossary)
docs.text:
1. Small Multiple (Trellis / Lattice Display) — A visual arrangement where an identical chart type and coordinate scale are replicated across a grid of adjacent panels, with each panel dedicated to a distinct category, cohort, or time segment.
  2. Spaghetti Chart — A degraded line chart containing numerous overlapping, entangled time-series lines of different colors, causing visual occlusion, color confusion, and severe cognitive fatigue.
  3. Scale Invariance — The mandatory design constraint in trellis displays requiring all sub-panels to share identical coordinate dimensions, axis ranges, and zero baselines, ensuring visual differences reflect genuine data differences.
  4. Preattentive Visual Variable — A visual feature (e.g., position, length, hue, size) processed unconsciously by the human primary visual cortex in under 200 milliseconds prior to conscious cognitive focus.
  5. Cleveland & McGill Hierarchy — An empirical ranking of 10 elementary graphical perceptual tasks ordered by human decoding accuracy, led by position along a common aligned scale and ending with color saturation.
  6. Data-Ink Ratio — Edward Tufte's fundamental metric defined as the proportion of graphic ink devoted to non-redundant data presentation relative to total ink printed.
  7. Big Ass Number (BAN) — A high-prominence Tier 1 executive dashboard KPI display presenting a critical aggregated metric in large, bold typography paired with a contextual delta indicator.
  8. Data Spotlight — An interactive mechanism that illuminates selected marks with vibrant color while desaturating unselected marks into neutral muted gray, preserving spatial context without filtering.
  9. Dynamic Query — A visual analytics technique providing direct-manipulation controls (sliders, range buttons, check facets) that update visual query results instantaneously with sub-100 ms latency.
  10. Data Brushing (Linking and Brushing) — An interactive coordination protocol where selecting or highlighting a cohort of data points in one visualization automatically highlights corresponding records across all other linked views.
  11. Local Zooming (Focus + Context) — An interaction technique that magnifies a localized subset of data in high resolution while retaining the surrounding global dataset in peripheral view.
  12. Shneiderman's Information Seeking Mantra — The foundational visual analytics interaction principle: "Overview first, zoom and filter, then details-on-demand."
  13. Radial Table — A circular visualization mapping Cartesian coordinates \((x, y)\) to polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\), ideal for continuous cyclical phenomena such as diurnal clocks or annual seasonality.
  14. Multi-Y Graph (Dual-Axis Chart) — A visualization displaying two or more quantitative measures with vastly differing numerical scales along a shared horizontal dimension by employing independent left and right vertical axes.
  15. Two-Axis Trap — The deceptive visual artifact in dual-axis charts where arbitrary zero baselines or range scaling create spurious visual correlations or false intersection points between unrelated series.
  16. Treemap — A space-filling visualization that recursively partitions a rectangular 2D canvas into nested rectangles proportional in area to a quantitative sizing metric and colored by a performance attribute.
  17. Squarified Treemap Algorithm — A computational tessellation method (Bruls et al.) that subdivides hierarchical data into rectangles whose aspect ratios approach 1:1, minimizing long, unreadable slivers.

Comparative analysis across multiple categories is a central objective of data analytics. When data analysts attempt to compare 10 different retail stores, 18 student cohorts, or 50 geopolitical territories on a single graph, they routinely produce illegible, tangled plots. Session 6 establishes the neuro-cognitive foundations, structural rules, and practical workflows of Small Multiples to resolve this challenge.

docs.title: Definition: Small Multiples (Trellis Display / Lattice Chart)
docs.text:
Meaning: A visual design technique that takes a single chart template and replicates it across multiple adjacent sub-panels, each displaying an isolated slice of the data across a uniform coordinate framework.

Formal Definition: A Trellis or Small Multiple display is a parameterized mapping:

\[ f: C_k \to \mathcal{G}(X, Y \mid \theta_0) \]

where \(C = \{c_1, c_2, \dots, c_K\}\) represents a discrete categorical conditioning dimension, and each sub-graph \(\mathcal{G}_k\) renders the quantitative relationship between variables \(X\) and \(Y\) using a strictly invariant coordinate transformation \(\theta_0\) (identical physical width, height, axis limits, and aspect ratio).

Intuition: Instead of forcing the human brain to disentangle 10 overlapping lines on one chart, the analyst gives each entity its own clean, quiet box. The eye sweeps effortlessly across the grid, instantly spotting spikes, troughs, and outliers because every box follows identical visual rules.

Example: A smartphone weather application displaying a 7-day forecast using 7 small, identical vertical cards side by side (Monday through Sunday), where each card features an identically scaled bar or temperature sparkline.

[Source: Session6_Small_Multiples.pdf, Slides 3–6]

docs.title: Neuro-Cognitive Foundations of Pattern Spotting
docs.text:
The efficacy of Small Multiples is grounded in human sensory perception:

  • Visual Cortex Parallelism: The human visual cortex processes parallel sensory inputs across the field of view in under 1 second (\(<1000\text{ ms}\)). When spatial structures are held identical, cognitive energy is not wasted decoding varying axes, legends, or color keys.
  • Pattern Spotting Mechanism: When multiple visual objects share identical geometries, any deviation in height, slope, or position creates immediate visual pop-out. The observer does not need to read numerical labels; the visual cortex registers the anomaly instantaneously.
  • Tabular Reading vs. Visual Scanning: Reading numbers from a tabular matrix requires serial, conscious, foveal scanning (left-to-right, top-to-bottom) mediated by working memory. Small multiples leverage preattentive parallel visual decoding, reducing cognitive cycle time by over 80%.

[Source: Session6_Small_Multiples.pdf, Slide 7]

docs.title: Small Multiples vs. The "Spaghetti Chart"
docs.text:
A recurring error in exploratory analytics is plotting dozens of multi-class series on a single coordinate plane:

Visual Attribute Single Crowded "Spaghetti" Chart Small Matching Multiples Display Line Geometry Lines cross and occlude each other repeatedly Each entity has its own dedicated, un-occluded spatial box Color Demand Requires 10–20 distinct hues; exceeds human color memory Uses 1 or 2 neutral hues across all sub-boxes Traceability Eye repeatedly tracks back and forth between line and legend Direct labeling on or above each sub-box eliminates legends Cognitive Fatigue High; causes mental exhaustion and misinterpretation Low; viewer scans calmly across an ordered visual grid Extremum Detection Obscured by overlapping lines and dense clusters Instantaneous; highest/lowest bars or lines stand out immediately

[Source: Session6_Small_Multiples.pdf, Slide 8]

docs.title: The Three Golden Design Rules of Small Multiples
docs.text: To construct robust, trustworthy Small Multiples, three strict architectural constraints must be enforced:

docs.title: Rule 1: Scale Invariance (Uniform Coordinate Axes)
docs.text:
• Constraint: Every sub-box must share an identical coordinate range \([Y_{\min}, Y_{\max}]\) and \([X_{\min}, X_{\max}]\).
  • Rationale: If software independently rescales each sub-box to optimize local fill, a minor fluctuation of 2 units in Store A will look visually identical to a catastrophic drop of 200 units in Store B. Independent scales destroy visual integrity and deceive decision-makers.
  • Implementation: In enterprise tools (e.g., Tableau, ggplot2, Vega-Lite), axis scales must be set to Uniform / Fixed across all rows and columns, never Independent.

docs.title: Rule 2: Logical Arrangement & Sorting
docs.text:
• Natural Order: When the conditioning dimension possesses an inherent sequence (days of the week, calendar months, financial quarters), maintain that chronological order.
  • Descending Rank Order: When comparing nominal categories (stores, disease classes, sales reps), order sub-boxes from highest to lowest based on the primary performance metric. This establishes an immediate perceptual winner-to-loser trajectory.
  • Matrix Grid Layout: Arrange boxes in a compact 2D matrix (\(R \times C\)) mimicking a calendar grid, allowing systematic horizontal and vertical eye sweeps.

docs.title: Rule 3: Minimalist Simplicity & Data-Ink Maximization
docs.text:
• Typography: Eliminate bulky per-box titles, subtitles, and redundant axis scales. Use a single compact micro-label per sub-box (e.g., Shop A, Mon).
  • Data-Ink Ratio: Remove numerical value labels from individual bars or data points; the relative geometry conveys the insight.
  • Color Discipline: Restrict color usage to 1–2 neutral tones (e.g., slate teal #0F766E or soft blue #2563EB). Reserve a high-contrast alert color (e.g., coral red #EF4444) strictly for highlighting a specific anomaly or KPI breach.
  • Dimensionality: Avoid pseudo-3D effects, gradient fills, and heavy drop shadows.

[Source: Session6_Small_Multiples.pdf, Slides 11–13]

docs.title: Mark Selection: Bar Marks vs. Line Marks
docs.text:
The mark type deployed inside each sub-multiple must match the mathematical continuity of the underlying data:

flowchart LR
    A["Mark Selection Decision"] --> B{"Is the independent variable continuous time?"}
    B -- "No: Point-in-Time Discrete Comparison" --> C["Use BAR Mark: Single discrete count, Common zero baseline, Encodes magnitude via length"]
    B -- "Yes: Sequential Temporal Progression" --> D["Use LINE Mark: Shows trajectory and slope, Connected points, Reveals rate of change"]
  • Use Bar Marks When: Comparing discrete, point-in-time quantitative sums, counts, or single-period values across entities (e.g., annual revenue by division, exam score by student).
  • Use Line Marks When: Tracking continuous temporal evolution over sequential intervals (e.g., 12-month sales trajectories, hourly server latency curves).

[Source: Session6_Small_Multiples.pdf, Slide 14]

docs.title: Cognitive Limits & Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. The Overload Threshold: When the count of sub-multiples exceeds 20 to 30 panels on a single viewport, the display crosses from clarity into visual cognitive overload. When \(K > 30\), partition the visualization into paginated views, hierarchical drill-down facets, or interactive scrolling containers.
  2. The Independent Scale Trap: Allowing sub-panels to auto-scale independently. This is the single most dangerous error in trellis design.
  3. Random Categorical Ordering: Displaying panels in arbitrary database ingestion order rather than sorted by rank or natural sequence.
  4. Color Clutter: Painting each sub-panel with a distinct categorical hue, re-introducing the cognitive chaos of the spaghetti chart.

[Source: Session6_Small_Multiples.pdf, Slide 15]

docs.title: Concrete Case Scenarios from Course Materials
docs.text:
• Scenario A: 18 Students' Academic Examination Scores: Arranged as a \(2 \times 9\) matrix of identical bar cards. Rather than reading a dense mark sheet, the educator scans 18 cards simultaneously. High-performing students (scores \(>85\)) pop out in emerald green, while students requiring academic intervention (scores \(<40\)) register in alert crimson.

  • Scenario B: 12 Retail Stores Across a Commercial Chain: Arranged in a \(2 \times 6\) grid. Store 1 through Store 12 display monthly sales bars on identical scales. Outlier stores suffering supply-chain stockouts are identified in under 1 second without inspecting raw spreadsheets.

  • Scenario C: 6-Year Geopolitical Election Map Multiples: Instead of bar or line marks, each sub-panel contains an identical choropleth map representing consecutive election cycles (2020 to 2025). The viewer tracks the geographic migration of political coalitions across time without cognitive dissonance.

[Source: Session6_Small_Multiples.pdf, Slides 10, 21, 23]

docs.title: Tableau 3-Step Construction Workflow
docs.text:
1. Step 1: Data Connection & Baseline Chart Generation: Drag the quantitative measure (e.g., SUM(Sales)) to Rows and the primary dimension (e.g., continuous Order_Date or discrete Sub-Category) to Columns. Establish the base line or bar chart.

  2. Step 2: Conditioning Shelf Partitioning: Drag the categorical grouping dimension (e.g., Store_Location, Region, Department) onto the Columns shelf (for horizontal layout) or Rows shelf (for vertical stacking), or both (to create a 2D matrix grid). Tableau automatically partitions the single chart into adjacent, synchronized trellis panels.

  3. Step 3: Axis Synchronization & Styling Simplification: Right-click the vertical axis \(\to\) ensure Uniform axis range for all rows and columns is selected. Remove unnecessary zero lines, lighten horizontal gridlines, format title labels to concise bold text, and assign a uniform monochromatic color palette.

[Source: Session6_Small_Multiples.pdf, Slide 25]

docs.title: Section 2: Organisational Models & Preattentive Visual Variables
docs.text:
Before an analyst can structure an effective dashboard, they must understand how the human visual apparatus receives, filters, and prioritizes graphical information. Session 7 establishes the bridge between cognitive psychology, psychophysics, and executive information design.

flowchart TD
    subgraph HumanPerceptionPipeline ["Human Neuro-Visual Perception Pipeline"]
        NP1["Retinal Light Input: Photoreceptors (Rods/Cones)"] --> NP2["Stage 1: Preattentive Processing: Duration under 200 ms, Parallel unconscious pop-out"]
        NP2 --> NP3["Stage 2: Attentive Processing: Duration over 250 ms, Serial focused conscious reading"]
    end

    subgraph DesignImplementation ["Dashboard Structural Implementation"]
        DI1["Tier 1: Hero BAN Cards (Immediate Pop-Out)"]
        DI2["Tier 2: Macro Trends & Geographic Choropleths"]
        DI3["Tier 3: Granular Auditing Tables & Cross-Tabs"]
    end

    NP2 -.-> DI1
    NP3 -.-> DI2
    NP3 -.-> DI3

docs.title: Preattentive Visual Processing (\(< 200\text{ ms}\))
docs.text:
Human vision operates in two distinct computational stages:

  1. Preattentive Processing: Occurs automatically, rapidly (\(<200\text{ ms}\)), and unconsciously across large areas of the visual field. It extracts low-level physical features without focused attention.
  2. Attentive Processing: Operates sequentially, slowly (\(>250\text{ ms}\)), and consciously, focusing on localized features to read text, decode numerical values, and synthesize complex relationships.

Visual analytics leverages preattentive attributes so that critical insights (e.g., KPI breaches, extreme losses) are decoded by the viewer's brain before conscious cognitive effort begins.

[Source: Session7_Organisational_Models.pptx; Session6_Small_Multiples.pdf, Slide 30]

docs.title: The Four Preattentive Visual Variable Families
docs.text:
classDiagram
    class PreattentiveVariables {
        <<Cognitive Classification>>
    }
    class FormAndPosition {
        +2D Position (x, y)
        +Length / Height
        +Width / Thickness
        +Size / 2D Area
        +Orientation / Angle
        +Shape / Curvature
        +Enclosure / Boundaries
    }
    class ColorChannels {
        +Hue (Wavelength Identity)
        +Luminance (Lightness / Value)
        +Saturation (Color Purity)
    }
    class GestaltSpatial {
        +Proximity (Spatial Nearness)
        +Similarity (Shared Attributes)
        +Continuity (Smooth Vectors)
        +Closure (Enclosed Regions)
        +Common Fate (Shared Motion)
    }
    class DynamicMotion {
        +Flicker / Flashing
        +Directional Velocity
        +Motion Trajectory
    }

    PreattentiveVariables <|-- FormAndPosition
    PreattentiveVariables <|-- ColorChannels
    PreattentiveVariables <|-- GestaltSpatial
    PreattentiveVariables <|-- DynamicMotion
  1. Form and Position Family:
  2. 2D Spatial Position \((x, y)\): The most perceptually powerful variable. Human vision detects aligned position differences with sub-millimeter precision.
  3. Length / Bar Height: Directly proportional to quantitative magnitude along an aligned baseline.
  4. Size and Area: Two-dimensional scaling (circles, squares). Subject to perceptual underestimation (Stevens' Power Law).
  5. Orientation / Slope: Direction of lines indicating rate of change or trend direction.
  6. Shape: Geometric identity (circle, triangle, cross) used exclusively for categorical differentiation.
  7. Color Channels Family:
  8. Hue: Psychological perception of light wavelength (Red, Green, Blue, Amber). Excellent for qualitative, nominal category mapping; useless for ordered magnitude unless paired with lightness.
  9. Luminance / Value: Perceived brightness from light to dark. Naturally interpreted as quantitative intensity or rank order.
  10. Saturation: Chroma purity from dull gray to vivid color. Functions well for highlighting priority or confidence bands.
  11. Spatial Grouping (Gestalt Principles):
  12. Proximity: Objects placed physically close together are perceived as belonging to a unified cohort.
  13. Similarity: Objects sharing identical color, shape, or size are grouped mentally.
  14. Enclosure: A subtle card background or border physically binds disparate metrics into a cohesive functional unit.
  15. Continuity: Aligned elements establish visual flow without requiring connecting vectors.
  16. Motion Family:
  17. Flicker and Directional Velocity: Highly preattentive but hazardous in enterprise interfaces; causes visual irritation and distraction. Restricted to critical physical alarm systems.

[Source: Session7_Organisational_Models.pptx]

docs.title: Cleveland & McGill Perceptual Accuracy Hierarchy (1984)
docs.text:
In their seminal psychophysical research, William S. Cleveland and Robert McGill empirically measured the mathematical error rates of human subjects decoding quantitative data encoded via different graphical channels. Their findings establish a strict operational hierarchy:

Rank Elementary Graphical Encoding Task Relative Decoding Accuracy Primary Chart Types Leveraging Channel Recommended Analytical Use Case 1 Position along a common aligned scale Highest (Most Precise) Standard Bar Charts, Dot Plots, Aligned Scatter Plots Core KPI comparisons, precise rankings 2 Position along non-aligned identical scales Very High Small Multiples, Trellis Displays Multi-category cohort comparisons 3 Length / Height High Stacked Bar Segments, Floating Range Bars Component volume, duration 4 Angle / Slope Moderate Pie Charts, Donut Charts, Line Chart Slopes Rough proportion of total, trend direction 5 Area (2D Square / Circle Size) Low (Subject to Bias) Bubble Charts, Treemap Rectangles, Proportional Circles Macro share-of-whole, hierarchical sizing 6 Volume (3D Cube / Sphere) Very Low Pseudo-3D Bar Charts, 3D Surface Plots Prohibited in scientific & BI charts 7 Color Saturation / Shading Intensity Lowest Quantitative Choropleth Maps, Heatmap Grids Secondary magnitude indicators, triage alerting

📝 Exam Note: Memorize the Cleveland-McGill hierarchy in exact descending order. When an exam question asks: "Why is a standard bar chart superior to a pie chart or bubble chart for comparing 5 division revenues?", the rigorous answer cites Cleveland & McGill: Bar charts encode data via Position along a common aligned scale (Rank 1), whereas pie charts rely on Angle (Rank 4) and bubble charts rely on Area (Rank 5), which suffer from non-linear psychophysical estimation error.

[Source: Session7_Organisational_Models.pptx]

docs.title: Dashboard Three-Tier Visual Hierarchy
docs.text:
Enterprise dashboards must structure information to serve executive decision-makers who have varying depths of inquiry:

flowchart TD
    subgraph Tier1 ["Tier 1: Executive Pulse (Hero BAN Cards)"]
        T1A["Revenue: $48.2M (+12.4% YoY)"] --- T1B["Gross Margin: 28.6% (-1.2% MoM)"] --- T1C["Operating Cash: $14.1M"]
    end

    subgraph Tier2 ["Tier 2: Contextual Drivers (Macro Trends & Geospatial Maps)"]
        T2A["10-Year Revenue vs Spending Trajectory: Dual-Line Macro Trend"]
        T2B["Regional Performance Choropleth Map: State-by-State Gain / Loss Spatial Distribution"]
    end

    subgraph Tier3 ["Tier 3: Granular Auditing (Micro-Detail Breakdown Tables)"]
        T3A["Itemized Regional Cross-Tab Table: Transaction Records, SKUs, Variance Diagnostics, Audit Log"]
    end

    Tier1 --> Tier2 --> Tier3
  • Tier 1: Hero BAN Cards (Big Ass Numbers): Positioned at the extreme top of the layout (highest visual prominence). Presents 3 to 5 core metrics in large, high-contrast typography, accompanied by small directional delta symbols (\(\blacktriangle / \blacktriangledown\)) and percentage comparisons against budget or prior period.
  • Tier 2: Macro Trends & Geospatial Choropleths: Positioned in the middle canvas. Provides longitudinal context (5 to 10 year time series) and geographic distribution, revealing where and when deviations occurred.
  • Tier 3: Granular Detail Tables & Cross-Tabs: Positioned at the bottom. Supplies the transactional, tabular data required by operational analysts to perform root-cause auditing.

[Source: Session7_Organisational_Models.pptx; Session9_Radial_MultiY_Treemaps_.pdf, Slide 26]

docs.title: Semantic Color Palettes
docs.text:
Color must never be deployed decoratively; it serves strict semantic functions:

Palette Type Visual Mechanics Mathematical / Logical Nature of Data Optimal Enterprise Use Cases Categorical (Nominal) Distinct hues with uniform visual luminance and saturation Unordered qualitative discrete classes (\(c_i \neq c_j\)) Customer Segments, Departments, Server Types Sequential Monotonic gradient of single hue from light (low) to dark (high) Continuous, ordered, non-negative quantitative data (\(x \ge 0\)) Total Headcount, Population Density, Invoice Totals Diverging Two contrasting hues separated by a neutral midpoint (white/gray) Ordered data with a critical central threshold or zero baseline Profit vs Loss (\(-\text{USD} \leftrightarrow +\text{USD}\)), YoY Growth Rate (\(\pm \%\)) Alert / RAG Red (Critical / Danger), Amber (Warning), Green (Normal) Qualitative operational threshold compliance SLA breaches, ICU bed saturation, claim denials

docs.title: Colorblind Accessibility Mandate
docs.text:
Standard Red-Green palettes fail for the 8% of male users with congenital color vision deficiencies (Deuteranopia and Protanopia). Designers must adopt accessible alternatives:

  • Substitute Red-Green with Navy Blue (Positive / Gain) versus Vermilion Orange (Negative / Loss).
  • Augment color encodings with redundant visual channels (e.g., text labels, directional arrows, distinct geometric shapes).

[Source: Session7_Organisational_Models.pptx; Session9_Radial_MultiY_Treemaps_.pdf, Slide 26]

docs.title: Edward Tufte's Data-Ink Maximization
docs.text:
Edward R. Tufte formulated the foundational rule of visual graphics:

\[ \text{Data-Ink Ratio} = \frac{\text{Data-Ink}}{\text{Total Ink Used to Print the Graphic}} = 1.0 - \text{Chartjunk Ratio} \]

docs.title: Architectural Principles:
docs.text:
1. Maximize Data-Ink: Every drop of ink or screen pixel must present non-redundant visual information.
  2. Eradicate Chartjunk: Eliminate decorative graphic elements that consume ink without conveying data:
  3. Heavy black gridlines (replace with faint gray dashed lines #E2E8F0 or omit entirely).
  4. Artificial 3D extrusions, cylindrical bars, and drop shadows.
  5. Redundant legends when direct labels can be placed on marks.
  6. Ornate background wallpaper and corporate watermarks.

[Source: Session7_Organisational_Models.pptx]

docs.title: Section 3: Interactive Charts & Visual Analytics Mechanisms
docs.text:
Static charts function as communication posters: they present a pre-compiled, author-driven perspective. In modern visual analytics, the data scale is too vast and user questions are too varied for static displays to suffice. Session 8 establishes the 4 core mechanisms that transform static charts into dynamic exploratory systems.

flowchart TD
    subgraph AnalyticalParadigm ["Visual Analytics Exploration Cycle"]
        U["Human Analyst"] -->|"Manipulates Direct Control"| DQ["Mechanism 2: Dynamic Queries (Sliders, Range Facets, Parameter Controls)"]
        DQ -->|"Sub-100ms In-Memory Query"| DS["Mechanism 1: Data Spotlight (Focal Brightness vs Gray Desaturation)"]
        DS -->|"Coordinates Across All Views"| DB["Mechanism 3: Data Brushing (Cross-View Linking and Highlighting)"]
        DB -->|"User Inspects Locus"| LZ["Mechanism 4: Local Zooming & Datatips (Focus + Context & Details on Demand)"]
        LZ -->|"Perceptual Feedback"| U
    end

docs.title: Static Posters vs. Interactive Exploratory Systems
docs.text:
Operational Dimension Static Visual Display (Poster Model) Interactive Visual Analytics (Exploratory System) Authoring Paradigm Created once by designer; fixed perspective Created as a configurable application canvas Audience Agency Passive observer; can only view pre-selected cuts Active explorer; poses ad-hoc queries via direct manipulation Audience Fit Generic, one-size-fits-all compromise Every user customizes the view to their operational cohort Delivery Medium Printed report, projected slide, static PDF / screenshot Digital screen interface with active hardware rendering Cognitive Velocity Slow; requires manual cross-referencing of appendixes Instantaneous; provides dynamic query-response feedback

[Source: Session8_Interactive_Charts_.pdf, Slide 5]

docs.title: The Four Core Visual Analytics Mechanisms
docs.text: Session 8 formalizes four fundamental interaction tools:

docs.title: Tool 1: Data Spotlight (Focal Luminance Modulation)
docs.text:
• Mechanical Definition: The technique of rendering a selected data cohort in vibrant, saturated color while simultaneously dropping all non-selected baseline marks into a soft, desaturated neutral gray.
  • Perceptual Logic: Like shining a flashlight in a dark room. Rather than deleting unselected items (which destroys global statistical context), the spotlight creates preattentive pop-out while retaining the peripheral distribution.
  • Enterprise Analogs: Google Maps highlighting the active transit route in bright blue while muting surrounding city roads into light gray; Spotify turning the active playing track bright green while playlist items remain white; Tableau Highlight Actions.

docs.title: Tool 2: Dynamic Queries (Zero-Latency Direct Manipulation)
docs.text:
• Mechanical Definition: The formulation of database queries through direct visual manipulation of interface controls (continuous range sliders, toggles, check facets) with real-time graphical feedback.
  • Temporal Constraint: The system must evaluate and re-render marks with latency under 100 milliseconds (\(<100\text{ ms}\)). If query latency exceeds 500 ms, user cognitive momentum collapses.
  • The Old Way vs. The Dynamic Way: The legacy paradigm forced users to fill SQL form fields, click Submit, and wait for a full-page server refresh. Dynamic queries allow an analyst to test 20 hypotheses in 60 seconds by moving a slider.
  • Enterprise Analogs: Amazon/Flipkart price range sliders; Zomato 4.0+ rating facets; Tableau Quick Filters and Parameters.

docs.title: Tool 3: Data Brushing (Cross-View Linking and Brushing)
docs.text:
• Mechanical Definition: An interactive protocol linking multiple distinct visualization sheets sharing a common relational key. Selecting a data subset in one chart (e.g., brushing a rectangle over points in a scatter plot) automatically highlights the identical records across all connected bar charts, maps, and tables on the canvas.
  • Brushing vs. Filtering Distinction:
  • Filtering: Deletes or hides unselected rows from view. Destroys peripheral context; makes it impossible to see what fraction of the total the cohort represents.
  • Brushing: Retains 100% of data points on screen, dynamically modulating color saturation or border outlines.
  • The Diagnostic Test: "After your click, can you still see the unselected items in faded form? If yes, it is Brushing. If no, it is Filtering."
  • Enterprise Analogs: A seller dashboard where selecting Diwali week on a time-series chart causes that specific week's revenue to glow inside the category bar chart and regional map; Tableau Dashboard Filter/Highlight Actions.

docs.title: Tool 4: Local Zooming (Focus + Context & Datatips)
docs.text:
• Mechanical Definition: Magnifying an area of localized interest to inspect high-frequency data while maintaining the global perimeter dataset in view.
  • Ben Shneiderman's Information Seeking Mantra:

    "Overview first, zoom and filter, then details-on-demand."

  • Datatips (Tooltips): Compact hover popover cards that remain hidden to preserve a clean Data-Ink ratio, appearing only when the user points at an individual mark to reveal micro-numerical attributes.
  • Enterprise Analogs: Pinch-to-zoom in navigation maps; hover image magnification on product catalogs; Tableau Viz-in-Tooltip micro-charts.

[Source: Session8_Interactive_Charts_.pdf, Slides 6–27]

docs.title: The Four-Question Functional Mapping
docs.text:
The 4 interaction mechanisms map directly to the four core questions an analyst asks during data exploration:

flowchart TD
    Q1["1. Where should I look?"] -->|"Focal Pop-Out"| A1["Data Spotlight: Illuminates primary focus, fades background"]
    Q2["2. Which ones fit my operational criteria?"] -->|"Direct Filtering"| A2["Dynamic Queries: Continuous sliders and discrete facets"]
    Q3["3. How does this specific cohort behave everywhere?"] -->|"Cross-View Linking"| A3["Data Brushing: Multi-coordinate relational illumination"]
    Q4["4. What micro-details exist in this small region?"] -->|"Local Inspection"| A4["Local Zooming and Datatips: Focus + Context, Tooltips"]

[Source: Session8_Interactive_Charts_.pdf, Slide 28]

docs.title: Negative Constraints: When NOT to Use Interactivity
docs.text:
Interactivity is not universally appropriate. Deploying interactive charts in unsuitable environments is a serious design failure:

  1. Static Physical & Digital Media:
  2. Printed Paper Reports: Clickable sliders, tooltips, and brushing mechanisms become useless paper artifacts.
  3. Projector Presentations & Keynotes: Interactive controls during executive presentations introduce technical latency, awkward mouse hunting, and audience detachment. Use pre-rendered spotlight graphics with bold static callouts.
  4. PDF Document Exports & Screen Captures: Interactivity is stripped away; un-spotlighted charts lose their communicative power.
  5. The "Too Many Filters" Anti-Pattern:
  6. Populating a dashboard with 15–20 dropdown filters overwhelms the user. Keep controls to 3–5 vital parameters.
  7. Absence of a Global Reset Mechanism:
  8. Every interactive dashboard must provide an unambiguous, 1-click "Reset All Filters" button. Without it, users become lost in complex cross-filtered states.

[Source: Session8_Interactive_Charts_.pdf, Slide 29]

docs.title: Tableau & Power BI Implementation Mapping
docs.text:
Visual Analytics Concept Tableau Desktop Implementation Mechanism Microsoft Power BI Equivalent Feature Data Spotlight Highlight Action (Dashboard \(\to\) Actions \(\to\) Add Highlight) Cross-highlighting mark behavior (Default interaction) Dynamic Queries Quick Filters & Tableau Parameters with Slider UI Interactive Slicers & Parameter Sliders Data Brushing Dashboard Filter Actions configured with Show all values Cross-filtering between visual cards on report page Local Zooming Canvas Zoom Controls + Viz-in-Tooltip (<Sheet name=...>) Drill-through pages + Tooltip report pages

[Source: Session8_Interactive_Charts_.pdf, Slide 31]

docs.title: Section 4: Specialized Chart Topologies
docs.text:
Standard Cartesian bar and line plots handle the majority of business reporting needs. However, specific structural data challenges—such as circular periodic phenomena, extreme numerical scale disparities, and deep hierarchical compositions—require specialized geometric chart topologies. Session 9 analyzes three such advanced architectures.

flowchart LR
    A["Specialized Chart Selection"] --> B{"Data Structure Profile"}
    B -- "Continuous Cyclical / Diurnal Time" --> C["Radial Table: Maps Cartesian (x,y) to Polar (r, theta), 360-degree cyclical continuity, 24h clock, 12 months"]
    B -- "Extreme Scale Disparity (Thousands vs Millions)" --> D["Multi-Y Graph (Dual-Axis): Shared horizontal time domain, Left & Right independent scales, Guard against Two-Axis Trap"]
    B -- "Hierarchical Part-to-Whole (>10 Categories)" --> E["Treemap: Space-filling recursive rectangles, Area = Size, Color = Growth/Margin, Outperforms pie charts at scale"]

docs.title: Mathematical Transformation:
docs.text:
A Radial Table translates standard rectilinear Cartesian coordinates \((x, y)\) into Polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\):

\[ x_i = r_i \cdot \cos(\theta_i), \quad y_i = r_i \cdot \sin(\theta_i) \]

where the angular displacement \(\theta_i\) encodes periodic cyclical time, and the radial vector distance \(r_i\) encodes quantitative magnitude:

\[ \theta_i = \theta_0 + 2\pi \left(\frac{t_i - t_0}{T}\right) \]

Here, \(T\) denotes the complete natural periodicity (e.g., \(T = 24\text{ hours}\) for diurnal cycles, \(T = 12\text{ months}\) for annual seasonality), and \(\theta_0\) represents the origin angle (standardized at 12 o'clock, \(\theta_0 = \frac{\pi}{2}\)).

docs.title: Optimal Domain & Real-World Use Cases:
docs.text:
• Natural Periodic Repetition: Phenomena that physically repeat in a loop, where the final interval connects seamlessly back to the first interval (\(23:59 \to 00:00\), or December \(\to\) January).
  • Apple Watch Activity Rings: Concentric radial arcs representing Move, Exercise, and Stand goals completing a \(360^\circ\) circle.
  • Spotify Wrapped Musical Wheels: Visualizing genre preference arcs radiating around a circular wheel.
  • Automotive Fuel Gauge & Speedometer: Circular needle dials indicating continuous reservoir status.

docs.title: Design Guidelines & Limitations:
docs.text:
• Do's: Anchor the start point clearly at 12 o'clock; restrict the display to 1 or 2 concentric rings; provide clean numerical datatips.
  • Don'ts: Never use a circle merely because it looks aesthetically pleasing. Human vision struggles to evaluate curved arc lengths compared to aligned straight bars (Cleveland-McGill Rank 4 vs. Rank 1). Do not partition a radial table into dozens of thin, unreadable pie wedges.

[Source: Session9_Radial_MultiY_Treemaps_.pdf, Slides 5–8]

docs.title: Resolving Extreme Scale Disparity:
docs.text:
In industrial monitoring, analysts frequently compare two metrics that share an identical timeline but operate on radically incompatible numerical scales. For example, in the CRSI Market Intelligence study:

  • Metric 1: Steel Producer Price Index (PPI) \(\approx 4,000\) points.
  • Metric 2: Total US Construction Spending \(\approx \$20,000,000\) (\(20\text{ Million USD}\)).

If plotted on a single shared vertical axis spanning 0 to 20,000,000, the Steel PPI line (values near 4,000) collapses into a flat, indistinguishable horizontal line along the bottom axis.

The Structural Solution: Implement a Multi-Y (Dual-Axis) Graph:

  • Metric 1 (Steel PPI) is plotted against the Left Vertical Axis (Scale: \(0\text{K}\) to \(4\text{K}\)).
  • Metric 2 (Construction Spending) is plotted against the Right Vertical Axis (Scale: \(\$0\text{M}\) to \(\$20\text{M}\)).
  • Both metrics share the Horizontal Axis (Timeline: 2015 to 2026).
flowchart TD
    subgraph MultiYArchitecture ["Dual-Axis Multi-Y Coordinate Architecture"]
        direction TB
        LA["Left Vertical Axis: Steel PPI (0 - 4K)"]
        RA["Right Vertical Axis: Construction Spending ($0M - $20M)"]
        HA["Shared Horizontal Time Axis: Years 2015 to 2026"]
        L1["Line 1: Steel Index (Color: Teal #0F766E)"]
        L2["Line 2: Construction ($) (Color: Amber #D97706)"]

        LA --- L1
        RA --- L2
        L1 --- HA
        L2 --- HA
    end

docs.title: The Dangerous "Two-Axis Trap"
docs.text:
While Multi-Y charts resolve scale disparity, they introduce severe visual risks:

flowchart LR
    subgraph TrapA ["Scale A: Uncompressed Axis (Baseline = 0)"]
        TA["Axis Range: 0 to 10,000 | Data: 4,800 to 5,100 | Visual Appearance: Flat line | Interpretation: Stable"]
    end

    subgraph TrapB ["Scale B: Squeezed Axis (Truncated Baseline)"]
        TB["Axis Range: 4,750 to 5,150 | Data: 4,800 to 5,100 | Visual Appearance: Jagged peaks and valleys | Interpretation: Crisis"]
    end
  • Deceptive Crossings: The point where two lines intersect on a dual-axis chart is a mathematical artifact of the arbitrary scaling chosen for the left and right axes. Changing either axis scale shifts the intersection point horizontally or eliminates it entirely. Viewers falsely interpret the intersection as an operational event (e.g., "Steel costs surpassed construction spending").
  • Spurious Correlation: An analyst can artificially scale the two axes to make two completely unrelated trends track each other visually.
  • Mandatory Design Safeguards:
  • Strict Color Coding: The color of the left axis labels and title must match Line 1 exactly; the right axis must match Line 2.
  • Limit to Exactly Two Lines: Never plot 3 or 4 disparate scales on one chart.
  • The Normalized Index Alternative: Convert both series to a Base-100 Relative Growth Index (\(I_t = \frac{X_t}{X_{\text{base}}} \times 100\)), enabling both series to be plotted honestly on a single Cartesian axis.

[Source: Session9_Radial_MultiY_Treemaps_.pdf, Slides 9–14]

docs.title: Mathematical & Geometric Topology:
docs.text:
A Treemap displays hierarchical, part-to-whole categorical data through recursive space-filling planar partitioning. The total canvas area represents 100% of the aggregated measure.

Let a category set have positive quantitative weights \(W = \{w_1, w_2, \dots, w_n\}\) within a bounding canvas of total area \(A_{\text{total}} = \text{Width} \times \text{Height}\). The area \(a_i\) allocated to rectangle \(R_i\) is strictly proportional to its relative weight:

\[ a_i = A_{\text{total}} \cdot \frac{w_i}{\sum_{j=1}^n w_j} \]

docs.title: Dual-Metric Visual Channel Encoding:
docs.text:
1. Primary Metric \(\to\) Rectangle Area: Quantifies total size, volume, or capacity (e.g., Gross Sales, Total Assets, Memory Allocation).
  2. Secondary Metric \(\to\) Fill Color: Encodes operational performance, percentage growth, or margin intensity via a diverging palette (e.g., Green for Profit / Orange for Loss; Red for Claim Rejection).

docs.title: The Aspect Ratio Optimization (\(\rho \approx 1\)):
docs.text:
Basic "slice-and-dice" treemaps produce long, thin, ribbon-like slivers that prevent human viewers from comparing areas and make text labeling impossible. Modern treemaps employ the Squarified Treemap Algorithm (Bruls, Huizing, van Wijk), which optimizes the rectangle aspect ratio \(\rho(R)\):

\[ \rho(R) = \max\left(\frac{w}{h}, \frac{h}{w}\right) \ge 1.0 \]

The algorithm recursively partitions space to drive \(\rho(R)\) as close to \(1.0\) (a perfect square) as possible.

        direction TB
        subgraph TopRow ["66% Total Canvas Area"]
            R1["Electronics: ₹42 Cr (Area = 42%), Color: Deep Navy"]
            R2["Fashion: ₹24 Cr (Area = 24%), Color: Slate Blue"]
        end
        subgraph BottomRow ["34% Total Canvas Area"]
            R3["Home: ₹14 Cr (14%)"]
            R4["Beauty: ₹8 Cr (8%)"]
            R5["Grocery: ₹6 Cr (6%)"]
            R6["Others: ₹6 Cr (Books, Toys, Sports)"]
        end
    end

docs.title: Deconstruction of the 5 Core Dashboard Components
docs.text:
1. The Executive Headline Narrative Banner: Positioned at the top of the canvas. Instead of a generic title (e.g., "Steel and Construction Report"), it provides an actionable executive summary:

    "Steel prices are up 9.87% year-over-year as of May 2026, while construction spending growth has slowed to under 1% — input costs are outpacing project demand, creating margin pressure for steel reinforcement buyers. Texas led construction job gains (+28,600), while California posted the steepest losses (-13,800) — a clear Sun Belt vs. coastal divergence in regional demand."

  2. The 4 Executive KPI Hero Cards (Tier 1 BANs):
  3. Steel YoY Growth: 9.87% (Input cost inflation)
  4. Construction YoY Growth: 0.88% (Market demand stagnation)
  5. Steel MoM Growth: 1.63% (Short-term acceleration)

  6. Construction MoM Growth: 0.37% (Short-term flattening) Each card displays a 24pt bold number paired with an explicit temporal baseline label.

  7. Dual Macroeconomic Trend Views (Tier 2): Rather than falling into the Two-Axis Trap by superimposing Steel PPI and Construction Spending onto a single deceptive dual-axis plot, the architect placed two coordinated line charts side by side:

  8. Chart A: Steel Price Producer Index from 2015 to 2026 (Scale: 0 to 4K).

  9. Chart B: Total US Construction Spending from 2015 to 2026 (Scale: $0 to $20M). This allows direct visual comparison of cyclical shapes and trajectories without generating spurious line intersections.

  10. Geospatial State Employment Choropleth Map (Tier 2): Encodes net 12-month construction job changes across all 50 US states using a diverging palette:

  11. Navy Blue: Positive employment expansion (Texas leading with \(+28,600\) positions).

  12. Vermilion Orange: Contraction and employment decline (California posting \(-13,800\) losses). The viewer decodes the macroeconomic geographic migration (Sun Belt boom vs. Coastal contraction) in under 2 seconds.

  13. Continuous Temporal Parameter Slider (Interaction Engine): Positioned in the upper right quadrant. Dragging the slider dynamically re-filters all 4 KPI BAN cards, updates the macro trend lines, and re-calculates state employment gains across the map with sub-100 ms latency.

[Source: Session9_Radial_MultiY_Treemaps_.pdf, Slides 21–25; Tableau Demo Solution.twbx]

docs.title: Formula 1: Edward Tufte's Data-Ink Ratio
docs.text: \[ \text{DIR} = \frac{\text{Data-Ink}}{\text{Total Ink Used to Print the Graphic}} = 1.0 - \frac{\text{Non-Data-Ink}}{\text{Total Ink}} \]

docs.title: Symbol Definitions
docs.text: Symbol Meaning Units / Range \(\text{DIR}\) Data-Ink Ratio Dimensionless, \([0.0, 1.0]\) \(\text{Data-Ink}\) Physical ink/pixels dedicated strictly to depicting non-redundant data values Area of ink (\(\text{mm}^2\) or pixels) \(\text{Total Ink}\) Total ink/pixels consumed by the entire graphic (data marks + borders + grid + text) Area of ink (\(\text{mm}^2\) or pixels) \(\text{Non-Data-Ink}\) Ink consumed by decorative elements, heavy borders, redundant text, and chartjunk Area of ink (\(\text{mm}^2\) or pixels)

docs.title: What It Represents:
docs.text: The efficiency of a visual display. A ratio approaching \(1.0\) indicates that nearly all ink conveys substantive data, minimizing cognitive clutter.

docs.title: Formula 2: Polar Coordinate Mapping for Radial Tables
docs.text: \[ \theta_i = \theta_0 + 2\pi \cdot \left(\frac{t_i - t_0}{T}\right) \] \[ r_i = r_{\text{inner}} + \left(\frac{v_i - V_{\min}}{V_{\max} - V_{\min}}\right) \cdot (r_{\text{outer}} - r_{\text{inner}}) \] \[ x_i = x_{\text{origin}} + r_i \cdot \cos(\theta_i), \quad y_i = y_{\text{origin}} + r_i \cdot \sin(\theta_i) \]

docs.title: Symbol Definitions
docs.text: Symbol Meaning Units / Range \(\theta_i\) Angular coordinate of \(i\)-th temporal interval Radians, \([0, 2\pi)\) \(\theta_0\) Origin reference angle (standardized at 12 o'clock) \(\frac{\pi}{2}\text{ rad}\) (\(90^\circ\)) \(t_i, t_0, T\) Active timestamp, baseline start time, and full cycle period Time units (Hours, Months) \(r_i\) Radial vector distance for \(i\)-th observation Length (pixels / mm) \(r_{\text{inner}}, r_{\text{outer}}\) Inner hole radius and outer boundary radius of the radial ring Length (pixels / mm) \(v_i, V_{\min}, V_{\max}\) Quantitative measure value, domain minimum, and domain maximum Original target measure units \(x_i, y_i\) Transformed Cartesian screen coordinates for rendering mark Pixel coordinates

docs.title: Formula 3: Squarified Treemap Aspect Ratio Penalty
docs.text: \[ \rho(R) = \max\left(\frac{w}{h}, \frac{h}{w}\right) \] \[ \text{Penalty}(R) = \rho(R) - 1.0 \ge 0.0 \]

docs.title: Symbol Definitions
docs.text: Symbol Meaning Units / Range \(\rho(R)\) Aspect ratio of bounding rectangle \(R\) Dimensionless, \([1.0, \infty)\) \(w, h\) Width and height of the subdivided rectangle Screen pixels / mm \(\text{Penalty}\) Geometric deviation from an optimal square Dimensionless, \([0.0, \infty)\) (\(0.0 = \text{Square}\))

docs.text: \[ I_t = \left(\frac{X_t}{X_{\text{base}}}\right) \times 100 \]

docs.title: Symbol Definitions
docs.text: Symbol Meaning Units / Range \(I_t\) Normalized base-100 index value at time \(t\) Index points, \([0, \infty)\) \(X_t\) Raw observed metric value at time \(t\) Original units (e.g., USD, PPI) \(X_{\text{base}}\) Baseline reference metric value at designated time \(t = 0\) Original units

docs.title: Formula 5: Stevens' Psychophysical Power Law (Cleveland-McGill Perception)
docs.text: \[ \psi(I) = k \cdot I^\beta \]

docs.title: Symbol Definitions
docs.text: Symbol Meaning Units / Range \(\psi(I)\) Perceived psychological sensation magnitude Dimensionless perceptual scale \(I\) Physical stimulus intensity (length, area, volume, brightness) Physical units (\(\text{mm}\), \(\text{mm}^2\), \(\text{cd/m}^2\)) \(k\) Empirical scaling constant Dimensionless constant \(\beta\) Sensory modality psychophysical exponent Dimensionless exponent

docs.title: Empirical Exponent Values:
docs.text:
• Aligned Length: \(\beta \approx 0.98 - 1.02\) (Linear perception; no cognitive distortion).
  • Two-Dimensional Area: \(\beta \approx 0.70 - 0.82\) (Severe underestimation of large areas).
  • Three-Dimensional Volume: \(\beta \approx 0.50 - 0.60\) (Extreme perceptual compression).

docs.title: Derivation: Proof of Perceptual Distortion in Area vs. Length Encodings
docs.text:
Goal: Prove mathematically, using Stevens' Power Law, why human observers experience non-linear underestimation when decoding 2D Area encodings (Treemaps, Proportional Circles, Bubble Charts) compared to 1D Length encodings (Bar Charts), explaining the Cleveland & McGill hierarchy ranking.

Starting Point: Stevens' Psychophysical Power Law relates perceived sensation \(\psi\) to physical stimulus intensity \(I\):

\[ \psi(I) = k \cdot I^\beta \]

Step-by-Step Derivation:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{For an Aligned Bar Chart (Length): } \beta_{\text{length}} &\approx 1.00 \\ \psi_{\text{length}}(L) &= k_1 \cdot L^{1.00} = k_1 \cdot L && \text{(Linear sensory transfer)} \\ \frac{d\psi_{\text{length}}}{dL} &= k_1 = \text{Constant} && \text{(Marginal sensitivity is perfectly invariant across scale)} \end{aligned} \]

Now, consider a 2D Area mark (circle or square) where physical area \(A\) encodes the quantitative value:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{For 2D Area: } \beta_{\text{area}} &\approx 0.75 \\ \psi_{\text{area}}(A) &= k_2 \cdot A^{0.75} && \text{(Sub-linear power relationship)} \\ \frac{d\psi_{\text{area}}}{dA} &= 0.75 \cdot k_2 \cdot A^{-0.25} = \frac{0.75 \cdot k_2}{A^{0.25}} && \text{(Derivative strictly decreases as Area increases)} \end{aligned} \]

Consider two data values: \(V_1 = 10\) units and \(V_2 = 100\) units (True ratio \(R_{\text{true}} = \frac{V_2}{V_1} = 10.0\)):

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{Perceived Ratio for Length: } R_{\text{perceived, length}} &= \frac{\psi(100)}{\psi(10)} = \frac{k_1 \cdot 100}{k_1 \cdot 10} = 10.0 && \text{(Accurate decoding)} \\ \text{Perceived Ratio for Area: } R_{\text{perceived, area}} &= \frac{\psi(100)}{\psi(10)} = \frac{k_2 \cdot 100^{0.75}}{k_2 \cdot 10^{0.75}} = \left(\frac{100}{10}\right)^{0.75} = 10^{0.75} \approx 5.623 \end{aligned} \]

Result:

\[ R_{\text{perceived, area}} \approx 5.62 \ll 10.0 = R_{\text{true}} \]

Interpretation: When an analyst doubles or increases a circle or rectangle's area by a factor of 10, the human visual cortex perceives an increase of only \(\sim 5.6\)-fold. Viewers systematically underestimate large areas unless explicit data labels are printed inside the marks. This empirical mathematical reality places Position and Length at Ranks 1–3 of the Cleveland-McGill hierarchy, while Area drops to Rank 5.

[Source: Session7_Organisational_Models.pptx]

docs.title: Section 7: Detailed Worked Numerical Problems (10–15 Mark Exam Caliber)
Numerical Problem 1: Quantitative Audit of Data-Ink Ratio & Chartjunk Optimization
docs.text:
Examination Level: 10 Marks Problem Statement: An analytics team deployed an operational dashboard displaying monthly departmental server expenses. A UI audit evaluates the ink consumption across a \(1000 \times 600\text{ pixel}\) canvas (Total Canvas Area \(= 600,000\text{ px}^2\)). The physical pixel breakdown reveals:

  • Total active screen pixels consumed by graphic elements: \(180,000\text{ pixels}\).
  • Essential data-ink (bars, line trajectories, and numerical value labels): \(54,000\text{ pixels}\).
  • Heavy decorative drop shadows and pseudo-3D bevels: \(45,000\text{ pixels}\).
  • Saturated dark background card panels: \(51,000\text{ pixels}\).
  • Dense black coordinate gridlines and redundant axis border frames: \(30,000\text{ pixels}\).

Required Targets:

  1. Compute the baseline Data-Ink Ratio (\(\text{DIR}_{\text{initial}}\)) and the Chartjunk Ratio.
  2. Formulate an engineering remediation plan removing non-data ink.
  3. Compute the re-engineered Data-Ink Ratio (\(\text{DIR}_{\text{final}}\)) assuming all 3D bevels and saturated cards are eliminated, and gridlines are replaced by subtle 1px dashed rules consuming only \(4,500\text{ pixels}\).
  4. State Tufte's core design prescription.

Step-by-Step Solution:

Step 1: Baseline Metrics Calculation

\[ \text{Data-Ink} = 54,000\text{ pixels} \] \[ \text{Total Printed Ink} = 180,000\text{ pixels} \] \[ \text{DIR}_{\text{initial}} = \frac{\text{Data-Ink}}{\text{Total Ink}} = \frac{54,000}{180,000} = 0.300 \quad (30.0\%) \] \[ \text{Non-Data Ink} = 45,000 + 51,000 + 30,000 = 126,000\text{ pixels} \] \[ \text{Chartjunk Ratio} = \frac{\text{Non-Data Ink}}{\text{Total Ink}} = \frac{126,000}{180,000} = 0.700 \quad (70.0\%) \]

Step 2: Remediation Plan Execution

  • Eliminate 3D bevels and drop shadows \(\to\) Recover \(45,000\text{ pixels}\).
  • Replace saturated dark background containers with pure white background #FFFFFF \(\to\) Recover \(51,000\text{ pixels}\).
  • Replace heavy black gridlines (\(30,000\text{ pixels}\)) with minimal dashed rules (\(4,500\text{ pixels}\)) \(\to\) Net non-data ink becomes \(4,500\text{ pixels}\).

Step 3: Post-Remediation Data-Ink Ratio

\[ \text{New Total Ink} = \text{Data-Ink} + \text{Remaining Non-Data Ink} = 54,000 + 4,500 = 58,500\text{ pixels} \] \[ \text{DIR}_{\text{final}} = \frac{54,000}{58,500} \approx 0.9231 \quad (92.31\%) \]

Step 4: Interpretation By eliminating chartjunk, the Data-Ink Ratio improved from an unacceptable \(30.0\%\) to an exceptional \(92.31\%\), a \(3.08\times\) efficiency gain. The visualization eliminates visual noise, allowing users to decode server expense anomalies instantly.

docs.title: Numerical Problem 2: Transforming Disparate Physical Measurements into a Normalized Base-100 Multi-Series Chart
docs.text:
Examination Level: 12 Marks Problem Statement: An executive visual analytics team at CRSI is analyzing steel input costs against commercial construction spending over a 5-year macro cycle (\(2020\) to \(2024\)). The raw data records:

Observation Year (\(t\)) Steel Producer Price Index (\(S_t\), Points) Total Construction Spending (\(C_t\), Billions USD) 2020 (Base Year) 2,000 $1,200 Billion 2021 3,600 $1,260 Billion 2022 3,200 $1,380 Billion 2023 2,800 $1,500 Billion 2024 2,600 $1,560 Billion

Required Targets:

  1. Demonstrate the failure mode of plotting both series on a single unnormalized Cartesian axis (\(0\) to \(\$1,600\)).
  2. Calculate the Normalized Base-100 Relative Growth Indices (\(I_{S, t}\) and \(I_{C, t}\)) for all years taking \(2020\) as Base Year (\(I_{2020} = 100.0\)).
  3. Compute the Year-over-Year (\(\text{YoY}\)) percentage growth rates for both series for 2021.
  4. Explain how this normalized transformation eliminates the "Two-Axis Trap".

Step-by-Step Solution:

Step 1: Failure Mode Analysis of Unnormalized Axis If plotted on a single vertical axis calibrated to Construction Spending (\(0\) to \(\$1,600\text{ Billion}\)), the Steel Index (\(2,000\) to \(3,600\)) operates in a completely mismatched numerical scale. If steel index values are mapped directly without conversion, they exceed the axis maximum (\(3,600 > 1,600\)); if scaled down by 1,000 (\(2.0\) to \(3.6\)), they collapse into an invisible flat line along the baseline (\(2.0 / 1600 \approx 0.12\%\)).

Step 2: Base-100 Normalized Index Calculation Formula: \(I_t = \left(\frac{X_t}{X_{2020}}\right) \times 100\)

  • For Steel Price Index (\(S_{\text{base}} = 2,000\)):
  • \(I_{S, 2020} = (2,000 / 2,000) \times 100 = \mathbf{100.0}\)
  • \(I_{S, 2021} = (3,600 / 2,000) \times 100 = \mathbf{180.0}\)
  • \(I_{S, 2022} = (3,200 / 2,000) \times 100 = \mathbf{160.0}\)
  • \(I_{S, 2023} = (2,800 / 2,000) \times 100 = \mathbf{140.0}\)

  • \(I_{S, 2024} = (2,600 / 2,000) \times 100 = \mathbf{130.0}\)

  • For Construction Spending (\(C_{\text{base}} = 1,200\)):

  • \(I_{C, 2020} = (1,200 / 1,200) \times 100 = \mathbf{100.0}\)
  • \(I_{C, 2021} = (1,260 / 1,200) \times 100 = \mathbf{105.0}\)
  • \(I_{C, 2022} = (1,380 / 1,200) \times 100 = \mathbf{115.0}\)
  • \(I_{C, 2023} = (1,500 / 1,200) \times 100 = \mathbf{125.0}\)
  • \(I_{C, 2024} = (1,560 / 1,200) \times 100 = \mathbf{130.0}\)

Summary Index Table:

Year Raw Steel (Pts) Raw Construct ($B) Steel Index (\(I_S\)) Construct Index (\(I_C\)) Spread (\(\Delta = I_S - I_C\)) 2020 2,000 $1,200 100.0 100.0 0.0 pts (Parity) 2021 3,600 $1,260 180.0 105.0 +75.0 pts (Cost Squeeze) 2022 3,200 $1,380 160.0 115.0 +45.0 pts 2023 2,800 $1,500 140.0 125.0 +15.0 pts 2024 2,600 $1,560 130.0 130.0 0.0 pts (Convergence)

Step 3: Year-over-Year (YoY) Percentage Growth Calculation for 2021

\[ \text{YoY}_{\text{Steel}, 2021} = \left(\frac{3,600 - 2,000}{2,000}\right) \times 100\% = \frac{1,600}{2,000} \times 100\% = \mathbf{+80.0\%} \] \[ \text{YoY}_{\text{Construct}, 2021} = \left(\frac{1,260 - 1,200}{1,200}\right) \times 100\% = \frac{60}{1,200} \times 100\% = \mathbf{+5.0\%} \]

Step 4: Analytical Conclusion: In 2021, steel input costs exploded by \(+80.0\%\) while project demand expanded by only \(+5.0\%\), producing severe contractor margin compression. By converting both disparate metrics to a shared Base-100 Relative Index on a single vertical axis, both series can be compared honestly without using misleading dual axes. The 2024 convergence at index \(130.0\) demonstrates that over the 5-year cycle, both steel prices and construction spending expanded by exactly \(+30.0\%\) relative to their 2020 baselines.

docs.title: Numerical Problem 3: Squarified Treemap Recursive Coordinate Partitioning
docs.text:
Examination Level: 15 Marks Problem Statement: An e-commerce executive dashboard partitions a total marketing revenue canvas of width \(W = 1000\text{ pixels}\) and height \(H = 600\text{ pixels}\) (\(A_{\text{total}} = 600,000\text{ px}^2\)). The portfolio consists of 4 commercial product categories whose revenue totals are:

  • Category A (Electronics): \(\$450,000\) (\(45\%\))
  • Category B (Apparel): \(\$270,000\) (\(27\%\))
  • Category C (Home Goods): \(\$180,000\) (\(18\%\))
  • Category D (Accessories): \(\$100,000\) (\(10\%\)) Total Revenue \(= \$1,000,000\).

Required Targets:

  1. Compute the exact pixel area allocated to each category rectangle (\(a_A, a_B, a_C, a_D\)).
  2. Perform a vertical split partitioning Category A along the left canvas boundary. Calculate its width \(w_A\), height \(h_A\), and aspect ratio \(\rho(A)\).
  3. Partition the remaining canvas area among Categories B, C, and D. Calculate the dimensions and aspect ratios for Category B under a horizontal sub-split.
  4. Evaluate whether Category A satisfies the squarified optimality criterion (\(\rho \le 2.0\)).

Step-by-Step Solution:

Step 1: Compute Target Pixel Areas Total Canvas Area \(A = 1000 \times 600 = 600,000\text{ px}^2\).

\[ a_i = A \times \left(\frac{\text{Revenue}_i}{\text{Total Revenue}}\right) \]
  • \(a_A = 600,000 \times 0.45 = \mathbf{270,000\text{ px}^2}\)
  • \(a_B = 600,000 \times 0.27 = \mathbf{162,000\text{ px}^2}\)
  • \(a_C = 600,000 \times 0.18 = \mathbf{108,000\text{ px}^2}\)
  • \(a_D = 600,000 \times 0.10 = \mathbf{60,000\text{ px}^2}\) Check sum: \(270,000 + 162,000 + 108,000 + 60,000 = 600,000\text{ px}^2\).

Step 2: Partitioning Category A (Left Vertical Slice) Because the canvas is wider than it is tall (\(W = 1000 > H = 600\)), the algorithm places the initial cut along the shorter dimension (\(H = 600\)). Category A spans the full height:

\[ h_A = 600\text{ pixels} \] \[ w_A = \frac{a_A}{h_A} = \frac{270,000}{600} = \mathbf{450\text{ pixels}} \]

Aspect ratio:

\[ \rho(A) = \max\left(\frac{w_A}{h_A}, \frac{h_A}{w_A}\right) = \max\left(\frac{450}{600}, \frac{600}{450}\right) = \frac{600}{450} \approx \mathbf{1.333} \]

Step 3: Partitioning Remaining Canvas (Categories B, C, D) The remaining bounding box has:

\[ w_{\text{rem}} = 1000 - 450 = 550\text{ pixels}, \quad h_{\text{rem}} = 600\text{ pixels} \] \[ a_{\text{rem}} = 550 \times 600 = 330,000\text{ px}^2 \]

Here, \(h_{\text{rem}} = 600 > w_{\text{rem}} = 550\). The algorithm splits horizontally across the width \(w_{\text{rem}} = 550\). Let Category B occupy a horizontal strip spanning full remaining width \(w_B = 550\text{ pixels}\):

\[ w_B = 550\text{ pixels} \] \[ h_B = \frac{a_B}{w_B} = \frac{162,000}{550} \approx \mathbf{294.55\text{ pixels}} \]

Aspect ratio of B:

\[ \rho(B) = \max\left(\frac{550}{294.55}, \frac{294.55}{550}\right) \approx \frac{550}{294.55} \approx \mathbf{1.867} \]

Sub-box remaining for Categories C and D:

\[ w_{\text{sub}} = 550\text{ pixels}, \quad h_{\text{sub}} = 600 - 294.55 = 305.45\text{ pixels} \]

Dividing vertically between C and D along \(h_{\text{sub}} = 305.45\):

\[ w_C = \frac{a_C}{h_{\text{sub}}} = \frac{108,000}{305.45} \approx \mathbf{353.58\text{ pixels}} \] \[ w_D = \frac{a_D}{h_{\text{sub}}} = \frac{60,000}{305.45} \approx \mathbf{196.42\text{ pixels}} \]

Check width: \(353.58 + 196.42 = 550.0\text{ pixels}\). Aspect ratios:

\[ \rho(C) = \max\left(\frac{353.58}{305.45}, \frac{305.45}{353.58}\right) \approx \mathbf{1.158} \] \[ \rho(D) = \max\left(\frac{196.42}{305.45}, \frac{305.45}{196.42}\right) \approx \mathbf{1.555} \]

Step 4: Layout Summary & Optimality Audit

Category Allocated Area Pixel Dimensions (\(w \times h\)) Aspect Ratio \(\rho(R)\) Quality Assessment A (Electronics) \(270,000\text{ px}^2\) (\(45\%\)) \(450.00 \times 600.00\text{ px}\) 1.333 Optimal (\(\rho < 1.5\), near square) B (Apparel) \(162,000\text{ px}^2\) (\(27\%\)) \(550.00 \times 294.55\text{ px}\) 1.867 Good (\(\rho < 2.0\)) C (Home Goods) \(108,000\text{ px}^2\) (\(18\%\)) \(353.58 \times 305.45\text{ px}\) 1.158 Exceptional (\(\rho \approx 1.16\), near square) D (Accessories) \(60,000\text{ px}^2\) (\(10\%\)) \(196.42 \times 305.45\text{ px}\) 1.555 Good (\(\rho < 2.0\))

All 4 category rectangles achieve an aspect ratio \(\rho < 2.0\), completely avoiding long, unreadable slivers. Category names and numerical metrics can be centered cleanly inside every cell.

docs.title: 1. Edward Tufte's Data-Ink Ratio
docs.text:
\[ \text{DIR} = \frac{\text{Data-Ink}}{\text{Total Ink Used to Print the Graphic}} = 1.0 - \text{Chartjunk Ratio} \]
  • \(\text{Data-Ink}\): Area of ink displaying non-redundant data marks (\(\text{px}^2\)).
  • \(\text{Total Ink}\): Total area of ink across all elements (\(\text{px}^2\)).
  • Range: \([0.0, 1.0]\) (Target: \(> 0.85\)).

docs.title: 2. Polar Coordinate Radial Table Mapping
docs.text:
\[ \theta_i = \theta_0 + 2\pi \left(\frac{t_i - t_0}{T}\right) \] \[ r_i = r_{\text{inner}} + \left(\frac{v_i - V_{\min}}{V_{\max} - V_{\min}}\right) \cdot (r_{\text{outer}} - r_{\text{inner}}) \]
  • \(\theta_i, r_i\): Polar coordinates of mark (radians, pixels).
  • \(T\): Cycle period (\(24\text{ hours}\) or \(12\text{ months}\)).
  • \(\theta_0\): Angular offset (\(90^\circ\) for 12 o'clock).

docs.text:
\[ \rho(R) = \max\left(\frac{w}{h}, \frac{h}{w}\right) \ge 1.0 \]
  • \(w, h\): Rectangle dimensions in screen pixels.
  • Optimal square: \(\rho = 1.0\); Acceptable threshold: \(\rho \le 2.0\).
