docs.title: Q-1(a) [6 Marks] — 8086 Processor Architecture Block Diagram & Explanation
docs.text: Question: Draw and explain block diagram of 8086 processor architecture.

docs.title: 1. Architectural Block Diagram
docs.text:
The 8086 architecture is divided into two independent, asynchronously operating processing sections: the Bus Interface Unit (BIU) and the Execution Unit (EU).

+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| BUS INTERFACE UNIT (BIU)                                                 |
|                                                                          |
|  Segment Registers:                                                      |
|  [ CS ] Code Segment           [ IP ] Instruction Pointer                |
|  [ DS ] Data Segment                                                     |
|  [ SS ] Stack Segment                |                                   |
|  [ ES ] Extra Segment                v                                   |
|       |                     20-bit Dedicated Adder                       |
|       +--------------------> (Segment * 16 + Offset)                     |
|                                      |                                   |
|                                      v                                   |
|                        20-bit System Address Bus                         |
|                        (AD0-AD15, A16/S3-A19/S6)                         |
|                                                                          |
|  +----------------------------------------------------+                  |
|  | 6-Byte Instruction FIFO Queue                      |                  |
|  | [Byte 1] [Byte 2] [Byte 3] [Byte 4] [Byte 5] [Byte 6]                 |
|  +-------------------------+--------------------------+                  |
+----------------------------|---------------------------------------------+
                             | 8-bit Prefetched Instruction Stream
+----------------------------v---------------------------------------------+
| EXECUTION UNIT (EU)                                                      |
|                                                                          |
|  [ Instruction Decoder & Machine Cycle Controller ]                      |
|                            |                                             |
|  General Purpose Data:     |   Pointer & Index:                          |
|  [ AH | AL ] (AX)          |   [ SP ] Stack Pointer                      |
|  [ BH | BL ] (BX)          +-> [ BP ] Base Pointer                       |
|  [ CH | CL ] (CX)              [ SI ] Source Index                       |
|  [ DH | DL ] (DX)              [ DI ] Destination Index                  |
|            |                        |                                    |
|            +-----------+------------+                                    |
|                        |                                                 |
|                        v                                                 |
|              [ 16-bit ALU ] <=======> [ 16-bit Flag Register / PSW ]     |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: 2. Functional Description of Units:
docs.text:
1. Bus Interface Unit (BIU):
  2. Role: Interfaces directly with external memory and peripheral devices.
  3. Segment Registers (CS, DS, SS, ES): Hold the base segment addresses.
  4. Instruction Pointer (IP): Contains the offset of the next instruction byte to fetch.
  5. 20-bit Dedicated Adder: Computes physical address (\(\text{Segment Base} \times 16_{10} + \text{Offset}\)) in hardware without consuming ALU time.

  6. 6-Byte Instruction Queue: Implements hardware pipelining by prefetching up to 6 bytes of instructions from memory whenever at least 2 bytes in the FIFO queue become vacant while the EU is busy executing.

  7. Execution Unit (EU):

  8. Role: Fetches instruction opcodes from the FIFO queue, decodes them, and executes arithmetic/logical operations.
  9. Control Logic & Instruction Decoder: Decodes instructions into microcode timing signals.
  10. 16-bit Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU): Performs 8-bit and 16-bit addition, subtraction, AND, OR, XOR, shifts, and rotates.
  11. General Purpose Registers (AX, BX, CX, DX): Store temporary calculation values.
  12. Pointer and Index Registers (SP, BP, SI, DI): Provide memory offset addresses for stack and data structures.
  13. Flag Register (PSW): 16-bit register containing 9 active condition and control flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, TF, IF, DF, OF).

docs.title: Q-1(b) [6 Marks] — Stack Operations in 8086 Assembly Language
docs.text: Question: Explain stack operations in 8086 assembly language.

docs.title: 1. Architectural Concept: Downward-Growing Stack
docs.text:
In 8086 architecture, the stack is a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) data structure located within the Stack Segment (SS).

  • The Stack Pointer (SP) points to the physical byte at the current top-of-stack.
  • The 8086 stack grows downward (toward lower memory addresses). Pushing decrements SP, and popping increments SP.
  • Stack operations always operate on 16-bit words (never single bytes).
Memory Address
    High   +-----------------------+
           | Unused Stack Space    |
           +-----------------------+ <--- Initial SP (e.g., 0100H)
           | Pushed Word 1 (High)  |
           | Pushed Word 1 (Low)   |
           +-----------------------+
           | Pushed Word 2 (High)  |
           | Pushed Word 2 (Low)   |
    Low    +-----------------------+ <--- Current SP after Pushes

docs.title: 2. Core Stack Instructions & Micro-Operations:
docs.text:
1. PUSH Source (Word Register or Memory):

  2. Micro-operations:

    \(SP \leftarrow SP - 1\)

    \([SS:SP] \leftarrow \text{High Byte of Operand}\)

    \(SP \leftarrow SP - 1\)

    \([SS:SP] \leftarrow \text{Low Byte of Operand}\)

  3. Effectively: \(SP \leftarrow SP - 2\), then writes 16-bit word at SS:SP.

  4. Example: PUSH AX, PUSH [BX]

  5. POP Destination (Word Register or Memory):

  6. Micro-operations:

    \(\text{Low Byte of Operand} \leftarrow [SS:SP]\)

    \(SP \leftarrow SP + 1\)

    \(\text{High Byte of Operand} \leftarrow [SS:SP]\)

    \(SP \leftarrow SP + 1\)

  7. Effectively: reads 16-bit word from SS:SP, then \(SP \leftarrow SP + 2\).

  8. Example: POP DX, POP [DI]

  9. PUSHF & POPF:

  10. PUSHF: Pushes entire 16-bit Processor Status Word (PSW/FLAGS) onto stack.

  11. POPF: Pops 16-bit word from stack directly into the Flag register.

  12. CALL & RET:

  13. Near CALL: Pushes 16-bit return IP onto stack (\(SP \leftarrow SP - 2\)). Near RET pops it back into IP.

  14. Far CALL: Pushes CS then IP (\(SP \leftarrow SP - 4\)). Far RET pops both IP and CS.

  15. Stack Frame Referencing via BP:

  16. Subroutines access parameters passed on the stack without popping: 
    PUSH BP          ; Save caller's base pointer
MOV BP, SP       ; Establish new stack frame
MOV AX, [BP+4]   ; Read parameter 1 passed before call
MOV BX, [BP+6]   ; Read parameter 2
...
MOV SP, BP       ; Destroy local variables
POP BP           ; Restore caller's BP
RET 4            ; Return and clean 4 parameter bytes from stack

docs.title: Q-1(c) [6 Marks] — Physical Address Calculations & Addressing Modes
docs.text:
Question: Compute physical address using given register values and also specify the addressing modes for the following instructions: \(BX=0222H, DS=1000H, SS=2000H, BP=0111H, DI=0111H\).

  1. MOV CX, [BP]
  2. MOV [DI + 3111h], AX
  3. MOV [BX - 5], BL

docs.title: Formula:
docs.text: \[\text{Physical Address (PA)} = (\text{Segment Base} \times 10\text{H}) + \text{Effective Address (EA)}\]

docs.title: 1. MOV CX, [BP]
docs.text:
• Addressing Mode: Based Indirect Addressing Mode.
  • Default Segment: Base Pointer BP defaults to Stack Segment (SS).
    • \(\text{Segment Base} = SS = 2000\text{H}\)
  • Effective Address: \(\text{EA} = [BP] = 0111\text{H}\)
  • Physical Address:

\(\text{PA} = (2000\text{H} \times 10\text{H}) + 0111\text{H} = 20000\text{H} + 0111\text{H} = \mathbf{20111}\text{H}\)

  • Accesses 16-bit word: Low byte (CL) from \(\mathbf{20111}\text{H}\), High byte (CH) from \(\mathbf{20112}\text{H}\).

docs.title: 2. MOV [DI + 3111h], AX
docs.text:
• Addressing Mode: Indexed Relative Addressing Mode (Indexed with 16-bit Displacement).
  • Default Segment: Destination Index DI defaults to Data Segment (DS).
    • \(\text{Segment Base} = DS = 1000\text{H}\)
  • Effective Address:

\(\text{EA} = [DI] + 3111\text{H} = 0111\text{H} + 3111\text{H} = 3222\text{H}\)

  • Physical Address:

\(\text{PA} = (1000\text{H} \times 10\text{H}) + 3222\text{H} = 10000\text{H} + 3222\text{H} = \mathbf{13222}\text{H}\)

  • Writes 16-bit word: Low byte (AL) to \(\mathbf{13222}\text{H}\), High byte (AH) to \(\mathbf{13223}\text{H}\).

docs.title: 3. MOV [BX - 5], BL
docs.text:
• Addressing Mode: Based Relative Addressing Mode (Based with Negative Displacement).
  • Default Segment: Base register BX defaults to Data Segment (DS).
    • \(\text{Segment Base} = DS = 1000\text{H}\)
  • Effective Address:

\(\text{EA} = [BX] - 5 = 0222\text{H} - 0005\text{H} = 021\text{DH}\)

  • Physical Address:

\(\text{PA} = (1000\text{H} \times 10\text{H}) + 021\text{DH} = 10000\text{H} + 021\text{DH} = \mathbf{1021D}\text{H}\)

  • Writes 8-bit byte from BL into physical memory address \(\mathbf{1021D}\text{H}\).

docs.title: Q-2(a) [6 Marks] — Syntax & Architectural Error Analysis in 6 Assembly Instructions
docs.text:
Question: Find the error in the following instructions: (VAR1 and VAR2 are word variables.)

  1. AAA DX
  2. XOR AL, VAR1
  3. ADD VAR1, VAR2
  4. DIV 2
  5. INC [BX]
  6. MUL AX, VAR2

docs.title: Technical Analysis & Corrections:
docs.text:
1. AAA DX
  2. Error: Instruction takes no operands.
  3. Explanation: ASCII Adjust After Addition (AAA) is an implicit single-byte instruction (opcode 37H). It implicitly checks and adjusts accumulator registers AL and AH. Specifying an explicit operand like DX is illegal.

  4. Correction: AAA

  5. XOR AL, VAR1

  6. Error: Operand Size Mismatch.
  7. Explanation: AL is an 8-bit byte register, whereas VAR1 is explicitly defined as a 16-bit WORD variable. 8086 instructions require both operands to have identical data types.

  8. Correction: XOR AX, VAR1 (for 16-bit) or XOR AL, BYTE PTR VAR1 (for 8-bit).

  9. ADD VAR1, VAR2

  10. Error: Memory-to-Memory operation is not permitted.
  11. Explanation: The 8086 instruction set architecture allows at most one memory operand per instruction. Both source and destination cannot reside in memory simultaneously.

  12. Correction: 

    MOV AX, VAR2
ADD VAR1, AX

  13. DIV 2

  14. Error: Immediate divisor is illegal in 8086.
  15. Explanation: In the 8086 instruction set, division instructions (DIV, IDIV) do not accept immediate operands. The divisor must reside in a general-purpose register or a memory location.

  16. Correction: 

    MOV BL, 2
DIV BL          ; Divides AX by BL

  17. INC [BX]

  18. Error: Ambiguous operand size (Cannot determine memory pointer type).
  19. Explanation: Since [BX] points to memory and there is no accompanying register to provide operand size context, the assembler cannot determine whether to increment an 8-bit byte (BYTE PTR) or a 16-bit word (WORD PTR).

  20. Correction: INC BYTE PTR [BX] or INC WORD PTR [BX].

  21. MUL AX, VAR2

  22. Error: Invalid operand count for MUL.
  23. Explanation: The 8086 unsigned multiplication instruction MUL accepts only a single operand (MUL source). The multiplicand is implicitly assumed to be in AL (for 8-bit) or AX (for 16-bit). Two-operand MUL is invalid.
  24. Correction: 
    MOV AX, VAR1    ; Ensure multiplicand is in AX
MUL VAR2        ; Multiplies AX by VAR2, result in DX:AX

docs.title: Q-2(b) [6 Marks] — Assembler Directives: EQU, LABEL, ORG, EVEN
docs.text: Question: Explain following assembler directives in brief: EQU, LABEL, ORG, EVEN.

docs.title: 1. EQU (Equate Directive):
docs.text:
• Function: Assigns a symbolic name to a numerical constant, register, or string expression. The assembler replaces every occurrence of the symbol with the assigned value at assembly time without allocating physical memory.
  • Example: 
    MAX_STUDENTS EQU 60
CR           EQU 0DH
MOV CX, MAX_STUDENTS   ; Assembles to MOV CX, 60

docs.title: 2. LABEL Directive:
docs.text:
• Function: Defines an alternate name and type attribute (BYTE, WORD, DWORD, FAR, NEAR) for the current location counter ($) without reserving new memory storage.
  • Example: 
    ARRAY_WORDS LABEL WORD      ; Access 100 bytes as 50 words
ARRAY_BYTES DB 100 DUP(0)
MOV AX, ARRAY_WORDS         ; Fetches 16-bit word from offset 0

docs.title: 3. ORG (Origin Directive):
docs.text:
• Function: Sets the assembler's Location Counter ($) to a specified numerical offset value within the current segment.
  • Significance: Standard for MS-DOS .COM executable files, which require the code segment origin set to offset 100H (to leave room for the 256-byte Program Segment Prefix - PSP).
  • Example: 
    CSEG SEGMENT
    ORG 100H        ; Start assembling code at offset 0100H
START:
    MOV AH, 4CH
CSEG ENDS

docs.title: 4. EVEN Directive:
docs.text:
• Function: Forces the subsequent instruction or data definition to align on an even memory address boundary (address divisible by 2). If the current location counter is odd, the assembler advances it by 1 by inserting a dummy NOP byte or zero pad byte.
  • Significance: Enables 16-bit words to be fetched in one single bus cycle (4 clocks) rather than two bus cycles (8 clocks).
  • Example: 
    DATA_SEG SEGMENT
    B_VAL DB 01H     ; Offset 0000H (1 byte)
    EVEN             ; Advances offset counter from 0001H to 0002H
    W_VAL DW 1234H   ; Aligned at even offset 0002H
DATA_SEG ENDS

docs.title: Q-2(c) [6 Marks] — 8086 Assembly Program: Count Blank Spaces in String
docs.text: Question: Write an assembly language program to count the blank spaces in given string.

docs.title: 1. Concept: Character Scanning & Space Comparison
docs.text:
• String is traversed character by character until the terminating null character (00H) or '$' symbol is reached.
  • Each character is compared against ASCII space ' ' (\(20\text{H}\)).
  • If a match is found, counter SPACE_COUNT is incremented.

docs.title: 2. Assembly Program Implementation
docs.text:
;====================================================================
; Program: Count blank spaces (' ', 20H) in a given string
;====================================================================
.MODEL SMALL
.STACK 64

.DATA
    STRING      DB 'Microprocessors and Interfacing CE701 Exam 2022', 0 ; Null-terminated
    SPACE_COUNT DW 0
    MSG_RESULT  DB 0DH, 0AH, 'Total blank spaces = $'

.CODE
MAIN PROC
    MOV AX, @DATA
    MOV DS, AX

    LEA SI, STRING        ; SI points to start of string
    XOR DX, DX            ; DX will accumulate total spaces (initially 0)

SCAN_LOOP:
    MOV AL, [SI]          ; Read current character
    CMP AL, 0             ; Check for end of string (null character)
    JE FINISHED

    CMP AL, ' '           ; Check if character is blank space (20H)
    JNE NOT_A_SPACE

    INC DX                ; Blank space detected, increment count

NOT_A_SPACE:
    INC SI                ; Point to next character
    JMP SCAN_LOOP

FINISHED:
    MOV SPACE_COUNT, DX   ; Store result in memory variable

    ; Display output message
    LEA DX, MSG_RESULT
    MOV AH, 09H
    INT 21H

    ; Print single digit count (for counts <= 9)
    MOV AX, SPACE_COUNT
    ADD AL, '0'
    MOV DL, AL
    MOV AH, 02H
    INT 21H

    ; Exit cleanly
    MOV AX, 4C00H
    INT 21H
MAIN ENDP
END MAIN

docs.title: Q-3(a) [7 Marks] — Interrupt Vector Table (IVT) Architecture & Layout
docs.text: Question: Draw and explain Interrupt vector table.

docs.title: 1. Interrupt Vector Table (IVT) Architecture
docs.text:
The IVT occupies the lowest 1024 bytes of physical memory (\(00000\text{H}\) to \(003\text{FFH}\)) in the 8086 address space:

  • Supports 256 distinct interrupt types (Type 0 to Type 255).
  • Each vector requires 4 bytes (32 bits) storing the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) entry pointer:
    • Byte 0: IP Low Byte
    • Byte 1: IP High Byte
    • Byte 2: CS Low Byte
    • Byte 3: CS High Byte
  • Formula:

\(\text{Vector Physical Address} = \text{Type Number } (N) \times 4\)

Physical Address Range:                 Interrupt Vector Assignment:
+-------------------------------+ 003FFH
| Type 255 Vector (CS:IP)       |       User Available Hardware & Software Interrupts
+-------------------------------+       (Types 32 to 255)
|              ...              |
+-------------------------------+ 00080H
| Type 32 Vector (CS:IP)        |
+-------------------------------+ 0007FH
| Reserved by Intel             |       Reserved for System Growth
+-------------------------------+ 00014H (Types 5 to 31)
| Type 4: INTO (Overflow)       | 00010H
+-------------------------------+ 0000FH
| Type 3: One-Byte Breakpoint   | 0000CH
+-------------------------------+ 0000BH
| Type 2: Non-Maskable (NMI)    | 00008H Dedicated Hardware & Processor Exceptions
+-------------------------------+ 00007H (Types 0 to 4)
| Type 1: Single Step (TF Trap) | 00004H
+-------------------------------+ 00003H
| Type 0: Divide by Zero Error  | 00000H
+-------------------------------+

docs.title: 2. Detailed Explanation of Dedicated Vectors (Types 0 to 4):
docs.text:
1. Type 0 (Divide Error): Generated automatically by the CPU whenever a DIV or IDIV instruction produces a quotient that overflows the destination register, or when division by zero is attempted.
  2. Type 1 (Single Step Trap): Generated automatically after every instruction if the Trap Flag (\(TF\)) is set to 1. Used by interactive debuggers to pause execution after each step.
  3. Type 2 (NMI — Non-Maskable Interrupt): Triggered by an external positive edge on the dedicated NMI input pin. Cannot be disabled by CLI. Used for catastrophic system events (power failure, RAM parity error).
  4. Type 3 (Breakpoint): Single-byte instruction INT 3 (opcode CCH). Inserted by debuggers over user instructions to set execution breakpoints.
  5. Type 4 (Overflow — INTO): Conditional software interrupt triggered by the INTO instruction if the Overflow Flag (\(OF\)) is set to 1.

docs.title: Q-3(a) OR [7 Marks] — 8086 Assembly Program: Multi-Precision Addition of 10 Packed BCD Numbers
docs.text: Question (OR): Write an assembly language program to add 10 packed BCD numbers.

docs.title: 1. Concept: Packed BCD Addition with DAA
docs.text:
• Packed BCD bytes store two decimal digits (\(00\)–\(99\)) per byte.
  • When two packed BCD numbers are added using binary addition (ADD or ADC), the result may produce non-BCD values (digits \(> 9\) or carries between nybbles).
  • The DAA (Decimal Adjust After Addition) instruction checks AF and CF and automatically adjusts AL to valid packed BCD by adding \(06\text{H}\) or \(60\text{H}\).
  • Carries out of AL into the next higher BCD place are captured in CF and accumulated into the high byte.

docs.title: 2. Assembly Program Implementation
docs.text:
;====================================================================
; Program: Add 10 Packed BCD numbers using DAA instruction
; Array:   10 Packed BCD bytes
; Result:  16-bit Packed BCD sum in DX:AX (or BCD_SUM_HIGH : BCD_SUM_LOW)
;====================================================================
.MODEL SMALL
.STACK 64

.DATA
    BCD_ARRAY    DB 15H, 25H, 35H, 45H, 55H, 10H, 20H, 30H, 40H, 50H ; 10 Packed BCD bytes
    ARRAY_LEN    EQU 10
    BCD_SUM_LOW  DB 0    ; Holds lower 2 BCD digits
    BCD_SUM_HIGH DB 0    ; Holds upper 2 BCD digits (carries)

.CODE
MAIN PROC
    MOV AX, @DATA
    MOV DS, AX

    LEA SI, BCD_ARRAY    ; SI points to start of array
    MOV CX, ARRAY_LEN    ; Counter CX = 10
    XOR AL, AL           ; Clear running BCD sum (lower 2 digits)
    XOR BL, BL           ; Clear carry accumulator (upper 2 digits)

ADD_BCD_LOOP:
    ADD AL, [SI]         ; Binary add next packed BCD byte
    DAA                  ; Decimal Adjust after Addition -> AL is valid BCD!
    JNC NO_BCD_CARRY     ; If no carry out of AL, skip high byte increment

    ; Carry occurred! Increment BCD high byte
    INC BL               ; Accumulate carry
    ; (If BL could exceed 9, use: PUSH AX; MOV AL, BL; ADD AL, 1; DAA; MOV BL, AL; POP AX)

NO_BCD_CARRY:
    INC SI               ; Advance to next packed BCD byte
    LOOP ADD_BCD_LOOP    ; Decrement CX and repeat

    ; Store results
    MOV BCD_SUM_LOW, AL  ; Lower 2 digits
    MOV BCD_SUM_HIGH, BL ; Upper carry digits

    ; Terminate cleanly
    MOV AX, 4C00H
    INT 21H
MAIN ENDP
END MAIN

docs.title: Q-3(b) [7 Marks] — 8254 PIT Operating Modes (0 to 5) with Practical Applications
docs.text: Question: Discuss different modes of 8254 programmable interval timer and give one application of each.

docs.title: The 6 Operating Modes of the 8254 PIT:
docs.text:
Mode 0: Interrupt on TC       Mode 1: Retriggerable One-Shot
  OUT __________/==========     OUT ======\___________/======
       <-- Count N -->                     <-- Count N -->

Mode 2: Rate Generator        Mode 3: Square Wave Generator
  OUT =====\__/=====\__/===     OUT ======\______/======\____
       <-N->   <-N->                       <-N/2-><-N/2->

Mode 4: Software Strobe       Mode 5: Hardware Strobe
  OUT ============\__/=====     OUT ============\__/=========
       <-- Count N -->               GATE _/--\

docs.title: Detailed Mode Descriptions & Applications:
docs.text:
1. Mode 0: Interrupt on Terminal Count:
  2. Operation: When the control word is written, OUT goes LOW and remains LOW until the count decrements to 0. At terminal count, OUT transitions HIGH and stays HIGH until reloaded. GATE = 1 enables counting; GATE = 0 freezes counting.

  3. Application: Event Counter / Timeout Interrupt (e.g., triggering a CPU interrupt after elapsed time).

  4. Mode 1: Hardware Retriggerable One-Shot:

  5. Operation: OUT is initially HIGH. A positive rising edge on GATE triggers the counter, driving OUT LOW on the next clock pulse. OUT remains LOW for the programmed \(N\) clock cycles, then returns HIGH. A new trigger on GATE while counting reloads the count and restarts the pulse.

  6. Application: Monostable Multivibrator / Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) for driving servo motors or generating fixed-width reset pulses.

  7. Mode 2: Rate Generator (Divide-by-N Counter):

  8. Operation: Acts as a frequency divider. OUT remains HIGH for \(N-1\) clock periods, drops LOW for exactly 1 clock period, and then automatically reloads and repeats indefinitely.

  9. Application: Real-Time Clock (RTC) Heartbeat / Baud Rate Generator for serial communication (8251 UART).

  10. Mode 3: Square Wave Generator:

  11. Operation: Similar to Mode 2, but produces a periodic symmetric square wave with a 50% duty cycle. If \(N\) is even, OUT stays HIGH for \(N/2\) clocks and LOW for \(N/2\) clocks. If \(N\) is odd, OUT is HIGH for \((N+1)/2\) and LOW for \((N-1)/2\).

  12. Application: PC Speaker Sound Tone Generation / System Master Clock Generation.

  13. Mode 4: Software Triggered Strobe:

  14. Operation: OUT starts HIGH. Once the count is written into the register, counting begins immediately. When count reaches zero, OUT pulses LOW for 1 clock period and immediately goes HIGH again.

  15. Application: Software Delay Generator / Digital Delay Line.

  16. Mode 5: Hardware Triggered Strobe:

  17. Operation: OUT starts HIGH. Counting does not start until a rising edge occurs on GATE. At terminal count, OUT pulses LOW for 1 clock period and returns HIGH. Retriggerable by subsequent GATE rising edges.
  18. Application: Hardware-Synchronized Strobe / External Event Sampler (e.g., triggering an ADC conversion precisely \(N\) microseconds after an external sensor trigger).

docs.title: Q-3(b) OR [7 Marks] — Step-by-Step Stack & Register Trace for INT 8 Instruction
docs.text: Question (OR): Given that \(SP=0100H, SS=0300H, PSW=0240H\) and the content of following location \(00020H=0040H\) and \(00022H=0100H\) and instruction INT 8 has an offset of \(00A0H\) and segment address is \(0900H\), determine the contents of \(SP, SS, IP, CS, PSW\) and the top three words on the stack after the interrupt sequence caused by the INT 8 instruction is executed.

docs.title: 1. Initial State & IVT Resolution:
docs.text:
• Current Registers:
    • Stack Pointer: \(SP = 0100\text{H}\)
    • Stack Segment: \(SS = 0300\text{H}\)
    • Processor Status Word: \(PSW = 0240\text{H}\)
    • Code Segment: \(CS = 0900\text{H}\)
    • Offset of INT 8: \(00\text{A0H}\)

  • INT 8 is a 2-byte instruction (CD 08H).

    • Next sequential instruction address (Return Address):

    \(\text{Return } IP = 00\text{A0H} + 2 = \mathbf{00A2}\text{H}\)

    \(\text{Return } CS = \mathbf{0900}\text{H}\)

  • Vector Base Address in IVT:

\(\text{Vector Address} = 8 \times 4 = 32_{10} = \mathbf{00020}\text{H}\)

- Given IVT Contents:
- $[00020\text{H}] = \mathbf{0040}\text{H} \implies \text{New } IP$
- $[00022\text{H}] = \mathbf{0100}\text{H} \implies \text{New } CS$

docs.title: 2. Detailed Interrupt Push Sequence onto Stack:
docs.text:
1. Push PSW (\(0240\text{H}\)):
  2. \(SP \leftarrow SP - 2 = 0100\text{H} - 2 = \mathbf{00FE}\text{H}\)
  3. Memory at \([SS:00FE\text{H}] \leftarrow \mathbf{0240}\text{H}\)
  4. Clear Control Flags (\(IF = 0, TF = 0\)):
  5. In initial \(PSW = 0240\text{H}\), Bit 9 (\(IF\)) is 1.

  6. Clearing \(IF\) and \(TF\) yields:

    \(\text{New } PSW = 0240\text{H} \text{ with } IF=0 \implies \mathbf{0040}\text{H}\)

  7. Push Return CS (\(0900\text{H}\)):

  8. \(SP \leftarrow SP - 2 = 00FE\text{H} - 2 = \mathbf{00FC}\text{H}\)
  9. Memory at \([SS:00FC\text{H}] \leftarrow \mathbf{0900}\text{H}\)
  10. Push Return IP (\(00A2\text{H}\)):
  11. \(SP \leftarrow SP - 2 = 00FC\text{H} - 2 = \mathbf{00FA}\text{H}\)
  12. Memory at \([SS:00FA\text{H}] \leftarrow \mathbf{00A2}\text{H}\)
  13. Load New CS and IP:
  14. \(IP \leftarrow \mathbf{0040}\text{H}\)
  15. \(CS \leftarrow \mathbf{0100}\text{H}\)

docs.title: 3. Summary of Resulting Registers & Stack Contents:
docs.text: Register / Memory Location Value (Hex) Description SP 00FAH Decremented by 6 bytes (3 word pushes) SS 0300H Unchanged IP 0040H ISR starting offset loaded from IVT \([00020\text{H}]\) CS 0100H ISR segment base loaded from IVT \([00022\text{H}]\) PSW 0040H \(IF\) (bit 9) and \(TF\) (bit 8) cleared to 0 Top Word on Stack ([SS:00FAH]) 00A2H Return Instruction Pointer (IP) Second Word on Stack ([SS:00FCH]) 0900H Return Code Segment (CS) Third Word on Stack ([SS:00FEH]) 0240H Saved Processor Status Word (PSW)

docs.text: Institution: Nirma University, Institute of Technology Degree & Semester: B.Tech. in Computer Engineering, Semester-VII Examination: Semester End Examination (IR), December 2017 Course Code & Title: CE701: Interfacing with Microprocessors Time Allowed: 3 Hours | Maximum Marks: 100 Marks Instructions: Attempt all questions. Figures to the right indicate full marks. Draw neat sketches wherever necessary. Assume necessary data wherever required.

docs.title: Q1(a) [5 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Show the physical address calculation process for 8086 microprocessor for various segments with neat illustration.

docs.title: 1. Concept & Architectural Formulation
docs.text:
The 8086 generates 20-bit physical addresses using 16-bit registers by shifting the segment base 4 bits left and adding the effective address:

\[\text{Physical Address} = (\text{Segment Base Register} \times 10\text{H}) + \text{Effective Address (Offset)}\] 
+------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------------+------------------------------------+
| Segment Type     | Segment Register Base | Pointer / Offset Registers  | Hardware Physical Mapping          |
+------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------------+------------------------------------+
| **Code Segment** | CS (Code Segment)     | IP (Instruction Pointer)    | PA = (CS * 16) + IP                |
| **Data Segment** | DS (Data Segment)     | BX, SI, DI, Displacement    | PA = (DS * 16) + EA                |
| **Stack Segment**| SS (Stack Segment)    | SP (Stack Pointer), BP      | PA = (SS * 16) + (SP or BP)        |
| **Extra Segment**| ES (Extra Segment)    | DI (String Destination)     | PA = (ES * 16) + DI                |
+------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------------+------------------------------------+

Segment Register (16-bit):  | S15 | S14 | ... | S1 | S0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |  (Appended 4 zeros = x16)
Offset Register (16-bit):               | O15 | O14 | ... | O1 | O0 |  (Effective Address)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Physical Address (20-bit):  | A19 | A18 | ... | A3 | A2 | A1 | A0 |  (1 MB physical range)

docs.title: Q1(b) [5 Marks]
docs.text:
Question: Given data: BX = 0017H, DI = 10C5H, Displacement = 1C58H and DS=1000H. Give example MOV instructions and determine the effective address and physical address for the following addressing modes:

  1. Direct addressing mode
  2. Register indirect assuming BX register
  3. Register relative assuming BX register
  4. Base indexed
  5. Register relative base indexed

docs.title: 1. Step-by-Step Calculations
docs.text:
• Base Physical Address: \(\text{DS} \times 10\text{H} = 1000\text{H} \times 10\text{H} = \mathbf{10000\text{H}}\).
# Addressing Mode Example Instruction Effective Address (EA) Formula & Value Physical Address Calculation 1 Direct MOV AX, [1C58H] \(\text{EA} = \text{Disp} = \mathbf{1\text{C}58\text{H}}\) \(10000\text{H} + 1\text{C}58\text{H} = \mathbf{11\text{C}58\text{H}}\) 2 Register Indirect (BX) MOV AX, [BX] \(\text{EA} = \text{BX} = \mathbf{0017\text{H}}\) \(10000\text{H} + 0017\text{H} = \mathbf{10017\text{H}}\) 3 Register Relative (BX) MOV AX, [BX + 1C58H] \(\text{EA} = \text{BX} + \text{Disp} = 0017\text{H} + 1\text{C}58\text{H} = \mathbf{1\text{C}6\text{F}\text{H}}\) \(10000\text{H} + 1\text{C}6\text{F}\text{H} = \mathbf{11\text{C}6\text{F}\text{H}}\) 4 Base Indexed MOV AX, [BX + DI] \(\text{EA} = \text{BX} + \text{DI} = 0017\text{H} + 10\text{C}5\text{H} = \mathbf{10\text{D}\text{C}\text{H}}\) \(10000\text{H} + 10\text{D}\text{C}\text{H} = \mathbf{110\text{D}\text{C}\text{H}}\) 5 Relative Base Indexed MOV AX, [BX + DI + 1C58H] \(\text{EA} = \text{BX} + \text{DI} + \text{Disp} = 0017\text{H} + 10\text{C}5\text{H} + 1\text{C}58\text{H} = \mathbf{2\text{D}34\text{H}}\) \(10000\text{H} + 2\text{D}34\text{H} = \mathbf{12\text{D}34\text{H}}\)

docs.title: Q1(c) [5 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Give the importance of DT/R, ALE, DEN, INTA and NMI control signals of 8086 microprocessor.

docs.title: 1. Signal Definitions
docs.text:
• \(\text{DT}/\overline{\text{R}}\) (Data Transmit/Receive, Pin 27): Output control signal used with bus transceivers (Intel 8286). When high (\(1\)), data flows from CPU to bus (Transmit/Write). When low (\(0\)), data flows into CPU from bus (Receive/Read).
  • ALE (Address Latch Enable, Pin 25): Output strobe pulse generated during clock state \(T_1\) of every bus cycle to latch valid memory/IO addresses from multiplexed lines \(AD_0 - AD_{15}\) into external latches (Intel 8282).
  • \(\overline{\text{DEN}}\) (Data Enable, Pin 26): Active-low output enabling external data bus transceivers during states \(T_2 - T_4\), isolating the data bus during \(T_1\) to prevent address/data bus contention.
  • \(\overline{\text{INTA}}\) (Interrupt Acknowledge, Pin 24): Active-low output pulse generated in response to an active INTR line, signaling the 8259A PIC to place its vector type byte on data bus lines \(D_0 - D_7\).
  • NMI (Non-Maskable Interrupt, Pin 17): High-priority, edge-triggered (low-to-high) input that bypasses the Interrupt Flag (IF). Automatically invokes Interrupt Type 2 for parity errors or power outages.

docs.title: Q2(a) [5 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Draw separate timing diagram of 8086 microprocessor with wait states for memory-read and IO-write machine cycles with all necessary control signals.

docs.title: 1. Concept: Wait State (\(T_w\)) Insertion
docs.text:
• The 8086 samples the READY pin at the end of state \(T_2\) and during each \(T_w\).
  • If READY is low, the CPU inserts one or more wait states (\(T_w\)) between \(T_3\) and \(T_4\) to allow slow memories or peripherals to respond.
Memory-Read Machine Cycle with Wait State (Tw):
CLK        |   T1   |   T2   |   T3   |   Tw   |   T4   |
ALE        |~~|_____|________|________|________|________|
AD0-AD15   |  Addr  | Float  |      Data In From Mem  |
READY      |~~~~~~~~|~~~~~~~~|________|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~| (Low at end of T2/T3)
RD#        |~~~~~~~~|________|________|________|~~~~~~~~|
M/IO#      |~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~| (1 = Memory)

IO-Write Machine Cycle with Wait State (Tw):
CLK        |   T1   |   T2   |   T3   |   Tw   |   T4   |
ALE        |~~|_____|________|________|________|________|
AD0-AD15   | IO-Addr|       Data Out to Peripheral      |
READY      |~~~~~~~~|~~~~~~~~|________|~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~|
WR#        |~~~~~~~~|________|________|________|~~~~~~~~|
M/IO#      |____________________________________________| (0 = I/O)

docs.title: Q2(b) [5 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Give pros and cons of 8086 microprocessor segmentation.

docs.title: 1. Pros of Segmentation
docs.text:
1. Dynamic Code Relocation: Programs can be placed anywhere in physical memory by changing base registers.
  2. Modular Organization: Natural division between executable instructions, variables, and stack frames.
  3. Addressing Beyond 16 Bits: Enables 16-bit registers to address a 1 MB physical address space.
  4. Shared Code Blocks: Multiple programs can execute the same reentrant code segment concurrently.

docs.title: 2. Cons of Segmentation
docs.text:
1. 64 KB Boundary Ceiling: A single segment cannot exceed 64 KB; large arrays spanning \(>64\text{ KB}\) require cumbersome segment switching.
  2. Translation Latency: Requires hardware adder latency to calculate \((\text{Segment} \times 16) + \text{Offset}\) on every bus access.
  3. Memory Fragmentation: Dynamic allocation of 64 KB segments leads to external physical memory fragmentation.

docs.title: Q2(b) OR [5 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Give the importance and the information stored in descriptor of 80286 processor.

docs.title: 1. 80286 Segment Descriptor Format (8 Bytes)
docs.text:
Byte 7: Reserved by Intel (Must be 0 in 80286)
Byte 6: Reserved by Intel (Must be 0 in 80286)
Byte 5: Access Rights Byte (P, DPL (2 bits), S, Type (4 bits))
Byte 4: Base Address Bits 23..16
Byte 3: Base Address Bits 15..8
Byte 2: Base Address Bits 7..0
Byte 1: Segment Limit Bits 15..8
Byte 0: Segment Limit Bits 7..0
  • Information Stored:
    1. 24-Bit Physical Base Address: Direct physical base location in 16 MB memory (\(2^{24} = 16,777,216\text{ bytes}\)).
    2. 16-Bit Segment Limit: Specifies segment size (\(0 \text{ to } 65,535\text{ bytes}\)). Offsets \(> \text{Limit}\) generate a General Protection Fault.
    3. Access Rights Byte:
    4. P (Present Bit): \(1 = \text{Segment loaded in RAM}\), \(0 = \text{Virtual memory fault}\).
    5. DPL (Descriptor Privilege Level, 2 bits): Privilege rings (0 Kernel to 3 User).
    6. S (System/Non-System): \(1 = \text{Code/Data segment}\), \(0 = \text{Control descriptor (Gate/TSS)}\).
    7. Type (4 bits): Read/Write/Execute permissions and direction (expand-down for stacks).

docs.title: Q2(c) [5 Marks]
docs.text: Question: With detailed 8086 memory bank organization show that it requires two machine cycles to complete one read or write operation if word data is stored beginning from odd address. Also specify the associated signals for byte and word operations.

docs.title: 1. Detailed Signal Table
docs.text: \(\overline{\text{BHE}}\) \(A_0\) Operation Performed Data Bus Lines Machine Cycles 0 0 16-bit Word at Even Address (Aligned) \(D_0 - D_{15}\) (Simultaneous) 1 1 0 8-bit Byte at Even Address \(D_0 - D_7\) (Lower Bank) 1 0 1 8-bit Byte at Odd Address \(D_8 - D_{15}\) (Upper Bank) 1 Two-Cycle Transfer 16-bit Word at Odd Address (Misaligned) 2

docs.title: 2. Two-Cycle Transfer Sequence for Misaligned Word
docs.text:
When accessing a 16-bit word starting at odd address \(N\):

  • Cycle 1 (Odd Byte Transfer): Address \(N\) is asserted. \(A_0 = 1\) and \(\overline{\text{BHE}} = 0\). The lower byte of the word is transferred through Upper Bank (\(D_8 - D_{15}\)).
  • Cycle 2 (Even Byte Transfer): The CPU increments address to \(N + 1\) (even). \(A_0 = 0\) and \(\overline{\text{BHE}} = 1\). The higher byte is transferred through Lower Bank (\(D_0 - D_7\)).
  • Therefore, accessing a word at an odd address requires two full 4-state bus cycles (8 T-states).

docs.title: Q3(a) [10 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Write 8086 microprocessor assembly program module with all necessary instructions to initialize a stack segment of 120 words. Write a reentrant recursive procedure to compute factorial of a given number and trace the contents of the stack for computing factorial of n=3.

docs.title: 1. Complete Assembly Program
docs.text:
.MODEL SMALL
.DATA
    N_VAL   DW 3
    RESULT  DW ?
.CODE
MAIN PROC
    MOV AX, @DATA
    MOV DS, AX

    ; Initialize stack segment of 120 words (240 bytes = 00F0H)
    MOV AX, 7000H
    MOV SS, AX
    MOV SP, 00F0H       ; Top of stack

    ; Push parameter n = 3
    PUSH N_VAL
    CALL FACTORIAL
    MOV RESULT, AX      ; AX holds 3! = 6

    MOV AH, 4CH
    INT 21H
MAIN ENDP

FACTORIAL PROC NEAR
    PUSH BP
    MOV BP, SP
    PUSH BX

    MOV BX, [BP+4]      ; Parameter n
    CMP BX, 1
    JLE BASE_CASE

    ; Recursive step: compute (n - 1)!
    DEC BX
    PUSH BX
    CALL FACTORIAL      ; Recursive call, result in AX

    ; Multiply n * (n - 1)!
    MOV BX, [BP+4]
    MUL BX              ; DX:AX = AX * BX
    JMP EXIT_FACT

BASE_CASE:
    MOV AX, 1           ; 1! = 1

EXIT_FACT:
    POP BX
    POP BP
    RET 2               ; Clean 1 parameter word
FACTORIAL ENDP
END MAIN

docs.title: 2. Stack Content Trace for \(n = 3\) (Peak Depth at \(n = 1\))
Q3(a) OR [10 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Write 8086 microprocessor interrupt service routine for a NMI interrupt to add byte type data stored in an array of size 100, starting at address 2000H: 5000H in memory with the corresponding data in another array of size 100, stored in memory starting at the address 3000H: 5000H. Store the result in another array in memory starting at the address 4000H: 5000H. Neglect the carry generated during addition.

docs.title: 1. Concept & IVT Vector for NMI
docs.text:
• NMI Vector: Type 2 interrupt located at physical memory address range \(00008\text{H} - 0000\text{B}\text{H}\) (\(\text{Base} = 2 \times 4 = 00008\text{H}\)).
  • Far Segment Access: Array 1 in 2000H, Array 2 in 3000H, Destination in 4000H.

docs.title: 2. Assembly ISR Implementation
docs.text:
.MODEL LARGE
.CODE
PUBLIC NMI_ISR

NMI_ISR PROC FAR
    PUSHA               ; Preserve AX, CX, DX, BX, SP, BP, SI, DI
    PUSH DS
    PUSH ES

    MOV CX, 100         ; 100 byte elements
    XOR SI, SI          ; Offset index = 0

ADD_LOOP:
    ; Read byte from Array 1 (2000H:5000H + SI)
    MOV AX, 2000H
    MOV DS, AX
    MOV AL, DS:[5000H + SI]

    ; Read byte from Array 2 (3000H:5000H + SI) and add
    MOV BX, 3000H
    MOV DS, BX
    ADD AL, DS:[5000H + SI]  ; Carry neglected as per instructions

    ; Store result into Array 3 (4000H:5000H + SI)
    MOV BX, 4000H
    MOV ES, BX
    MOV ES:[5000H + SI], AL

    INC SI
    LOOP ADD_LOOP

    POP ES
    POP DS
    POPA
    IRET                ; Return from interrupt
NMI_ISR ENDP
END

docs.title: Q3(b) [10 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Assume a symbol table with name as TABLE consisting of 100 entries. Each entry has 80 bytes with the first 8 bytes representing the name field of an entity and the remaining 72 bytes represents information about the name entity. Write 8086 assembly program sequence to search this TABLE for a given name stored in a variable SEARCH_NAME and if SEARCH_NAME is found in TABLE then the program should copy 72 bytes of information in variable NAME_INFO. If SEARCH_NAME is not found then NAME_INFO should contain '$' symbol.

docs.title: 1. Assembly Solution
docs.text:
.MODEL SMALL
.STACK 100H
.DATA
    ENTRY_COUNT EQU 100
    ENTRY_SIZE  EQU 80
    NAME_LEN    EQU 8
    INFO_LEN    EQU 72

    TABLE       DB ENTRY_COUNT * ENTRY_SIZE DUP(0) ; 8,000 bytes
    SEARCH_NAME DB 'MATH_VAR'                     ; 8 bytes
    NAME_INFO   DB INFO_LEN DUP(?)

.CODE
MAIN PROC
    MOV AX, @DATA
    MOV DS, AX
    MOV ES, AX

    LEA BX, TABLE       ; BX points to base of current entry
    MOV CX, ENTRY_COUNT

TABLE_SCAN:
    ; Compare 8-byte Name Field
    LEA SI, SEARCH_NAME
    MOV DI, BX          ; DI points to entry name
    PUSH CX
    MOV CX, NAME_LEN
    CLD
    REPE CMPSB
    POP CX
    JE ENTRY_FOUND      ; Match found!

    ADD BX, ENTRY_SIZE  ; Advance to next 80-byte record
    LOOP TABLE_SCAN

    ; NOT FOUND: Store `'$'` into NAME_INFO
    MOV BYTE PTR NAME_INFO, `'$'`
    JMP FINISH_PROGRAM

ENTRY_FOUND:
    ; Copy 72 bytes of Info Field (located at BX + 8) into NAME_INFO
    LEA SI, [BX + 8]
    LEA DI, NAME_INFO
    MOV CX, INFO_LEN
    CLD
    REP MOVSB

FINISH_PROGRAM:
    MOV AH, 4CH
    INT 21H
MAIN ENDP
END MAIN

docs.title: Q4(a) [5 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Identify the conditions that causes type 0, type 1, type 3, and type 4 interrupts. Give the importance of IF and TF flag while handling interrupts from hardware and software sources.

docs.title: 1. Conditions Causing Dedicated Interrupts
docs.text:
• Type 0 (Divide Overflow Error): Triggered by CPU hardware when a DIV or IDIV instruction generates a quotient that exceeds destination capacity (or division by zero).
  • Type 1 (Single-Step / Trap): Triggered after every single instruction execution whenever the Trap Flag \(\text{TF} = 1\).
  • Type 3 (Breakpoint): Triggered by the 1-byte opcode 0CCH (INT 3), used by debuggers to set breakpoints without shifting trailing code bytes.
  • Type 4 (Overflow Trap): Triggered by the INTO instruction if and only if the Overflow Flag \(\text{OF} = 1\).

docs.title: 2. Importance of IF and TF during Interrupt Handling
docs.text:
• Automatic Clearing: Upon accepting any interrupt (hardware or software), the 8086 hardware automatically clears both IF and TF:
    • Clearing IF (\(\text{IF} \leftarrow 0\)): Disables maskable hardware interrupts (INTR), preventing higher-level or nested interrupts from corrupting the ISR state before the handler is ready.
    • Clearing TF (\(\text{TF} \leftarrow 0\)): Disables single-stepping inside the ISR itself, ensuring the interrupt handler executes at normal speed.

docs.title: Q4(b) [5 Marks]
docs.text:
Question: Illustrate with a neat diagram the effect of the following instructions on the stack pointer and on the contents of the stack and other used registers if the values of the registers are given as SS = 2000h, SP=6000h, SI=1111h, CX = 2222h, DX=3333h and AX=4444h: 

PUSH SI
PUSH CX
PUSH DX
CALL SAMPLE
POP SI
JMP NEXT
SAMPLE PROC NEAR
    PUSHF
    PUSH DX
    ADD AX, DX
    POP DX
    POPF
    RET 4
SAMPLE ENDP
NEXT: END

docs.title: 1. Step-by-Step Stack Execution Trace
docs.text:
1. PUSH SI: \(\text{SP} = 5\text{FFEH}\); \([\text{SS}:5\text{FFEH}] = 1111\text{H}\).
  2. PUSH CX: \(\text{SP} = 5\text{FFCH}\); \([\text{SS}:5\text{FFCH}] = 2222\text{H}\).
  3. PUSH DX: \(\text{SP} = 5\text{FFAH}\); \([\text{SS}:5\text{FFAH}] = 3333\text{H}\).
  4. CALL SAMPLE: Near call pushes return address \(\text{IP}_{\text{POP\_SI}}\):
  5. \(\text{SP} = 5\text{FF8H}\); \([\text{SS}:5\text{FF8H}] = \text{IP}_{\text{POP\_SI}}\).
  6. Inside SAMPLE:
  7. PUSHF: \(\text{SP} = 5\text{FF6H}\); \([\text{SS}:5\text{FF6H}] = \text{PSW}\).
  8. PUSH DX: \(\text{SP} = 5\text{FF4H}\); \([\text{SS}:5\text{FF4H}] = 3333\text{H}\).
  9. ADD AX, DX: \(\text{AX} = 4444\text{H} + 3333\text{H} = \mathbf{7777\text{H}}\).
  10. POP DX: \(\text{DX} = 3333\text{H}\); \(\text{SP} = 5\text{FF6H}\).
  11. POPF: Restores Flags; \(\text{SP} = 5\text{FF8H}\).

  12. RET 4: Pops return address into IP (\(\text{SP} = 5\text{FFAH}\)), then adds 4 to SP:

    \(\text{SP} = 5\text{FFAH} + 4 = \mathbf{5\text{FFEEH}}\) (Effect: Cleans both parameters DX and CX off the stack!)

  13. Returning to caller:

  14. POP SI: Reads from \([\text{SS}:5\text{FFEEH}]\), which holds the original \(1111\text{H}\) from step 1: \(\text{SI} = 1111\text{H}\); \(\mathbf{\text{SP} = 6000\text{H}}\).
  15. JMP NEXT: Terminates with \(\mathbf{\text{SP} = 6000\text{H}}\), \(\mathbf{\text{AX} = 7777\text{H}}\), and all other registers preserved.

docs.title: Q4(c) [5 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Identify the difference between the following: (i) RET and IRET (ii) ENDS and ENDP (iii) GLOBAL and PUBLIC (iv) DQ and DT

docs.title: 1. Detailed Comparative Analysis
docs.text:
1. RET vs IRET:
  2. RET: Subroutine return. Pops 16-bit IP (near) or IP then CS (far) from stack.
  3. IRET: Interrupt return. Pops IP, then CS, and then pops the saved 16-bit Flags (PSW) back into the CPU flag register.
  4. ENDS vs ENDP:
  5. ENDS: Assembler directive signaling the end of a Segment (SEGMENT ... ENDS) or a Structure (STRUC ... ENDS).
  6. ENDP: Assembler directive signaling the end of a Procedure / Subroutine (PROC ... ENDP).
  7. GLOBAL vs PUBLIC:
  8. PUBLIC: Declares labels, variables, or procedures in the current source module to be exportable and visible to external linking modules.
  9. GLOBAL: Used in modern assemblers/linkers to declare symbols that are both defined and exported if defined locally, or imported (EXTRN) if defined externally.
  10. DQ vs DT:
  11. DQ (Define Quadword): Allocates 8 bytes (64 bits) of storage.
  12. DT (Define Tenbytes): Allocates 10 bytes (80 bits) of storage, standardly used for 18-digit packed BCD integers or 80-bit IEEE extended precision floats.

docs.title: Q5(a) [5 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Write an 8086 assembly language code to multiply two double word unsigned number. Store the result in consecutive memory locations of extra segment.

docs.title: 1. Concept: 32-bit by 32-bit Multiplication using 16-bit MUL
docs.text:
Let \(X = (X_H \times 2^{16}) + X_L\) and \(Y = (Y_H \times 2^{16}) + Y_L\). The 64-bit product is computed via 4 cross partial products:

\[\text{Product} = (X_L \times Y_L) + (X_L \times Y_H \times 2^{16}) + (X_H \times Y_L \times 2^{16}) + (X_H \times Y_H \times 2^{32})\]

docs.title: 2. Assembly Program
docs.text:
.MODEL SMALL
.DATA
    X_LOW   DW 1234H
    X_HIGH  DW 5678H
    Y_LOW   DW 0ABCDH
    Y_HIGH  DW 00EFH
.CODE
MAIN PROC
    MOV AX, @DATA
    MOV DS, AX
    MOV AX, 5000H       ; Extra Segment target
    MOV ES, AX
    XOR DI, DI          ; ES:DI points to destination buffer (8 bytes)

    ; Partial Product 1: X_LOW * Y_LOW
    MOV AX, X_LOW
    MUL Y_LOW           ; DX:AX = X_L * Y_L
    MOV ES:[DI+0], AX   ; Result Word 0
    MOV CX, DX          ; CX = Carry word for Word 1

    ; Partial Product 2: X_LOW * Y_HIGH
    MOV AX, X_LOW
    MUL Y_HIGH          ; DX:AX = X_L * Y_H
    ADD AX, CX          ; Add carry
    ADC DX, 0
    MOV BX, AX          ; BX = Accumulator for Word 1
    MOV BP, DX          ; BP = Carry for Word 2

    ; Partial Product 3: X_HIGH * Y_LOW
    MOV AX, X_HIGH
    MUL Y_LOW           ; DX:AX = X_H * Y_L
    ADD AX, BX          ; Accumulate into Word 1
    ADC DX, BP          ; Accumulate carry into Word 2
    MOV ES:[DI+2], AX   ; Result Word 1
    MOV BX, DX          ; BX = Word 2
    MOV CX, 0
    ADC CX, 0           ; CX = Carry for Word 3

    ; Partial Product 4: X_HIGH * Y_HIGH
    MOV AX, X_HIGH
    MUL Y_HIGH          ; DX:AX = X_H * Y_H
    ADD AX, BX
    ADC DX, CX
    MOV ES:[DI+4], AX   ; Result Word 2
    MOV ES:[DI+6], DX   ; Result Word 3

    MOV AH, 4CH
    INT 21H
MAIN ENDP
END MAIN

docs.title: Q5(a) OR [5 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Write 8086 program that contains macro definition which accepts two string variables STR1 and STR2 and concatenates them into a third string variable STR3.

docs.title: 1. Assembly Solution
docs.text:
.MODEL SMALL
.STACK 100H

; Macro definition for string concatenation
CONCAT_MACRO MACRO STR1, STR2, STR3
    LOCAL CPY1, CPY2, DONE_M
    LEA SI, STR1
    LEA DI, STR3
    CLD

CPY1:
    LODSB
    CMP AL, `'$'`
    JE CPY2_PREP
    CMP AL, 0
    JE CPY2_PREP
    STOSB
    JMP CPY1

CPY2_PREP:
    LEA SI, STR2
CPY2:
    LODSB
    STOSB
    CMP AL, `'$'`
    JE DONE_M
    CMP AL, 0
    JE DONE_M
    JMP CPY2

DONE_M:
ENDM

.DATA
    S1 DB 'Data ', `'$'`
    S2 DB 'Structure$', 0
    S3 DB 64 DUP(0)

.CODE
MAIN PROC
    MOV AX, @DATA
    MOV DS, AX
    MOV ES, AX

    CONCAT_MACRO S1, S2, S3

    LEA DX, S3
    MOV AH, 09H
    INT 21H

    MOV AH, 4CH
    INT 21H
MAIN ENDP
END MAIN

docs.title: Q5(b) [5 Marks]
docs.text:
Question: Identify the errors for each of the given instructions referring the following data segment: 

DATA SEGMENT WORD PUBLIC
    A DW 45H
    B DW 60H
DATA ENDS

  1. AAA DX
  2. SUB AL, A
  3. JNZ A
  4. ADD A, B
  5. MOV [DX], AL

docs.title: 1. Error Identification
docs.text:
1. AAA DX: Error. AAA takes no operands.
  2. SUB AL, A: Error. Size mismatch error. AL is 8 bits; A is declared as word (DW).
  3. JNZ A: Error. The target of a conditional jump must be a code label in Code Segment, not a memory variable in Data Segment.
  4. ADD A, B: Error. Memory-to-memory operations are illegal in 8086 machine code.
  5. MOV [DX], AL: Error. Register DX is illegal as a base/index pointer in memory addressing modes.

docs.title: Q5(c) [5 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Write an assembly language code to convert ten, 8 bit packed BCD number to unpacked BCD number.

docs.title: 1. Assembly Solution
docs.text:
.MODEL SMALL
.DATA
    PACKED_BCD   DB 12H, 34H, 56H, 78H, 90H, 23H, 45H, 67H, 89H, 11H ; 10 bytes
    UNPACKED_BCD DB 20 DUP(0)                                         ; 20 bytes output
.CODE
MAIN PROC
    MOV AX, @DATA
    MOV DS, AX

    LEA SI, PACKED_BCD
    LEA DI, UNPACKED_BCD
    MOV CX, 10

UNPACK_LOOP:
    MOV AL, [SI]        ; Read packed BCD byte
    MOV AH, AL          ; Copy into AH

    ; Extract lower nibble (units digit)
    AND AL, 0FH
    MOV [DI], AL        ; Store unpacked units digit

    ; Extract upper nibble (tens digit)
    MOV AL, AH
    MOV CL, 4
    SHR AL, CL          ; Shift tens into lower nibble
    MOV [DI+1], AL      ; Store unpacked tens digit

    ADD DI, 2
    INC SI
    DEC CX
    JNZ UNPACK_LOOP

    MOV AH, 4CH
    INT 21H
MAIN ENDP
END MAIN

docs.title: Q6(a) [5 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Describe the paging mechanism in 80286 through Core2 microprocessors and other advance 80x86 architectures.

docs.title: 1. Two-Level Paging Architecture (80386 to Core 2)
docs.text:
Paging divides linear address space into fixed-size 4 KB pages:

\[\text{Linear Address (32 bits)} \implies [ \text{Directory (10 bits)} ] \; [ \text{Page Table (10 bits)} ] \; [ \text{Offset (12 bits)} ]\]
  • Page Directory (4 KB): 1,024 entries pointing to page tables. Base address in CR3.
  • Page Table (4 KB): 1,024 entries pointing to physical 4 KB page frames.
  • Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB): Hardware associative cache caching the most recent page translations, delivering 1-cycle address resolution.

docs.title: Q6(b) [5 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Draw and state the function of each component of 8259 Programmable Interrupt Controller.

docs.title: 1. Component Functional Summary
docs.text:
1. Interrupt Request Register (IRR): Latches pending interrupt requests arriving on \(IR_0 - IR_7\).
  2. In-Service Register (ISR): Tracks which interrupt level is actively being serviced by the CPU.
  3. Interrupt Mask Register (IMR): Stores mask bits written via OCW1; disables unneeded interrupt lines.
  4. Priority Resolver: Logic block selecting the highest priority active request in IRR relative to ISR.
  5. Control Logic & Bus Buffer: Generates INT output to CPU and handles dual \(\overline{\text{INTA}}\) handshakes.

docs.title: Q6(c) [5 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Give the block diagram of 8255A programmable peripheral interface and different modes of operation.

docs.title: 1. Operating Modes
docs.text:
• Mode 0 (Basic I/O): Unlatched inputs, latched outputs. Ports A, B, and C function as simple input or output ports.
  • Mode 1 (Strobed I/O): Handshake I/O. Port A and/or Port B transfer data using Port C lines as handshaking control signals (STB#, IBF, INTR).
  • Mode 2 (Strobed Bidirectional Bus): Port A functions as an 8-bit bidirectional data bus using 5 lines of Port C for handshaking control.

docs.title: Q6(c) OR [5 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Describe the functional block diagram of 8254 Programmable Interval Timer and write an assembly program module to generate a square wave.

docs.title: 1. Control Word & Count Calculation
docs.text:
• For 1 kHz square wave from 2 MHz clock: \(\text{Count} = 2,000,000 / 1,000 = \mathbf{2000_{10}} = \mathbf{07\text{D}0\text{H}}\).
  • Control Word: Counter 0 (00), LSB then MSB (11), Mode 3 Square Wave (011), Binary (0) \(\implies\) 36H.

docs.title: 2. Assembly Module
docs.text:
MOV DX, 0043H        ; 8254 Control Register port
MOV AL, 36H          ; Counter 0, Mode 3, LSB then MSB, Binary
OUT DX, AL

MOV DX, 0040H        ; Counter 0 Data port
MOV AL, 0D0H         ; Write LSB
OUT DX, AL
MOV AL, 07H          ; Write MSB
OUT DX, AL

docs.title: Q6(d) [5 Marks]
docs.text: Question: Discuss in detail different modes of operation of 8237 DMA controller and why read and write control signals are bidirectional.

docs.title: 1. Operating Modes of 8237 DMAC
docs.text:
1. Single Transfer Mode: Transfers one single byte per DMA request (DREQ), releasing the bus after each byte.
  2. Block Transfer Mode: Activated by DREQ; transfers an entire block of data until terminal count (TC) is reached.
  3. Demand Transfer Mode: Continues transferring data as long as DREQ remains asserted active.
  4. Cascade Mode: Allows multiple 8237 chips to be cascaded together to expand DMA channels.

docs.title: 2. Why Control Signals (\(\text{MEMR}\#, \text{MEMW}\#, \text{IOR}\#, \text{IOW}\#\)) are Bidirectional
docs.text:
• During CPU Programming (Slave Mode): The 8237 is a slave peripheral. \(\overline{\text{IOR}}\) and \(\overline{\text{IOW}}\) act as inputs driven by the CPU to read status or write control parameters into 8237 registers.
  • During DMA Transfer (Bus Master Mode): The 8237 seizes control of the system bus via HOLD/HLDA. \(\overline{\text{MEMR}}, \overline{\text{MEMW}}, \overline{\text{IOR}}, \overline{\text{IOW}}\) become outputs driven by the 8237 to command memory and peripheral transfers directly.
