Source Index SI 16-bit None Source data offset pointer in DS; source string pointer (DS:SI). Destination Index DI 16-bit None Destination data offset pointer in DS; string target pointer (ES:DI). Code Segment CS 16-bit None Base paragraph address of active Code Segment. Data Segment DS 16-bit None Base paragraph address of active Data Segment. Stack Segment SS 16-bit None Base paragraph address of active Stack Segment. Extra Segment ES 16-bit None Base paragraph address of active Extra Segment (string destinations). Instruction Pointer IP 16-bit None Offset address of next instruction to execute within CS (CS:IP).

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture part 1, Slides 8–14, 19]

docs.title: 5. 8086 Flag Register Specifications
docs.text:
The 8086 Flag Register is a 16-bit register containing 9 active flags (6 Status Flags and 3 Control Flags):

Bit Position Flag Name Symbol Category Functional Description \(D_0\) Carry Flag CF Status Set to 1 if unsigned math produces carry out of MSB or borrow; otherwise 0. \(D_2\) Parity Flag PF Status Set to 1 if lower 8 bits of result contain even number of 1s (Even Parity). \(D_4\) Auxiliary Carry AF Status Set to 1 if carry generated from bit 3 to bit 4 during BCD math. \(D_6\) Zero Flag ZF Status Set to 1 if operation result is zero; reset to 0 if non-zero. \(D_7\) Sign Flag SF Status Set to 1 if MSB of result is 1 (negative signed value). \(D_8\) Trap Flag TF Control Set to 1 to enable single-step debugging mode (CPU generates Type 1 interrupt after each instruction). \(D_9\) Interrupt Flag IF Control Set to 1 to enable maskable hardware interrupts (INTR); 0 disables INTR. \(D_{10}\) Direction Flag DF Control Determines auto increment/decrement for string operations: 0 = Increment (forward), 1 = Decrement (backward). \(D_{11}\) Overflow Flag OF Status Set to 1 if signed arithmetic result exceeds signed capacity of destination register.

docs.title: Comprehensive Flag Calculation Example
docs.text:
Consider execution of ADD AL, 1 when register AL contains 7FH (\(0111\,1111_2\)):

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{Initial AL:} & \quad 0111\,1111_2 \quad (7\text{FH}) \\ + \text{Value } 1: & \quad 0000\,0001_2 \quad (01\text{H}) \\ \hline \text{New AL Result:} & \quad 1000\,0000_2 \quad (80\text{H}) \end{aligned} \]

  • AL Output: \(80\text{H}\)(Decimal \(-128\) in signed 2's complement).

  • Carry Flag (CF): 0 (No carry out of bit 7).

  • Parity Flag (PF): 0 (Result \(1000\,0000_2\) has one 1 bit \(\rightarrow\) odd parity).

  • Auxiliary Carry (AF): 1 (Carry generated out of bit 3 into bit 4).

  • Zero Flag (ZF): 0 (Result \(80\text{H}\) is non-zero).

  • Sign Flag (SF): 1 (Bit \(D_7\) is 1).

  • Overflow Flag (OF): 1 (Positive \(+127\) added to \(+1\) resulted in negative \(-128\), triggering signed overflow).

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture part 1, Slides 15–17]

docs.title: Concept of Segmented Memory
docs.text:
The 8086 addresses \(1\text{ MB}\) (\(1,048,576\text{ bytes}\)) of physical memory using a 20-bit address. However, all internal registers are 16-bit wide. To bridge this gap, memory is organized into logical Segments.

  • A Segment is a contiguous block of up to \(64\text{ KB}\) (\(65,536\text{ bytes}\)) of memory.

  • A segment can begin at any memory address divisible by 16 (\(10\text{H}\)), known as a Paragraph Boundary (where the lower 4 hex digits of physical address are 0000_2).

  • Four active logical segments are accessible at any instant: Code Segment (CS), Data Segment (DS), Stack Segment (SS), and Extra Segment (ES).

docs.title: Key Architectural Advantages of Memory Segmentation
docs.text:
1. Expands Memory Capacity: Allows 16-bit registers to address \(1\text{ MB}\) of physical memory using segment:offset combinations.

  2. Code and Data Protection: Separates executable code, data variables, and stack buffers into distinct logical areas, preventing accidental program overwrite.

  3. Dynamic Program Relocation: Programs can be loaded into any physical memory location without altering internal offset addresses—only the segment register values are updated.

  4. Supports Programs \(>\) 64 KB: Code, data, or stack structures exceeding \(64\text{ KB}\) can be handled by defining multiple logical segments.

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture part 1, Slides 21–24]

docs.title: Memory Banking (Physical Organization)
docs.text:
Although the 8086 has a 20-bit address bus to access 1 MB of physical memory, the memory is physically organized as two independent 512 KB banks: the Even Bank (Low Bank) and the Odd Bank (High Bank). This allows the 16-bit CPU to access either an 8-bit byte or a 16-bit word in a single bus cycle.

  • Even Bank (Low Bank): Contains all even-numbered physical addresses (00000H, 00002H, ... FFFFEH). Connected to the lower half of the data bus (\(D_7 - D_0\)). It is enabled when address line \(A_0 = 0\).

  • Odd Bank (High Bank): Contains all odd-numbered physical addresses (00001H, 00003H, ... FFFFFH). Connected to the upper half of the data bus (\(D_{15} - D_8\)). It is enabled when Bus High Enable (\(\overline{\text{BHE}}\)) pin is active low (\(\overline{\text{BHE}} = 0\)).


flowchart TD

    subgraph Mem ["8086 1 MB Physical Memory Space"]

        subgraph Even ["Even Bank / Low Bank (Enables D7-D0, Activated when A0 = 0)"]

            even_mem["512 KB Even Addresses: 00000H, 00002H, ... FFFFEH"]

        end

        subgraph Odd ["Odd Bank / High Bank (Enables D15-D8, Activated when BHE = 0)"]

            odd_mem["512 KB Odd Addresses: 00001H, 00003H, ... FFFFFH"]

        end

    end

    8086["8086 CPU"] -->|BHE Signal| Odd

    8086 -->|A0 Signal| Even

docs.title: Bank Selection and Alignment Scenarios (Exam Twisters)
docs.text:
The 8086 uses \(A_0\) and \(\overline{\text{BHE}}\) status signals to select the appropriate memory bank(s) according to this truth table:

\(\overline{\text{BHE}}\) \(A_0\) Data Bus Width Used Memory Bank Accessed Bus Cycles Required 0 0 16-bit (\(D_{15} - D_0\)) Both Banks (Aligned Word access at Even Address) 1 Cycle 0 1 8-bit (\(D_{15} - D_8\)) Odd Bank only (Byte access at Odd Address) 1 Cycle 1 0 8-bit (\(D_7 - D_0\)) Even Bank only (Byte access at Even Address) 1 Cycle 1 1 None (Idle) No Bank selected -

CRITICAL EXAM TWISTER (Unaligned Word Access):

If the CPU attempts to read/write a 16-bit word starting at an odd address (e.g., 00001H), it is called an unaligned word access. This requires two consecutive bus cycles:

  1. First Bus Cycle: CPU accesses the Odd Bank (\(\overline{\text{BHE}}=0, A_0=1\)) to read the low byte of the word from 00001H using \(D_{15}-D_8\).

  2. Second Bus Cycle: CPU accesses the Even Bank (\(\overline{\text{BHE}}=1, A_0=0\)) to read the high byte of the word from 00002H using \(D_7-D_0\).

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture part 1, Slide 25]

docs.title: Figure 3.3: 8086 Physical Address Summing Block
docs.text:
flowchart LR

    Seg["Segment Register (e.g., CS = 3000H)"] -->|Shift Left 4 Bits / Multiply by 10H| Shift["Base Segment Address: 30000H"]

    Offset["Offset Register (e.g., IP = 1234H)"] --> Add

    Shift --> Add((20-Bit Adder))

    Add -->|Sum| PA["Physical Address: 31234H"]

docs.title: Mathematical Formula
docs.text:
\[ \text{Physical Address} = (\text{Segment Register Value} \times 16_{10}) + \text{Offset Address} \]

In Hexadecimal notation:

\[ \text{Physical Address} = (\text{Segment Register Value} \times 10_H) + \text{Offset Address} \] 
Segment Register (16-bit):  [ S3  S2  S1  S0 ] 0H    (Shifted 4 bits left = x 16)

+ Offset Register (16-bit):      [ O3  O2  O1  O0 ]

---------------------------------------------------

Physical Address (20-bit):  [ P4  P3  P2  P1  P0 ]

CRITICAL EXAM TWISTER (Physical Address Wrap-around in Real Mode):

What happens if the segment and offset combination computes an address exceeding the 1 MB addressable boundary (FFFFFH)?

For example: \(\text{Segment} = \text{FFFFH}\), \(\text{Offset} = \text{FFFFH}\).

\[ \text{Base Segment Address} = \text{FFFFH} \times 10\text{H} = \text{FFFF0H} \] \[ \text{Physical Address} = \text{FFFF0H} + \text{FFFFH} = \text{10FFEFH} \]

Since the 8086 has only 20 physical address lines (\(A_{19} - A_0\)), the 21st bit (the leading 1 in 10FFEFH) is discarded (there is no 21st line).

The address wraps around to the very beginning of physical memory space, specifically to:

\[ \text{Wrapped Address} = \text{0FFEFH} \]

This is a classic real-mode memory limitation and an extremely common trick question in university examinations.

docs.title: Standard Segment and Offset Register Pairs
docs.text:
Segment Type Segment Register Default Offset Register Alternative Offset Registers Physical Address Purpose Instruction Fetch CS IP None Next instruction byte to fetch (CS:IP). Stack Operation SS SP BP Top of stack (SS:SP) or stack frame (SS:BP). General Data DS BX SI, DI, Direct Address General variable data (DS:BX, DS:SI, DS:DI). String Destination ES DI None Destination operand in string commands (ES:DI).

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture part 1, Slides 26, 32]

docs.title: Numerical Problem 3.1
docs.text:
Problem: The Data Segment (DS) starts at physical address 10000H (Segment value 1000H). A data reference specifies an offset of 0029H. Calculate the physical address of the data operand.

Given: \(\text{DS} = 1000\text{H}\), \(\text{Offset} = 0029\text{H}\).

Required: Physical Address.

Formula: \(\text{Physical Address} = \text{DS} \times 10\text{H} + \text{Offset}\).

Solution Steps:

  1. Shift DS value left by 4 hex bits: \(1000\text{H} \times 10\text{H} = 10000\text{H}\).

  2. Add offset: \(10000\text{H} + 0029\text{H} = 10029\text{H}\).

Final Answer: Physical Address = 10029H.

docs.title: Numerical Problem 3.2
docs.text:
Problem: A program code segment starts at physical address 70400H.

  1. What value is stored in the Code Segment register (CS)?

  2. If the Instruction Pointer (IP) contains 539CH, what physical address is fetched?

Given: \(\text{Physical Base} = 70400\text{H}\), \(\text{IP} = 539\text{CH}\).

Required: CS register value, physical fetch address.

Formula: \(\text{CS} = \frac{\text{Physical Base}}{16_{10}}\), \(\text{Physical Address} = \text{CS} \times 10\text{H} + \text{IP}\).

Solution Steps:

  1. \(\text{CS} = \frac{70400\text{H}}{10\text{H}} = 7040\text{H}\).

  2. \(\text{Physical Address} = 70400\text{H} + 539\text{CH} = 7579\text{CH}\).

Final Answer: CS = 7040H, Physical Address = 7579CH.

docs.title: Numerical Problem 3.3
docs.text:
Problem: The Stack Segment register (SS) contains 3000H and Stack Pointer (SP) contains 8434H. Find the physical address of the top of stack.

Given: \(\text{SS} = 3000\text{H}\), \(\text{SP} = 8434\text{H}\).

Required: Physical Address of Top of Stack.

Formula: \(\text{Physical Address} = \text{SS} \times 10\text{H} + \text{SP}\).

Solution Steps:

\[ \text{Physical Address} = 30000\text{H} + 8434\text{H} = 38434\text{H} \]

Final Answer: Top of Stack Physical Address = 38434H.

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture part 1, Slides 31, 33]

docs.title: Key 8086 Pin Signals
docs.text:
1. \(AD_{15} - AD_0\)(Pins 1–16, 39): Multiplexed Address/Data bus. Carries memory address during \(T_1\), and data during \(T_2, T_3, T_4\).

  2. \(A_{19}/S_6 - A_{16}/S_3\) (Pins 35–38): Multiplexed high address lines and system status lines.

  3. \(\overline{\text{BHE}}/S_7\) (Pin 34): Bus High Enable / Status. Active low signal used to enable upper data byte (\(D_{15} - D_8\)) on memory bus.

  4. \(\text{MN}/\overline{\text{MX}}\) (Pin 33): Minimum / Maximum mode select. High selects Minimum mode; Low selects Maximum mode.

  5. \(RD\) (Pin 32): Read signal. Active low.

  6. \(TEST\) (Pin 23): Tested by WAIT instruction. If low, CPU continues execution; if high, CPU waits.

  7. \(READY\) (Pin 22): Bus ready input for interfacing slow memories.

  8. \(RESET\) (Pin 21): Reset input. Clears flags, IP to 0000H, CS to FFFFH.

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture part 1, Slide 4]

docs.title: 9. 8086 Addressing Modes
docs.text: The 8086 provides 7 primary addressing modes for accessing instruction operands:

docs.title: Summary Comparison Table of Addressing Modes
docs.text: Addressing Mode Effective Address (\(EA\)) Formula Advantage Disadvantage Typical Assembly Example Register \(EA = R\) Fastest (No memory reference) Limited addressable space (registers only) MOV BX, DX Immediate \(EA = \text{Instruction Constant}\) Fast operand loading Fixed constant value MOV AX, 2550H Direct \(EA = [\text{Displacement}]\) Simple to program Fixed memory offset MOV AX, [2400H] Register Indirect \(EA = [\text{BX/BP/SI/DI}]\) Large addressable memory Requires prior register load MOV AX, [BX] Base Relative \(EA = [\text{BX/BP}] + \text{Disp}\) Flexible for structures Requires 16-bit register addition MOV AX, 12H[BX] Indexed Relative \(EA = [\text{SI/DI}] + \text{Disp}\) Ideal for array indexing Requires 16-bit register addition MOV DX, ARRAY[SI] Base Indexed Relative \(EA = [\text{BX/BP}] + [\text{SI/DI}] + \text{Disp}\) Extremely flexible (2D arrays) Complex address calculation MOV AX, BETA[BX][SI]

docs.title: Detailed Breakdown of Each Addressing Mode
1. Register Addressing Mode
docs.text: Operand is stored inside an internal CPU register.

docs.title: Figure 3.5: Register Addressing Mode
docs.text:
• Formula: \(EA = R\)

  • Example: MOV BX, DX (Copies contents of DX into BX).

docs.title: 2. Immediate Addressing Mode
docs.text: Operand data is encoded directly as part of the machine instruction byte sequence.

docs.title: Figure 3.6: Immediate Addressing Mode
docs.text:
• Formula: \(\text{Operand} = A\)

  • Example: MOV AX, 2550H (Loads immediate word 2550H into AX).

CRITICAL EXAM WARNING (Segment Register Load Restriction):

Inside the 8086 Instruction Set Architecture, immediate data cannot be loaded directly into any Segment Register (CS, DS, SS, ES).

  • Invalid/Illegal: MOV DS, 1000H (Will result in a compiler/assembler error).

  • Correct Workaround: You must load the immediate value into a 16-bit general purpose register (like AX, BX, CX, DX) first, and then copy that register into the target Segment Register:

MOV AX, 1000H   ; Load immediate data into AX

MOV DS, AX      ; Transfer from AX to DS

docs.title: 3. Direct Addressing Mode
docs.text: The 16-bit effective address (offset) of the operand is explicitly written inside the instruction.

docs.title: Figure 3.7: Direct Addressing Mode
docs.text:
• Formula: \(EA = A\), \(\text{Physical Address} = \text{DS} \times 10\text{H} + A\)

  • Example: MOV AX, [2400H] (If \(\text{DS} = 2000\text{H}\), \(\text{Physical Address} = 20000\text{H} + 2400\text{H} = 22400\text{H}\)).

docs.title: 4. Register Indirect Addressing Mode
docs.text: The 16-bit offset address of the operand in memory is held inside a Base register (BX, BP) or Index register (SI, DI).

docs.title: Figure 3.8: Register Indirect Addressing Mode
docs.text:
• Formula: \(EA = [R]\) where \(R \in \{\text{BX}, \text{BP}, \text{SI}, \text{DI}\}\)

  • Example: MOV AX, [BX] (If \(\text{DS} = 1010\text{H}\) and \(\text{BX} = 1122\text{H}\), \(\text{Physical Address} = 10100\text{H} + 1122\text{H} = 11222\text{H}\)).

  • Pointer Operator Requirement: In ambiguous memory operations, BYTE PTR or WORD PTR must specify data size (e.g., INC BYTE PTR [BX]).

docs.title: 5. Base Relative Addressing Mode
docs.text: Effective address is computed by adding an 8-bit or 16-bit displacement to the contents of a Base register (BX or BP).

docs.title: Figure 3.9: Base Relative Addressing Mode
docs.text:
• Formula: \(EA = [\text{Base Reg}] + \text{Displacement}\)

    • Default Segment for BX is DS.

    • Default Segment for BP is SS.

  • Displacement Limits: 8-bit signed (\(-128\) to \(+127\)) or 16-bit signed (\(-32768\) to \(+32767\)).

  • Example: MOV AX, 1234H[BX] (If \(\text{DS} = 4000\text{H}\), \(\text{BX} = 1000\text{H}\), \(\text{Physical Address} = 40000\text{H} + 1000\text{H} + 1234\text{H} = 42234\text{H}\)).

docs.title: 6. Indexed Relative Addressing Mode
docs.text: Effective address is computed by adding an 8-bit or 16-bit displacement to an Index register (SI or DI).

docs.title: Figure 3.10: Indexed Relative Addressing Mode
docs.text:
• Formula: \(EA = [\text{Index Reg}] + \text{Displacement}\)

  • Example: MOV DX, ARRAY[SI] (If \(\text{DS} = 2000\text{H}\), \(\text{SI} = 5000\text{H}\), \(\text{ARRAY} = 1234\text{H}\), \(\text{Physical Address} = 20000\text{H} + 5000\text{H} + 1234\text{H} = 26234\text{H}\)).

docs.title: 7. Base Indexed Relative Addressing Mode
docs.text: Combines Base register, Index register, and an optional displacement to compute the effective address.

docs.title: Figure 3.11: Base Indexed Relative Addressing Mode
docs.text:
• Formula: \(EA = [\text{Base Reg}] + [\text{Index Reg}] + \text{Displacement}\)

  • Example: MOV AX, BETA[BX][SI] (If \(\text{DS} = 1200\text{H}\), \(\text{BX} = 1000\text{H}\), \(\text{SI} = 2000\text{H}\), \(\text{BETA} = 1234\text{H}\), \(\text{Physical Address} = 12000\text{H} + 1000\text{H} + 2000\text{H} + 1234\text{H} = 15234\text{H}\)).

[Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture, Slides 34–54]

docs.title: 10. 8086 Instruction Format & Machine Encoding
docs.text: 8086 instructions range from 1 to 6 bytes in length.

docs.title: Field Descriptions in Machine Code Byte
docs.text:
1. Opcode (6 bits): Identifies basic instruction operation (e.g., 100010_2 for MOV).

  2. D (Direction Bit, 1 bit):

  3. \(D = 0\): Data flows from Register specified in REG field to operand in R/M.

  4. \(D = 1\): Data flows to Register specified in REG field from operand in R/M.

  5. W (Word/Byte Bit, 1 bit):

  6. \(W = 0\): 8-bit Byte operation.

  7. \(W = 1\): 16-bit Word operation.

  8. MOD (Mode Field, 2 bits): Specifies addressing mode (Register vs Memory with displacement):

  9. \(\text{MOD} = 11\): Register-to-Register mode (No memory displacement).

  10. \(\text{MOD} = 00\): Memory mode with no displacement (except direct addressing when \(\text{R/M} = 110\)).

  11. \(\text{MOD} = 01\): Memory mode with 8-bit sign-extended displacement.

  12. \(\text{MOD} = 10\): Memory mode with 16-bit displacement.

  13. REG (Register Field, 3 bits): Identifies register operand.

  14. R/M (Register/Memory Field, 3 bits): Specifies second operand or memory addressing combination.

docs.title: Figure 3.13: 8086 MOD and R/M Encoding Matrix
docs.text: [Source: 3CS526CC23 8086 Architecture, Slides 55–66]

docs.title: 1. Chapter Overview
docs.text: This chapter provides an exhaustive breakdown of the 8086 microprocessor instruction set. Instructions are classified into functional categories: Data Transfer, Arithmetic, Logical, Shift/Rotate, String Manipulation, Branch/Control Transfer, and Processor Control. Each instruction is detailed with syntax, operational mechanics, flag impacts, constraints, worked code examples, and practical programming patterns.

docs.title: 2. General Assembler Instruction Syntax
docs.text:
The standard format for an 8086 assembly language instruction line is:

Label:   Mnemonic   Destination, Source   ; Comments

docs.title: Example
docs.text: START:   MOV        AX, [BX]              ; Load word from memory address BX into AX

docs.title: Pointer (PTR) Operator Resolution
docs.text:
When an instruction contains a memory operand without an explicit register to specify operand size, the assembler cannot determine whether to execute a 8-bit byte or 16-bit word operation. The PTR operator must be used to resolve ambiguity:

  • INC [BX] \(\rightarrow\) AMBIGUOUS (Compiler Error).

  • INC BYTE PTR [BX] \(\rightarrow\) Increments the 8-bit byte at memory address [BX].

  • INC WORD PTR [BX] \(\rightarrow\) Increments the 16-bit word at memory address [BX].

[Source: 8086_instruction_set_Basic, Slides 3, 5]

docs.title: 3. Data Transfer Instructions
docs.text: Data transfer instructions move data between registers, memory locations, and I/O ports. No status flags are affected by standard data transfer instructions.

docs.title: MOV (Move Data)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Copies data byte or word from source to destination.

  • Syntax: MOV Destination, Source

  • Operation: \((\text{Destination}) \leftarrow (\text{Source})\)

  • Constraints:

    • Both operands cannot be memory locations simultaneously.

    • Both operands cannot be segment registers simultaneously.

    • Immediate data cannot be moved directly into segment registers.

  • Flags Affected: None.

  • Examples:

MOV CX, 037AH        ; Load immediate word 037AH into CX

MOV AL, BL           ; Copy byte from BL to AL

MOV BX, [0301H]      ; Load word from memory offset 0301H into BX

docs.title: XCHG (Exchange Data)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Swaps contents of source and destination operands.

  • Syntax: XCHG Destination, Source

  • Operation: \((\text{Destination}) \leftrightarrow (\text{Source})\)

  • Constraints: Cannot exchange two memory locations directly. One operand must be a register. Segment registers cannot be exchanged.

  • Flags Affected: None.

  • Examples:

XCHG BX, AX          ; Swap contents of BX and AX

XCHG [5000H], AX     ; Swap word in memory location 5000H with AX

docs.title: LEA (Load Effective Address)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Computes the 16-bit effective address (offset) of the source memory operand and stores it in the destination register.

  • Syntax: LEA Reg16, Memory

  • Operation: \(\text{EA} \rightarrow (\text{Reg16})\)

  • Flags Affected: None.

  • Example:

LEA BX, ARRAY        ; Load offset address of ARRAY into register BX

docs.title: LDS (Load Pointer Using DS)
docs.text: • Purpose: Loads a 32-bit far pointer from a 4-byte memory location into a 16-bit general register and the Data Segment register (DS).

docs.title: Figure 4.1: LDS and LES Memory Pointer Loading Mechanism
docs.text:
• Syntax: LDS Reg16, MEM32

  • Operation:

    • \((\text{MEM32}) \rightarrow (\text{Reg16})\) (Offset loaded into destination register)

    • \((\text{MEM32} + 2) \rightarrow (\text{DS})\) (Segment selector loaded into DS)

  • Flags Affected: None.

  • Example:

LDS SI, [0301H]      ; Loads offset into SI and segment into DS from memory 0301H

docs.title: LES (Load Pointer Using ES)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Loads a 32-bit far pointer from memory into a specified 16-bit register and the Extra Segment register (ES).

  • Syntax: LES Reg16, MEM32

  • Operation:

    • \((\text{MEM32}) \rightarrow (\text{Reg16})\)

    • \((\text{MEM32} + 2) \rightarrow (\text{ES})\)

  • Flags Affected: None.

  • Example:

LES BX, STRING_PTR   ; Loads string offset into BX and segment into ES

[Source: 8086_instruction_set_Basic, Slides 7–14]

docs.title: 4. Arithmetic Instructions
docs.text: Arithmetic instructions perform binary addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, increment, decrement, and sign extension. All conditional flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF) are affected unless explicitly noted.

docs.title: ADD (Add Words or Bytes)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Adds contents of source operand to destination operand and stores sum in destination.

  • Syntax: ADD Destination, Source

  • Operation: \((\text{Destination}) \leftarrow (\text{Destination}) + (\text{Source})\)

  • Flags Affected: All status flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF).

  • Examples:

ADD AX, 2020H        ; AX = AX + 2020H

ADD AX, BX           ; AX = AX + BX

docs.title: ADC (Add with Carry)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Adds source operand, destination operand, and the current Carry Flag (CF) bit together.

  • Syntax: ADC Destination, Source

  • Operation: \((\text{Destination}) \leftarrow (\text{Destination}) + (\text{Source}) + \text{CF}\)

  • Flags Affected: All status flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF).

  • Examples:

ADC AX, 2020H        ; AX = AX + 2020H + CF

ADC AX, BX           ; AX = AX + BX + CF

docs.title: SUB (Subtract)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Subtracts source operand from destination operand.

  • Syntax: SUB Destination, Source

  • Operation: \((\text{Destination}) \leftarrow (\text{Destination}) - (\text{Source})\)

  • Flags Affected: All status flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF).

  • Examples:

SUB AX, 1000H        ; AX = AX - 1000H

SUB AX, BX           ; AX = AX - BX

docs.title: SBB (Subtract with Borrow)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Subtracts source operand and Carry Flag (Borrow) from destination operand.

  • Syntax: SBB Destination, Source

  • Operation: \((\text{Destination}) \leftarrow (\text{Destination}) - (\text{Source}) - \text{CF}\)

  • Flags Affected: All status flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF).

  • Examples:

SBB AX, 1000H        ; AX = AX - 1000H - CF

SBB AX, BX           ; AX = AX - BX - CF

docs.title: INC (Increment) & DEC (Decrement)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Adds 1 to (INC) or subtracts 1 from (DEC) the operand.

  • Syntax: INC Source, DEC Source

  • CRITICAL FLAG RULE: INC and DEC affect PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF, but DO NOT affect the Carry Flag (CF)!

  • Constraints: Operand cannot be immediate data.

  • Examples:

INC AX               ; Increment AX by 1

DEC BYTE PTR [5000H] ; Decrement byte in memory location 5000H by 1

CRITICAL EXAM TWISTER (Why INC/DEC do not affect CF):

If you have a loop that performs multi-word additions using ADC (Add with Carry), you typically use a register like SI or DI to point to the array elements, and a loop register like CX or BX as a counter. After each array addition, you increment the pointer using INC SI and decrement the counter using DEC CX.

If INC or DEC affected the Carry Flag, they would overwrite the carry status generated by the ADC instruction. This would ruin the addition of the next word/byte in the sequence!

By leaving CF untouched, the 8086 allows developers to update pointers and counters inside multi-word arithmetic loops without losing valuable carry information.

docs.title: NEG (Negate / Two's Complement)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Replaces operand contents with its two's complement (\(0 - \text{Operand}\)).

  • Syntax: NEG Source

  • Flags Affected: All status flags. CF is set to 1 for any non-zero operand.

  • Example:

NEG AX               ; AX = -AX

docs.title: CMP (Compare)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Subtracts source operand from destination operand to update status flags without altering destination contents.

  • Syntax: CMP Operand1, Operand2

  • Operation: Flags updated based on \((\text{Operand1}) - (\text{Operand2})\). Result is discarded.

  • Flags Affected: All status flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF).

  • Examples:

CMP AX, 1000H        ; Compare AX with 1000H

CMP AX, BX           ; Compare AX with BX

docs.title: CBW (Convert Byte to Word) & CWD (Convert Word to Doubleword)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Sign-extends signed operands for division/arithmetic.

    • CBW: Extends sign bit of AL (\(D_7\)) across all bits of AH.

    • CWD: Extends sign bit of AX (\(D_{15}\)) across all bits of DX.

  • Syntax: CBW, CWD (No explicit operands).

  • Flags Affected: None.

  • Example Code Sequence (Adding Signed Byte Y to Signed Word X):

MOV AL, Y            ; Load signed byte Y into AL

CBW                  ; Sign extend AL into AX (AX now holds 16-bit signed Y)

ADD AX, X            ; Add signed word X to AX

docs.title: MUL (Unsigned Multiplication) & IMUL (Signed Multiplication)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Multiplies accumulator by source operand.

  • Operational Mechanics:

    • 8-bit Multiplication: \(\text{AL} \times \text{Operand8} \rightarrow \text{AX}\) (16-bit product stored in AX).

    • 16-bit Multiplication: \(\text{AX} \times \text{Operand16} \rightarrow (\text{DX:AX})\) (32-bit product stored across DX:AX, where DX holds high word).

  • Flags Affected: OF and CF are set to 1 if upper half of product contains significant digits (non-zero for MUL, non-sign extension for IMUL); otherwise reset to 0. Other flags are undefined.

  • Constraints: Source operand cannot be immediate data.

  • Examples:

MUL BH               ; AX = AL * BH (Unsigned)

IMUL CX              ; (DX:AX) = AX * CX (Signed)

docs.title: DIV (Unsigned Division) & IDIV (Signed Division)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Divides accumulator by source operand.

  • Operational Mechanics:

    • 8-bit Division: Dividend in AX \(\div\) Operand8 \(\rightarrow \text{AL} = \text{Quotient}\), \(\text{AH} = \text{Remainder}\).

    • 16-bit Division: Dividend in (DX:AX) \(\div\) Operand16 \(\rightarrow \text{AX} = \text{Quotient}\), \(\text{DX} = \text{Remainder}\).

  • Flags Affected: All status flags are undefined.

  • Examples:

MOV AX, 0203H

MOV BL, 04H

DIV BL               ; AX / BL -> AL = 50H (Quotient), AH = 03H (Remainder)

[Source: 8086_instruction_set_Basic, Slides 15–32]

docs.title: 5. Logical Instructions
docs.text:
Logical instructions perform bitwise boolean operations. CF and OF are cleared to 0 by all bitwise logical operations; SF, ZF, and PF are updated accordingly; AF is undefined.

Instruction Syntax Boolean Operation Flag Rules NOT NOT OPR \((\text{OPR}) \leftarrow \overline{\text{OPR}}\) (One's Complement) No flags affected. AND AND DST, SRC \((\text{DST}) \leftarrow (\text{DST}) \land (\text{SRC})\) CF=0, OF=0, updates SF, ZF, PF. OR OR DST, SRC \((\text{DST}) \leftarrow (\text{DST}) \lor (\text{SRC})\) CF=0, OF=0, updates SF, ZF, PF. XOR XOR DST, SRC \((\text{DST}) \leftarrow (\text{DST}) \oplus (\text{SRC})\) CF=0, OF=0, updates SF, ZF, PF. TEST TEST OPR1, OPR2 \((\text{OPR1}) \land (\text{OPR2})\) (Result discarded) CF=0, OF=0, updates SF, ZF, PF.

docs.title: Applied Bitwise Logic Program Example
docs.text:
Task: Selectively set bits 0 and 2 of DL; toggle (invert) bits 1 and 6; clear bits 3 and 4; then test bits 1 and 7 and branch to EXIT if both test bits are set.

OR  DL, 00000101B      ; Set bits 0 and 2 of DL (Mask: 05H)

XOR DL, 01000010B      ; Toggle bits 1 and 6 of DL (Mask: 42H)

AND DL, 11100111B      ; Clear bits 3 and 4 of DL (Mask: E7H)

TEST DL, 10000010B     ; Test bits 1 and 7 of DL (Mask: 82H)

JZ  EXIT               ; Jump to EXIT if tested bits are zero

[Source: 8086_instruction_set_Basic, Slides 33–34]

docs.title: 6. Shift and Rotate Instructions
docs.text:
Shift and Rotate instructions manipulate operand bits by shifting them left or right.

  • Count Rule: The shift/rotate count CNT can be 1 (specified as immediate constant) or stored in register CL for multi-bit shifts.
Instruction Name / Type Operational Behavior Carry Flag (CF) Impact SHL / SAL Shift Logical/Arithmetic Left Shifts bits left; fills right with 0. MSB shifted out enters CF. SHR Shift Logical Right Shifts bits right; fills left with 0. LSB shifted out enters CF. SAR Shift Arithmetic Right Shifts bits right; retains original MSB (sign bit) on left. LSB shifted out enters CF. ROL Rotate Left Circular bit rotation left. MSB rotates into LSB AND into CF. ROR Rotate Right Circular bit rotation right. LSB rotates into MSB AND into CF. RCL Rotate Left Through Carry 9-bit/17-bit circular rotation left through CF. CF bit enters LSB; MSB enters CF. RCR Rotate Right Through Carry 9-bit/17-bit circular rotation right through CF. CF bit enters MSB; LSB enters CF.

[Source: 8086_instruction_set_Basic, Slides 35–36]

docs.title: 7. Branch & Control Transfer Instructions
docs.text: Branch instructions alter program execution flow by modifying IP (and CS for Far branches).

docs.title: Unconditional Jump
docs.text: • JMP Target: Unconditionally branches to Target address.

docs.title: Conditional Jumps (Depend on Flag States)
docs.text:
• JZ / JE Target: Jump if Zero (\(ZF = 1\)).

  • JNZ / JNE Target: Jump if Not Zero (\(ZF = 0\)).

  • JC / JB Target: Jump if Carry / Below (\(CF = 1\)).

  • JNC / JNB Target: Jump if No Carry / Above or Equal (\(CF = 0\)).

  • JS Target: Jump if Sign / Negative (\(SF = 1\)).

  • JNS Target: Jump if No Sign / Positive (\(SF = 0\)).

  • JO Target: Jump if Overflow (\(OF = 1\)).

  • JPO / JNP Target: Jump if Parity Odd (\(PF = 0\)).

  • JPE / JP Target: Jump if Parity Even (\(PF = 1\)).

docs.title: Loop Control Instructions
docs.text:
• LOOP Target: Decrements CX by 1; jumps to Target if \( ext{CX} eq 0\).

  • LOOPE / LOOPZ Target: Decrements CX; jumps if \( ext{CX} eq 0\) AND \(ZF = 1\).

  • LOOPNE / LOOPNZ Target: Decrements CX; jumps if \( ext{CX} eq 0\) AND \(ZF = 0\).

docs.title: Subroutine Control
docs.text:
• CALL ProcedureName: Pushes return address (IP) onto stack and branches to procedure.

  • RET: Pops return address off stack into IP to return from procedure.

docs.title: 8. Processor Control & Flag Manipulation Instructions
docs.text:
• CLC: Clear Carry Flag (\(CF \leftarrow 0\)).

  • STC: Set Carry Flag (\(CF \leftarrow 1\)).

  • CMC: Complement Carry Flag (\(CF \leftarrow \overline{CF}\)).

  • CLD: Clear Direction Flag (\(DF \leftarrow 0\), Auto-increment string pointers).

  • STD: Set Direction Flag (\(DF \leftarrow 1\), Auto-decrement string pointers).

  • CLI: Clear Interrupt Flag (\(IF \leftarrow 0\), Disable maskable INTR).

  • STI: Set Interrupt Flag (\(IF \leftarrow 1\), Enable maskable INTR).

  • NOP: No Operation (Consumes 3 T-states, performs no operation).

  • HLT: Halt CPU execution until hardware interrupt or reset occurs.

docs.title: 1. 8085 Clock Period & T-State Duration
docs.text:
\[ T = \frac{1}{f_{\text{CLK}}} \]

Where \(f_{\text{CLK}}\) is CPU operating frequency (e.g.,\(3\text{ MHz} \rightarrow T = 333.33\text{ ns}\)).

docs.title: 2. 8085 Hardware Interrupt Vector Address
docs.text:
\[ \text{Vector Address (Hex)} = (N \times 8_{10}) \quad \text{converted to 16-bit Hex} \]

Where \(N\) is restart vector number (e.g.,\(RST 7.5 \rightarrow 7.5 \times 8 = 60_{10} = 003C_H\)).

docs.title: 3. Physical Address Calculation
docs.text:
\[ \text{Physical Address} = (\text{Segment Register Value} \times 16_{10}) + \text{Offset Address} \] \[ \text{Physical Address} = (\text{Segment Register Value} \times 10_H) + \text{Offset Address} \]

Where:

  • \(\text{Segment Register} \in \{\text{CS}, \text{DS}, \text{SS}, \text{ES}\}\) (16-bit Base Selector).

  • \(\text{Offset Address} \in \{\text{IP}, \text{SP}, \text{BP}, \text{BX}, \text{SI}, \text{DI}, \text{Direct Address}\}\) (16-bit Offset).

docs.title: 4. Effective Address (\(EA\)) Formulas
docs.text:
• Register: \(EA = R\)

  • Immediate: \(\text{Operand} = A\)

  • Direct: \(EA = A\)

  • Register Indirect: \(EA = [R] \quad (R \in \{\text{BX}, \text{BP}, \text{SI}, \text{DI}\})\)

  • Base Relative: \(EA = [\text{Base Reg}] + \text{Displacement} \quad (\text{Base} \in \{\text{BX}, \text{BP}\})\)

  • Indexed Relative: \(EA = [\text{Index Reg}] + \text{Displacement} \quad (\text{Index} \in \{\text{SI}, \text{DI}\})\)

  • Base Indexed Relative: \(EA = [\text{Base Reg}] + [\text{Index Reg}] + \text{Displacement}\)

docs.title: Appendix B — Definition Sheet
docs.text:
• Accumulator: Primary register used to store inputs and output results of ALU operations.

  • Address Bus: Unidirectional bus lines used by CPU to select memory or I/O locations.

  • Address Latch Enable (ALE): Signal issued to demultiplex address/data bus during \(T_1\).

  • Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU): Digital circuit performing binary math and logic operations.

  • Bus Interface Unit (BIU): 8086 section responsible for fetching instructions, bus access, and address translation.

  • Execution Unit (EU): 8086 section responsible for instruction decoding and execution.

  • Instruction Queue: FIFO buffer in 8086 BIU holding prefetched instruction bytes.

  • Machine Cycle: Fundamental CPU bus operation (Fetch, Read, Write) composed of T-states.

  • Paragraph Boundary: Physical memory address divisible by 16 (ending in lower hex 0).

  • Pipelining: Overlapping instruction fetch and execution cycles to increase CPU throughput.

  • Segment Register: 16-bit register holding upper 16 bits of a 64 KB memory segment base address.

  • T-State: Single clock period of CPU system clock.

  • Vector Address: Fixed memory location to which CPU transfers execution upon receiving an interrupt.

docs.title: Appendix E — Exam Review & Questions
docs.text: This section provides an Exam-oriented review and question bank to test core microprocessor concepts.

docs.title: Section 1: Conceptual & Short Answer Questions
docs.text:
1. Explain the purpose of the ALE signal in Intel 8085 and 8086 microprocessors.

Answer: \(ALE\)(Address Latch Enable) is a positive pulse emitted during \(T_1\) of a machine cycle to signal external latches (e.g., 74LS373) to capture and hold the lower address byte from the multiplexed Address/Data bus (\(AD_7 - AD_0\) or \(AD_{15} - AD_0\)).

  1. Why does the INC instruction in 8086 not affect the Carry Flag (CF)?

Answer: INC (and DEC) instructions intentionally leave CF unaffected so that loop counter increments do not overwrite the carry state resulting from prior multi-word arithmetic operations.

  1. What is the difference between MUL and IMUL instructions in 8086?

Answer: MUL performs unsigned binary multiplication, interpreting operands as positive magnitudes. IMUL performs signed two's complement multiplication, preserving operand sign bits.

  1. State two primary advantages of memory segmentation in the 8086 microprocessor.

Answer: 1) Allows 16-bit registers to address \(1\text{ MB}\) of physical memory. 2) Enables dynamic code and data relocation without modifying internal program offset addresses.

docs.title: Section 2: Architectural & Diagram-Based Questions
docs.text:
1. Draw and explain the internal architecture of 8086, highlighting BIU and EU interaction.

Review Requirement: Draw Figure 3.1. Explain prefetch queue operations, asynchronous execution, address generation, and queue flushing during branches.

  1. Explain the 8085 Interrupt structure in order of priority.

Review Requirement: List priority: TRAP \(>\) RST 7.5 \(>\) RST 6.5 \(>\) RST 5.5 \(>\) INTR. Detail vector addresses, triggering mechanisms (edge vs level), and masking via SIM.

docs.title: Section 3: Numerical & Address Calculation Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. If \(\text{CS} = 24A0\text{H}\) and \(\text{IP} = 1082\text{H}\), determine the physical memory address.

Solution:

\[ \text{Physical Address} = 24A00\text{H} + 1082\text{H} = 25A82\text{H} \]
  1. Find the effective address (\(EA\)) and physical address for MOV AX, [BX+SI+0100H] given \(\text{DS} = 3000\text{H}\), \(\text{BX} = 0200\text{H}\), \(\text{SI} = 0050\text{H}\).

Solution:

\[ EA = 0200\text{H} + 0050\text{H} + 0100\text{H} = 0350\text{H} \] \[ \text{Physical Address} = 30000\text{H} + 0350\text{H} = 30350\text{H} \]

docs.title: Section 4: Assembly Code & Algorithm Synthesis
docs.text:
1. Write an 8086 assembly program sequence to add two 32-bit numbers stored in memory.

Solution:

MOV AX, WORD PTR [NUM1_LOW]     ; Load low word of Number 1

ADD AX, WORD PTR [NUM2_LOW]     ; Add low word of Number 2

MOV WORD PTR [SUM_LOW], AX      ; Store low word sum



MOV AX, WORD PTR [NUM1_HIGH]    ; Load high word of Number 1

ADC AX, WORD PTR [NUM2_HIGH]    ; Add high word of Number 2 with Carry

MOV WORD PTR [SUM_HIGH], AX     ; Store high word sum

docs.title: 8. Exam-Oriented Worked Numerical Examples & Step-by-Step Traces
Problem 1: 8086 Physical Address Generation
docs.text:
Question: Calculate the 20-bit Physical Address generated by the 8086 CPU for the following segment and offset register pairs:

  1. \(\text{CS} = 2500\text{H}, \text{IP} = 1200\text{H}\)

  2. \(\text{DS} = 4000\text{H}, \text{BX} = 0050\text{H}, \text{SI} = 0100\text{H}\) (Based-Indexed Addressing)

  3. \(\text{SS} = 7000\text{H}, \text{SP} = 0FF0\text{H}\)

Step-by-Step Solution & Calculation:

  1. Case 1 (Code Segment Fetch):

  2. Formula: \(\text{Physical Address} = (\text{CS} \times 16_{10}) + \text{IP} = (\text{CS} \ll 4) + \text{IP}\)

  3. \(\text{CS} \times 10\text{H} = 25000\text{H}\)

  4. Add Offset \(\text{IP} = 01200\text{H}\)

  5. \(\text{Physical Address} = 25000\text{H} + 01200\text{H} = \mathbf{26200\text{H}}\)

  6. Case 2 (Data Segment Based-Indexed Fetch):

  7. Formula: \(\text{Effective Address (EA)} = \text{BX} + \text{SI} = 0050\text{H} + 0100\text{H} = 0150\text{H}\)

  8. \(\text{Physical Address} = (\text{DS} \times 10\text{H}) + \text{EA} = 40000\text{H} + 0150\text{H} = \mathbf{41500\text{H}}\)

  9. Case 3 (Stack Segment Operation):

  10. Formula: \(\text{Physical Address} = (\text{SS} \times 10\text{H}) + \text{SP}\)

  11. \(\text{SS} \times 10\text{H} = 70000\text{H}\)

  12. Add Offset \(\text{SP} = 00FF0\text{H}\)

  13. \(\text{Physical Address} = 70000\text{H} + 00FF0\text{H} = \mathbf{70FF0\text{H}}\)

Step-by-Step Solution:

  1. Formula: \(\text{Vector Address} = (\text{Interrupt Number}) \times 8_{10}\) converted to 16-bit Hexadecimal.

  2. For RST 5:

docs.title: Problem 3: 8259 PIC Vector Address Calculation
docs.text:
Question: If 8259 ICW1 is initialized with vector base address \(T_7 - T_3 = 10000_2\) (80H), determine the interrupt vector address for Interrupt Request Line IR3.

Step-by-Step Solution:

  1. Vector Offset for IR3: \(3 \times 4\text{ bytes} = 12_{10} = 0C\text{H}\)(or in 8086 mode, Vector Type Number =\(\text{Base Type} + 3\)).

  2. In 8086 mode, Type Number = \(80\text{H} + 3 = 83\text{H}\).

  3. Vector Table Entry Location = \(83\text{H} \times 4 = 20C\text{H}\).

  4. The 4 bytes at 0020CH to 0020FH store the 16-bit \(\text{IP}\) and 16-bit \(\text{CS}\) for IR3's Interrupt Service Routine (ISR).

docs.title: Microprocessors & Interfacing: Comprehensive Master Guide
docs.text: Generated from source slides (MI_Sem5/Slides).

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Microprocessors and Assembly Language
1.1 What is a Microprocessor?
docs.text: A Microprocessor is an integrated circuit (IC) that contains the core functions of a central processing unit (CPU) of a computer. It is driven by a clock, accepts binary data as input, processes it according to instructions stored in its memory, and provides results as output.

docs.title: The System Bus Architecture
docs.text:
To communicate with memory and input/output (I/O) peripherals, the microprocessor uses a collection of communication lines called a Bus. The system bus is divided into three distinct categories:

  1. Data Bus (Bidirectional): Carries the actual binary data between the CPU and memory or I/O devices. A wider data bus (e.g., 16-bit vs 8-bit) allows more data to be transferred simultaneously.
  2. Address Bus (Unidirectional): Carries the memory address or I/O port number from the CPU to the memory/peripherals. It tells the system where the data should go or come from. The width of the address bus determines the maximum memory capacity (e.g., 20 address lines = \(2^{20} = 1\text{ MB}\)).
  3. Control Bus: Carries control signals (like Read RD/, Write WR/, Memory/IO select IO/M/) to coordinate and synchronize the activities of the system.

docs.title: 1.2 The Software Hierarchy
docs.text: Microprocessors execute binary code, but humans write programs using text. Software acts as the bridge.

docs.title: Levels of Programming Languages
docs.text:
1. Machine Language: The lowest level. Consists entirely of binary \(0\) s and \(1\) s. This is the only language the microprocessor actually understands.
  2. Assembly Language: A low-level programming language where machine instructions are represented by readable abbreviations called Mnemonics (e.g., MOV, ADD, JMP).
  3. High-Level Language: Human-readable code (like C, C++, Python) that abstracts away hardware details.

docs.title: System Software & Translators
docs.text:
To convert human code into machine code, the computer uses translators:

  • Assembler: Translates Assembly Language code (mnemonics) directly into Machine Language (binary object code).
  • Compiler / Interpreter: Translates High-Level Language into Machine Language.
  • Linker (Linkage Editor): Takes one or more object files generated by a compiler or assembler and combines them into a single executable program.
  • Resident Monitor / Operating System: The core program that is always loaded in memory to handle I/O and execute user programs.

docs.title: 1.3 Features of Assembly Language Programming
docs.text:
Writing programs in Assembly language gives you absolute control over the microprocessor.

  1. Machine Dependent: Assembly code is tied directly to the specific architecture of the CPU. Code written for an x86 processor (like the 8086) will not run on an ARM processor.
  2. Low-Level Language: It is one step above machine code. You manage the exact memory locations and CPU registers.
  3. Mnemonic Instructions: Uses short, readable operation codes (e.g., SUB for subtract) instead of raw binary hex values.
  4. Fast Execution & High Performance: Since there is no heavy overhead from high-level abstractions, assembly programs execute incredibly fast.
  5. Efficient Memory Usage: Programmers have direct control over exactly how many bytes are used, preventing memory bloat.
  6. Direct Hardware Access: Capable of interacting directly with I/O ports and specific memory addresses to control peripheral devices (like timers or displays).
  7. Register-Based Operations: Most computations avoid slow RAM by performing math directly inside the CPU's internal high-speed memory cells (Registers).
  8. Limited Portability: Code must be rewritten if migrating to a different CPU family.

docs.title: 1.4 Common Assembly Development Tools
docs.text:
To write, assemble, and debug x86 Assembly code, several software environments and toolchains are commonly used in academia and industry:

  • MASM (Microsoft Macro Assembler): Microsoft's assembler for the x86 architecture. Highly popular in legacy DOS/Windows environments.
  • NASM (Netwide Assembler): A free, open-source assembler widely used today. It supports a variety of output formats (Linux, Windows, macOS).
  • TASM (Turbo Assembler): Developed by Borland, popular in educational environments alongside Turbo C/C++.
  • DOSBox-X / EMU8086 (Emulator): Since modern 64-bit operating systems do not natively run 16-bit DOS programs, an emulator like DOSBox or EMU8086 is required to safely simulate the 8086 microprocessor environment.
  • SASM (SimpleASM IDE): A modern, open-source Integrated Development Environment (IDE) specifically designed for NASM, MASM, GAS, and FASM. It provides syntax highlighting and a built-in debugger.

docs.title: Example: A Basic Assembly Program Structure
docs.text:
If you are writing complete code, your file will typically have segments defined for data and code.

; A typical complete code structure in MASM/TASM

DATA SEGMENT           ; Define the start of the data segment
    NUM1 DB 05H        ; DB = Define Byte. Variable NUM1 initialized to 05H
    NUM2 DB 03H        ; Variable NUM2 initialized to 03H
    RESULT DB ?        ; Uninitialized byte to store the answer
DATA ENDS              ; End of data segment

CODE SEGMENT           ; Define the start of the code segment
    ASSUME CS:CODE, DS:DATA  ; Tell the assembler which segments to use

START: 
    MOV AX, DATA       ; Initialize Data Segment register (DS)
    MOV DS, AX         ; DS cannot be loaded directly with immediate data

    MOV AL, NUM1       ; Load the value of NUM1 into register AL
    ADD AL, NUM2       ; Add the value of NUM2 to AL. (AL = AL + NUM2)
    MOV RESULT, AL     ; Store the final sum from AL into memory variable RESULT

    MOV AH, 4CH        ; Setup DOS interrupt to terminate program gracefully
    INT 21H            ; Call DOS interrupt
CODE ENDS              ; End of code segment

END START              ; End of file, specify the entry point 'START'

docs.title: 2.1 The 8085 Microprocessor: Overview and Architecture
docs.text: The Intel 8085 is an 8-bit microprocessor introduced in the late 1970s. While modern computers use 64-bit processors, studying the 8085 is fundamental for understanding how the core principles of CPU architecture work.

docs.title: Main Technical Specifications
docs.text:
• Data Bus: 8-bit. It can process 8 bits of data simultaneously.
  • Address Bus: 16-bit. It can address up to \(2^{16} = 65,536\text{ bytes}\) (\(64\text{ KB}\)) of memory.
  • Clock Speed: Typically runs at \(3\text{ MHz}\) (8085A) or \(5\text{ MHz}\) (8085A-2).
  • Power Supply: Single \(+5\text{V}\) power supply.
  • Instruction Set: Contains exactly 80 machine instructions.

docs.title: Pin Functions and Hardware Signals
docs.text:
The 8085 chip communicates with the outside world via 40 pins. Key signals include:

  1. X1 and X2: Input pins connected to an external crystal oscillator to provide the clock rhythm.
  2. SID (Serial Input Data) & SOD (Serial Output Data): Used for single-bit serial communication. Manipulated via the RIM (Read Interrupt Mask) and SIM (Set Interrupt Mask) instructions.
  3. AD0 - AD7 (Multiplexed Address/Data Bus): To save physical pins on the chip, these 8 lines serve a dual purpose. During the first clock cycle (\(T_1\)), they transmit the lower 8 bits of the memory address. During subsequent cycles (\(T_2, T_3\)), they switch roles to transfer actual data.
  4. A8 - A15 (Address Bus): An 8-bit unidirectional bus that always carries the higher-order 8 bits of the memory address.
  5. ALE (Address Latch Enable): Because AD0-AD7 switches roles between Address and Data, the CPU sends a positive pulse on the ALE pin during \(T_1\). This signals external latches (hardware memory buffers) to capture and hold the address before the lines switch to data mode.
  6. IO/M/ (Input/Output / Memory Select): A signal that tells the external circuitry whether the CPU is trying to talk to RAM (Memory Mode, active low) or a peripheral device (I/O Mode, active high).
  7. READY: An input pin. If the CPU is communicating with a slow memory chip, the memory can pull READY low, forcing the CPU to pause (enter WAIT states) until the slow memory catches up.
  8. HOLD and HLDA (Hold Acknowledge): Used for Direct Memory Access (DMA). An external device requests control of the buses by asserting HOLD. The CPU finishes its current cycle and responds with HLDA, disconnecting itself from the buses so the device can transfer data directly to RAM.

docs.title: 2.2 Register Organization (The CPU's Internal Memory)
docs.text: Registers are ultra-fast, temporary storage pockets located directly inside the CPU.

docs.title: General Purpose Registers (8-bit)
docs.text:
The 8085 has six 8-bit general-purpose registers: B, C, D, E, H, and L. Because a memory address is 16 bits long, these 8-bit registers can be paired up to form 16-bit pairs to hold addresses:

  • BC Pair
  • DE Pair
  • HL Pair: This is the most important pair. The HL pair is primarily used as the default Memory Pointer (Data Pointer). When an instruction targets the abstract memory register M, the CPU looks at the 16-bit address held in the HL pair to know where in RAM to go.

docs.title: Special Purpose Registers
docs.text:
1. Accumulator (A Register, 8-bit): The most important register. All math and logic operations (Addition, Subtraction, AND, OR) are performed here. The final result is also stored back in the Accumulator.
  2. Flag Register (8-bit): Holds 5 individual bits (Flags) that act as a dashboard warning light to report the status of the last arithmetic operation:
    • S (Sign Flag): Set to 1 if the result is negative (MSB is 1).
    • Z (Zero Flag): Set to 1 if the result is exactly zero.
    • AC (Auxiliary Carry Flag): Used internally for BCD (Binary Coded Decimal) math. Set if there is a carry from bit 3 to bit 4.
    • P (Parity Flag): Set to 1 if the binary result contains an even number of 1s (Even Parity).
    • CY (Carry Flag): Set to 1 if the math operation resulted in an overflow or required a borrow.
  3. Stack Pointer (SP, 16-bit): Points to the top of the Stack (a temporary LIFO storage area in RAM).
  4. Program Counter (PC, 16-bit): Holds the exact memory address of the next instruction the CPU needs to fetch. Automatically increments after every fetch.

docs.title: 2.3 Addressing Modes in 8085
docs.text:
"Addressing Mode" simply means "How do we tell the CPU where to find the data for this instruction?" The 8085 has five modes:

  1. Immediate Addressing: The data is hardcoded directly inside the instruction itself. 

    MVI A, 45H    ; Move Immediate: Load the hex value 45 directly into Accumulator A

  2. Register Addressing: The data is already in a CPU register. 

    MOV B, A      ; Copy the contents of Register A into Register B

  3. Direct Addressing: The 16-bit memory address of the data is explicitly stated in the instruction. 

    LDA 2050H     ; Load Accumulator directly from memory address 2050 Hex

  4. Register Indirect Addressing: The CPU looks inside a register pair (like HL) to find the memory address, then goes to that address to get the data. 

    MOV A, M      ; Move to A from Memory. (Memory address is defined by the HL pair)

  5. Implied (Implicit) Addressing: The instruction doesn't need an operand because the target is understood (usually the Accumulator). 

    CMA           ; Complement Accumulator: Invert all bits in Register A

docs.title: 2.4 Interrupt Processing & The 8259 PIC
docs.text:
An interrupt is a hardware signal sent to the CPU, telling it to pause its current program and execute an emergency subroutine (Interrupt Service Routine - ISR).

The 8085 has 5 hardware interrupt pins, ranked by strict priority:

Interrupt Line Trigger Type Priority Vector Address (Hex) Maskable? TRAP (RST 4.5) Edge AND Level 1 (Highest) 0024H Non-Maskable RST 7.5 Rising Edge 2 003CH Maskable via SIM RST 6.5 High Level 3 0034H Maskable via SIM RST 5.5 High Level 4 0020H Maskable via SIM INTR High Level 5 (Lowest) Provided by external IC Maskable via EI/DI

docs.title: How Hardware Interrupts Work
docs.text:
1. TRAP: This is an absolute emergency (e.g., power failure). It is "Non-Maskable" meaning no software command can ignore it. It instantly forces the CPU to jump to memory address 0024H.
  2. RST (Restart) 7.5, 6.5, 5.5: These are "Vectored" interrupts. When triggered, the CPU calculates a specific mathematical address (the Vector) and jumps there. You can disable (Mask) them using the SIM (Set Interrupt Mask) instruction.
  3. Formula to calculate Vector Address: Vector Address = N x 8
  4. Example for RST 5.5: \(5.5 \times 8 = 44_{10}\). Convert 44 to Hexadecimal = 002CH.
  5. INTR (Handshake Interrupt): The lowest priority. It is "Non-Vectored," meaning it doesn't have a hardcoded jump address.

docs.title: The 8259 Programmable Interrupt Controller (PIC)
docs.text:
Because the 8085 only has a few interrupt pins, computers use an external chip (the 8259 PIC) to manage multiple devices (keyboard, mouse, hard drive) trying to interrupt the CPU simultaneously.

  • The 8259 can accept up to 8 external interrupts (IR0 to IR7).
  • It checks priority. If IR1 and IR4 trigger at the same time, it serves the highest priority first.
  • It sends a single INTR signal to the 8085.
  • The 8085 responds with INTA/ (Interrupt Acknowledge).
  • The 8259 then places the appropriate CALL opcode and 16-bit subroutine address directly onto the data bus so the 8085 knows exactly where to jump to handle the device.

docs.title: 3.1 Overview of the 8086 Microprocessor
docs.text: The Intel 8086 is a monumental upgrade over the 8085. It is a true 16-bit microprocessor designed to handle significantly more data and larger programs.

docs.title: Key Technical Features
docs.text:
• Data Bus: 16-bit. It can read or write a full 16-bit Word in a single operation.
  • Address Bus: 20-bit. It can address up to \(2^{20} = 1,048,576\text{ bytes}\) (\(1\text{ MB}\)) of physical memory.
  • I/O Ports: Supports up to \(64\text{K}\) (\(65,536\)) separate Input/Output ports.
  • Registers: Fourteen 16-bit registers.
  • Power & Clock: Requires a single \(+5\text{V}\) supply and operates between \(5\text{ MHz}\) and \(8\text{ MHz}\).
  • Operating Modes: Can operate in Minimum Mode (single processor system) or Maximum Mode (multi-processor system with coprocessors like the 8087 math chip).

docs.title: 3.2 The Two-Unit Architecture: BIU and EU
docs.text: To drastically speed up execution, the 8086 is internally divided into two completely separate processing units that work in parallel. This overlapping of fetching and executing is known as Pipelining.

docs.title: 1. The Bus Interface Unit (BIU)
docs.text:
The BIU handles all communication with the outside world (the buses).

  • Responsibilities: Fetching instructions from memory, reading/writing operands, and calculating physical memory addresses.
  • The Instruction Queue (Q): To prevent the Execution Unit from waiting for memory reads, the BIU "looks ahead." When the buses are idle, the BIU prefetches up to 6 bytes of upcoming instructions and stores them in a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue.
  • Components: Contains the Segment Registers, the Instruction Pointer (IP), the Queue, and the Address Summing Block.

docs.title: 2. The Execution Unit (EU)
docs.text:
The EU does the actual brainwork. It does not connect to the system buses directly.

  • Responsibilities: Decodes instructions pulled from the BIU's Queue, generates control signals, and performs arithmetic/logic via the ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit).
  • Components: Contains the General Purpose Registers, Index/Pointer Registers, the Flag Register, and the ALU.

docs.title: 3.3 The 8086 Register Set
docs.text: The 8086 provides 14 internal 16-bit registers.

docs.title: General Purpose Registers
docs.text:
These can be used as full 16-bit registers or split into two independent 8-bit registers (High and Low).

  1. AX (Accumulator Register - AH & AL): Primary register for arithmetic, logic, and data transfer. Multiplication and division instructions force the use of AX.
  2. BX (Base Register - BH & BL): Frequently used to hold the base address of data structures (like arrays) in memory.
  3. CX (Count Register - CH & CL): Automatically used by the hardware as a countdown timer for looping instructions (LOOP) and bit shift/rotate operations.
  4. DX (Data Register - DH & DL): Used to hold the upper 16 bits in 32-bit multiplication/division, and holds the port address for I/O operations (IN, OUT).

docs.title: Pointer and Index Registers
docs.text:
Always 16-bit. They hold memory offsets (relative addresses).

  1. SP (Stack Pointer): Points to the current top of the stack.
  2. BP (Base Pointer): Used to access data inside the stack, usually parameters passed into subroutines.
  3. SI (Source Index): Points to the source string/array in string operations.
  4. DI (Destination Index): Points to the destination string/array in string operations.

docs.title: The Flag Register (Status & Control)
docs.text:
A 16-bit register where 9 bits are active. Status Flags (Math Results):

  • CF (Carry Flag): Set if an addition produces a carry or subtraction needs a borrow.
  • PF (Parity Flag): Set if the lower 8 bits of the result have an even number of 1s.
  • AF (Auxiliary Carry): Carry from bit 3 to bit 4 (used for BCD math).
  • ZF (Zero Flag): Set to 1 if the result is exactly zero.
  • SF (Sign Flag): Set to 1 if the result is negative (MSB is 1).
  • OF (Overflow Flag): Set if signed arithmetic exceeds the register's capacity (e.g., adding two positive numbers results in a negative number).

Control Flags (Hardware Behavior):

  • TF (Trap Flag): If set, CPU enters single-step debugging mode, executing one instruction at a time.
  • IF (Interrupt Flag): If set (STI), maskable hardware interrupts (INTR) are enabled. If cleared (CLI), they are disabled.
  • DF (Direction Flag): Controls string operations. If 0 (CLD), string pointers (SI/DI) auto-increment (forward). If 1 (STD), they auto-decrement (backward).

docs.title: 3.4 Segmented Memory Architecture
docs.text:
The 8086 has 20 address pins, allowing \(1\text{ MB}\) of memory. However, the internal registers (IP, BX, SI, etc.) are only 16 bits wide, meaning they can only count up to \(65,535\) (\(64\text{ KB}\)).

To solve this, memory is divided into \(64\text{ KB}\) blocks called Segments. The CPU addresses memory by combining a Segment Base Address with a 16-bit Offset.

docs.title: The 4 Segment Registers
docs.text:
1. CS (Code Segment): Holds the base address for the running program's instructions.
  2. DS (Data Segment): Holds the base address for the program's variables.
  3. SS (Stack Segment): Holds the base address for the stack.
  4. ES (Extra Segment): Usually serves as a secondary data segment, specifically for the destination in string operations.

docs.title: Physical Address Calculation
docs.text:
Inside the BIU, a dedicated hardware adder (the Address Summing Block) calculates the true 20-bit physical address using this formula:

\[ \text{Physical Address} = (\text{Segment Register} \times 16_{10}) + \text{Offset Register} \]

(In Hexadecimal: Multiply the Segment by 10H (shift left 1 hex digit), then add the Offset)

Example Calculation: If the Data Segment (DS) is 4000H and the Base Register (BX) offset is 0150H:

  • Shift DS left: 4000H \(\rightarrow\) 40000H
  • Add Offset: 40000H + 0150H = 40150H (This is the exact byte in the 1MB RAM).

docs.title: 3.5 The 7 Addressing Modes of 8086
docs.text:
How does the CPU know where an operand is? It relies on the Addressing Mode.

  1. Register Addressing: Data is in an internal register. (Fastest, no memory access). 

    MOV AX, BX       ; Copy 16-bit contents of BX into AX

  2. Immediate Addressing: The actual data value is hardcoded into the instruction. 

    MOV CX, 2550H    ; Load the literal hex value 2550 into CX

[!WARNING] You cannot load immediate data directly into a Segment Register. MOV DS, 1000H is illegal. You must go through a general register: MOV AX, 1000H then MOV DS, AX.

  1. Direct Addressing: The 16-bit offset address is hardcoded in brackets. 

    MOV AL, [2400H]  ; Fetch the byte from offset 2400H in the Data Segment

  2. Register Indirect Addressing: The offset address is held inside BX, BP, SI, or DI. 

    MOV AX, [BX]     ; Fetch the word from memory at the offset stored in BX

  3. Base Relative Addressing: Offset = Base Register (BX or BP) + an 8/16-bit displacement. 

    MOV AL, [BX + 5] ; Fetch byte from memory at offset (BX + 5)

  4. Indexed Relative Addressing: Offset = Index Register (SI or DI) + an 8/16-bit displacement. Used heavily for array traversal. 

    MOV DX, ARRAY[SI]; Fetch data from offset (ARRAY_Base + SI)

  5. Base Indexed Relative Addressing: The ultimate flexible mode. Offset = Base + Index + Displacement. Excellent for 2D arrays. 

    MOV AX, [BX + SI + 10H] ; Fetch word from offset (BX + SI + 16 decimal)

docs.title: 3.6 Machine Instruction Format Encoding
docs.text:
When you write MOV CX, BX, the assembler translates it into binary machine code. 8086 instructions range from 1 to 6 bytes. A typical instruction byte is structured as:

  • Opcode (6 bits): Identifies the operation (e.g., 100010 = MOV).
  • D (Direction Bit, 1 bit):
    • 0: Data flows from the specified REG to the R/M location.
    • 1: Data flows to the specified REG from the R/M location.
  • W (Word/Byte Bit, 1 bit):
    • 0: 8-bit Byte operation.
    • 1: 16-bit Word operation.
  • MOD (Mode Field, 2 bits) & R/M (Register/Memory, 3 bits): Together these 5 bits dictate which of the 7 addressing modes is being used, and whether there is an 8-bit or 16-bit displacement attached.
  • REG (Register Field, 3 bits): Dictates exactly which register (AX, BX, etc.) is involved.

docs.title: Chapter 4: 8086 Instruction Set Basics
docs.text: The 8086 supports over 20,000 instruction variations. To understand them, we classify them into logical groups.

docs.title: 4.1 General Assembler Instruction Syntax
docs.text:
Every assembly instruction follows a strict format: 

Label:   Mnemonic   Destination, Source   ; Comments

If an instruction interacts with memory and the size (byte vs word) is ambiguous, the Assembler will throw an error. You must explicitly define the size using the PTR (Pointer) operator. 

INC [BX]               ; ERROR: Ambiguous! Are we incrementing a byte or a 16-bit word?
INC BYTE PTR [BX]      ; Correct: Increments the 8-bit byte at memory address [BX]
INC WORD PTR [BX]      ; Correct: Increments the 16-bit word at memory address [BX]

docs.title: 4.2 Data Transfer Instructions
docs.text: These instructions move data. Critical Rule: Data transfer instructions NEVER affect the Status Flags.

docs.title: MOV (Move Data)
docs.text:
Copies data from Source to Destination. 

MOV AX, 1234H          ; Load immediate word into AX
MOV BX, AX             ; Copy AX into BX
MOV CX, [5000H]        ; Load word from memory address 5000H into CX

Constraints: You cannot move memory to memory directly (e.g., MOV [1000H], [2000H] is invalid). You cannot move immediate data directly into a Segment Register (e.g., MOV DS, 1000H is invalid).

docs.title: XCHG (Exchange)
docs.text:
Swaps the contents of two operands. At least one must be a register. Segment registers cannot be exchanged. 

XCHG AX, BX            ; Swap AX and BX
XCHG AL, [1000H]       ; Swap AL with the memory byte at 1000H

docs.title: Pointer Loading: LEA, LDS, LES
docs.text:
These instructions deal with memory addresses (pointers) rather than raw numerical data.

  • LEA (Load Effective Address): Calculates the offset address of a memory variable and loads the address itself into a register, not the data at the address. 

    LEA BX, ARRAY        ; BX now holds the 16-bit memory address of ARRAY

  • LDS (Load Pointer to DS) & LES (Load Pointer to ES): Loads a full 32-bit far pointer (Segment + Offset) from memory into a designated register AND a segment register. 

    LDS SI, [0301H]      ; Loads the 16-bit offset into SI, and the 16-bit Segment into DS
LES DI, [POINTER]    ; Loads offset into DI, Segment into ES

docs.title: 4.3 Arithmetic Instructions
docs.text: Arithmetic operations always affect the Status Flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF) depending on the result, with a few notable exceptions.

docs.title: Addition and Subtraction
docs.text:
• ADD / SUB: Standard addition and subtraction.
  • ADC (Add with Carry) / SBB (Subtract with Borrow): Includes the current state of the Carry Flag in the calculation. Vital for multi-word math (like adding two 32-bit numbers in a 16-bit system). 
    ADD AX, BX           ; AX = AX + BX
ADC DX, CX           ; DX = DX + CX + Carry Flag
SUB AX, 0005H        ; AX = AX - 5
SBB BX, CX           ; BX = BX - CX - Carry Flag

docs.title: Increment, Decrement, and Negation
docs.text:
• INC / DEC: Adds or subtracts 1.

    [!IMPORTANT] CRITICAL RULE: INC and DEC affect all flags EXCEPT the Carry Flag (CF). This allows you to increment loop counters without destroying the carry state from a previous addition. 

    INC CX               ; CX = CX + 1
DEC BYTE PTR [SI]    ; Decrement the memory byte pointed to by SI

  • NEG: Performs Two's Complement negation (multiplies by -1). 

    NEG AL               ; If AL was 5, it becomes -5 (Two's Complement binary)

docs.title: Compare and Sign Extension
docs.text:
• CMP (Compare): Exactly the same as SUB, but it throws away the result. It is used purely to set the Status Flags so a conditional Jump can be performed immediately after. 

    CMP AX, BX           ; Internally calculates AX - BX and sets flags, but AX remains untouched.

  • CBW (Convert Byte to Word) & CWD (Convert Word to Doubleword): Extends the sign bit of a number so 8-bit math can be safely expanded into 16-bit math. Affects NO flags. 

    MOV AL, -5           ; AL holds 8-bit negative 5
CBW                  ; Expands AL into AX by copying the sign bit into AH. AX now holds 16-bit -5.

docs.title: Multiplication and Division
docs.text:
Multiplication and Division have rigid register requirements. You cannot use immediate data (e.g., MUL 5 is illegal).

  • MUL (Unsigned) & IMUL (Signed Multiplication):

    • 8-bit multiply: AL is implicitly multiplied by the operand. Result goes to AX.
    • 16-bit multiply: AX is implicitly multiplied by the operand. Result goes to DX:AX (DX holds high 16 bits, AX holds low 16 bits). 
      MUL BL               ; AX = AL * BL (Unsigned)
IMUL CX              ; DX:AX = AX * CX (Signed)

  • DIV (Unsigned) & IDIV (Signed Division):

    • 8-bit divide: AX divided by operand. Quotient in AL, Remainder in AH.
    • 16-bit divide: DX:AX divided by operand. Quotient in AX, Remainder in DX. 
      DIV BL               ; AX / BL -> Quotient in AL, Remainder in AH

docs.title: 4.4 Logical and Bit Manipulation Instructions
docs.text:
Logical instructions perform bitwise Boolean algebra. They always force CF=0 and OF=0, and update SF, ZF, and PF based on the result.

  • AND, OR, XOR: Standard bitwise operations. Used for masking, setting, or toggling specific bits. 

    AND AL, 0FH          ; Clears upper 4 bits, keeps lower 4 bits
OR  BL, 80H          ; Forces the MSB (bit 7) to 1
XOR CX, CX           ; Fastest way to clear a register to 0 (CX = 0)

  • NOT: Inverts all bits (One's Complement). Does NOT affect any flags.

  • TEST: Exactly like AND, but throws away the result. Used purely to set flags to test if a specific bit is a 1 or 0.

docs.title: Shift and Rotate Instructions
docs.text:
Used to move bits left or right. The CF (Carry Flag) acts as an extra 17th bit that catches bits pushed out the end. The count must be 1, or stored in the CL register.

  • SHL / SAL (Shift Left): Multiplies by 2. Pushes 0 in from the right. MSB goes to Carry Flag.
  • SHR (Shift Logical Right): Divides unsigned numbers by 2. Pushes 0 in from the left. LSB goes to Carry Flag.
  • SAR (Shift Arithmetic Right): Divides signed numbers by 2. Retains the original sign bit by copying it back into the MSB, preserving negativity. LSB goes to CF.
  • ROL / ROR (Rotate Left / Right): Bits pushed out one end wrap around and enter the other end, while ALSO copying into the Carry Flag.
  • RCL / RCR (Rotate through Carry): Includes the Carry Flag in the rotation ring, effectively making it a 9-bit or 17-bit rotation. 
    SHL AX, 1            ; Shift AX left by 1 bit
MOV CL, 4            
ROR BX, CL           ; Rotate BX right by 4 bits (CL is required for count > 1)

docs.title: Chapter 5: 8086 Advanced Instructions (Branching, Strings, and Stacks)
5.1 Branching and Flow Control
docs.text: Normally, the CPU executes instructions sequentially by automatically incrementing the Instruction Pointer (IP). Branching instructions force the IP to load a new address, jumping to a different part of the code.

docs.title: Unconditional Jumps
docs.text:
• JMP Target_Label: Immediately jumps to the specified label. No flags are checked, and no flags are affected. 
    START: 
    MOV AX, 0000H
    JMP START        ; Infinite loop back to START

docs.title: Conditional Jumps
docs.text:
These jumps check the current state of the Status Flags (usually set by a previous CMP or arithmetic instruction). If the condition is met, it jumps. If not, it falls through to the next instruction.

  • JZ / JE Target: Jump if Zero / Jump if Equal. (Jumps if ZF = 1)
  • JNZ / JNE Target: Jump if Not Zero / Jump if Not Equal. (Jumps if ZF = 0)
  • JC / JB Target: Jump if Carry / Jump if Below. (Jumps if CF = 1)
  • JNC / JAE Target: Jump if No Carry / Jump if Above or Equal. (Jumps if CF = 0)
  • JS Target: Jump if Sign (Negative). (Jumps if SF = 1)
  • JNS Target: Jump if No Sign (Positive). (Jumps if SF = 0)

Complete Code Example: Finding the Maximum of Two Numbers 

DATA SEGMENT
    NUM1 DB 45H
    NUM2 DB 8AH
    MAX  DB ?
DATA ENDS

CODE SEGMENT
    ASSUME CS:CODE, DS:DATA
START:
    MOV AX, DATA
    MOV DS, AX

    MOV AL, NUM1       ; Load first number
    MOV BL, NUM2       ; Load second number
    CMP AL, BL         ; Compare AL and BL (Internally: AL - BL)
    JC SECOND_IS_BIGGER ; If AL < BL, subtraction requires a borrow, setting Carry Flag (CF=1)

    ; If we reach here, AL >= BL
    MOV MAX, AL        ; Store NUM1 as maximum
    JMP FINISH         ; Skip the next block

SECOND_IS_BIGGER:
    MOV MAX, BL        ; Store NUM2 as maximum

FINISH:
    MOV AH, 4CH        ; DOS terminate
    INT 21H
CODE ENDS
END START

docs.title: 5.2 Looping Mechanics
docs.text:
To execute a block of code multiple times, the 8086 uses the CX (Count Register) alongside dedicated LOOP instructions.

  • LOOP Target: When executed, the CPU automatically decrements CX by 1. If CX is not zero, it jumps to Target. If CX is zero, the loop ends.

    [!TIP] The hardware specifically designs LOOP so that it does not affect any flags. This is crucial, as you usually have math happening inside the loop that needs the flags preserved.

Complete Code Example: Adding 5 Numbers in an Array 

DATA SEGMENT
    ARRAY DB 10H, 20H, 30H, 40H, 50H
    SUM   DB 0
DATA ENDS

CODE SEGMENT
    ASSUME CS:CODE, DS:DATA
START:
    MOV AX, DATA
    MOV DS, AX

    LEA SI, ARRAY      ; Load offset of ARRAY into Source Index
    MOV CX, 0005H      ; Set loop counter to 5
    MOV AL, 00H        ; Clear AL to hold the running total

ADD_LOOP:
    ADD AL, [SI]       ; Add the current array element to AL
    INC SI             ; Point to the next element
    LOOP ADD_LOOP      ; Decrement CX. If CX != 0, jump back to ADD_LOOP

    MOV SUM, AL        ; Store final sum

    MOV AH, 4CH
    INT 21H
CODE ENDS
END START

docs.title: 5.3 Hardware String Primitives
docs.text: Moving large blocks of memory (arrays/strings) byte-by-byte using loops is slow. The 8086 has dedicated hardware "String Primitives" that act like conveyor belts.

docs.title: The Strict Rules of String Operations
docs.text:
1. Source: MUST be pointed to by DS:SI (Data Segment : Source Index).
  2. Destination: MUST be pointed to by ES:DI (Extra Segment : Destination Index).
  3. Direction: Controlled by the Direction Flag (DF).
  4. CLD (Clear Direction): DF = 0. Pointers (SI/DI) auto-increment (move forward).
  5. STD (Set Direction): DF = 1. Pointers auto-decrement (move backward).

docs.title: The String Instructions
docs.text:
• MOVSB / MOVSW (Move String Byte/Word): Copies a byte/word from [DS:SI] to [ES:DI], then auto-updates SI and DI.
  • CMPSB / CMPSW (Compare String): Compares byte/word at [DS:SI] with [ES:DI] and updates flags.
  • SCASB / SCASW (Scan String): Searches for a specific character. Compares the Accumulator (AL/AX) with the memory at [ES:DI].
  • LODSB / LODSW (Load String): Copies memory at [DS:SI] into the Accumulator (AL/AX).
  • STOSB / STOSW (Store String): Copies the Accumulator (AL/AX) into memory at [ES:DI].

docs.title: The REP Prefix
docs.text:
You can attach a REP (Repeat) prefix to string instructions. It tells the CPU to automatically repeat the instruction CX times, effectively turning a single instruction into an ultra-fast hardware loop.

Complete Code Example: Copying a String 

DATA SEGMENT
    SOURCE_STR DB 'HELLO WORLD'
    DEST_STR   DB 11 DUP(?)     ; Allocate 11 bytes of uninitialized space
DATA ENDS

EXTRA_SEG SEGMENT                 ; Define Extra Segment for string destination
EXTRA_SEG ENDS

CODE SEGMENT
    ASSUME CS:CODE, DS:DATA, ES:EXTRA_SEG
START:
    MOV AX, DATA
    MOV DS, AX
    MOV AX, EXTRA_SEG
    MOV ES, AX         ; Initialize Extra Segment

    LEA SI, SOURCE_STR ; Setup Source Pointer (DS:SI)
    LEA DI, DEST_STR   ; Setup Destination Pointer (ES:DI)
    MOV CX, 000BH      ; String length is 11 bytes (0BH)

    CLD                ; Clear Direction Flag to move forward

    REP MOVSB          ; Repeat "Move String Byte" CX times!

    MOV AH, 4CH
    INT 21H
CODE ENDS
END START

docs.title: 5.4 The Stack and Modular Programming
docs.text:
The Stack is a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) temporary memory structure. It grows "upside down" in memory—meaning as you add items, the memory address decreases.

  • PUSH Source: Subtracts 2 from the Stack Pointer (SP), then writes a 16-bit word to [SS:SP]. You cannot push 8-bit bytes, only 16-bit words.
  • POP Destination: Reads a 16-bit word from [SS:SP] into the destination, then adds 2 to the Stack Pointer.

docs.title: Procedures (CALL and RET)
docs.text:
Procedures (functions/subroutines) allow you to write reusable code blocks.

  • CALL Procedure_Name:
    1. The CPU takes the address of the next instruction (the return address) and PUSHes it onto the stack to save it.
    2. The CPU jumps to the Procedure_Name.
  • RET (Return):
    1. The CPU POPs the saved return address off the stack and loads it back into the Instruction Pointer (IP).
    2. Execution resumes right after the original CALL.

Complete Code Example: Reusable Procedure 

DATA SEGMENT
    NUM1 DW 1234H
    NUM2 DW 5678H
DATA ENDS

CODE SEGMENT
    ASSUME CS:CODE, DS:DATA
START:
    MOV AX, DATA
    MOV DS, AX

    MOV AX, NUM1       ; Load first parameter
    MOV BX, NUM2       ; Load second parameter

    CALL SWAP_REGS     ; Call the subroutine. Hardware pushes return address to Stack.

    ; At this point, AX will be 5678H and BX will be 1234H
    MOV AH, 4CH
    INT 21H

; ---------------------------------
; Procedure: SWAP_REGS
; Purpose: Swaps contents of AX and BX
; ---------------------------------
SWAP_REGS PROC NEAR
    PUSH CX            ; Save CX so we don't destroy its original value

    MOV CX, AX         ; Temp = AX
    MOV AX, BX         ; AX = BX
    MOV BX, CX         ; BX = Temp

    POP CX             ; Restore CX's original value
    RET                ; Pop return address to IP and go back to main program
SWAP_REGS ENDP

CODE ENDS
END START

docs.title: Chapter 6: Assembler Directives
docs.text: Directives (also called Pseudo-Operations) are instructions for the Assembler program itself (like MASM or TASM), not for the microprocessor. They do not generate machine code instructions for the CPU to execute. Instead, they tell the assembler how to allocate memory, organize segments, and evaluate mathematical expressions.

docs.title: 6.1 Data Definition and Storage Allocation
docs.text:
These directives allocate physical bytes in RAM and initialize them with data.

  • DB (Define Byte): Allocates 8-bit memory.
  • DW (Define Word): Allocates 16-bit memory.
  • DD (Define Doubleword): Allocates 32-bit memory.

docs.title: Complete Examples of Data Allocation
docs.text:
DATA SEGMENT
    ; Defining simple numeric variables
    DATA_BYTE   DB 10, 4, 10H        ; Allocates 3 bytes: decimal 10, decimal 4, hex 10
    DATA_WORD   DW 100, 100H, -5     ; Allocates 3 words (6 bytes total)
    DATA_DWORD  DD 3*20, 0FFFDH      ; Allocates 2 doublewords. Evaluates 3*20 at compile time.

    ; Defining strings
    MESSAGE1    DB 'H', 'E', 'L', 'L', 'O' ; 5 bytes
    MESSAGE2    DB 'HELLO'                 ; Exactly identical to MESSAGE1

    ; Uninitialized Data
    ABC         DB 0, ?, ?, ?, 0     ; '?' means allocate 1 byte but leave it uninitialized
    DEF         DW ?, 52, ?          ; Allocates 3 words. Middle word is initialized to 52.
DATA ENDS

docs.title: The DUP (Duplicate) Operator
docs.text:
Used to generate large blocks of data or arrays without typing each element. Syntax: Exp DUP (OP1, OP2, ... OPN) 

DATA SEGMENT
    ARRAY1 DB 2 DUP(0, 1, 2, ?)         ; Allocates 8 bytes: 0, 1, 2, ?, 0, 1, 2, ?
    ARRAY2 DB 100 DUP(?)                ; Allocates an array of 100 uninitialized bytes
    ARRAY3 DB 100 DUP(0, 2 DUP(1,2), 0, 3) ; Nested DUPs are allowed!
DATA ENDS

docs.title: Creating Arrays of Pointers
docs.text:
You can allocate arrays that hold the memory addresses of other variables. 

DATA SEGMENT
    PAR1 DW 1234H
    PAR2 DW 5678H

    ; This table holds the 16-bit offset addresses of PAR1 and PAR2
    PARAMETER_TABLE DW PAR1
                    DW PAR2
DATA ENDS

docs.title: 6.2 Overriding Types and Ambiguity Resolution
