docs.text: Sometimes you must perform an operation where the size (byte vs word) is ambiguous or contradicts the original variable definition.

docs.title: The PTR (Pointer) Operator
docs.text:
Forces the assembler to treat a memory location as a specific size. 

DATA SEGMENT
    OPER1 DB ?, ?      ; Two 8-bit bytes
    OPER2 DW ?, ?      ; Two 16-bit words
DATA ENDS

CODE SEGMENT
    ASSUME CS:CODE, DS:DATA
START:
    ; ERROR: OPER1 is defined as DB (Byte), but AX is 16-bit!
    ; MOV OPER1+1, AX  

    ; CORRECT: Force assembler to treat OPER1+1 as the start of a 16-bit word
    MOV WORD PTR OPER1+1, AX

    ; CORRECT: Force assembler to treat OPER2 as just an 8-bit byte to fit into AL
    MOV BYTE PTR OPER2, AL
CODE ENDS

docs.title: The LABEL Directive
docs.text:
Assigns a secondary name and type to an existing memory offset, allowing you to access the same memory as either bytes or words without needing PTR everywhere. 

DATA SEGMENT
    BYTE_ARRAY LABEL BYTE       ; Treat the following data as bytes
    WORD_ARRAY DW 50 DUP(?)     ; Actually allocates 50 words (100 bytes)
DATA ENDS

CODE SEGMENT
    MOV WORD_ARRAY+2, 0         ; Clears a 16-bit word
    MOV BYTE_ARRAY+2, 0         ; Clears an 8-bit byte at the exact same physical location
CODE ENDS

docs.title: 6.3 Aliases and Macros (EQU)
docs.text:
• EQU (Equate): Works like #define in C. It acts as a find-and-replace for the assembler. It does NOT allocate any memory.
NUM EQU 6                            ; Define a constant named NUM
INDXD_CHAR EQU CHAR_ARRAY[SI+10]     ; Define an alias for a complex memory operation

CODE SEGMENT
    ADD BX, NUM                      ; Assembler translates to: ADD BX, 6
    MOV AL, INDXD_CHAR               ; Assembler translates to: MOV AL, CHAR_ARRAY[SI+10]
CODE ENDS

docs.title: 6.4 Segment Definitions
docs.text:
Used to tell the assembler how to organize your logical memory blocks.

  • SEGMENT and ENDS (End Segment): Demarcates the boundaries of a segment.
  • ASSUME: Tells the assembler which physical segment register corresponds to which logical segment you defined.
  • END: Marks the absolute physical end of the source code file. Everything below END is ignored.
DATA SEGMENT
    VAR1 DB 55H
DATA ENDS

CODE SEGMENT
    ASSUME CS:CODE, DS:DATA      ; Link CS to CODE segment, DS to DATA segment
START:
    ; Main code goes here
CODE ENDS
END START                        ; Denotes the end of the file and the entry label

docs.title: 6.5 Alignment Directives
docs.text:
• EVEN: Forces the next variable to be placed at an even memory address. Essential because 16-bit word fetches from even addresses take 1 bus cycle, while odd addresses take 2 bus cycles (Unaligned Memory Access).
  • ORG (Origin): Forces the assembler to set the internal location counter to a specific physical offset.
VECTORS SEGMENT
    ORG 10H             ; Force next variable to be at physical offset 0010H
    VECT1 DW 1234H

    ORG 20H             ; Jump to offset 0020H
    VECT2 DW 5678H
VECTORS ENDS

docs.title: 6.6 Value Returning Attribute Operators
docs.text:
These operators ask the assembler to calculate and return metadata about a variable during compile time.

DATA SEGMENT
    A DW 100 DUP(0)      ; An array of 100 words (200 bytes total)
DATA ENDS

CODE SEGMENT
    ; LENGTH: Returns the number of elements in an array defined by DUP.
    MOV CX, LENGTH A     ; CX = 100

    ; SIZE: Returns the total number of bytes allocated (LENGTH x TYPE).
    MOV CX, SIZE A       ; CX = 200 (100 words * 2 bytes/word)

    ; OFFSET: Returns the 16-bit offset address of the variable inside its segment.
    MOV BX, OFFSET A     ; BX = 0000H (Assuming 'A' is the very first variable in DATA segment)

    ; SEG: Returns the 16-bit Segment Base Address.
    MOV AX, SEG A        ; Equivalent to loading DS

    ; TYPE: Returns the size of a single element in bytes (DB=1, DW=2, DD=4).
    ADD SI, TYPE A       ; SI = SI + 2 (Since A is a DW)
CODE ENDS

docs.title: Chapter: 8086 Macros and Interrupts
docs.text: Course: Microprocessors (MI) — Semester 5 Primary Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf (31 slides) Files Integrated: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf

docs.title: 1. Chapter Overview
docs.text:
This chapter covers two major topics:

  1. Macros in ASM-86 — a text-substitution mechanism that allows blocks of code to be written once and expanded inline at each point of use, without the overhead of procedure call linkage.
  2. 8086 Interrupts — the hardware and software mechanism by which normal program execution is temporarily suspended to handle a special event (divide-by-zero, keypress, timer tick, etc.), after which execution resumes.

Additionally, the XLAT (Table Translation) instruction is introduced as a useful data-lookup mechanism.

docs.title: 2.1 Why Use Macros?
docs.text:
Procedures and macros both promote code reuse, but they work differently:

Feature Procedure Macro Reuse mechanism CALL/RET linkage Inline text substitution Memory for code Written once in memory Code repeated at each expansion point Execution overhead PUSH return address, POP, JMP None (no linkage) Best for Long, frequently called code Short code repeated at several places Parameters Registers, stack, memory Dummy parameter substitution

Key idea: Macros save programmer effort (write once). The expanded code is repeated in memory and the binary — unlike procedures where code exists only once.

📝 Exam Note: A macro does NOT generate a CALL/RET. The assembler (or macro pre-processor) replaces each macro call with a copy of the expanded code. This is called inline expansion.

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slide 2]

docs.title: 2.2 Macro Terminology
docs.text:
Term Definition Prototype code The code that is to be repeated (the body of the macro) Macro definition Prototype code plus the %*DEFINE header and terminator Macro call A statement using the macro name (preceded by %) at the point where the code is needed Macro expansion The assembler's (or pre-processor's) act of replacing the macro call with the prototype code, substituting actual parameters

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slide 3]

docs.title: 2.3 ASM-86 Macro Syntax
docs.text: ASM-86 uses the %*DEFINE directive for macro definitions. This syntax is specific to Intel's ASM-86 assembler (and PLM-86 environments).

docs.title: Definition Syntax
docs.text:
%*DEFINE (MacroName (DummyParam1, DummyParam2, ...))
(
    ; Prototype code
    ; Each dummy parameter is prefixed with % in the body
)

docs.title: Call Syntax
docs.text:
%MacroName (ActualParam1, ActualParam2, ...)

Rules:

  • The macro name must be an identifier beginning with a letter, containing letters, numbers, and underscores.
  • Dummy parameters in the definition are listed in the DummyParameterList.
  • Inside the prototype code, each dummy parameter is referenced with a % prefix: %OPR1, %RESULT.
  • Actual parameters in the call are character strings that replace the dummy parameters positionally (first actual → first dummy, etc.).

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slide 4]

docs.title: 2.4 Dummy and Actual Parameters — How Substitution Works
docs.text:
During macro expansion, the assembler performs textual substitution:

  • The 1st actual parameter replaces every occurrence of the 1st dummy parameter in the prototype code.
  • The 2nd actual parameter replaces every occurrence of the 2nd dummy parameter, and so on.
  • The substitution is purely textual — the resulting code must be syntactically valid assembly.

docs.title: Example: MSGGEN Macro (String Generation)
docs.text:
; Definition
%*DEFINE (MSGGEN (LAB, NUM, XYZ))
(
    %LAB%NUM   DB   'HELLO MR. %XYZ'
)

; Call
%MSGGEN (MSG, 1, TAYLOR)

; Expansion
MSG1   DB   'HELLO MR. TAYLOR'

The actual parameters are: LAB='MSG', NUM='1', XYZ='TAYLOR'. The prototype code concatenates %LAB and %NUM to produce the label MSG1, and substitutes %XYZ inside the string literal.

📝 Exam Note: Concatenation of dummy parameters (as in %LAB%NUM) is a key ASM-86 feature. The % prefix is not a modulo operator here — it is the parameter-reference prefix in the macro language.

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slide 5]

docs.title: 2.5 MULTIPLY Macro — Full Example
docs.text:
Goal: Multiply two word operands and store the result. Pushes/pops AX and DX to preserve them.

; Definition
%*DEFINE (MULTIPLY (OPR1, OPR2, RESULT))
(
    PUSH DX
    PUSH AX
    MOV  AX, %OPR1       ; load first operand
    IMUL %OPR2           ; signed multiply: DX:AX = AX × OPR2
    MOV  %RESULT, AX     ; store low word of result
    POP  AX
    POP  DX
)

; Call
%MULTIPLY (CX, VAR, XYZ[BX])

; Expansion
PUSH DX
PUSH AX
MOV  AX, CX             ; OPR1 = CX
IMUL VAR                ; OPR2 = VAR
MOV  XYZ[BX], AX        ; RESULT = XYZ[BX]
POP  AX
POP  DX

Important constraint: The actual parameters must produce syntactically valid instructions after substitution. An invalid operand form (e.g., %MULTIPLY (5, 10, [5]) — immediate as destination) causes an assembler error.

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slide 6]

docs.title: 2.6 Macros Without Parameters
docs.text:
A macro can be defined with no dummy parameters. In this case, the call must also include no parameters. The call form %SAVEREG (no parentheses) is used.

; Definition — no parameters
%*DEFINE (SAVEREG)
(
    PUSH AX
    PUSH BX
    PUSH CX
    PUSH DX
    PUSH SI
    PUSH DI
)

; Call
%SAVEREG

; Expansion
PUSH AX
PUSH BX
PUSH CX
PUSH DX
PUSH SI
PUSH DI

Usage: Write %SAVEREG at the start of any procedure to save all general-purpose registers in one line.

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slide 7]

docs.title: 2.7 Macro Processor Architecture
docs.text:
The assembler can handle macros in two ways:

Approach 1: Include macro expansion in the first pass of the assembler itself.

Approach 2: Use a separate pre-pass (macro processor) before normal assembly:

flowchart TD
    A["Source Code (.ASM with macro definitions and calls)"]
    A --> B["Macro Processor (pre-pass)"]
    B --> C["Expanded Source Code (no macro calls, all expanded)"]
    C --> D["Assembler"]
    D --> E["Object Module (.OBJ)"]

What the macro processor does:

  1. Scans the source for %*DEFINE directives → stores each in a macro-definition table.
  2. Scans for %MacroName calls → retrieves definition from table, substitutes actual parameters, emits the expanded code.
  3. Produces an expanded source file ready for normal assembly.

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slide 8]

docs.title: 2.8 Local Labels — Preventing Name Conflicts
docs.text:
Problem: If a macro contains a label (e.g., NEXT), the first expansion defines NEXT as a label. A second expansion would redefine NEXT — causing an assembly error ("duplicate label").

; PROBLEM: no local labels
%*DEFINE (ABSOL (OPER))
(
    CMP  %OPER, 0
    JGE  %NEXT         ; uses label NEXT
    NEG  %OPER
%NEXT: NOP
)

%ABSOL(VAR)   ; defines label NEXT
%ABSOL(BX)    ; ERROR: NEXT already defined!

Solution: Declare labels as LOCAL in the macro definition. ASM-86 auto-appends a two-digit numeric suffix (starting at 00, incrementing by 1 for each expansion).

docs.title: LOCAL Syntax
docs.text:
%*DEFINE (ABSOL (OPER)) LOCAL NEXT
(
    CMP  %OPER, 0
    JGE  %NEXT
    NEG  %OPER
%NEXT: NOP
)

LOCAL NEXT is attached at the end of the first statement of the macro definition.

docs.title: Two Expansions of ABSOL
docs.text:
; First call: %ABSOL(VAR)          ; Second call: %ABSOL(BX)
CMP  VAR, 0                        CMP  BX, 0
JGE  NEXT00                        JGE  NEXT01
NEG  VAR                           NEG  BX
NEXT00: NOP                        NEXT01: NOP

Each expansion gets a distinct suffix (NEXT00, NEXT01), eliminating collisions.

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slides 9–10]

docs.title: 2.9 Nested Macros — Calling One Macro from Another
docs.text:
A macro call can appear inside another macro's prototype code. This is nested macro expansion.

Rule: All macros used inside a macro definition must be defined before the macro that calls them.

docs.title: Nested Macro Example
docs.text:
; First, define DIF (computes X - Y, result in AX)
%*DEFINE (DIF (X, Y))
(
    MOV AX, %X
    SUB AX, %Y
)

; Then define DIFSQR (computes (OPR1 - OPR2)^2)
%*DEFINE (DIFSQR (OPR1, OPR2, RESULT))
(
    PUSH DX
    PUSH AX
    %DIF (%OPR1, %OPR2)   ; nested call: expands DIF with OPR1 and OPR2
    IMUL AX               ; AX × AX = AX^2  (DX:AX = result)
    MOV  %RESULT, AX
    POP  AX
    POP  DX
)

; Usage
%DIFSQR (V1, V2, ERROR)

; Expands to:
PUSH DX
PUSH AX
MOV  AX, V1
SUB  AX, V2
IMUL AX
MOV  ERROR, AX
POP  AX
POP  DX

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slide 11]

docs.title: 2.10 Macros That Define Other Macros
docs.text:
A macro can be parameterized to generate new macro definitions as its output. This is an advanced technique for creating families of similar operations.

; DEFMAC: generates a macro for a binary operation
%*DEFINE (DEFMAC (MACNAM, OPERATOR))
(
    %*DEFINE (%MACNAM (X, Y, Z))
    (
        PUSH AX
        MOV  AX, %X
        %OPERATOR AX, %Y     ; actual instruction (e.g., SUB, OR)
        MOV  %Z, AX
        POP  AX
    )
)

; Generate two new macros using DEFMAC
%DEFMAC (SUBTRACT, SUB)    ; creates %SUBTRACT macro using SUB instruction
%DEFMAC (LOGOR, OR)        ; creates %LOGOR macro using OR instruction

; Using the generated macro
%SUBTRACT (V1, V2, V3)    ; expands to: PUSH AX; MOV AX,V1; SUB AX,V2; MOV V3,AX; POP AX

Benefit: One DEFMAC call generates an entire family of operation macros (add, sub, and, or, xor, etc.) without writing each one individually.

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slide 12]

docs.title: 3. XLAT — Table Translation Instruction
docs.text: The XLAT instruction provides fast byte-to-byte translation using a lookup table in memory. It is commonly used for character code conversion (e.g., BCD digit → 7-segment display code, ASCII code → custom encoding).

docs.title: Definition: XLAT
docs.text:
Mnemonic: XLAT (or XLATB)

Operation:

\[ AL \leftarrow [BX + AL] \]

Meaning: The byte at memory address BX + AL (in the data segment) is loaded into AL. BX points to the base of the translation table; AL is the index into that table; AL receives the translated value.

Requirements:

  • BX must contain the base address of the translation table.
  • AL must contain the index (0-based) of the byte to translate.
  • The table is in the data segment.

docs.title: XLAT Application: BCD to 7-Segment Display
docs.text:
The table maps decimal digits (0–9) to their 7-segment LED codes:

TABLE   DB  3FH    ; 0 → 7-seg code
        DB  06H    ; 1
        DB  5BH    ; 2
        DB  4FH    ; 3
        DB  66H    ; 4
        DB  6DH    ; 5
        DB  7DH    ; 6
        DB  07H    ; 7
        DB  7FH    ; 8
        DB  6FH    ; 9

Usage:

        LEA       BX, TABLE         ; BX = base of lookup table
        LEA       SI, STG_BCD       ; SI → BCD digit string
        LEA       DI, STG_DISP      ; DI → output display buffer
        CLD
        MOV       CX, LENGTH STG_BCD  ; CX = number of digits
CONVERT:
        LODS      STG_BCD           ; AL = next BCD digit, SI++
        CMP       AL, 9
        JA        INVALID           ; digit > 9 → error
        XLAT      TABLE             ; AL = TABLE[BX + AL] = 7-seg code
        STOS      STG_DISP          ; store display code, DI++
        LOOP      CONVERT

Flow:

  1. LODS reads the next BCD digit into AL.
  2. Validate: if \(\text{AL} > 9\), handle as invalid.
  3. XLAT replaces AL with TABLE[AL] — the corresponding 7-segment code.
  4. STOS writes the translated code to the output buffer.

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slides 14–15]

docs.title: Definition: Interrupt
docs.text:
Meaning: An interrupt is a signal that causes the CPU to temporarily suspend normal program execution, save its state, and execute a special routine (the Interrupt Service Routine or ISR) to handle the event. After the ISR completes, execution resumes from where it was interrupted.

Formal definition: An interrupt is a mechanism for breaking the normal sequential execution of a program in response to an internal or external event, causing the CPU to vector to the appropriate Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) and return to the main program via IRET.

Intuition: Think of it as an emergency signal. The CPU finishes its current instruction, handles the emergency (ISR), and then resumes whatever it was doing — the main program never "knows" it was paused.

flowchart TD
    A["Main Program executing"] --> B{"Interrupt signal?"}
    B -- No --> A
    B -- Yes --> C["Complete current instruction"]
    C --> D["Save FLAGS, CS, IP on stack"]
    D --> E["Load CS:IP from Interrupt Vector Table"]
    E --> F["Execute ISR"]
    F --> G["IRET: restore IP, CS, FLAGS from stack"]
    G --> A

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slides 16–17]

docs.title: 4.2 Types of Interrupts
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    I["Interrupts"] --> H["Hardware Interrupts"]
    I --> S["Software Interrupts"]
    H --> M["Maskable (INTR pin)"]
    H --> N["Non-Maskable (NMI pin)"]
    S --> SW["INT n instruction"]
    S --> D["Divide Error (automatic)"]
    S --> T["Trap / Single Step"]
Type Trigger Source Can be disabled? Hardware — Maskable External signal on INTR pin Yes (by clearing IF flag with CLI) Hardware — Non-Maskable External signal on NMI pin No Software INT n instruction No Internal/Exception Divide by zero, INTO overflow No Single-step (Trap) TF flag set Cleared by hardware on ISR entry

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slides 18–20]

docs.title: 4.3 Sources of Interrupts
docs.text:
The 8086 can be interrupted in four ways:

  1. External signal on NMI or INTR pin — hardware interrupts from external devices (keyboard, timer, disk).
  2. INT n instruction — software-initiated; n is the interrupt type number (0–255).
  3. Error conditions — divide-by-zero or quotient overflow triggers automatic Type 0 interrupt.
  4. Trap interrupt — when the Trap Flag (TF) is set, the CPU generates a Type 1 interrupt after every instruction (used for single-step debugging).

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slide 19]

docs.title: 4.4 The 256 Interrupt Types
docs.text:
The 8086 supports 256 interrupt types (numbered 0–255, or 00H–FFH). They are divided into three groups:

Group Type Numbers Count Description Dedicated 0–4 5 Fixed purposes (divide error, single-step, NMI, breakpoint, overflow) Reserved 5–32 27 Reserved by Intel for future use User-available 33–255 223 Available for DOS services, user ISRs, device drivers

Dedicated Interrupt Details:

Type Name Description 0 Divide Error Generated when DIV/IDIV causes divide-by-zero or quotient overflow 1 Single-Step / Trap Generated after every instruction when TF = 1; used by debuggers 2 NMI Non-Maskable hardware interrupt; used for power failure, critical events 3 Breakpoint Generated by INT 3 (single-byte opcode); used by debuggers to set breakpoints 4 Overflow Generated by INTO instruction when OF = 1

📝 Exam Note: INT 21H (Type 33 = 21H) is the primary DOS service interrupt. INT 21H AH=09H prints a string; INT 21H AH=4CH exits to DOS.

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slides 20, 27–28]

docs.title: 4.5 Interrupt Processing Sequence
docs.text:
When the 8086 acknowledges an interrupt, it performs the following exactly:

Step 1: Finish executing the current instruction.

Step 2: SP ← SP − 2 ; push FLAGS (PSW) onto stack.

Step 3: Clear IF (Interrupt Flag) — disables further maskable interrupts (so no interrupt-within-interrupt for INTR).

Step 4: Clear TF (Trap Flag) — disables single-step mode during ISR.

Step 5: SP ← SP − 2 ; push CS onto stack.

Step 6: SP ← SP − 2 ; push IP onto stack.

Step 7: Read the Interrupt Vector Table at address Type × 4 to get the new CS:IP of the ISR.

Step 8: Load new IP (from Type×4) and new CS (from Type×4 + 2) → jump to ISR.

Summary of stack state at ISR entry:

Stack (growing down):
[SP+4]  FLAGS (original)
[SP+2]  CS (return segment)
[SP+0]  IP (return offset)    ← SP points here

IRET restores the state: 

IP ← pop stack
CS ← pop stack
FLAGS ← pop stack
SP ← SP + 6

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slides 22–23]

docs.title: Definition: Interrupt Vector Table (IVT)
docs.text:
Meaning: A table in the first 1 KB of physical memory (addresses 00000H to 003FFH) that stores the starting address (CS:IP) of every ISR. Each entry is 4 bytes: IP (2 bytes) followed by CS (2 bytes).

Formula for IVT entry address:

\[ \text{IVT entry address} = \text{Interrupt Type} \times 4 \]

Example: For Type 02H (NMI):

\[ \text{Address} = 02H \times 4 = 00008H \]

Memory layout at address 00008H:

Address Content Meaning 00008H IP Low byte Return IP (low) of NMI ISR 00009H IP High byte Return IP (high) of NMI ISR 0000AH CS Low byte CS (low) of NMI ISR 0000BH CS High byte CS (high) of NMI ISR

IVT Layout:

Address Range Interrupt Types Group 00000H–0000FH Types 0–3 Dedicated (4 × 4 bytes) 00010H–00013H Type 4 Dedicated 00014H–0007FH Types 5–31 Reserved 00080H–003FFH Types 32–255 User-available

📝 Exam Note: The entire IVT occupies exactly \(256 \times 4 = 1024\) bytes = 1 KB.

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slides 24–27]

docs.title: 4.7 Interrupt Priority
docs.text:
When multiple interrupt sources compete simultaneously, the 8086 handles them in the following priority order (highest to lowest):

Priority Source Highest Divide error / INT n / INTO (software/internal) ↓ NMI (Non-Maskable Interrupt) ↓ INTR (Maskable hardware interrupt) Lowest Single-step / Trap (TF)

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slide 29]

docs.title: 4.8 Complete Example: Divide Error ISR
docs.text: The following two-module example installs a custom ISR for Type 0 (divide error) and uses it to gracefully handle division-by-zero cases in a scaling loop.

docs.title: Main Module
docs.text:
DATA SEGMENT WORD PUBLIC
    INPUT_VALUES  DW  0035H, 0855H, 2011H, 1359H  ; 4 values to scale
    SCALED_VALUES DB  4 DUP(0)                     ; results
    SCALE_FACTOR  DB  09                           ; divisor
    BAD_DIV_FLAG  DB  0                            ; flag set by ISR on error
DATA ENDS

STACK_SEG SEGMENT STACK
    DW 100 DUP (0)
    TOP_STACK LABEL WORD
STACK_SEG ENDS

PUBLIC BAD_DIV_FLAG                ; make flag accessible to other modules

INT_PROC SEGMENT WORD PUBLIC
    EXTRN BAD_DIV:FAR              ; ISR defined in another module
INT_PROC ENDS

CODE SEGMENT WORD PUBLIC
    ASSUME CS:CODE, DS:DATA, SS:STACK_SEG
START:
    MOV AX, STACK_SEG
    MOV SS, AX
    MOV SP, OFFSET TOP_STACK

    MOV AX, DATA
    MOV DS, AX

    ; Install the divide-error ISR into IVT (Type 0 = address 00000H)
    MOV AX, 0000H
    MOV ES, AX
    MOV WORD PTR ES:0002H, SEG BAD_DIV    ; store CS of ISR at IVT+2
    MOV WORD PTR ES:0000H, OFFSET BAD_DIV ; store IP of ISR at IVT+0

    MOV SI, OFFSET INPUT_VALUES
    MOV BX, OFFSET SCALED_VALUES
    MOV CX, 0004H                         ; process 4 values
NEXT:
    MOV AX, [SI]
    DIV SCALE_FACTOR                      ; AX / SCALE_FACTOR → if div error, ISR runs
    CMP BAD_DIV_FLAG, 01
    JNE OK                                ; no error → use quotient
    MOV BYTE PTR [BX], 00                 ; error → store 0 as result
    JMP SKIP
OK:
    MOV [BX], AL                          ; store quotient (byte result)
SKIP:
    MOV BAD_DIV_FLAG, 0                   ; reset flag for next iteration
    ADD SI, 02
    INC BX
    LOOP NEXT

STOP: NOP
CODE ENDS
END START

docs.title: ISR Module (Divide Error Handler)
docs.text:
DATA SEGMENT WORD PUBLIC
    EXTRN BAD_DIV_FLAG:BYTE         ; flag defined in main module
DATA ENDS

PUBLIC BAD_DIV
INT_PROC SEGMENT WORD PUBLIC
BAD_DIV PROC FAR
    ASSUME CS:INT_PROC, DS:DATA
    PUSH AX                          ; preserve all used registers
    PUSH DS
    MOV AX, DATA
    MOV DS, AX
    MOV BAD_DIV_FLAG, 01             ; signal that divide error occurred
    POP DS
    POP AX
    IRET                             ; restore FLAGS, CS, IP → return to main
BAD_DIV ENDP
INT_PROC ENDS
END

How it works:

flowchart TD
    A["Main program: DIV SCALE_FACTOR"] --> B{"Divide error?"}
    B -- No --> C["Continue: store AL in SCALED_VALUES"]
    B -- Yes --> D["CPU pushes FLAGS, CS, IP"]
    D --> E["CPU reads IVT[0]: BAD_DIV address"]
    E --> F["Execute BAD_DIV ISR"]
    F --> G["Set BAD_DIV_FLAG = 01"]
    G --> H["IRET: restore FLAGS, CS, IP"]
    H --> I["Return to instruction AFTER DIV"]
    I --> J["Check BAD_DIV_FLAG → store 0 as result"]

📝 Exam Note: The ISR must end with IRET, not RET. IRET restores FLAGS in addition to CS and IP, re-enabling interrupts (IF) and restoring the original processor state.

[Source: 8086_Macros and Interrupt.pdf, Slides 30–31]

docs.title: 5. Abbreviation / Acronym Index
docs.text: Abbr. Full Form Brief Meaning ISR Interrupt Service Routine Code that executes in response to an interrupt IVT Interrupt Vector Table Table at 00000H–003FFH storing ISR addresses IF Interrupt Flag Flag bit; IF=1 enables maskable interrupts TF Trap Flag Flag bit; TF=1 causes single-step (Type 1) interrupt after each instruction NMI Non-Maskable Interrupt Hardware interrupt that cannot be disabled INTR Interrupt Request Maskable hardware interrupt pin PSW Program Status Word Synonym for the FLAGS register BCD Binary Coded Decimal Representation where each decimal digit is encoded in 4 bits IRET Interrupt Return Instruction to return from ISR (pops IP, CS, FLAGS) XLAT Translate Instruction: AL ← [BX + AL] (table lookup) ASM Assembler / Assembly The assembler tool or the assembly language OF Overflow Flag Set when signed arithmetic overflows CLI Clear Interrupt Flag Instruction: IF ← 0 (disable maskable interrupts) STI Set Interrupt Flag Instruction: IF ← 1 (enable maskable interrupts) INTO Interrupt on Overflow Software interrupt instruction; generates Type 4 if OF=1

docs.title: IVT Entry Address Formula
docs.text: \[ \text{IVT Address} = \text{Type Number} \times 4 \]

docs.title: IVT Size
docs.text: \[ 256 \text{ types} \times 4 \text{ bytes/type} = 1024 \text{ bytes} = 1 \text{ KB} \]

docs.title: XLAT Operation
docs.text: \[ AL \leftarrow DS:[BX + AL] \]

docs.title: Macro Expansion (No Parameters)
docs.text: %MacroName  →  (Prototype code, verbatim copy)

docs.title: Macro Expansion (With Parameters)
docs.text: %MacroName(a1, a2, ..., an)  →  (Prototype code with dummy1→a1, dummy2→a2, ..., dummyn→an)

docs.title: 7. Definition Sheet
docs.text:
• Macro: A named block of prototype code that the assembler (or pre-processor) expands inline at each call site; no CALL/RET linkage overhead.
  • Macro Definition: The %*DEFINE block specifying the macro name, dummy parameters, and prototype code.
  • Macro Call: A %MacroName(actuals) statement that triggers expansion.
  • Macro Expansion: The textual substitution of actual parameters for dummy parameters, producing inline assembly code.
  • Local Label: A label in a macro definition declared with LOCAL; ASM-86 appends a unique numeric suffix to each expansion to prevent duplicate-label errors.
  • Nested Macro: A macro whose prototype code contains a call to another macro.
  • Interrupt: A CPU mechanism that temporarily suspends normal execution to handle an event, saving FLAGS, CS, and IP on the stack before vectoring to the ISR.
  • ISR (Interrupt Service Routine): The routine that handles an interrupt; must end with IRET.
  • IVT (Interrupt Vector Table): The 1 KB table at physical addresses 00000H–003FFH storing the CS:IP pairs of all 256 ISRs.
  • IRET: Instruction that ends an ISR; restores IP, CS, and FLAGS from the stack.
  • NMI (Non-Maskable Interrupt): Hardware interrupt on NMI pin; cannot be disabled by clearing IF.
  • Maskable Interrupt (INTR): Hardware interrupt that can be disabled by clearing IF (CLI).
  • Divide Error (Type 0): Automatically generated when DIV/IDIV results in quotient too large to fit in the destination register or divides by zero.
  • Single-Step (Type 1): Interrupt generated after each instruction when TF = 1; used by debuggers.
  • XLAT: Table translation instruction; replaces AL with the byte at address [BX + AL].

docs.title: Important Concepts
docs.text:
• Macro vs procedure: code expansion vs CALL/RET linkage
  • How dummy/actual parameter substitution works (first→first, second→second, textual)
  • Local labels in macros: why needed, how ASM-86 implements them (auto-suffix)
  • The macro processor pre-pass approach
  • Nested and macro-generating macros
  • Interrupt processing sequence (7 steps): push FLAGS, clear IF, clear TF, push CS, push IP, read IVT, jump to ISR
  • IRET vs RET: IRET also restores FLAGS
  • IVT address calculation: Type × 4
  • The 3 groups of interrupts (dedicated 0–4, reserved 5–32, user 33–255)
  • Dedicated interrupts and their types (0=divide, 1=single-step, 2=NMI, 3=breakpoint, 4=overflow)
  • XLAT operation: AL ← [BX + AL]

docs.title: Important Definitions
docs.text:
• Macro expansion: inline substitution of prototype code with actual parameters for dummy parameters; no linkage overhead
  • IVT: 1 KB table at 00000H–003FFH; each entry is 4 bytes (IP, CS) for the ISR of one interrupt type
  • IRET: pops IP, CS, FLAGS — restoring full CPU state at the point of interruption

docs.title: Important Comparisons
docs.text: Feature Macro Procedure Code in memory Repeated at each call site Written once Execution overhead None CALL + RET Parameter mechanism Textual substitution Registers / stack Label conflicts Possible (use LOCAL) No (scope is proc) Best for Short, repeated code Long, frequently reused code Feature INT n CALL :------ :---- :--- Saves to stack FLAGS + CS + IP IP (NEAR) or CS+IP (FAR) Vector lookup IVT at Type×4 Direct address Return instruction IRET RET Can be masked No (software INT always runs) N/A

docs.title: Potential Exam Questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between a macro and a procedure? When would you use each?
  2. Write an ASM-86 macro PUSH_ALL that pushes AX, BX, CX, DX, SI, DI onto the stack.
  3. Define the macro ADD_OP(A, B, C) that computes C = A + B using the ADD instruction.
  4. What is a local label in a macro? Why is it needed? Show an example of two expansions with LOCAL labels.
  5. What is the purpose of the macro pre-processor? Draw the flow from source to machine code with a macro pre-processor.
  6. Write a nested macro example: define NEG_OP(X) and use it inside ABS_OP(X).
  7. Explain the complete 8086 interrupt processing sequence step-by-step.
  8. What is the Interrupt Vector Table? Where is it located? How is the ISR address found for interrupt Type N?
  9. Calculate the IVT address for interrupt Type 21H (DOS). What are the four bytes stored there?
  10. What is the difference between INTR and NMI? How can you disable INTR?
  11. What is the difference between IRET and RET? Why must an ISR use IRET?
  12. List the five dedicated interrupt types (0–4) with their names and trigger conditions.
  13. Explain the XLAT instruction. Write a code fragment that uses XLAT to convert a single BCD digit to a 7-segment code.
  14. Write a complete ISR for a divide-error handler that sets a flag variable and returns with IRET.
  15. What is the difference between maskable and non-maskable interrupts?

docs.title: Chapter: 8086 Modular Programming, Linking, Relocation & Segment Combination
docs.text: Course: Microprocessors (MI) — Semester 5 Primary Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf (48 slides, Dr. Pimal Khanpara) Files Integrated: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf

docs.title: 1. Chapter Overview
docs.text:
As programs grow in complexity, writing everything in a single source file becomes unmanageable. Modular programming divides the program into smaller, independently understandable and testable modules, each performing one well-defined task.

Once modules are written and assembled separately, they must be linked together to form an executable. This chapter covers:

  • Why modular programming matters and the six-step development process
  • How separately assembled object modules are linked into a load module
  • Segment combination types: PUBLIC, COMMON, STACK, AT, MEMORY
  • Alignment directives: EVEN, ALIGN
  • Naming directives: LABEL, NAME, TITLE
  • External identifier resolution: EXTRN and PUBLIC declarations
  • How and when offsets and segment addresses are inserted (assembler vs linker vs loader)
  • Relocation — assigning final segment addresses
  • Complete multi-module example with FAR jumps and segment register setup

docs.title: 2. Why Modular Programming?
docs.text:
Real programs are too large and complex to write as a single monolithic source file. Modular programming breaks the problem into pieces:

Benefit Explanation Comprehensibility Each module is small enough to understand independently Parallel development Different modules assigned to different programmers Orderly testing Each module can be tested in isolation Documentation Smaller units are easier to document Localized modifications A bug fix or change affects only one module Library reuse Common tasks stored in libraries and reused by multiple programs

Analogy to hardware design: Break a large circuit into sub-modules (ALU, registers, bus controller), implement each, then integrate — the same philosophy applies to software modules.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 2, 6]

docs.title: 3. Six-Step Program Development Process
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    S1["1. Precisely state what the program must do"]
    S2["2. Break the overall problem into tasks (decompose)"]
    S3["3. Define what each task does and how it communicates with others"]
    S4["4. Write tasks as ASM modules; connect them to form the program"]
    S5["5. Debug and test"]
    S6["6. Document the program"]
    S1 --> S2 --> S3 --> S4 --> S5 --> S6

Key point: Step 3 is critical — defining the interface (what data a module expects, what it produces, and how it communicates) before writing any code prevents integration problems later.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slide 3]

docs.title: 4. Module Hierarchy and Structure
docs.text:
A modular program is organized as a hierarchy with a single main module at the top:

flowchart TD
    MAIN["Main Module"] --> A["Module A"]
    MAIN --> B["Module B"]
    A --> C["Module C"]
    A --> D["Module D"]
    B --> D
  • A submodule may be subordinate to more than one module (Module D is shared by A and B).
  • The main module contains the program's entry point (the first instruction to execute).

docs.title: Simple Example: INPUT / PROCESS / OUTPUT
docs.text:
MAIN
          /       \
       INPUT     PROCESS
                    |
                  OUTPUT
  • INPUT — obtains data from user or memory
  • PROCESS — performs computation
  • OUTPUT — displays or stores result

Each module has exactly one well-defined responsibility.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 4–5]

docs.title: 5. Module Design: Control and Data Coupling
docs.text:
When designing modules:

  • Control coupling should be kept simple — ideally, a module is entered at one point and exited at one point (no messy jumps in/out).
  • Data coupling should be minimized — modules should share only the data they absolutely need; hidden dependencies between modules cause maintenance nightmares.

Three ways ASM-86 supports modularization:

  1. Data structuring — data can be organized so multiple modules can access it.
  2. Subroutines — sections of code exposed as procedures callable from other modules.
  3. Macros — code that appears as a single statement and accepts programmer-supplied arguments.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slide 7]

docs.title: 6. Linking and Relocation — Why Needed?
docs.text: When modules are assembled separately, each object module contains machine code with incomplete addresses — the assembler cannot fill in addresses that depend on where other modules will be placed in memory. The linker and loader complete this process.

docs.title: Definition: Object Module
docs.text: Meaning: The output of the assembler for one source module. Contains machine code with unresolved (placeholder) addresses for external references and segment addresses.

docs.title: Definition: Load Module
docs.text: Meaning: The output of the linker. Contains machine code with all addresses resolved and all object modules combined, ready to be loaded into memory and executed.

docs.title: Definition: Relocation
docs.text:
Meaning: The process of assigning final physical segment addresses to relocatable segments. Performed by the linker/locator after it determines where each segment will be placed in memory.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 8, 36]

docs.title: 7. Creation and Execution Pipeline
docs.text:
The complete journey from source code to execution:

flowchart TD
    SRC1["Module1.ASM"] --> ASM1["Assembler"]
    SRC2["Module2.ASM"] --> ASM2["Assembler"]
    LIB["Libraries (.LIB)"] --> LNK
    ASM1 --> OBJ1["Module1.OBJ"]
    ASM2 --> OBJ2["Module2.OBJ"]
    OBJ1 --> LNK["Linker / Locator"]
    OBJ2 --> LNK
    LNK --> LOAD["Load Module (.EXE / .COM)"]
    OS["OS / I/O Drivers"] --> EXEC
    LOAD --> LDR["Loader"]
    LDR --> EXEC["Execution in Memory"]

Pipeline stages explained:

Stage Tool Input Output Assembly Assembler (ASM-86) Source .ASM files Object .OBJ files Linking Linker (LINK-86) .OBJ files + libraries Partially resolved load module Location/Relocation Locator (LOC-86) Linked module Final load module with absolute addresses Loading Loader (OS) Load module Program in memory, ready to run

Note: In practice on DOS systems, the linker and locator are combined. The assembler cannot fill in segment addresses because those depend on where all modules are placed — only the linker knows the final layout.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 8–10]

docs.title: 8. What the Linker/Loader Must Do
docs.text:
The linker must:

  1. Find all object modules named in the linker command.
  2. Assign positions to all segments from all object modules (determine the load layout).
  3. Fill in offsets that could not be determined by the assembler (e.g., offsets of external symbols).
  4. Fill in segment addresses (relocation — load all segment-address references).
  5. Load the program into memory for execution.

The linker also produces a memory map showing the starting address and length of each combined segment in the load module.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slide 11]

docs.title: 9. Two-Module Program: Assembly → Linking → Loading
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    M1["MODULE1.ASM"] --> A1["Assembler"] --> OBJ1["MODULE1.OBJ"]
    M2["MODULE2.ASM"] --> A2["Assembler"] --> OBJ2["MODULE2.OBJ"]
    OBJ1 --> LNK["LINKER"]
    OBJ2 --> LNK
    LNK --> LM["LOAD MODULE"]
    LM --> LDR["LOADER"]
    LDR --> MEM["MEMORY (Execution)"]

Key rule: The main module (containing the entry point) ends with END <entry_label>. All other modules end with just END (no entry label operand).

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 12–13]

docs.title: 10. Segment Combination
docs.text: ASM-86 provides combine types as modifiers on the SEGMENT directive that control how the linker handles segments with the same name from different object modules.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
SegmentName  SEGMENT  [alignment]  [combine-type]  [class]
    ; segment contents
SegmentName  ENDS

Rules:

  • Segments with different names cannot be combined.
  • Same-named segments with no combine-type cause a linker error.
  • The combine-type determines the linkage behavior.

docs.title: 10.1 PUBLIC — Concatenate Segments
docs.text:
Behaviour: Same-named PUBLIC segments from different modules are joined end-to-end (concatenated) into one larger segment. The total size is the sum of all individual sizes.

; Module 1
CODE SEGMENT PUBLIC
    ; 20 words of code
CODE ENDS

; Module 2
CODE SEGMENT PUBLIC
    ; 30 words of code
CODE ENDS

; After linking:
; ONE CODE SEGMENT of 50 words (20 + 30)

Benefit of PUBLIC for code: When multiple code sections are concatenated into one CODE segment, CS does not need to change as execution passes between instruction groups. Intersegment (FAR) branches become intrasegment (NEAR) branches — more efficient.

Benefit of PUBLIC for data: Multiple data sections are concatenated into one larger DATA segment.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 15–16, 18]

docs.title: 10.2 COMMON — Overlay Segments
docs.text:
Behaviour: Same-named COMMON segments all start at the same address — they overlay each other. The combined size is the size of the longest segment.

; Module 1
DATA SEGMENT COMMON
    ; 100 bytes
DATA ENDS

; Module 2
DATA SEGMENT COMMON
    ; 150 bytes
DATA ENDS

; After linking:
; ONE DATA region at the SAME start address
; Combined size = 150 bytes (longest)
; NOT 100 + 150 = 250 bytes

Use case: COMMON creates a shared memory pool accessible by multiple modules simultaneously. Variables defined at the same offset in two COMMON segments of the same name will overlap (occupy the same memory location).

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 15, 17]

docs.title: 10.3 STACK — Add Lengths
docs.text:
Behaviour: Same-named STACK segments are concatenated like PUBLIC, but each module contributes to a shared stack. Total stack size = sum of all individual stack sizes.

; Module 1
STACK_SEG SEGMENT STACK
    DW 20 DUP(?)     ; 20 words = 40 bytes
STACK_SEG ENDS

; Module 2
STACK_SEG SEGMENT STACK
    DW 30 DUP(?)     ; 30 words = 60 bytes
STACK_SEG ENDS

; After linking:
; Total stack = 50 words = 100 bytes

Purpose: Allows each module to specify how much stack it needs, and the linker builds one unified stack of the combined size.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 15, 19]

docs.title: 10.4 AT — Absolute Segment Address
docs.text:
Behaviour: AT expression fixes the segment at a specific physical address specified by the programmer. Variables and labels in AT segments have absolute addresses (set by programmer/assembler, not relocated by linker).

IOBUF SEGMENT AT 0B800H      ; fixed at video memory address
    ; ... screen buffer data ...
IOBUF ENDS

Use cases:

  • I/O port buffers at known fixed addresses
  • Special memory-mapped hardware registers
  • BIOS data area at fixed locations

Contrast: Variables in non-AT segments are relocatable — their final segment address is determined by the linker. AT segments are absolute — the programmer specifies the exact location.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 15, 21]

docs.title: 10.5 MEMORY — Highest Address Segment
docs.text:
Behaviour: The MEMORY segment is placed at the highest address in the load module (at the end). If multiple MEMORY segments are linked, only the first gets true MEMORY treatment; subsequent ones are treated as COMMON.

Use case: Placing an overlay area or a data buffer at the top of the program's memory space.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 15, 21]

docs.title: 10.6 Combine-Type Comparison Table
docs.text:
Combine-Type Combined Size Address Relationship Use Case PUBLIC Sum of all sizes Concatenated end-to-end Shared code or data, one segment COMMON Largest individual size All start at same address Shared variable pool (overlapping) STACK Sum of all sizes Concatenated (like PUBLIC) Shared stack; each module contributes AT expr As declared Fixed at expr (absolute) Hardware-mapped I/O, BIOS areas MEMORY As declared At highest address Overlay area, top-of-memory buffer

Quick numerical comparison:

Scenario Module 1 Module 2 PUBLIC result COMMON result STACK result Size 20 units 30 units 50 units 30 units 50 units

📝 Exam Note: STACK behaves the same as PUBLIC in terms of size (sum), but it specifically forms the unified stack segment.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 15, 20]

docs.title: 11. Segment Alignment
docs.text:
Alignment controls the boundary at which a segment begins in memory.

  • The default alignment places a segment at an address divisible by 16 (paragraph boundary).
    • Example boundaries: 1000H, 1010H, 1020H, 1030H, …
  • The alignment is specified before the combine-type in the SEGMENT directive.

Do not confuse segment alignment with item alignment (EVEN/ALIGN — see next section). Segment alignment applies to where the whole segment starts; item alignment applies to where a variable within a segment starts.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 18, 23]

docs.title: 12.1 EVEN Directive
docs.text:
EVEN ensures that the next item in the segment starts at an even byte address (a 2-byte boundary). If the current address is already even, no padding is needed. If odd, one padding byte is inserted.

A  DB  11H       ; A starts at offset 1000H (1 byte)
EVEN             ; next item must be at even address → 1001H is odd → insert 1 byte padding
B  DW  1234H     ; B starts at offset 1002H (word-aligned)

Memory layout:

Offset Content Label 1000H 11H A 1001H padding (e.g., NOP or 00H) — 1002H 34H B (low byte) 1003H 12H B (high byte)

Why important: The 8086 accesses words faster at even addresses (one bus cycle instead of two for odd-addressed words).

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slide 24]

docs.title: 12.2 ALIGN Directive
docs.text:
ALIGN n ensures the next item starts at an address that is a multiple of n bytes (where n is typically 2, 4, or 16). The assembler inserts padding bytes as needed.

ALIGN 2          ; next item on 2-byte boundary

EVEN and ALIGN 2 are equivalent.

Note: EVEN and ALIGN are assembler directives — they generate padding in the object file but are not executed as 8086 instructions.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slide 25]

docs.title: 13.1 LABEL Directive
docs.text:
LABEL gives a symbolic name and type to the current location in a segment without allocating any new memory.

VALUE   DW   1234H      ; allocates 2 bytes at current offset
NEXT    LABEL WORD      ; NEXT = name for the next address after VALUE; no memory allocated

LABEL:

  • Gives a name and type to a position
  • Does not allocate new memory

Use cases:

  • Referencing a stack position (e.g., TOS LABEL WORD at the end of a stack segment)
  • Providing alternative types to the same memory location

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slide 26]

docs.title: 13.2 NAME Directive
docs.text:
NAME MYPROGRAM

Assigns a name to the object module. Used for linker identification. Not an executed instruction.

docs.title: 13.3 TITLE Directive
docs.text:
TITLE 8086 Modular Programming

Sets the title string printed at the top of each page of the assembler's listing output. Useful for documentation. Not an executed instruction.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slide 27]

docs.title: 14. External Identifiers: EXTRN and PUBLIC
docs.text:
When multiple modules are linked together, one module may need to access a variable or procedure defined in a different module. ASM-86 provides two directives to manage this:

Directive Meaning Module Usage Context EXTRN Identifier:Type "I need this identifier from another module" References the identifier but does not define it PUBLIC Identifier "I provide this identifier to other modules" Defines the identifier and makes it visible externally

Symmetry rule: For each EXTRN X in one module, there must be a PUBLIC X in exactly one other module. The linker matches them.

flowchart LR
    M1["Module 1
EXTRN VAR1:WORD"] -- "needs VAR1" --> M2["Module 2
PUBLIC VAR1
VAR1 DW ?"]
    M1 -- "provides LAB1" --> M3["Module 3
EXTRN LAB1:NEAR"]
    M1pu["Module 1
PUBLIC LAB1"]

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 28–29]

docs.title: 14.1 EXTRN and PUBLIC Syntax
docs.text:
EXTRN  Identifier:Type, Identifier:Type, ...
PUBLIC Identifier, Identifier, ...

External type specifiers:

Category Type keywords Variable BYTE, WORD, DWORD Label / Procedure NEAR, FAR

Examples:

; Declaring external variables
EXTRN VAR1:WORD, VAR2:BYTE, PTR3:DWORD

; Declaring external labels
EXTRN SUBROUTINE:NEAR, FARPROC:FAR

; Making local identifiers public
PUBLIC VAR1, LAB1, MYFUNC

📝 Exam Note: The assembler needs the type of each external identifier to generate correct machine code (e.g., a BYTE access generates an 8-bit instruction; a WORD access generates a 16-bit instruction). EXTRN is purely a declaration — it does not create or allocate the identifier.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 30–32]

docs.title: 14.2 Linker External Reference Resolution
docs.text:
The linker matches each EXTRN declaration with a PUBLIC declaration. If no match is found, the linker reports an Unresolved External error.

Example of linker error:

; Module 1
EXTRN VAR4:WORD          ; declares need for VAR4

; Module 2
VAR4 DW ?                ; defines VAR4 in memory
; BUT: no PUBLIC VAR4   → LINKER ERROR: unresolved external VAR4

Fix:

; Module 2
PUBLIC VAR4
VAR4 DW ?

Important note: A PUBLIC symbol that is never referenced by any EXTRN does not cause an error — it is simply unused.

flowchart TD
    E["EXTRN VAR4:WORD in Module 1"] --> S["Linker searches all modules for PUBLIC VAR4"]
    S --> F{"Found?"}
    F -- Yes --> R["Resolve: fill in address of VAR4"]
    F -- No --> ERR["LINKER ERROR: Unresolved External"]

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 33–35]

docs.title: 15. Address Insertion: What Is Known When?
docs.text:
Different parts of an address (offset and segment address) become available at different stages of the build pipeline:

Address component Determined by When Offset of a local variable/label Assembler During assembly of its module Offset of an external variable/label Linker During linking Segment address of any segment Linker/Locator During relocation

docs.title: Example: Address Analysis
docs.text:
DATA_SEG SEGMENT
    POINTER  DD  VAR2         ; 4-byte far pointer to VAR2 (external)
    VAR1     DW  2            ; local variable
DATA_SEG ENDS

EXTRA SEGMENT
    VAR2  DW  2               ; another variable (may be external)
EXTRA ENDS

CODE_SEG SEGMENT
    ASSUME CS:CODE_SEG, DS:DATA_SEG, ES:EXTRA
    MOV AX, DATA_SEG          ; segment address → must be filled by linker
    MOV DS, AX
    DEC VAR1                  ; VAR1 is local → offset inserted by assembler
    LES DI, POINTER           ; POINTER is local → offset by assembler; VAR2's address in linker
    ADD BX, ES:[DI]
    JMP FAR PTR LAB           ; FAR jump → both segment and offset of LAB from linker
CODE_SEG ENDS

What the assembler CAN fill: The offset of local VAR1 and the offset of local POINTER. What the linker MUST fill: The segment address of DATA_SEG in MOV AX, DATA_SEG; the segment and offset of external VAR2 in POINTER DD VAR2; the target of JMP FAR PTR LAB if LAB is external.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 37, 40–41]

docs.title: 16. Physical Address Calculation
docs.text:
The 8086 uses a segmented memory model. Every logical address consists of a Segment (16-bit) and an Offset (16-bit). The physical address is:

\[ \text{Physical Address} = \text{Segment} \times 10H + \text{Offset} \] \[ = \text{Segment} \times 16 + \text{Offset} \]

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Given:

  • Segment = 1234H
  • Offset = 0050H
\[ \text{Physical Address} = 1234H \times 10H + 0050H = 12340H + 0050H = 12390H \]

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slide 38]

docs.title: 17. Relocation — Assigning Final Segment Addresses
docs.text:
During assembly, the assembler does not know the final segment addresses. It uses a placeholder offset (e.g., VAR1 offset = 0010H) and notes that the segment address is unknown. The linker/locator performs relocation:

  1. Linker determines the layout of all segments in memory.
  2. Assigns each segment's final base address.
  3. Updates all segment-address references in the code.

docs.title: Relocation Example
docs.text:
Stage VAR1 knowledge Assembly Offset = 0010H; segment = unknown After linking / locating DATA segment placed at 2500H Final logical address VAR1 = 2500H:0010H Physical address \(2500H \times 10H + 0010H = 25010H\)

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slide 39]

docs.title: 18. Accessing External Variables: Segment Register Setup
docs.text:
Knowing that a variable is external (EXTRN) is not enough at runtime. The appropriate segment register must be loaded with the variable's segment address before the variable is accessed.

; Correct: load ES before accessing external VAR
MOV AX, SEG VAR       ; SEG operator → segment address of VAR (filled by linker)
MOV ES, AX            ; ES now holds the segment where VAR lives
ADD DX, ES:VAR        ; access VAR through ES

Critical distinction:

  • ASSUME ES:EXTDATA tells the assembler to associate ES with the EXTDATA segment — it is a declaration, not an instruction.
  • MOV AX, SEG VAR; MOV ES, AX is the runtime code that actually loads ES.
  • EXTRN does not automatically load any segment register.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 42–43, 47]

docs.title: 19. Complete Multi-Module Example
docs.text: This example shows three modules linked together: Module 1 (main), Module 2 (provides VAR1), Module 3 (provides VAR2 and OUTPUT).

docs.title: Module 1 — Main Program
docs.text:
EXTRN VAR1:WORD, VAR2:WORD, OUTPUT:FAR   ; declare external needs

LOCAL_DATA SEGMENT
    VAR3  DW  ?                          ; local variable
LOCAL_DATA ENDS

CODE SEGMENT
    ASSUME CS:CODE, DS:LOCAL_DATA
START:
    MOV AX, LOCAL_DATA
    MOV DS, AX                           ; DS → local data segment

    MOV BX, VAR3                         ; access local variable (DS:VAR3)

    MOV AX, SEG VAR2                     ; get segment address of external VAR2
    MOV ES, AX                           ; ES → segment containing VAR2
    MOV BX, ES:VAR2                      ; access external VAR2 through ES

    JMP OUTPUT                           ; FAR jump to external routine
CODE ENDS
END START

docs.title: Module 2 — Provides VAR1
docs.text:
PUBLIC VAR1                    ; make VAR1 available to other modules

EXTDATA1 SEGMENT
    VAR1  DW  ?                ; the actual storage for VAR1
EXTDATA1 ENDS
END

docs.title: Module 3 — Provides VAR2 and OUTPUT routine
docs.text:
PUBLIC VAR2                    ; make VAR2 available
EXTDATA2 SEGMENT
    VAR2  DW  ?
EXTDATA2 ENDS

PUBLIC OUTPUT                  ; make OUTPUT label available
ROUTINE SEGMENT
OUTPUT LABEL FAR               ; FAR label = entry point for far jumps
    ; ... output code ...
ROUTINE ENDS
END

docs.title: Cross-Reference Table
docs.text:
EXTRN in Module 1 Matched PUBLIC Defined in EXTRN VAR1:WORD PUBLIC VAR1 Module 2 EXTRN VAR2:WORD PUBLIC VAR2 Module 3 EXTRN OUTPUT:FAR PUBLIC OUTPUT Module 3

Key points:

  • DS is loaded for LOCAL_DATA (local segment).
  • Before accessing VAR2, ES is explicitly loaded using SEG VAR2.
  • JMP OUTPUT is a FAR jump; both CS and IP are provided by the linker.

[Source: 8086_Modular_Programming_Segment_Combination.pdf, Slides 44–46, 48]

docs.title: 20. Abbreviation / Acronym Index
docs.text: Abbr. Full Form Brief Meaning ASM Assembler / Assembly Language Tool that translates assembly source to object code OBJ Object Module Output of assembler; machine code with unresolved references EXE Executable Load module ready for execution DS Data Segment Segment register for data ES Extra Segment Extra segment register (for additional data segments) CS Code Segment Segment register for code SS Stack Segment Segment register for stack SP Stack Pointer Points to top of stack BP Base Pointer Used to access stack frame NEAR Near (same segment) Call/jump within the same segment FAR Far (different segment) Call/jump across segments EXTRN External Directive declaring an identifier defined in another module PUBLIC Public Directive making an identifier available to other modules IVT Interrupt Vector Table Table of ISR addresses (for interrupt chapter context) LOC Locator Tool that assigns final physical addresses (relocation)

docs.title: Physical Address Calculation
docs.text: \[ \text{Physical Address} = \text{Segment Register} \times 10H + \text{Offset} \] \[ = \text{Segment} \times 16_{10} + \text{Offset} \]

docs.title: IVT Entry (for context)
docs.text: \[ \text{IVT entry address for type } N = N \times 4 \]

docs.title: Combine-Type Size Rules
docs.text: \[ \text{PUBLIC size} = \sum \text{all individual sizes (sum)} \] \[ \text{COMMON size} = \max(\text{all individual sizes (largest)}) \] \[ \text{STACK size} = \sum \text{all individual sizes (sum)} \]

docs.title: 22. Definition Sheet
docs.text:
• Modular programming: Dividing a complex program into smaller, independently developed and testable modules, each performing one well-defined task.
  • Object module: Output of the assembler for one source file; contains machine code with placeholder (unresolved) addresses for external references and segment addresses.
  • Load module: Output of the linker; all object modules combined with all addresses resolved; ready for execution.
  • Linker: Tool that combines object modules, resolves external references, and assigns relative positions to all segments.
  • Locator/Loader: Assigns final physical (absolute) addresses to segments (relocation) and loads the program into memory.
  • Relocation: The process of updating segment-address references in the object code after the linker determines the final memory layout.
  • PUBLIC (directive): Declares that the following identifiers (variables or labels) in this module are visible to other linked modules.
  • EXTRN (directive): Declares that the following identifiers (with their types) are defined in another linked module; the linker will resolve them.
  • Unresolved external: A linker error when an EXTRN identifier has no matching PUBLIC declaration in any of the linked modules.
  • Segment combine type: A modifier (PUBLIC, COMMON, STACK, AT, MEMORY) on the SEGMENT directive that controls how same-named segments from different modules are merged by the linker.
  • PUBLIC (combine type): Join same-named segments end-to-end; combined size = sum.
  • COMMON (combine type): Overlay same-named segments at the same start address; combined size = largest.
  • STACK (combine type): Join same-named stack segments; combined size = sum (forms one unified stack).
  • AT (combine type): Fix segment at a specific absolute address; variables are not relocatable.
  • MEMORY (combine type): Place segment at the highest address in the load module.
  • EVEN directive: Insert padding to align the next item to an even (2-byte) boundary; no new memory allocated for the EVEN itself.
  • ALIGN n directive: Insert padding to align the next item to an n-byte boundary.
  • LABEL directive: Give a symbolic name and type to the current location; no memory allocated.
  • NAME directive: Assign a name to the object module (for linker identification); not executable.
  • SEG operator: In assembly, SEG identifier returns the segment address of the identifier; inserted by the linker/locator.
  • Relocatable: Address determined at link/load time; can be placed anywhere in memory.
  • Absolute: Address fixed at assembly time (using AT); cannot be relocated.

docs.title: Important Concepts
docs.text:
• The six-step program development process
  • Creation/execution pipeline: ASM → OBJ → LINKER → LOAD MODULE → LOADER → EXECUTION
  • What the linker/locator does and why it is needed
  • Segment combine types: PUBLIC, COMMON, STACK, AT, MEMORY — how each behaves, size formula
  • EXTRN/PUBLIC: syntax, type specifiers (BYTE/WORD/DWORD for variables; NEAR/FAR for labels), unresolved external error
  • When offsets are known (assembler) vs when segment addresses are filled (linker)
  • Physical address calculation: Segment × 10H + Offset
  • Why ES must be loaded explicitly before accessing an external variable
  • EVEN/ALIGN: word alignment for performance
  • LABEL: symbolic name, no memory allocated

docs.title: Important Comparisons
docs.text: Combine-Type Size Result Memory Layout Use Case PUBLIC Sum End-to-end Shared code/data COMMON Largest Overlapping (same address) Shared pool STACK Sum End-to-end Unified stack AT As declared Fixed absolute Hardware I/O MEMORY As declared At top of load module Overlay buffer Stage What is resolved Assembly Offsets of local variables/labels Linking Offsets of external symbols; segment placements Relocation Segment addresses (final physical addresses)

docs.title: Potential Exam Questions
docs.text:
1. What is modular programming? List any four advantages.
  2. Draw and explain the complete build pipeline from source code to execution.
  3. What is the difference between an object module and a load module?
  4. Explain the five segment combine types with examples and size formulas.
  5. What is the difference between PUBLIC and COMMON segment combination? Give a numerical example.
  6. Two modules each define a STACK_SEG SEGMENT STACK of 20 words. What is the total stack size after linking?
  7. What is the purpose of EXTRN and PUBLIC directives? What causes an "unresolved external" linker error?
  8. What type specifiers can be used with EXTRN? When would you use NEAR vs FAR?
  9. What information can the assembler insert, and what must be deferred to the linker?
  10. Calculate the physical address for logical address 2500H:0050H.
  11. What is relocation? Who performs it (assembler, linker, or loader)?
  12. Write a two-module program in 8086 assembly where Module 1 defines a variable COUNT:WORD and Module 2 increments it using EXTRN and PUBLIC.
  13. What is the EVEN directive? Why is word alignment important on the 8086?
  14. What is the difference between the LABEL directive and a normal variable declaration (DW, DB)?
  15. What is the SEG operator? Why must you load a segment register before accessing an external variable, even after declaring it with EXTRN?
  16. Explain ASSUME vs actually loading a segment register at runtime. Why is ASSUME not sufficient?

docs.title: Chapter: 8086 Procedures (Subroutines)
docs.text: Course: Microprocessors (MI) — Semester 5 Primary Source: 8086 procedures.pdf (35 slides, Dr. Pimal Khanpara) Files Integrated: 8086 procedures.pdf

docs.title: 1. Chapter Overview
docs.text:
A procedure (also called a subroutine) is a named, reusable block of assembly instructions that performs a specific task. Instead of repeating the same code at multiple points in a program, the program issues a CALL instruction; the procedure executes and returns control to the next instruction after the CALL using RET.

This chapter covers:

  • Stack fundamentals (PUSH, POP) needed for procedure linkage
  • Defining and calling procedures (PROC/ENDP, CALL, RET)
  • What happens at the hardware level during CALL and RET
  • Saving and restoring registers (PUSH/POP convention, LIFO discipline)
  • Three parameter-passing methods: registers, memory variables, stack
  • The BP register and the standard stack frame (prologue/epilogue)
  • RET n for callee stack cleanup
  • Caller-saved vs callee-saved register conventions
  • Nested and recursive procedure calls
  • FAR vs NEAR procedures

docs.title: 2. Stack Review
docs.text: The stack is a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) data structure in memory, used by the 8086 for procedure call linkage, register saving, and parameter passing. The Stack Segment Register (SS) holds the segment base, and SP (Stack Pointer) holds the current top-of-stack offset.

docs.title: Stack Instructions
docs.text:
Instruction Effect on SP Data Movement PUSH SRC SP ← SP − 2 (SP+1 : SP) ← SRC (stores high byte at SP+1, low byte at SP) POP DST SP ← SP + 2 DST ← (SP+1 : SP) PUSHF SP ← SP − 2 FLAGS register pushed onto stack POPF SP ← SP + 2 FLAGS register restored from stack

Key rule: The 8086 stack grows downward — PUSH decrements SP, POP increments SP. The stack always operates on 16-bit (word) quantities.

docs.title: Stack Initialization Example
docs.text:
STACK_SEG SEGMENT
    DW 30 DUP(?)          ; reserve 30 words = 60 bytes for stack
    TOS LABEL WORD        ; TOS = Top of Stack label (points just past stack)
STACK_SEG ENDS

CODE SEGMENT
    ASSUME CS:CODE, DS:DATA, SS:STACK_SEG
    START:
        MOV AX, STACK_SEG
        MOV SS, AX             ; load stack segment
        MOV SP, OFFSET TOS     ; SP points to top of reserved stack area

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slides 2–3]

docs.title: Definition: Procedure (NEAR)
docs.text:
Meaning: A named block of assembly instructions enclosed between PROC and ENDP directives, callable from anywhere in the same code segment.

Formal definition: A procedure is a contiguous sequence of instructions beginning at a named entry point and ending with a RET instruction. It is invoked by CALL <name> and returns to the caller via RET.

Intuition: Procedures are assembly's equivalent of functions in high-level languages. They encapsulate a task so it can be reused without code duplication.

Basic control flow:

flowchart LR
    A["MAIN Program"] --> B["CALL PROCEDURE"]
    B --> C["PROCEDURE executes"]
    C --> D["RET"]
    D --> E["Instruction after CALL"]
    E --> F["Continue MAIN"]

docs.title: Why Use Procedures?
docs.text:
Without Procedures With Procedures Repeated code at every use site Write once, CALL many times Longer programs Better modularity Harder debugging Each task tested independently More duplication Common operations centralized Difficult maintenance Changes made in one place

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slides 4–5]

docs.title: 4. Procedure Definition Syntax
docs.text:
procedure_name  PROC  NEAR      ; NEAR = same code segment
    ; procedure instructions
    RET                          ; return to caller
procedure_name  ENDP             ; end of procedure
  • PROC marks the beginning of the procedure.
  • NEAR means the procedure is in the same code segment as the caller.
  • ENDP marks the logical end (the assembler directive — execution reaches RET before ENDP).
  • RET is the actual runtime instruction that pops the return address and resumes execution at the caller.

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slide 6]

docs.title: Example 1 — Simplified (segment-based syntax)
docs.text:
STACK_SEG SEGMENT
    DW 30 DUP(?)
    TOS LABEL WORD
STACK_SEG ENDS

DATA SEGMENT
    MSG DB "hello$"
DATA ENDS

CODE SEGMENT
    ASSUME CS:CODE, DS:DATA, SS:STACK_SEG
    START:
        MOV AX, STACK_SEG
        MOV SS, AX
        MOV SP, OFFSET TOS          ; initialize stack
        MOV AX, DATA
        MOV DS, AX
        CALL DISPLAY                ; push IP of next instruction, jump to DISPLAY
        MOV AH, 4CH
        INT 21H

    DISPLAY PROC NEAR               ; procedure begins here
        MOV AH, 09H
        LEA DX, MSG
        INT 21H                     ; print MSG
        RET                         ; pop saved IP, return to instruction after CALL
    DISPLAY ENDP
CODE ENDS
END START

docs.title: Example 2 — Simplified model syntax (.MODEL SMALL)
docs.text:
.MODEL SMALL
.STACK 100H
.DATA
    MSG DB 'Hello from procedure!$'
.CODE
MAIN PROC
    MOV AX, @DATA
    MOV DS, AX
    CALL DISPLAY_MSG           ; call the procedure
    MOV AH, 4CH
    INT 21H
MAIN ENDP

DISPLAY_MSG PROC NEAR
    LEA DX, MSG
    MOV AH, 09H
    INT 21H
    RET
DISPLAY_MSG ENDP
END MAIN

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slides 7–8]

docs.title: 6. What Happens During CALL and RET
docs.text: Understanding the hardware-level sequence is critical for stack debugging and for writing correct procedures.

docs.title: NEAR CALL — Step by Step
docs.text:
CALL <procedure_name>
  1. SP ← SP − 2 (make room on stack)
  2. (SP+1 : SP) ← IP (push return address — the IP of the instruction after the CALL)
  3. IP ← address of procedure (jump to procedure)

docs.title: RET — Step by Step
docs.text:
RET
  1. IP ← (SP+1 : SP) (pop saved return address from stack)
  2. SP ← SP + 2 (restore SP)
  3. Execution resumes at the restored IP (the instruction after the original CALL)

docs.title: Hardware Flow Diagram
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["CALL PROCEDURE"] --> B["SP ← SP − 2"]
    B --> C["Stack: (SP+1:SP) ← IP (return address)"]
    C --> D["IP ← address of PROCEDURE"]
    D --> E["Procedure executes"]
    E --> F["RET instruction"]
    F --> G["IP ← (SP+1:SP) (pop stack)"]
    G --> H["SP ← SP + 2"]
    H --> I["Execution resumes after CALL"]

docs.title: Intrasegment (NEAR) vs Intersegment (FAR) CALL
docs.text:
Intrasegment CALL (NEAR): 

CALL DST
; SP = SP − 2
; (SP+1 : SP) = IP
; IP = IP + displacement (D16)

Intersegment CALL (FAR): 

CALL DST
; SP = SP − 2 ; (SP+1 : SP) = CS   ← CS saved first
; SP = SP − 2 ; (SP+1 : SP) = IP   ← then IP saved
; CS = segment address of target
; IP = D16 (offset of target)

RET variants:

Instruction Effect RET IP ← (SP+1:SP) ; SP ← SP + 2 RET exp Pop IP, then SP ← SP + exp (removes exp argument bytes)

📝 Exam Note: A NEAR CALL saves only IP (2 bytes); a FAR CALL saves CS and IP (4 bytes). The matching RET/RETF must match the CALL type.

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slides 9–11]

docs.title: 7. Stack During CALL/RET — Memory Layout
docs.text:
After MAIN executes CALL ADD_TWO:

Stack (growing downward):
┌──────────────┐ ← higher address
│  ...         │
│  Return IP   │ ← (SP points here after CALL, before PUSH BP)
└──────────────┘ ← lower address

When ADD_TWO executes RET, it pops the saved IP and SP returns to its pre-CALL value.

docs.title: Critical Stack Rule
docs.text:
A CALL and its matching RET must leave the stack in exactly the same state.

  • If a procedure PUSHes data during execution, it must POP that data before RET (unless using RET n).

Correct: 

MYPROC PROC NEAR
    PUSH AX        ; save AX
    ; ... use AX ...
    POP AX         ; restore AX
    RET            ; stack is clean
MYPROC ENDP

Incorrect: 

MYPROC PROC NEAR
    PUSH AX        ; pushed AX
    ; ... use AX ...
    RET            ; ERROR: RET pops AX as return address → wrong IP!
MYPROC ENDP

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slides 12–13]

docs.title: 8. Saving and Restoring Registers
docs.text: A procedure may use registers that the caller still needs after the call returns. The procedure is responsible for preserving such registers using PUSH/POP.

docs.title: Standard Register-Save Pattern
docs.text:
MYPROC PROC NEAR
    PUSH AX           ; save caller's registers
    PUSH BX
    PUSH CX
    ; --- procedure body ---
    POP CX            ; restore in REVERSE order (LIFO)
    POP BX
    POP AX
    RET
MYPROC ENDP

docs.title: PUSH/POP LIFO Discipline
docs.text:
The stack is Last-In-First-Out. If you push AX → BX → CX, you must pop CX → BX → AX.

PUSH AX  →  PUSH BX  →  PUSH CX
                         Stack top = CX

POP CX   →  POP BX   →  POP AX

📝 Exam Note: Reversing the POP order is a common mistake. Always POP in the exact reverse order of PUSH.

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slides 14–15]

docs.title: 9. Parameter Passing Methods
docs.text: The 8086 does not enforce one parameter-passing convention. Three common methods are used:

docs.title: 9.1 Method 1 — Through Registers
docs.text:
Fastest method; limited to a small number of parameters (limited register set).

  • Input parameters: loaded into registers before the CALL.
  • Output: returned in a designated register (typically AX).

docs.title: Example: Add Two 16-bit Numbers
docs.text:
; -----------------------------------------
; ADD_TWO: adds AX and BX, result in AX
; Input : AX = first number, BX = second
; Output: AX = sum
; Preserves: BX, CX, DX
; Modifies : AX, Flags
; -----------------------------------------
ADD_TWO PROC NEAR
    ADD AX, BX         ; AX = AX + BX
    RET
ADD_TWO ENDP

; Caller:
MOV AX, 25
MOV BX, 17
CALL ADD_TWO
; After: AX = 42

Note: AX is not preserved here because it intentionally carries the return value.

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slides 16–17]

docs.title: 9.2 Method 2 — Through Memory Variables
docs.text:
Useful when many parameters are needed or when parameters are large data structures.

  • Input: procedure reads named variables from the DATA segment.
  • Output: procedure writes to a named result variable.
; DATA segment
NUM1   DW 25
NUM2   DW 17
RESULT DW ?

; Procedure
ADD_MEMORY PROC NEAR
    MOV AX, NUM1       ; load first operand
    ADD AX, NUM2       ; add second operand
    MOV RESULT, AX     ; store result
    RET
ADD_MEMORY ENDP

; Caller:
CALL ADD_MEMORY
; RESULT now contains 42

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slide 18]

docs.title: 9.3 Method 3 — Through the Stack
docs.text:
Most flexible method; supports any number of parameters; essential for recursion.

Protocol:

  1. Caller PUSHes arguments onto the stack.
  2. Caller issues CALL.
  3. Procedure uses BP to access the stacked arguments.
  4. Procedure returns result (typically in AX).
  5. Caller or procedure cleans up the stack (see RET n).

docs.title: The BP Register — Stable Stack Frame Reference
docs.text:
SP changes with every PUSH/POP. BP is used as a stable base pointer that doesn't change during the procedure body, giving reliable access to arguments.

Standard prologue: 

PUSH BP           ; save caller's BP
MOV BP, SP        ; BP now points to top of stack

Stack layout after prologue (NEAR call):

Address     Content
[BP+6]      second argument  (pushed first by caller)
[BP+4]      first argument   (pushed second by caller)
[BP+2]      return IP        (saved by CALL)
[BP+0]      saved old BP     (saved by PUSH BP)
[BP-2]      local variable 1 (if SUB SP, 2 was done)
[BP-4]      local variable 2
↓ lower addresses (stack grows down)

docs.title: Complete Stack-Based Add Example
docs.text:
; Procedure: add two numbers passed on stack
ADD_STACK PROC NEAR
    PUSH BP
    MOV BP, SP             ; establish stack frame
    MOV AX, [BP+4]         ; first argument
    ADD AX, [BP+6]         ; second argument (add to first)
    POP BP                 ; restore caller's BP
    RET 4                  ; return and remove 4 bytes of arguments (2 args × 2 bytes)
ADD_STACK ENDP

; Caller:
MOV AX, 25
PUSH AX                   ; push first argument
MOV AX, 17
PUSH AX                   ; push second argument
CALL ADD_STACK
; AX = 42; stack is clean (RET 4 removed both args)

Stack trace:

Before CALL:
SP → [17]   ← last pushed argument
     [25]   ← first pushed argument

After CALL (return IP pushed):
SP → [ret IP]
     [17]
     [25]

After PUSH BP:
SP → [old BP]  ← BP (and SP) now point here
     [ret IP]
     [25]   = [BP+4]
     [17]   = [BP+6]

Wait — the push order matters:
Caller pushes 25 first, then 17.
Stack (top = lowest address):
[BP+0] = saved BP
[BP+2] = return IP
[BP+4] = 17 (last pushed = at lower offset)
[BP+6] = 25 (first pushed = at higher offset)

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slides 19–21]

docs.title: 10. Procedure Prologue and Epilogue
docs.text:
MYPROC PROC NEAR
    ; --- PROLOGUE ---
    PUSH BP            ; save old BP
    MOV BP, SP         ; set frame pointer

    ; --- BODY ---
    ; access [BP+4], [BP+6] for parameters
    ; use [BP-2], [BP-4] for local variables

    ; --- EPILOGUE ---
    MOV SP, BP         ; restore SP (collapse local variables)
    POP BP             ; restore caller's BP
    RET
MYPROC ENDP
  • Prologue: establishes the stack frame for the procedure.
  • Epilogue: tears down the stack frame, restores BP, and returns.

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slide 22]

docs.title: 11. RET vs RET n
docs.text:
Instruction Meaning RET Pop return IP; continue at caller RET 2 Pop return IP; additionally SP ← SP + 2 (remove 1 word argument) RET 4 Pop return IP; additionally SP ← SP + 4 (remove 2 word arguments)

RET n is the callee-cleans-stack convention (common in Pascal/Windows API style). The caller pushes arguments; the procedure removes them via RET n.

📝 Exam Note: If RET n is used, n must exactly equal the total bytes of arguments pushed by the caller. Too small → leftover bytes on stack; too large → SP points past valid data.

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slide 23]

docs.title: 12. Caller-Saved vs Callee-Saved Registers
docs.text:
A calling convention defines which registers a procedure may freely destroy and which it must preserve.

Convention Responsibility Typical Rule Caller-saved Caller saves the register before CALL if it needs the value after RET Procedure may freely modify it Callee-saved Procedure saves/restores the register if it uses it Caller can rely on finding it unchanged after RET

Good documentation practice:

; ------------------------------------------------
; ADD_TWO
; Input : AX = first number, BX = second number
; Output: AX = sum
; Preserves: BX, CX, DX
; Modifies : AX, Flags
; ------------------------------------------------
ADD_TWO PROC NEAR
    ADD AX, BX
    RET
ADD_TWO ENDP

Every procedure should have a header comment stating inputs, outputs, preserved registers, and modified registers.

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slides 24–25]

docs.title: 13.1 Find Maximum of Two Numbers
docs.text:
; Input : AX = first number, BX = second number
; Output: AX = larger of AX and BX
MAX_TWO PROC NEAR
    CMP AX, BX         ; compare AX with BX
    JAE MAX_DONE       ; if AX >= BX, AX is already max
    MOV AX, BX         ; else BX is larger, put in AX
MAX_DONE:
    RET
MAX_TWO ENDP

; Caller:
MOV AX, 45
MOV BX, 72
CALL MAX_TWO
; After: AX = 72

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slide 26]

docs.title: 13.2 Sum of an Array
docs.text:
; Input : SI = address of word array, CX = number of elements
; Output: AX = sum of all elements
; Preserves: SI, CX
SUM_ARRAY PROC NEAR
    PUSH SI            ; save SI (callee-saved)
    PUSH CX            ; save CX
    XOR AX, AX         ; AX = 0 (sum accumulator)
SUM_LOOP:
    ADD AX, [SI]       ; add current word to sum
    ADD SI, 2          ; advance SI to next word
    LOOP SUM_LOOP      ; CX--; repeat if CX ≠ 0
    POP CX             ; restore CX
    POP SI             ; restore SI
    RET
SUM_ARRAY ENDP

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slide 27]

docs.title: 13.3 Common Mistake: Restoring the Result Register
docs.text:
; WRONG — destroys the calculated sum
WRONG_SUM PROC NEAR
    PUSH AX            ; save old AX value
    XOR AX, AX
    ; ... calculate sum into AX ...
    POP AX             ; BUG: restores old AX, discards the sum!
    RET
WRONG_SUM ENDP

Rule: Do not PUSH/POP the register that carries the return value.

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slide 28]

docs.title: 14. Nested Procedure Calls
docs.text:
A procedure can call another procedure. The 8086 handles this naturally because each CALL pushes its own return address, and RETs pop them in LIFO order.

Example chain: 

MAIN → CALL PROC_A → CALL PROC_B → RET (to PROC_A) → RET (to MAIN)

Stack state after MAIN calls A, and A calls B:

Stack (growing down):
[MAIN's return addr]   ← pushed when MAIN called A
[A's return addr]      ← pushed when A called B
                       ← SP points here (top of stack)

B executes RET → pops A's return address → returns to A. A executes RET → pops MAIN's return address → returns to MAIN.

sequenceDiagram
    participant MAIN
    participant PROC_A
    participant PROC_B
    MAIN->>PROC_A: CALL PROC_A (push ret_MAIN)
    PROC_A->>PROC_B: CALL PROC_B (push ret_A)
    PROC_B-->>PROC_A: RET (pop ret_A)
    PROC_A-->>MAIN: RET (pop ret_MAIN)

[Source: 8086 procedures.pdf, Slides 29–30]

docs.title: 15. Recursive Procedures
docs.text: A recursive procedure calls itself. Each recursive call creates a new stack frame with its own copy of local data and the return address. The stack naturally provides this storage.
