docs.title: 9. The C4.5 Algorithm
docs.text: [Source: KNN Naive Bayes and DT1.pdf, Slides 82–85]

docs.title: 9.1 High-Cardinality Bias of Information Gain
docs.text:
A major flaw in ID3 is its systemic bias toward high-cardinality attributes (e.g., Customer_ID or SSN). If an attribute assigns a unique value to every instance, partitioning on it produces \(m\) pure single-item subsets with \(H(S_v) = 0\), yielding maximum Information Gain:

\[ IG(S, \text{ID}) = H(S) - 0 = H(S) \]

This creates a shallow tree with \(m\) branches that memorizes the data but has zero predictive power on unseen samples.

docs.title: 9.2 Split Information & Gain Ratio Formulations
docs.text:
1. Split Information:

Measures the intrinsic entropy of the partition itself:

\[ \text{SplitInfo}_A(S) = -\sum_{v=1}^{c} \frac{|S_v|}{|S|} \log_2\left( \frac{|S_v|}{|S|} \right) \]

Attributes with many small branches produce large \(\text{SplitInfo}\), penalizing fragmented partitions.

  1. Gain Ratio:
\[ \text{GainRatio}(S, A) = \frac{IG(S, A)}{\text{SplitInfo}_A(S)} \]

docs.title: C4.5 Attribute Selection Rule:
docs.text:
To prevent selecting attributes with near-zero Information Gain whose Split Information is infinitesimally small:

  1. Calculate average Information Gain across all candidate attributes.

  2. Select the attribute that maximizes Gain Ratio among those attributes whose Information Gain is at or above average.

docs.title: 9.3 Additional Advances in C4.5
docs.text:
1. Continuous Attribute Handling (Dynamic Thresholding):

  2. For continuous feature \(A\), sort distinct training values: \(v_1 < v_2 < \dots < v_n\).

  3. Evaluate binary split thresholds at midpoints: \(\theta_i = \frac{v_i + v_{i+1}}{2}\).

  4. Partition into \(S_1 = \{x \mid A \le \theta_i\}\) and \(S_2 = \{x \mid A > \theta_i\}\), computing \(IG\) for each midpoint and selecting threshold \(\theta^*\) maximizing Gain.

  5. Handling Missing Feature Values:

  6. If an instance lacks a value for test attribute \(A\), C4.5 assigns it fractional weights proportional to branch sizes: \(w_v = \frac{|S_v|}{|S|}\).

docs.title: 9.4 Step-by-Step Solved Exam Problem: C4.5 Gain Ratio Calculation
docs.text:
Exam Question:

A company dataset (\(m = 8\)) evaluates employee promotion based on Employee_ID (unique), Department (\(\text{Sales, IT}\)), and Performance_Rating (\(\text{High, Medium}\)):

Employee_ID Department Performance_Rating Promoted (\(y\)) E1 Sales High Yes E2 Sales High Yes E3 Sales Medium No E4 IT High Yes E5 IT High Yes E6 IT Medium No E7 IT Medium No E8 Sales Medium No

Target distribution: 4 Yes, 4 No (\(|S|=8\)).

Task: Demonstrate how C4.5 overcomes the high-cardinality bias of Employee_ID by computing \(IG\), \(\text{SplitInfo}\), and \(\text{GainRatio}\) for Employee_ID and Performance_Rating.

Step 1: Compute Base Entropy \(H(S)\):

\(p_+ = \frac{4}{8} = 0.5, p_- = 0.5 \implies H(S) = \mathbf{1.0000 \text{ bit}}\).

Step 2: Evaluate Employee_ID (8 unique values, 8 branches):

  • Each subset \(S_v\) has 1 instance (\(H(S_v) = 0\)).

  • Weighted entropy = \(0 \implies IG(S, \text{Employee\_ID}) = 1.0000 - 0 = \mathbf{1.0000 \text{ bit}}\) (Maximum possible!).

  • Split Information:

\[ \text{SplitInfo}_{\text{ID}}(S) = -\sum_{i=1}^{8} \frac{1}{8} \log_2\left(\frac{1}{8}\right) = -\log_2\left(\frac{1}{8}\right) = \mathbf{3.0000 \text{ bits}} \]
  • Gain Ratio:
\[ \text{GainRatio}(S, \text{Employee\_ID}) = \frac{1.0000}{3.0000} = \mathbf{0.3333} \]

Step 3: Evaluate Performance_Rating (\(\{\text{High}, \text{Medium}\}\)):

  • High (\(4\) instances: E1, E2, E4, E5 \(\implies 4+, 0-\)): \(H = 0\).

  • Medium (\(4\) instances: E3, E6, E7, E8 \(\implies 0+, 4-\)): \(H = 0\).

  • Weighted entropy = \(0 \implies IG(S, \text{Performance}) = 1.0000 - 0 = \mathbf{1.0000 \text{ bit}}\).

  • Split Information:

\[ \text{SplitInfo}_{\text{Performance}}(S) = -\left[ \frac{4}{8}\log_2\left(\frac{4}{8}\right) + \frac{4}{8}\log_2\left(\frac{4}{8}\right) \right] = \mathbf{1.0000 \text{ bit}} \]
  • Gain Ratio:
\[ \text{GainRatio}(S, \text{Performance}) = \frac{1.0000}{1.0000} = \mathbf{1.0000} \]

Conclusion: Although both attributes have \(IG = 1.0\), Performance_Rating has a significantly higher Gain Ratio (\(1.0000\)) than Employee_ID (\(0.3333\)). C4.5 correctly penalizes the high cardinality of Employee_ID and selects Performance_Rating!

docs.title: 10. The CART Algorithm (Classification and Regression Trees)
docs.text: [Source: KNN Naive Bayes and DT1.pdf, Slides 86–100]

docs.title: 10.1 Mathematical Formulation of Gini Impurity
docs.text:
CART constructs strictly binary decision trees using Gini Impurity:

\[ \text{Gini}(S) = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{c} p_i^2 \]

For binary classification (\(p_1\) positive,\(p_2 = 1 - p_1\) negative):

\[ \text{Gini}(S) = 1 - (p_1^2 + p_2^2) = 2 p_1 (1 - p_1) \]

docs.title: Figure 6.16: Gini Impurity Formulation
docs.text:
Key Properties:

  • Pure node (\(p_1=1\) or \(p_1=0\)): \(\text{Gini} = 0\).

  • Maximum impurity (\(p_1=0.5, p_2=0.5\)): \(\text{Gini} = 0.50\).

  • Computationally faster than entropy because it avoids logarithmic operations.

docs.title: 10.2 Binary Subset Partitioning & Gini Gain
docs.text:
For a categorical attribute \(A\) with values \(\{v_1, \dots, v_k\}\), CART tests all proper non-empty binary subset splits \((S_1, S_2)\). The weighted Gini index of partition \((S_1, S_2)\) is:

\[ \text{Gini}_A(S) = \frac{|S_1|}{|S|} \text{Gini}(S_1) + \frac{|S_2|}{|S|} \text{Gini}(S_2) \]

Gini Gain (Impurity Reduction):

\[ \Delta\text{Gini}(A) = \text{Gini}(S) - \text{Gini}_A(S) \]

CART selects the split maximizing \(\Delta\text{Gini}(A)\) (minimizing weighted Gini index).

docs.title: 10.3 Step-by-Step Solved Exam Problem: CART Job Offer Induction
docs.text:
Exam Question:

Induce a binary CART tree using the Job Offer dataset (\(m = 10\)):

ID CGPA Interactiveness Practical Knowledge Communication Skills Job Offer (\(y\)) 1 \(\ge 9\) Yes Very Good Good Yes 2 \(\ge 8\) No Good Moderate Yes 3 \(\ge 9\) No Average Poor No 4 \(< 8\) No Average Good No 5 \(\ge 8\) Yes Good Moderate Yes 6 \(\ge 9\) Yes Good Moderate Yes 7 \(< 8\) Yes Good Poor No 8 \(\ge 9\) No Very Good Good Yes 9 \(\ge 8\) Yes Good Good Yes 10 \(\ge 8\) Yes Average Good Yes

Step 1: Base Gini Impurity \(\text{Gini}(T)\):

\(|T| = 10\): \(7\) Yes,\(3\) No (\([7+, 3-]\)).

\[ \text{Gini}(T) = 1 - \left(\frac{7}{10}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{3}{10}\right)^2 = 1 - 0.49 - 0.09 = \mathbf{0.4200} \]

Step 2: Candidate Root Binary Split Evaluation:

  1. CGPA Split: \(\{\ge 9, \ge 8\}\) vs.\(\{< 8\}\):

  2. \(S_1\) (\(\text{CGPA} \in \{\ge 9, \ge 8\}\), 8 instances: IDs 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 \(\implies 7+, 1-\)):

\[ \text{Gini}(S_1) = 1 - \left(\frac{7}{8}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^2 = 1 - \frac{49}{64} - \frac{1}{64} = \mathbf{0.21875} \]
  • \(S_2\) (\(\text{CGPA} < 8\), 2 instances: IDs 4, 7 \(\implies 0+, 2-\)):
\[ \text{Gini}(S_2) = 0 \quad (\text{Pure}) \]
  • Weighted Gini:
\[ \text{Gini}(T, \text{CGPA}) = \frac{8}{10}(0.21875) + \frac{2}{10}(0) = \mathbf{0.1755} \]
  • Impurity Reduction:
\[ \Delta\text{Gini}(\text{CGPA}) = 0.4200 - 0.1755 = \mathbf{0.2445} \]

  1. Communication Skills Split: \(\{\text{Good}, \text{Moderate}\}\) vs.\(\{\text{Poor}\}\):

  2. \(S_{\text{Poor}}\)(2 instances: IDs 3, 7 \(\implies 0+, 2-\)): \(\text{Gini} = 0\).

  3. \(S_{\text{Good/Mod}}\)(8 instances \(\implies 7+, 1-\)): \(\text{Gini} = 0.21875\).

-

\[ \text{Gini}(T, \text{Comm}) = \frac{8}{10}(0.21875) + 0 = \mathbf{0.1755} \implies \Delta\text{Gini} = \mathbf{0.2445} \]
  1. Selecting Root Split:

Both CGPA and Communication Skills tie at \(\Delta\text{Gini} = 0.2445\). CART selects \(\text{CGPA} < 8\) as the primary root test.

  • Branch \(\text{CGPA} < 8\)(Right)\(\implies\) Pure \(\implies\) Leaf: Job Offer = No.

docs.title: Step 3: Subtree Induction on Left Branch (\(\text{CGPA} \in \{\ge 9, \ge 8\}\))
docs.text:
Dataset at left node: 8 instances (\(7+, 1-\)), \(\text{Gini} = 0.21875\).

Evaluating Communication Skills on remaining left branch samples:

  • Comm Skills == Poor (ID 3): Job Offer = No (\(0+, 1- \implies \text{Gini} = 0\)).

  • Comm Skills != Poor (7 instances: IDs 1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10): Job Offer = Yes (\(7+, 0- \implies \text{Gini} = 0\)).

  • Weighted Gini = \(0 \implies \Delta\text{Gini} = 0.21875\) (Perfect Purity!).

docs.title: 11. Decision Tree Pruning & Overfitting Prevention
docs.text:
[Source: KNN Naive Bayes and DT1.pdf, Slide 100]

Unconstrained decision trees tend to memorize sample noise, resulting in high variance and poor generalization.

docs.title: Figure 6.19: Tree Pruning and Generalization Tradeoff
11.1 Pre-Pruning (Early Stopping)
docs.text:
Halts tree expansion during induction if a stopping condition is met:

  1. Max Depth Cap: Stop growth when tree depth exceeds \(d_{\max}\).

  2. Min Node Samples: Stop if a node contains fewer than \(n_{\min}\) instances.

  3. Impurity Threshold: Stop if node impurity falls below \(\epsilon\).

  4. Statistical Significance: Stop if split gain is not statistically significant (\(\chi^2\) test).

Limitation: Susceptible to the horizon effect (premature stopping where an uninformative split would have enabled a decisive subsequent split).

docs.title: 11.2 Post-Pruning (Cost-Complexity Pruning)
docs.text: Grows the tree to full max depth and systematically prunes subtrees from the bottom up using validation data.

docs.title: Cost-Complexity Objective (Weakest Link Pruning):
docs.text:
\[ R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha |T| \]

Where \(R(T)\) is training error rate,\(|T|\) is the number of terminal leaves, and \(\alpha \ge 0\) is the complexity penalty parameter.

docs.text: \[ \text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN}, \quad \text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}, \quad \text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}, \quad F_1 = \frac{2 \cdot TP}{2 \cdot TP + FP + FN} \]

docs.title: 6. Shannon Entropy and Information Gain (ID3)
docs.text: \[ H(S) = -\sum_{i=1}^c p_i \log_2(p_i), \quad IG(S, A) = H(S) - \sum_{v \in \text{Values}(A)} \frac{|S_v|}{|S|} H(S_v) \]

docs.text: \[ \text{SplitInfo}_A(S) = -\sum_{v=1}^c \frac{|S_v|}{|S|} \log_2\left( \frac{|S_v|}{|S|} \right), \quad \text{GainRatio}(S, A) = \frac{IG(S, A)}{\text{SplitInfo}_A(S)} \]

docs.title: 14. Important Definitions Sheet
docs.text:
• Lazy Learner: An algorithm that stores training instances and defers all hypothesis formulation until an active inference query arrives (e.g., KNN).

  • Curse of Dimensionality: The phenomenon where high-dimensional feature spaces become exponential in volume, making pairwise distances equidistant.

  • Conditional Independence: The condition where random variables \(X_i\) and \(X_j\) provide no information about each other when conditioned on class \(C\).

  • Laplace Smoothing: Adding 1 to observation counts and \(|V|\) to denominators to eliminate zero probabilities in categorical likelihood estimation.

  • Sensitivity (Recall): The probability that a positive instance is correctly identified by the model (\(TP / (TP + FN)\)).

  • Specificity: The probability that a negative instance is correctly identified by the model (\(TN / (TN + FP)\)).

  • Shannon Entropy: The expected amount of information (in bits) produced by a stochastic source.

  • Information Gain: The expected reduction in entropy obtained by splitting on a specific attribute.

  • Gain Ratio: Information Gain normalized by Split Information to penalize attributes with excessive branches.

  • Gini Impurity: A quadratic measure of node impurity representing expected misclassification probability.

  • Pre-Pruning: Stopping decision tree growth before full expansion using validation metrics or depth caps.

  • Post-Pruning: Collapsing branches of a fully grown decision tree to optimize test set generalization.

docs.title: 15.1 High-Probability Theory Questions
docs.text:
1. Explain the differences between lazy and eager learners. Why is KNN classified as a lazy learner?

  2. Answer: Eager learners (Naïve Bayes, Decision Trees) construct an explicit, compiled hypothesis model during training, discarding original training data. Lazy learners (KNN) perform \(O(1)\) storage during training, deferring all computational effort (\(O(m \cdot d)\) distance computations) to the inference query phase.

  3. State the conditional independence assumption of Naïve Bayes. Why is it called "naïve", and why does it perform surprisingly well in practice?

  4. Answer: It assumes \(P(\mathbf{x} \mid C) = \prod_{j=1}^d P(x_j \mid C)\). It is "naïve" because real-world features frequently correlate. It performs well because classification only requires picking the maximum posterior class, which remains correct even if probability magnitudes are distorted, provided relative ranking order is preserved.

  5. Why does ID3 favor high-cardinality attributes, and how does C4.5 resolve this issue?

  6. Answer: High-cardinality attributes (e.g., ID numbers) partition data into tiny, pure single-item subsets with zero subset entropy (\(H=0\)), yielding maximal Information Gain. C4.5 resolves this by normalizing Information Gain by Split Information, defining the Gain Ratio.

  7. Differentiate between Information Gain and Gini Impurity.

  8. Answer: Information Gain is logarithmic (\(-\sum p_i \log_2 p_i\)), maximizing entropy reduction; Gini Impurity is quadratic (\(1 - \sum p_i^2\)), computationally faster, and tends to isolate the largest class into pure binary splits.

docs.title: 6.1 Foundations of Biological and Artificial Neural Networks
docs.text: The field of Artificial Neural Networks originated from the quest to replicate the computational versatility, robustness, and fault tolerance of the biological human brain within synthetic computing systems. While conventional digital architectures excel at rapid sequential arithmetic and algorithmic precision, biological nervous systems demonstrate unparalleled superiority in perceptual tasks, pattern recognition, contextual understanding, and adaptive learning through experience. This section establishes the structural, functional, and mathematical analogies connecting biological neurobiology to foundational artificial computational models.

docs.title: Core Terminology Dictionary
docs.text:
1. Neuron (Biological): An electrically excitable biological cell that processes and transmits information throughout the nervous system via electrochemical signaling mechanisms.
  2. Synapse: The microscopic junction and biochemical interface across which an action potential is transmitted from the presynaptic axon terminal to the postsynaptic dendrite.
  3. Dendrite: The highly branched cellular projections of a biological neuron that receive incoming electrical or chemical stimuli from adjacent neurons.
  4. Soma (Cell Body): The central metabolic and computational hub of a neuron containing the cell nucleus; it aggregates postsynaptic electrical potentials across dendrites.
  5. Axon: A single, elongated cellular fiber extending from the soma that propagates generated action potentials (nerve impulses) toward downstream target neurons or effector cells.
  6. Net Input (\(net\)): The aggregated scalar sum of all weighted input signals arriving at an artificial neuron, combined with an internal bias parameter.
  7. Activation Function (\(f\)): A mathematical transfer function applied to the net input scalar that determines the final activation level and output state of an artificial neuron.
  8. Linear Activation Function: A transfer function producing an output directly proportional to its net input (\(f(net) = net\)), providing no non-linear transformation.
  9. Binary Step Activation Function: A discontinuous threshold function yielding binary values (\(0\) or \(1\)) based on whether the net input meets or exceeds a predefined threshold.
  10. Ramp (Saturating Linear) Function: A piecewise linear function that clips output values to a bounded range \([0, 1]\) when the net input exceeds specified upper and lower saturation limits.
  11. Sigmoid (Logistic) Function: A smooth, S-shaped non-linear activation function mapping the real number line \((-\infty, +\infty)\) into a bounded probability interval \((0, 1)\).
  12. Hyperbolic Tangent (Tanh) Function: A zero-centered, smooth S-shaped activation function mapping real inputs into the bounded interval \((-1, +1)\).
  13. Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU): A non-linear activation function defined as \(f(net) = \max(0, net)\), widely used in deep neural architectures to prevent gradient saturation.
  14. Leaky Rectified Linear Unit (Leaky ReLU): A modified ReLU function introducing a small non-zero slope \(\alpha\) for negative net inputs to prevent the "dying ReLU" failure mode.
  15. Parametric Rectified Linear Unit (PReLU): A generalization of Leaky ReLU where the negative slope coefficient \(\alpha\) is treated as an adaptive parameter learned during training.
  16. Randomized Rectified Linear Unit (RReLU): A stochastic variation of Leaky ReLU where the negative slope parameter \(\alpha_{ji}\) is randomly sampled from a uniform distribution during training and fixed during evaluation.
  17. Perceptron: The fundamental supervised learning model introduced by Frank Rosenblatt, consisting of a single-layer threshold neuron capable of learning linearly separable binary classification boundaries.
  18. Epoch: Exactly one complete presentation and forward-backward training cycle of the entire training dataset through a machine learning model.
  19. Backpropagation (BP): A supervised gradient descent algorithm that computes the partial derivatives of an objective error function with respect to all network weights via the multivariate calculus chain rule.
  20. Competitive Learning: An unsupervised neural learning paradigm wherein output neurons compete with one another for the exclusive right to respond to a given input pattern.
  21. Winner-Take-All (WTA): The operational principle of competitive networks where only the single neuron with the highest activation (or minimum metric distance) updates its synaptic weights.
  22. Lateral Inhibition: Biological and artificial inhibitory synaptic cross-connections between adjacent neurons that suppress surrounding units while reinforcing the dominant winning unit.
  23. Self-Organizing Map (SOM): An unsupervised neural network architecture introduced by Teuvo Kohonen that maps high-dimensional input spaces onto a low-dimensional (typically 1D or 2D) regular grid while preserving topological relationships.
  24. Topological Neighborhood: A geometrically defined local region surrounding the winning neuron in an SOM lattice within which neighboring neurons also update their synaptic weights.
  25. K-Means Clustering: A partitioning clustering algorithm that partitions \(N\) observations into \(K\) disjoint clusters by iteratively assigning points to the nearest mean vector and recomputing cluster centroids.
  26. Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS): The objective optimization metric in K-Means measuring the total squared Euclidean distance between each data point and its assigned cluster centroid.
  27. K-Medoids Clustering: A robust partitioning clustering algorithm that designates actual observed data points (medoids) as cluster centers instead of fictitious arithmetic means.
  28. Partitioning Around Medoids (PAM): The classic, deterministic realization of K-Medoids that iteratively swaps medoid and non-medoid points to minimize total absolute dissimilarity.
  29. Hierarchical Clustering: A clustering approach that builds a continuous nested hierarchy of cluster partitions, organized either bottom-up (agglomerative) or top-down (divisive).
  30. Linkage Criteria: Mathematical distance functions determining the pairwise dissimilarity between two multi-point clusters in hierarchical clustering (e.g., Single, Complete, Average, Centroid).
  31. Dendrogram: A two-dimensional tree diagram illustrating the sequential merges or divisions of data clusters in hierarchical clustering across varying proximity thresholds.

docs.title: Biological Neural Networks (BNN)
docs.text:
The biological human nervous system is divided anatomically into the Central Nervous System (CNS), comprising the brain and spinal cord, and the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS), which interfaces sensory organs and muscular effectors. The structural and computational core of the human brain exhibits the following biological characteristics:

  • Scale: Contains between \(10^{10}\) and \(10^{11}\) biological neurons (\(10\) to \(100\) billion neurons).
  • Connectivity: Each individual neuron forms between \(1,000\) and \(10,000\) synaptic junctions with adjacent cells, yielding in excess of \(10^{14}\) (over \(100\) trillion) simultaneous synaptic interconnections.
  • Processing Architecture: A massively parallel, distributed biological system where individual computational elements operate slowly (\(\approx 10^{-3}\text{ s}\) per synaptic transmission compared to \(\approx 10^{-9}\text{ s}\) in silicon transistors), yet outperform supercomputers in visual processing and speech comprehension due to vast parallelism.
  • Fault Tolerance & Graceful Degradation: The network continues to function reliably even when individual neurons or synapses degrade or die, avoiding catastrophic system failures.
  • Energy Efficiency: The human brain operates at peak computational capacity on an extraordinarily modest metabolic power budget of approximately \(20\text{ Watts}\).

docs.title: Written Analysis of Biological Neuron Components
docs.text:
1. Dendrites: Serve as the input receptive field. Tree-like arborizations extending from the cell body that receive incoming neurotransmitter chemicals released by upstream neurons.
  2. Soma (Cell Body): Integrates incoming postsynaptic electrical potentials across all dendrites over time. Contains the biological nucleus and cellular infrastructure.
  3. Axon: Propagates action potentials initiated at the axon hillock when the integrated potential crosses an excitation threshold (\(\approx -55\text{ mV}\)). The axon acts as an active transmission line.
  4. Synapse & Synaptic Terminals: The terminal boutons convert electrical action potentials into chemical neurotransmitters (e.g., acetylcholine, GABA, glutamate) that diffuse across the synaptic cleft (\(\approx 20\text{ nm}\) gap) to excite or inhibit the receiving postsynaptic dendrite.

    BIAS["Bias (b)"] --> SUM
    SUM -->|"net"| ACT["Activation Function: f(net)"]
    ACT -->|"y"| OUT["Output y"]

docs.title: Component Breakdown and Operational Flow
docs.text:
1. Input Vector: A feature vector \(\mathbf{x} = [x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n]^T \in \mathbb{R}^n\) representing quantitative observations.
  2. Weight Vector: A vector of synaptic connection strengths \(\mathbf{w} = [w_1, w_2, \dots, w_n]^T \in \mathbb{R}^n\).
  3. Bias Parameter: An independent scalar \(b \in \mathbb{R}\) equivalent to a weight with a permanently clamped input of \(+1\). It acts as an adjustable threshold: \(b = -\theta\).
  4. Summation Junction: Computes the net internal activation scalar \(net\) as the algebraic inner product plus bias:
\[ net = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i + b \]
  1. Activation Operator: Transforms the net input through a linear or non-linear operator \(f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\), yielding the output:
\[ y = f(net) \]

[Source: NN and Clustering.pdf, Slides 1–8]

docs.title: 6.2 Activation Functions and Mathematical Transfer Functions
docs.text: Activation functions inject non-linear computational capacity into artificial neural networks. Without non-linear activation functions, any multi-layer neural network collapses mathematically into a single linear matrix transformation, regardless of layer depth. The choice of activation function dictates gradient propagation, convergence velocity, numerical stability, and representational capacity.

docs.title: 1. Binary Step Function (Threshold / Heaviside)
docs.text:
\[ f(net) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } net \ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{if } net < 0 \end{cases} \] Symbol Meaning Units / Range \(net\) Net aggregated input to the neuron \(\mathbb{R} \in (-\infty, +\infty)\) \(f(net)\) Binary discrete firing state \(\{0, 1\}\)
  • Characteristics: Discontinuous at \(net = 0\); derivative is zero everywhere and undefined at \(0\).
  • Gradient Limitation: \(f'(net) = 0\) for all \(net \neq 0\). Prevents gradient-based backpropagation learning. Used primarily in Rosenblatt perceptrons.

docs.title: 2. Linear (Identity) Activation Function
docs.text:
\[ f(net) = net \] Symbol Meaning Units / Range \(net\) Net aggregated input \(\mathbb{R} \in (-\infty, +\infty)\) \(f(net)\) Linear output \(\mathbb{R} \in (-\infty, +\infty)\)
  • Characteristics: Continuous and unbounded.
  • Derivative: \(f'(net) = 1\). Constant gradient.
  • Limitation: Stacking multiple linear layers yields \(y = \mathbf{W}_k \dots \mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{W}^* \mathbf{x}\), providing zero non-linear feature representation.

docs.title: 3. Ramp Function (Saturating Linear)
docs.text:
\[ f(net) = \begin{cases} 0, & \text{if } net < 0 \\ net, & \text{if } 0 \le net \le 1 \\ 1, & \text{if } net > 1 \end{cases} \] Symbol Meaning Units / Range \(net\) Net aggregated input \(\mathbb{R} \in (-\infty, +\infty)\) \(f(net)\) Bounded piecewise output \([0, 1]\)
  • Characteristics: Piecewise linear; non-differentiable at boundary points \(net = 0\) and \(net = 1\).
  • Derivative: \(f'(net) = 1\) when \(0 < net < 1\); \(f'(net) = 0\) when \(net < 0\) or \(net > 1\).

docs.title: 4. Sigmoid (Logistic) Function
docs.text:
\[ f(net) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-net}} = \sigma(net) \] Symbol Meaning Units / Range \(net\) Net aggregated input \(\mathbb{R} \in (-\infty, +\infty)\) \(f(net)\) Probability distribution output \((0, 1)\) \(e\) Base of the natural logarithm \(\approx 2.71828\)
  • Mathematical Derivation of First Derivative: Let \(f(net) = (1 + e^{-net})^{-1}\). Applying the chain rule:
\[ \frac{d f(net)}{d(net)} = -1(1 + e^{-net})^{-2}(-e^{-net}) = \frac{e^{-net}}{(1 + e^{-net})^2} \]

Decomposing the fraction:

\[ f'(net) = \left(\frac{1}{1 + e^{-net}}\right) \left(\frac{e^{-net}}{1 + e^{-net}}\right) = f(net) [1 - f(net)] \]
  • Pros and Cons: Smooth, infinitely differentiable, maps outputs strictly to probabilities \((0, 1)\). However, it suffers from the vanishing gradient problem when \(|net| \gg 0\) (\(f'(net) \to 0\)) and its output is not zero-centered.

docs.title: 5. Hyperbolic Tangent (Tanh) Function
docs.text:
\[ f(net) = \tanh(net) = \frac{e^{net} - e^{-net}}{e^{net} + e^{-net}} = \frac{2}{1 + e^{-2 net}} - 1 = 2\sigma(2 net) - 1 \] Symbol Meaning Units / Range \(net\) Net aggregated input \(\mathbb{R} \in (-\infty, +\infty)\) \(f(net)\) Zero-centered continuous output \((-1, +1)\)
  • Mathematical Derivation of Derivative:
\[ \frac{d}{d(net)}\tanh(net) = \frac{(e^{net}+e^{-net})(e^{net}+e^{-net}) - (e^{net}-e^{-net})(e^{net}-e^{-net})}{(e^{net}+e^{-net})^2} = 1 - \tanh^2(net) = 1 - f(net)^2 \]
  • Pros and Cons: Zero-centered (mean output is near zero), which facilitates gradient descent optimization across layers. Still susceptible to vanishing gradients at extreme values.

docs.title: 6. Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU)
docs.text:
\[ f(net) = \max(0, net) \] Symbol Meaning Units / Range \(net\) Net aggregated input \(\mathbb{R} \in (-\infty, +\infty)\) \(f(net)\) Non-negative rectified output \([0, +\infty)\)
  • Derivative:
\[ f'(net) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } net > 0 \\ 0, & \text{if } net < 0 \end{cases} \]

(Subgradient convention sets \(f'(0) = 0\) or \(f'(0) = 0.5\)).

  • Pros and Cons: Computationally trivial (no exponentials), does not saturate in the positive regime, preventing vanishing gradients. Subject to the "Dying ReLU" failure mode where neurons receiving large negative biases permanently output zero with zero gradient.

docs.title: 7. Leaky Rectified Linear Unit (Leaky ReLU)
docs.text:
\[ f(net) = \max(\alpha \cdot net, net) = \begin{cases} net, & \text{if } net \ge 0 \\ \alpha \cdot net, & \text{if } net < 0 \end{cases} \] Symbol Meaning Units / Range \(net\) Net aggregated input \(\mathbb{R} \in (-\infty, +\infty)\) \(\alpha\) Fixed small leakage slope Typically \(\alpha = 0.01\) \(f(net)\) Leaky rectified output \((-\infty, +\infty)\)
  • Derivative:
\[ f'(net) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } net \ge 0 \\ \alpha, & \text{if } net < 0 \end{cases} \]
  • Pros: Solves the dying ReLU problem by guaranteeing a small, constant gradient \(\alpha\) for negative net inputs.

docs.title: 8. Parametric Rectified Linear Unit (PReLU)
docs.text:
\[ f(net) = \begin{cases} net, & \text{if } net \ge 0 \\ \alpha_i \cdot net, & \text{if } net < 0 \end{cases} \] Symbol Meaning Units / Range \(net\) Net aggregated input \(\mathbb{R} \in (-\infty, +\infty)\) \(\alpha_i\) Learnable channel/neuron-specific parameter Initialized to small positive value (e.g., \(0.25\)) \(f(net)\) Adaptive rectified output \((-\infty, +\infty)\)
  • Pros: Allows the network to learn the optimal slope for negative activations via gradient descent rather than fixing it heuristically.

docs.title: 9. Randomized Rectified Linear Unit (RReLU)
docs.text:
\[ f(net) = \begin{cases} net, & \text{if } net \ge 0 \\ a_{ji} \cdot net, & \text{if } net < 0 \end{cases} \]

where \(a_{ji} \sim U(l, u)\) with \(l < u\) (typically \(l = 1/8\), \(u = 1/3\)).

Symbol Meaning Units / Range \(net\) Net aggregated input \(\mathbb{R} \in (-\infty, +\infty)\) \(a_{ji}\) Random leakage coefficient \(a_{ji} \sim U(l, u)\) during training; \(\frac{l+u}{2}\) during testing \(f(net)\) Stochastically rectified output \((-\infty, +\infty)\)
  • Pros: Introduces regularization during training, reducing overfitting risk in deep convolutional networks.

docs.title: Table 6.2: Comprehensive Activation Functions Comparison Matrix
docs.text:

Primary Advantages & Disadvantages Binary Step \(1 \text{ if } net \ge 0 \text{ else } 0\) \(\{0, 1\}\) No (Discontinuous at \(0\)) \(0 \text{ for } net \ne 0\) Total (Gradient is \(0\)) Pro: Clean binary thresholding. Con: Cannot be used with gradient descent. Linear \(net\) \((-\infty, +\infty)\) Yes \(1\) None Pro: Preserves scale for regression. Con: Multi-layer networks collapse to single linear model. Ramp Piecewise linear \([0, 1]\) \([0, 1]\) No (Kinks at \(0, 1\)) \(1 \text{ if } 0 < net < 1 \text{ else } 0\) High outside \((0, 1)\) Pro: Bounds output. Con: Gradient dies outside active linear band. Sigmoid \(\frac{1}{1 + e^{-net}}\) \((0, 1)\) Yes \(f(net)[1 - f(net)]\) High for \(\|net\| > 3\) Pro: Smooth probabilistic interpretation. Con: Vanishing gradient; non-zero-centered. Con: Vanishing gradient at saturation plateaus. Con: Dying ReLU phenomenon on negative inputs. Con: Non-deterministic training step.

[Source: NN and Clustering.pdf, Slides 9–10, 27]

docs.title: 6.3 Neural Network Topologies and Architectures
docs.text: The architectural layout of an artificial neural network defines the flow of information, the presence or absence of recurrent temporal memory, and the structural partition of computational nodes. Networks range from single-layer arrangements to deep layered feedforward networks and feedback architectures.

docs.title: Structural Classifications of Network Topologies
docs.text:
1. Fully Connected Network (Asymmetric): Every node in the network possesses a directed synaptic connection to every other node with independent, asymmetric weights (\(w_{ij} \neq w_{ji}\)).
  2. Fully Connected Network (Symmetric): Every node is bidirectionally connected to every other node with identical mutual coupling weights (\(w_{ij} = w_{ji}\) and \(w_{ii} = 0\)), typical of energy-minimizing Hopfield networks.
  3. Layered Network: Computational units are partitioned into discrete subsets called layers: an Input Layer, zero or more Hidden Layers, and an Output Layer. Intra-layer connections within the same layer are prohibited.
  4. Acyclic Network: A subclass of layered networks containing no closed feedback loops or cycles; signal flow follows a strict directed acyclic graph (DAG).
  5. Feedforward Network: A subclass of acyclic networks where connections are permitted solely from a node in layer \(l\) to nodes in layer \(l+1\) (or strictly higher layers in skip-connection topologies).
  6. Recurrent / Feedback Network: Networks containing cyclic feedback loops wherein the outputs of downstream neurons (or internal hidden states) are redirected back as inputs to upstream neurons or to themselves, maintaining dynamic temporal state.

docs.title: Component Breakdown and Signal Flow in Feedforward Networks
docs.text:
• Input Layer: Does not perform computational transformations; acts as a fan-out buffer passing feature elements \(x_i\) to downstream units.
  • Hidden Layer: Evaluates non-linear transformations: \(h_j = f(\sum_i w_{ji} x_i + \theta_j)\). Hidden units extract intermediate abstract latent representations of the input space.
  • Output Layer: Synthesizes extracted hidden features into the final network prediction: \(y_k = g(\sum_j v_{kj} h_j + \theta_k)\).
  • Signal Flow: Purely unidirectional left-to-right propagation without feedback loops or delay elements.

docs.title: 6.4 Learning Paradigms and Linear Separability
docs.text:
Machine learning systems are governed by the nature and availability of instructional feedback. Artificial neural networks implement two dominant learning paradigms alongside reinforcement paradigms:

  1. Supervised Learning: The network is supplied with paired training tuples \(\{(\mathbf{x}_p, \mathbf{t}_p)\}_{p=1}^P\). An external supervisor or teacher provides the ground-truth target vector \(\mathbf{t}_p\). Learning proceeds by calculating an error signal \(e = \mathbf{t} - \mathbf{y}\) and adjusting synaptic parameters to minimize this discrepancy.
  2. Unsupervised Learning: The network receives unlabeled feature vectors \(\{\mathbf{x}_p\}_{p=1}^P\) without external teacher guidance. The network autonomously discovers statistical regularities, correlations, and geometric clusters within the data manifold.
  3. Reinforcement Learning: An agent interacts with an environment, receiving scalar evaluative reward or penalty feedback rather than explicit corrective instructions.

docs.title: The Geometric Concept of Linear Separability
docs.text:
A binary classification problem involving two classes \(\mathcal{C}_1\) and \(\mathcal{C}_2\) in an \(n\)-dimensional Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is defined as linearly separable if and only if there exists an \((n-1)\)-dimensional affine hyperplane that completely separates the vectors of \(\mathcal{C}_1\) from \(\mathcal{C}_2\) without misclassification.

graph TD
    subgraph LinearSeparable ["Linearly Separable (AND / OR)"]
        A1["Class 0: (0,0), (0,1), (1,0)"]
        A2["Class 1: (1,1)"]
        SEP["Separating Line: x₁ + x₂ - 1.5 = 0"]
        A1 -.-> SEP
        A2 -.-> SEP
    end
    subgraph NonLinearSeparable ["Non-Linearly Separable (XOR)"]
        B1["Class 0: (0,0), (1,1)"]
        B2["Class 1: (0,1), (1,0)"]
        FAIL["No single straight line can separate Class 0 from Class 1"]
        B1 -.-> FAIL
        B2 -.-> FAIL
    end

docs.title: Dimensional Manifestations of Linear Separability
docs.text:
1. One-Dimensional Space (\(\mathbb{R}^1\)):
  2. The boundary is a single threshold point \(x = \theta\).
  3. Slide 19 Example: 7 students with body weight measurements categorized into "Not Obese" (NO) and "Obese" (O):
\[ \{(50, \text{NO}), (55, \text{NO}), (60, \text{NO}), (65, \text{NO}), (70, \text{O}), (75, \text{O}), (80, \text{O})\} \] 
 A clean separating threshold exists at any boundary point $x^* \in (65, 70)$, e.g., $x^* = 67.5\text{ kg}$. This problem is linearly separable in 1D.
  1. Two-Dimensional Space (\(\mathbb{R}^2\)):
  2. The boundary is a straight line governed by:
\[ w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b = 0 \implies x_2 = -\frac{w_1}{w_2} x_1 - \frac{b}{w_2} \]
  • Logical AND & OR Functions: Both are linearly separable in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
  • Logical XOR (Exclusive OR) Problem:
\[ \mathcal{C}_0 = \{(0,0), (1,1)\}, \quad \mathcal{C}_1 = \{(0,1), (1,0)\} \] 
 No single line $w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b = 0$ can simultaneously satisfy:
\[ \begin{cases} w_1(0) + w_2(0) + b < 0 \implies b < 0 \\ w_1(0) + w_2(1) + b \ge 0 \implies w_2 + b \ge 0 \\ w_1(1) + w_2(0) + b \ge 0 \implies w_1 + b \ge 0 \\ w_1(1) + w_2(1) + b < 0 \implies w_1 + w_2 + b < 0 \end{cases} \] 
 Summing inequalities 2 and 3 yields $w_1 + w_2 + 2b \ge 0$. Since $b < 0$, this requires $w_1 + w_2 + b > 0$, directly contradicting inequality 4 ($w_1 + w_2 + b < 0$). This proof (formalized by Minsky and Papert in 1969) proved the fundamental limitation of single-layer perceptrons.
  1. Three-Dimensional Space (\(\mathbb{R}^3\)):
  2. The boundary is a flat two-dimensional plane:
\[ w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + w_3 x_3 + b = 0 \]
  1. N-Dimensional Space (\(\mathbb{R}^n\)):
  2. The boundary is an \((n-1)\)-dimensional separating hyperplane:
\[ \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i + b = 0 \]

[Source: NN and Clustering.pdf, Slides 18–21]

docs.title: 6.5 The Single-Layer Perceptron and Learning Rule
Definition: Perceptron
docs.text:
Meaning: A Perceptron is a supervised learning classifier that maps an incoming feature vector to a binary class decision by computing a linear combination of features and applying a hard threshold activation function.

Formal Definition: A mathematical operator \(P: \mathbb{R}^n \to \{0, 1\}\) defined as:

\[ y = f(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } \sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i + b \ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{if } \sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i + b < 0 \end{cases} \]

where \(\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is the synaptic weight vector, \(b \in \mathbb{R}\) is the bias scalar, and \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is the input pattern.

Intuition: The perceptron establishes a flat decision boundary across the input space. All points lying on or to one side of the hyperplane are classified as Class 1, while points on the opposing side are assigned to Class 0.

Example: Classifying patient medical indicators (e.g., blood glucose and insulin levels) into diabetic (\(1\)) or non-diabetic (\(0\)).

docs.title: The Perceptron Learning Algorithm
docs.text: The Perceptron Learning Rule adjusts the weight vector \(\mathbf{w}\) and bias \(b\) iteratively whenever a training pattern is misclassified.

docs.title: Governing Equations
docs.text: \[ e = t - y \] \[ \mathbf{w}^{(new)} = \mathbf{w}^{(old)} + \eta \cdot e \cdot \mathbf{x} \] \[ b^{(new)} = b^{(old)} + \eta \cdot e \] Symbol Meaning Units / Range \(\mathbf{w}\) Synaptic weight vector \(\mathbb{R}^n\) \(b\) Bias scalar parameter \(\mathbb{R}\) \(\eta\) Learning rate hyperparameter Real positive scalar, typically \(\eta \in (0, 1]\) \(\mathbf{x}\) Current input training vector \(\mathbb{R}^n\) \(t\) Desired ground-truth target label \(\{0, 1\}\) \(y\) Actual binary perceptron output \(\{0, 1\}\) \(e\) Quantified classification error \(\{-1, 0, +1\}\)

docs.title: What It Represents
docs.text: The update shifts the separating hyperplane toward misclassified points. When \(e = 0\), no weight adjustment occurs. When \(e = +1\) (false negative), the weight vector rotates toward \(\mathbf{x}\). When \(e = -1\) (false positive), the weight vector rotates away from \(\mathbf{x}\).

docs.title: Conditions and Convergence Theorem
docs.text: If the training dataset is linearly separable, the Perceptron Learning Rule is guaranteed to converge to a separating hyperplane in a finite number of weight updates (Perceptron Convergence Theorem). If the data is non-linearly separable, the algorithm will oscillate indefinitely without terminating.

docs.title: Key Practical Issues in Perceptron Design
docs.text:
1. Why Use Bias (\(b\))? Without an independent bias parameter (\(b=0\)), the separating hyperplane is constrained to pass through the coordinate origin: \(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} = 0\). Including \(b\) allows the decision boundary to translate anywhere in the coordinate space.

  2. Termination Criteria: Learning halts when: (a) Zero misclassification errors occur across an entire epoch, (b) The total squared error drops below a predefined tolerance, or (c) A preset maximum epoch budget is exhausted.

  3. Role of Learning Rate (\(\eta\)): Controls the step size of weight corrections. An excessively large \(\eta\) causes erratic oscillations around the optimal boundary, while an overly small \(\eta\) requires excessive training iterations.

  4. Handling Non-Numeric Inputs: Qualitative or categorical attributes must be converted to numerical representations using techniques such as one-hot encoding or ordinal feature scaling before presentation to the perceptron.

  5. Epoch Definition: An epoch represents exactly one complete sequential pass of all training instances through the network.

docs.title: Multiclass Discrimination via Layered Perceptrons
docs.text:
To classify input vectors into \(K > 2\) distinct classes, a layer of \(K\) independent perceptrons operating in parallel is used:

graph LR
    X["Input Vector x"] --> P1["Perceptron 1 (Class 1)"]
    X --> P2["Perceptron 2 (Class 2)"]
    X --> Pk["Perceptron K (Class K)"]
    P1 --> Y1["y₁"]
    P2 --> Y2["y₂"]
    Pk --> Yk["yₖ"]

docs.title: Decision Logic and Failure Modes
docs.text:
• One-Hot Encoding Criterion: A presented pattern \(\mathbf{x}\) is classified as belonging to Class \(i\) if and only if the \(i\)-th perceptron fires (\(y_i = 1\)) and all other perceptrons remain inactive (\(y_j = 0\) for all \(j \neq i\)).
  • Ambiguity and Failure Modes:
  • Dead Zone / Null Classification: If all perceptrons output zero (\(\sum_k y_k = 0\)), the pattern lies in an unassigned region; the network fails to classify.
  • Conflict Zone / Overlap: If two or more perceptrons output one simultaneously (\(\sum_k y_k \ge 2\)), the decision boundaries overlap, creating an ambiguous prediction.

docs.title: Mandatory Worked Numerical Problem 1: Perceptron 1D Classification (10–15 Marks)
Problem Statement
docs.text:
Assume 7 one-dimensional input patterns:

\[ X = \{0.0, 0.17, 0.33, 0.50, 0.67, 0.83, 1.0\} \]

The first four patterns belong to Class 0 (desired output \(t = 0\)), and the remaining three patterns belong to Class 1 (desired output \(t = 1\)). Design a single-layer perceptron to classify these patterns using the perceptron learning rule. Assume a learning rate \(\eta = 0.1\), and initial weight and bias values of \(w^{(0)} = -0.36\) and \(b^{(0)} = -0.10\). Show full step-by-step arithmetic computations for two complete epochs.

docs.title: Given Values and Initial Conditions
docs.text:
• Input patterns and targets:
  • \(P_1: x_1 = 0.00, \quad t_1 = 0\)
  • \(P_2: x_2 = 0.17, \quad t_2 = 0\)
  • \(P_3: x_3 = 0.33, \quad t_3 = 0\)
  • \(P_4: x_4 = 0.50, \quad t_4 = 0\)
  • \(P_5: x_5 = 0.67, \quad t_5 = 1\)
  • \(P_6: x_6 = 0.83, \quad t_6 = 1\)
  • \(P_7: x_7 = 1.00, \quad t_7 = 1\)
  • Learning rate: \(\eta = 0.1\)
  • Initial parameters: \(w = -0.36, \quad b = -0.10\)
  • Activation function:
\[ y = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } net \ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{if } net < 0 \end{cases} \]
  • Parameter update rules:
\[ e = t - y \] \[ w_{new} = w_{old} + \eta \cdot e \cdot x \] \[ b_{new} = b_{old} + \eta \cdot e \]

docs.title: Pattern 3: \(x = 0.33, t = 0\)
docs.text:
• Current state: \(w = -0.1270, \quad b = 0.0000\)
  • Net input:
\[ net = (-0.1270)(0.33) + 0.0000 = -0.0419 \]
  • Output: Since \(net = -0.0419 < 0\), \(y = 0\).
  • Error: \(e = 0 - 0 = 0\) (Correct).
  • Weight update:
\[ w_{new} = -0.1270, \quad b_{new} = 0.0000 \]

docs.title: Pattern 4: \(x = 0.50, t = 0\)
docs.text:
• Current state: \(w = -0.1270, \quad b = 0.0000\)
  • Net input:
\[ net = (-0.1270)(0.50) + 0.0000 = -0.0635 \]
  • Output: Since \(net = -0.0635 < 0\), \(y = 0\).
  • Error: \(e = 0 - 0 = 0\) (Correct).
  • Weight update:
\[ w_{new} = -0.1270, \quad b_{new} = 0.0000 \]

docs.title: Pattern 7: \(x = 1.00, t = 1\)
docs.text:
• Current state: \(w = -0.0600, \quad b = 0.1000\)
  • Net input:
\[ net = (-0.0600)(1.00) + 0.1000 = -0.0600 + 0.1000 = +0.0400 \]
  • Output: Since \(net = +0.0400 \ge 0\), \(y = 1\).
  • Error: \(e = 1 - 1 = 0\) (Correct).
  • Weight update:
\[ w_{new} = -0.0600, \quad b_{new} = 0.1000 \]

Parameters at the end of Epoch 2: \(w = -0.0600, \quad b = 0.1000\).

Final Interpretation
docs.text:
Over the course of two epochs, the perceptron parameters transitioned from \((w=-0.36, b=-0.10)\) to \((w=-0.06, b=0.10)\). By the end of Epoch 2, the decision boundary \(w \cdot x + b = 0\) yields a classification threshold \(x^* = -b/w = -(0.10)/(-0.06) \approx 1.67\). While the perceptron has not reached complete convergence by Epoch 2 (patterns \(P_3, P_4, P_6, P_7\) are correctly classified, while \(P_1, P_2, P_5\) showed misclassifications earlier in the epoch), the learning dynamics demonstrate monotonic movement of the decision boundary toward the separating margin between \(x=0.50\) and \(x=0.67\).

[Source: NN and Clustering.pdf, Slides 22–26]

docs.title: 6.6 Multi-Layer Perceptrons and the Backpropagation Algorithm
docs.text: Single-layer perceptrons are strictly limited to linearly separable decision regions. To resolve complex, non-linear classification boundaries (such as XOR) and approximate arbitrary continuous functions, Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) incorporate one or more hidden layers equipped with non-linear, continuously differentiable activation functions. The Backpropagation algorithm, popularized by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams (1986), provides the mathematical framework for training such multi-layer architectures via gradient descent.

docs.title: Multivariate Calculus Derivation of Backpropagation
docs.text:
Consider a layered feedforward network where an input layer connects to a hidden layer of units \(j\), which in turn connects to an output layer of units \(k\).

graph LR
    I["Input Unit i (xᵢ)"] -->|"wᵢⱼ"| H["Hidden Unit j (Oⱼ)"]
    H -->|"wⱼₖ"| O["Output Unit k (Oₖ)"]
    TH["Bias θⱼ"] --> H
    TO["Bias θₖ"] --> O

docs.title: Notation Definitions
docs.text:
• \(x_i\): Input feature presented to input unit \(i\).
  • \(I_j\): Net input to hidden unit \(j\):
\[ I_j = \sum_i w_{ij} O_i + \theta_j \]
  • \(O_j\): Output of hidden unit \(j\) using activation function \(f\):
\[ O_j = f(I_j) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-I_j}} \]
  • \(I_k\): Net input to output unit \(k\):
\[ I_k = \sum_j w_{jk} O_j + \theta_k \]
  • \(O_k\): Output of output unit \(k\):
\[ O_k = f(I_k) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-I_k}} \]
  • \(T_k\): Target ground-truth value for output unit \(k\).
  • \(E\): Total sum of squared errors across all output units for the given pattern:
\[ E = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k} (T_k - O_k)^2 \]

docs.title: Derivation 1: Output Layer Weight Update (\(\Delta w_{jk}\))
docs.text:
To adjust the weight \(w_{jk}\) between hidden unit \(j\) and output unit \(k\) using gradient descent:

\[ \Delta w_{jk} = -\eta \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{jk}} \]

Applying the multivariate calculus chain rule:

\[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{jk}} = \frac{\partial E}{\partial O_k} \cdot \frac{\partial O_k}{\partial I_k} \cdot \frac{\partial I_k}{\partial w_{jk}} \]

docs.title: Step 1: Differentiating Total Error with respect to Output \(O_k\)
docs.text: \[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial O_k} = \frac{\partial}{\partial O_k} \left[ \frac{1}{2} (T_k - O_k)^2 \right] = -(T_k - O_k) \]

docs.title: Step 2: Differentiating Output \(O_k\) with respect to Net Input \(I_k\)
docs.text:
For the standard logistic sigmoid activation function:

\[ \frac{\partial O_k}{\partial I_k} = \frac{d}{d I_k} \left( \frac{1}{1 + e^{-I_k}} \right) = O_k (1 - O_k) \]

docs.title: Step 3: Differentiating Net Input \(I_k\) with respect to Weight \(w_{jk}\)
docs.text:
Since \(I_k = \sum_j w_{jk} O_j + \theta_k\):

\[ \frac{\partial I_k}{\partial w_{jk}} = O_j \]

docs.title: Step 4: Synthesizing the Output Gradient
docs.text:
Combining these components:

\[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{jk}} = -(T_k - O_k) \cdot O_k (1 - O_k) \cdot O_j \]

Defining the output error gradient \(Err_k\) (as adopted in Han & Kamber):

\[ Err_k = -\frac{\partial E}{\partial I_k} = (T_k - O_k) O_k (1 - O_k) \]

Therefore:

\[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{jk}} = -Err_k \cdot O_j \]

Applying the gradient descent learning rule with learning rate \(\eta\):

\[ \Delta w_{jk} = \eta \cdot Err_k \cdot O_j \] \[ w_{jk}^{(new)} = w_{jk}^{(old)} + \Delta w_{jk} \]

For the output bias \(\theta_k\):

\[ \Delta \theta_k = \eta \cdot Err_k \] \[ \theta_k^{(new)} = \theta_k^{(old)} + \Delta \theta_k \]

docs.title: Derivation 2: Hidden Layer Weight Update (\(\Delta w_{ij}\))
docs.text:
Now consider a synaptic weight \(w_{ij}\) connecting input unit \(i\) to hidden unit \(j\). Applying the multivariate chain rule across all downstream output units \(k\):

\[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}} = \frac{\partial E}{\partial I_j} \cdot \frac{\partial I_j}{\partial w_{ij}} \]

where:

\[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial I_j} = \frac{\partial E}{\partial O_j} \cdot \frac{\partial O_j}{\partial I_j} \]

Because the output \(O_j\) influences error \(E\) through all output units \(k\) connected to unit \(j\):

\[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial O_j} = \sum_k \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial I_k} \cdot \frac{\partial I_k}{\partial O_j} \right) \]

Recall that \(\frac{\partial E}{\partial I_k} = -Err_k\) and \(\frac{\partial I_k}{\partial O_j} = w_{jk}\). Substituting these relations:

\[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial O_j} = \sum_k (-Err_k \cdot w_{jk}) = -\sum_k (Err_k \cdot w_{jk}) \]

Next, differentiating the activation of hidden unit \(j\):

\[ \frac{\partial O_j}{\partial I_j} = O_j (1 - O_j) \]

Thus, defining the hidden unit error gradient \(Err_j\):

\[ Err_j = -\frac{\partial E}{\partial I_j} = -\left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial O_j} \cdot \frac{\partial O_j}{\partial I_j} \right) = O_j (1 - O_j) \sum_k (Err_k \cdot w_{jk}) \]

Finally, since \(I_j = \sum_i w_{ij} x_i + \theta_j\), we have \(\frac{\partial I_j}{\partial w_{ij}} = x_i\). Therefore:

\[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{ij}} = -Err_j \cdot x_i \]

The gradient descent weight and bias updates for the hidden layer are:

\[ \Delta w_{ij} = \eta \cdot Err_j \cdot x_i \] \[ w_{ij}^{(new)} = w_{ij}^{(old)} + \Delta w_{ij} \] \[ \Delta \theta_j = \eta \cdot Err_j \] \[ \theta_j^{(new)} = \theta_j^{(old)} + \Delta \theta_j \]

docs.title: Mandatory Worked Numerical Problem 2: Backpropagation on 3-2-1 Network (10–15 Marks)
Problem Statement (Han & Kamber Benchmark)
docs.text:
Consider a fully connected multi-layer feedforward network with three input units (\(1, 2, 3\)), two hidden units (\(4, 5\)), and one output unit (\(6\)). The network uses logistic sigmoid activation functions:

\[ f(I) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-I}} \]

A training pattern \(\mathbf{x} = [1, 0, 1]^T\) with desired target \(T_6 = 1\) is presented. The learning rate is \(\eta = 0.9\). Compute the forward pass (net inputs and outputs), error gradients (\(Err_6, Err_5, Err_4\)), and updated weights and biases.

  • Learning rate: \(\eta = 0.9\)
  • Initial weights:
  • Input to Hidden:
\[ w_{14} = 0.2, \quad w_{15} = -0.3 \] \[ w_{24} = 0.4, \quad w_{25} = 0.1 \] \[ w_{34} = -0.5, \quad w_{35} = 0.2 \]

  • Initial biases:

Final Interpretation
docs.text:
The initial output \(O_6 = 0.474\) was substantially below the desired target \(T = 1.0\), resulting in an initial squared error \(E = \frac{1}{2}(1 - 0.474)^2 \approx 0.1383\). Applying backpropagation increased the output bias \(\theta_6\) from \(0.10\) to \(0.2180\) and shifted the output synaptic weights in the positive direction (\(w_{46}: -0.3 \to -0.2608\), \(w_{56}: -0.2 \to -0.1380\)), driving the net input higher to align subsequent predictions closer to \(1.0\).

[Source: NN and Clustering.pdf, Slides 27–32]

docs.title: 6.7 Unsupervised Competitive Learning and Self-Organizing Maps (SOM)
docs.text: Unsupervised neural learning discards target labels in favor of identifying natural clusterings, latent geometric manifolds, and continuous feature representations directly from input data. Two prominent connectionist architectures embody this paradigm: Simple Competitive Learning and Kohonen's Self-Organizing Feature Maps (SOM).

docs.title: Simple Competitive Learning and Winner-Take-All (WTA)
docs.text:
In competitive learning, output neurons compete with one another for the exclusive right to represent input patterns. The network topology consists of a feedforward layer from inputs to output units, coupled with reciprocal lateral inhibitory connections among output units.

graph TD
    X["Input Vector x = (x₁, x₂, x₃)"]
    X -->|"W_A"| NA["Neuron A"]
    X -->|"W_B"| NB["Neuron B"]
    X -->|"W_C"| NC["Neuron C"]

    NA <-->|"Lateral Inhibition (-)"| NB
    NB <-->|"Lateral Inhibition (-)"| NC
    NA <-->|"Lateral Inhibition (-)"| NC

    WIN["Winner-Take-All: argmin ||x - Wᵢ||"]
    NA -.-> WIN
    NB -.-> WIN
    NC -.-> WIN

docs.title: The Winner-Take-All Adaptation Rule
docs.text:
1. Distance Metric Evaluation: For an presented input vector \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d\), each competing neuron \(i\) calculates its Euclidean distance:
\[ d_i = \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{w}_i\| = \sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^d (x_k - w_{ik})^2} \]
  1. Winner Selection: The winning unit \(k^*\) is identified as:
\[ k^* = \arg\min_i \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{w}_i\| \]
  1. Synaptic Weight Update: Only the winning neuron adjusts its weight vector toward the input vector:
\[ \mathbf{w}_{k^*}^{(new)} = \mathbf{w}_{k^*}^{(old)} + \eta (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{w}_{k^*}^{(old)}) \]

For all non-winning units (\(i \neq k^*\)):

\[ \mathbf{w}_i^{(new)} = \mathbf{w}_i^{(old)} \]

docs.title: Key Behavioral Observations in Competitive Learning
docs.text:
• Neuron Specialization: Over repeated iterations, individual neurons move toward dense clusters of inputs, effectively acting as adaptive cluster centers.
  • Sensitivity to Initial Positions: Random weight initialization strongly dictates the final partition. If initial weights are biased toward one quadrant, convergence can become skewed.
  • The "Dead Unit" Problem: A neuron initialized far from all training data may never win a competition (\(d_i > d_{others}\) for all \(\mathbf{x}\)). Because non-winners receive zero updates, the unit remains permanently inactive ("dead"), wasting computational capacity.

docs.title: Mandatory Worked Numerical Problem 3: Simple Competitive Learning Trace (10–15 Marks)
Problem Statement
docs.text:
Given six 3-dimensional training samples:

\[ \mathbf{x}_1 = (1.1, 1.7, 1.8), \quad \mathbf{x}_2 = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), \quad \mathbf{x}_3 = (0.0, 0.5, 1.5) \] \[ \mathbf{x}_4 = (1.0, 0.0, 0.0), \quad \mathbf{x}_5 = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5), \quad \mathbf{x}_6 = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) \]

Train a competitive learning output layer of three neurons (\(A, B, C\)) with initial random weights:

\[ \mathbf{w}_A = (0.2, 0.7, 0.3), \quad \mathbf{w}_B = (0.1, 0.1, 0.9), \quad \mathbf{w}_C = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) \]

Use a learning rate \(\eta = 0.5\). Track the winner selection and weight vector updates across two full training epochs (12 iterations).

docs.title: Final Interpretation
docs.text:
Across both training epochs, the three neurons specialize into distinct feature subspaces:

  • Neuron C captures high-magnitude input samples (\(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_6\)).
  • Neuron B specializes in patterns dominated by the third coordinate with small first components (\(\mathbf{x}_3\)).
  • Neuron A captures distributed low-magnitude and origin-adjacent patterns (\(\mathbf{x}_2, \mathbf{x}_4, \mathbf{x}_5\)). Neuron A won three patterns per epoch, while C won two and B won one, illustrating that cluster density and initial positioning govern winning frequency.

docs.title: Self-Organizing Maps (SOM / Kohonen Networks)
docs.text:
Introduced by Teuvo Kohonen, Self-Organizing Maps extend competitive learning by mapping high-dimensional inputs onto a low-dimensional discrete lattice (usually 1D or 2D) while preserving the topological and metric properties of the input manifold.

graph TD
    subgraph SOMGrid ["2D Lattice Array of Neurons"]
        N11["(1,1)"] --- N12["(1,2)"] --- N13["(1,3)"]
        N21["(2,1)"] --- BMU["(2,2) BMU (Winner)"] --- N23["(2,3)"]
        N31["(3,1)"] --- N32["(3,2)"] --- N33["(3,3)"]
        N11 --- N21 --- N31
        N12 --- BMU --- N32
        N13 --- N23 --- N33
    end
    X["Input Vector x"] --> BMU

docs.title: The Four Phases of SOM Algorithm Execution
docs.text:
1. Initialization: Synaptic weight vectors \(\mathbf{w}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d\) are initialized to small random values or sampled along the primary principal components of the dataset.
  2. Competition (BMU Selection): For an input \(\mathbf{x}(t)\), every neuron on the grid calculates its Euclidean distance \(\|\mathbf{x}(t) - \mathbf{w}_i(t)\|\). The Best Matching Unit (BMU) \(c\) is selected as:
\[ c = \arg\min_i \|\mathbf{x}(t) - \mathbf{w}_i(t)\| \]
  1. Cooperation (Topological Neighborhood): Rather than updating only the winner, a topological neighborhood function \(h_{ci}(t)\) defines the spatial influence of BMU \(c\) across the lattice:
\[ h_{ci}(t) = \exp\left( -\frac{\|\mathbf{r}_c - \mathbf{r}_i\|^2}{2\sigma^2(t)} \right) \]

where \(\mathbf{r}_c, \mathbf{r}_i\) are grid coordinates, and \(\sigma(t)\) is the neighborhood radius decaying over time:

\[ \sigma(t) = \sigma_0 \exp\left( -\frac{t}{\tau_1} \right) \]
  1. Adaptation & Cooling: All neurons within the neighborhood update their weights:
\[ \mathbf{w}_i(t+1) = \mathbf{w}_i(t) + \eta(t) \cdot h_{ci}(t) [\mathbf{x}(t) - \mathbf{w}_i(t)] \]

where the learning rate \(\eta(t)\) decays monotonically:

\[ \eta(t) = \eta_0 \exp\left( -\frac{t}{\tau_2} \right) \]

docs.title: Mandatory Worked Numerical Problem 4: SOM 1D Chain B–A–C Trace (10–15 Marks)
Problem Statement
docs.text:
Consider an SOM configured as a one-dimensional linear lattice of three neurons ordered:

\[ \text{Neuron } B \longleftrightarrow \text{Neuron } A \longleftrightarrow \text{Neuron } C \]

The grid distances are \(d_{grid}(B, A) = 1\), \(d_{grid}(A, C) = 1\), and \(d_{grid}(B, C) = 2\). The dataset consists of the six 3D vectors from Problem 3 presented cyclically:

\[ T = \{\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \mathbf{x}_3, \mathbf{x}_4, \mathbf{x}_5, \mathbf{x}_6\} \]

Initial weight vectors are:

\[ \mathbf{w}_A(0) = (0.2, 0.7, 0.3), \quad \mathbf{w}_B(0) = (0.1, 0.1, 0.9), \quad \mathbf{w}_C(0) = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) \]

The neighborhood radius \(D(t)\) and learning rate \(\eta(t)\) follow the schedule:

  • For \(t \le 6\): \(D(t) = 1\) (BMU and its immediate 1-hop lattice neighbors update); \(\eta(t) = 0.5\).
  • For \(7 \le t \le 12\): \(D(t) = 0\) (only BMU updates, winner-take-all); \(\eta(t) = 0.25\).
  • For \(t \ge 13\): \(D(t) = 0\); \(\eta(t) = 0.10\). Execute the trace for 15 iterations and analyze inter-neuron distance evolution.

docs.title: Step \(t = 1\): Present \(\mathbf{x}_1 = (1.1, 1.7, 1.8)\)
docs.text:
• \(D(1) = 1, \quad \eta(1) = 0.5\)
  • Input space Euclidean distances:
  • \(d_A = 2.015, \quad d_B = 2.091, \quad d_C = 1.068 \implies \text{Winner is } \mathbf{C}\).
  • Lattice neighbors within \(D=1\) of \(C\): Unit \(C\) (distance \(0\)) and Unit \(A\) (distance \(1\)). Unit \(B\) is excluded (\(d_{grid}=2\)).
  • Weight updates:
\[ \mathbf{w}_C(1) = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) + 0.5[(1.1, 1.7, 1.8) - (1.0, 1.0, 1.0)] = (1.050, 1.350, 1.400) \] \[ \mathbf{w}_A(1) = (0.2, 0.7, 0.3) + 0.5[(1.1, 1.7, 1.8) - (0.2, 0.7, 0.3)] = (0.650, 1.200, 1.050) \] \[ \mathbf{w}_B(1) = (0.100, 0.100, 0.900) \quad \text{(Unchanged)} \]

docs.title: Topological Distance Evolution and Interpretation
docs.text:
Calculating Euclidean distances between neurons in feature space at \(t = 15\):

  • \(\|\mathbf{w}_A - \mathbf{w}_B\| = \sqrt{(0.828-0.474)^2 + (0.770-0.234)^2 + (0.814-0.300)^2} = \sqrt{0.125 + 0.287 + 0.264} = \sqrt{0.676} \approx 0.822\)
  • \(\|\mathbf{w}_A - \mathbf{w}_C\| = \sqrt{(0.828-0.611)^2 + (0.770-0.953)^2 + (0.814-1.339)^2} = \sqrt{0.047 + 0.033 + 0.276} = \sqrt{0.356} \approx 0.597\)
  • \(\|\mathbf{w}_B - \mathbf{w}_C\| = \sqrt{(0.474-0.611)^2 + (0.234-0.953)^2 + (0.300-1.339)^2} = \sqrt{0.019 + 0.517 + 1.080} = \sqrt{1.616} \approx 1.271\)

Notice that:

\[ \|\mathbf{w}_B - \mathbf{w}_C\| \approx 1.271 > \|\mathbf{w}_A - \mathbf{w}_B\| \text{ and } \|\mathbf{w}_A - \mathbf{w}_C\| \]

The metric distances in feature space reflect the 1D lattice topology (\(B \longleftrightarrow A \longleftrightarrow C\)), where \(B\) and \(C\) are separated by intermediate unit \(A\). The SOM successfully preserved topological adjacency during self-organization.

[Source: NN and Clustering.pdf, Slides 33–45]

docs.title: 6.8 Partitioning Clustering Methods: K-Means and K-Medoids
docs.text: Cluster analysis aims to partition an unlabeled set of observations into groups such that objects within the same cluster exhibit high mutual similarity, while objects across distinct clusters exhibit pronounced dissimilarity.

docs.title: Definition: K-Means Clustering
docs.text:
Meaning: K-Means is an iterative, centroid-based partitioning algorithm that divides an unlabeled dataset into \(K\) non-overlapping clusters by minimizing the total squared distance between data points and their assigned cluster means.

Formal Definition: Given a dataset \(D = \{\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \dots, \mathbf{x}_n\}\) with \(\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d\), K-Means partitions \(D\) into \(K\) disjoint clusters \(\mathcal{C} = \{C_1, C_2, \dots, C_K\}\) that minimize the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) objective function:

\[ J = \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{\mathbf{x}_i \in C_k} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2 \]

where \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\) is the arithmetic centroid of cluster \(C_k\):

\[ \boldsymbol{\mu}_k = \frac{1}{|C_k|} \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in C_k} \mathbf{x} \]

Intuition: The algorithm acts as an alternating minimization process: it assigns points to the nearest current cluster center, recalculates the centers as the means of the newly formed clusters, and repeats until the centroids stabilize.

Example: Customer segmentation in e-commerce grouping consumers by annual expenditure and site browsing duration.

docs.title: The K-Means Algorithmic Procedure
docs.text:
1. Centroid Initialization: Select \(K\) initial points as initial cluster seeds \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1^{(0)}, \dots, \boldsymbol{\mu}_K^{(0)}\) (chosen randomly or via K-Means++).
  2. Assignment Step: Assign each data point \(\mathbf{x}_i\) to its nearest centroid based on Euclidean distance:
\[ C_k^{(t)} = \left\{ \mathbf{x}_i : \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{(t)}\|^2 \le \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_j^{(t)}\|^2, \quad \forall j \in \{1, \dots, K\} \right\} \]
  1. Centroid Recalculation Step: Recompute the arithmetic mean of all vectors assigned to each cluster:
\[ \boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{(t+1)} = \frac{1}{|C_k^{(t)}|} \sum_{\mathbf{x}_i \in C_k^{(t)}} \mathbf{x}_i \]
  1. Convergence Check: Repeat steps 2 and 3 until cluster assignments no longer change, centroid shifts fall below a threshold \(\epsilon\), or a maximum iteration limit is reached.

docs.title: Strengths and Limitations of K-Means
docs.text:
• Strengths: Simple implementation, computationally efficient with time complexity \(\mathcal{O}(t \cdot K \cdot n \cdot d)\) where \(t \ll n\).
  • Limitations: Sensitive to initial centroid placement (risk of suboptimal local minima), prone to distortion from extreme outliers, requires specifying \(K\) in advance, and implicitly assumes spherical, equal-variance clusters.

docs.title: Definition: K-Medoids Clustering (PAM - Partitioning Around Medoids)
docs.text:
Meaning: K-Medoids is a partitioning clustering algorithm that designates actual observed data points (medoids) as cluster centers instead of fictitious arithmetic means, making it substantially more robust to noise and extreme outliers.

Formal Definition: Given an arbitrary dissimilarity metric \(d(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)\), K-Medoids identifies \(K\) representative medoid objects \(\{m_1, m_2, \dots, m_K\} \subset D\) that minimize the total absolute dissimilarity:

\[ J_{medoid} = \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{\mathbf{x}_i \in C_k} d(\mathbf{x}_i, m_k) \]

Intuition: Just as the median is more robust than the mean in univariate statistics, using an actual observed data point as the cluster representative prevents extreme outlier values from shifting the cluster center.

Example: Clustering DNA sequences or graph structures where arithmetic means cannot be computed, but pairwise sequence alignments provide valid distances.

docs.title: Table 6.4: K-Means vs K-Medoids In-Depth Comparison
docs.text: Dimension / Property K-Means Algorithm K-Medoids (PAM) Algorithm Cluster Representative Fictitious arithmetic mean (\(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k = \frac{1}{\vert C_k \vert}\sum \mathbf{x}\)) Actual observed data point (Medoid \(m_k \in D\)) Objective Function Within-Cluster Sum of Squared Errors (WCSS): \(\sum \|\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}\|^2\) Absolute Dissimilarity Error: \(\sum d(\mathbf{x}, m)\) Sensitivity to Outliers High (Squaring distances amplifies outlier leverage) Low (Medoid resists distortion from distant points) Computational Complexity \(\mathcal{O}(t \cdot K \cdot n \cdot d)\) — highly scalable to large \(n\) \(\mathcal{O}(t \cdot K \cdot (n - K)^2)\) for PAM — computationally heavy Applicable Data Types Continuous Euclidean vector spaces only Continuous, categorical, graphs, sequence data Distance Metric Flexibility Restricted to Euclidean distance Supports arbitrary distance metrics (Manhattan, Cosine, Jaccard)

docs.title: Mandatory Worked Numerical Problem 5: K-Means 8-Point Clustering (10–15 Marks)
Problem Statement (Slide 47 Benchmark)
docs.text:
Perform K-Means clustering (\(K = 3\)) on a two-dimensional dataset of eight individual points:

\[ A_1 = (2, 10), \quad A_2 = (2, 5), \quad A_3 = (8, 4) \] \[ B_1 = (5, 8), \quad B_2 = (7, 5), \quad B_3 = (6, 4) \] \[ C_1 = (1, 2), \quad C_2 = (4, 9) \]

Designate the initial cluster centers as:

\[ m_1^{(0)} = A_1 = (2, 10), \quad m_2^{(0)} = B_1 = (5, 8), \quad m_3^{(0)} = C_1 = (1, 2) \]

Use Euclidean distance \(d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{m}) = \sqrt{(x_1 - m_1)^2 + (x_2 - m_2)^2}\). Show the full distance evaluation, cluster assignment, and centroid recalculation for Iteration 1.

docs.title: Step 1: Distance Computations to Initial Centroids
Point \(B_2 = (7, 5)\)
docs.text:
• \(d(B_2, m_1) = \sqrt{(7-2)^2 + (5-10)^2} = \sqrt{25 + 25} = \sqrt{50} \approx 7.07\)
  • \(d(B_2, m_2) = \sqrt{(7-5)^2 + (5-8)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 9} = \sqrt{13} \approx 3.61\)
  • \(d(B_2, m_3) = \sqrt{(7-1)^2 + (5-2)^2} = \sqrt{36 + 9} = \sqrt{45} \approx 6.71\)
  • Minimum distance is \(3.61 \implies\) Assignment: Cluster 2

docs.title: Point \(B_3 = (6, 4)\)
docs.text:
• \(d(B_3, m_1) = \sqrt{(6-2)^2 + (4-10)^2} = \sqrt{16 + 36} = \sqrt{52} \approx 7.21\)
  • \(d(B_3, m_2) = \sqrt{(6-5)^2 + (4-8)^2} = \sqrt{1 + 16} = \sqrt{17} \approx 4.12\)
  • \(d(B_3, m_3) = \sqrt{(6-1)^2 + (4-2)^2} = \sqrt{25 + 4} = \sqrt{29} \approx 5.39\)
  • Minimum distance is \(4.12 \implies\) Assignment: Cluster 2

docs.title: Point \(C_2 = (4, 9)\)
docs.text:
• \(d(C_2, m_1) = \sqrt{(4-2)^2 + (9-10)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 1} = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.24\)
  • \(d(C_2, m_2) = \sqrt{(4-5)^2 + (9-8)^2} = \sqrt{1 + 1} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41\)
  • \(d(C_2, m_3) = \sqrt{(4-1)^2 + (9-2)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 49} = \sqrt{58} \approx 7.62\)
  • Minimum distance is \(1.41 \implies\) Assignment: Cluster 2

docs.title: Final Interpretation
docs.text:
In a single iteration, the cluster centroids moved from the arbitrary seeds \((2, 10), (5, 8), (1, 2)\) to updated positions:

\[ \boldsymbol{\mu}_1 = (2, 10), \quad \boldsymbol{\mu}_2 = (6, 6), \quad \boldsymbol{\mu}_3 = (1.5, 3.5) \]

Points \(A_3, B_1, B_2, B_3, C_2\) form a cohesive central cluster around \((6,6)\), while \(A_2\) and \(C_1\) form a low-magnitude cluster around \((1.5, 3.5)\). Point \(A_1\) remains an isolated high-value cluster at \((2, 10)\).

[Source: NN and Clustering.pdf, Slides 46–48]

docs.title: 6.9 Hierarchical Clustering Methods
docs.text:
Hierarchical clustering builds a continuous nested tree of partitions, avoiding the requirement to specify the number of clusters \(K\) beforehand. Hierarchical algorithms follow one of two paradigms:

  1. Agglomerative (Bottom-Up): Starts with every data point as an independent singleton cluster (\(N\) clusters for \(N\) points). At each successive step, the two closest clusters are merged until all entities unite into a single root cluster.
  2. Divisive (Top-Down): Starts with the entire dataset grouped into one monolithic root cluster, then recursively splits clusters into smaller fragments until each point forms its own singleton.

docs.title: Linkage Criteria for Cluster Distance Evaluation
docs.text:
When clusters contain multiple points, their pairwise dissimilarity is measured using a linkage criterion:

graph TD
    subgraph Linkages ["Hierarchical Linkage Formulations"]
        SL["Single Linkage: min d(x, y) (Chaining)"]
        CL["Complete Linkage: max d(x, y) (Compact Spheres)"]
        AL["Average Linkage: mean d(x, y) (Robust Balance)"]
        CEN["Centroid Linkage: ||μ₁ - μ₂|| (Mean Distance)"]
    end

docs.title: 1. Single Linkage (Minimum Distance / Nearest Neighbor)
docs.text:
\[ d(A, B) = \min_{\mathbf{x} \in A, \mathbf{y} \in B} d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) \]
  • Properties: Can track non-elliptical, elongated, concentric cluster geometries.
  • Limitation: Susceptible to the chaining effect, where noisy bridging points between two distinct clusters can cause them to merge prematurely.

docs.title: 2. Complete Linkage (Maximum Distance / Furthest Neighbor)
docs.text:
\[ d(A, B) = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in A, \mathbf{y} \in B} d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) \]
  • Properties: Enforces tight, compact, spherical clusters of roughly equal diameters.
  • Limitation: Highly sensitive to outliers, which can disproportionately inflate cluster distances.

docs.title: 3. Average Linkage (UPGMA - Unweighted Pair Group Method with Arithmetic Mean)
docs.text:
\[ d(A, B) = \frac{1}{|A| \cdot |B|} \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in A} \sum_{\mathbf{y} \in B} d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) \]
  • Properties: Evaluates overall pairwise similarity across all points, providing a balanced compromise between single and complete linkage.

docs.title: Table 6.5: Linkage Criteria Comparison Matrix
docs.text: Linkage Criterion Mathematical Formulation Cluster Shape Bias Sensitivity to Noise / Outliers Chaining Tendency? Single Linkage \(\min_{\mathbf{x} \in A, \mathbf{y} \in B} d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})\) Arbitrary, non-elliptical, elongated chains High (Sensitive to noise bridges) High (Dominant failure mode) Complete Linkage \(\max_{\mathbf{x} \in A, \mathbf{y} \in B} d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})\) Compact, spherical, uniform diameter High (Outliers dominate maximums) None Average Linkage \(\frac{1}{\vert A \vert \vert B \vert}\sum \sum d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})\) Moderately spherical, balanced clusters Low (Averaging dampens outliers) Low Centroid Linkage \(\Vert \boldsymbol{\mu}_A - \boldsymbol{\mu}_B \Vert\) Spherical clusters Moderate Low (Can invert non-monotonically)

docs.title: The Dendrogram Representation
docs.text:
A dendrogram is a two-dimensional tree diagram that illustrates the hierarchy of nested cluster merges. The vertical axis represents the merge distance (or similarity threshold), while the horizontal axis arrays individual data points. Cutting the dendrogram horizontally at a chosen threshold \(q\) partitions the dataset into disjoint clusters.

    C123["Cluster (1, 2, 3) (Level 0.80)"]
    C45["Cluster (4, 5) (Level 0.90)"]
    P6["Point 6"]

    P2["Point 2"]

    P4["Point 4"]

    ROOT --- C123
    ROOT --- C45
    C123 --- P1
    C123 --- C23["Cluster (2, 3) (Level 0.85)"]
