docs.title: 4.3 Service Layer and Thread-Safe Storage
docs.text:
package com.deepcollege.fsd.unit3.service;

import com.deepcollege.fsd.unit3.dto.OrderDto.*;
import com.deepcollege.fsd.unit3.exception.ResourceNotFoundException;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final Map<String, OrderResponse> orderDatabase = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final AtomicLong idSequence = new AtomicLong(1000);

    public OrderResponse createOrder(CreateOrderRequest request) {
        String generatedId = "ORD-" + idSequence.incrementAndGet();

        BigDecimal total = request.getItems().stream()
                .map(item -> item.getUnitPrice().multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(item.getQuantity())))
                .reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add);

        Instant now = Instant.now();
        OrderResponse response = new OrderResponse(
                generatedId,
                request.getCustomerId(),
                new ArrayList<>(request.getItems()),
                total,
                OrderStatus.PENDING,
                request.getShippingAddress(),
                now,
                now
        );

        orderDatabase.put(generatedId, response);
        return response;
    }

    public OrderResponse getOrderById(String orderId) {
        OrderResponse order = orderDatabase.get(orderId);
        if (order == null) {
            throw new ResourceNotFoundException("Order with ID '" + orderId + "' does not exist");
        }
        return order;
    }

    public List<OrderResponse> getAllOrders() {
        return new ArrayList<>(orderDatabase.values());
    }

    public OrderResponse updateOrderStatus(String orderId, OrderStatus newStatus) {
        OrderResponse existing = getOrderById(orderId);
        existing.setStatus(newStatus);
        existing.setUpdatedAt(Instant.now());
        orderDatabase.put(orderId, existing);
        return existing;
    }

    public void deleteOrder(String orderId) {
        if (!orderDatabase.containsKey(orderId)) {
            throw new ResourceNotFoundException("Order with ID '" + orderId + "' does not exist");
        }
        orderDatabase.remove(orderId);
    }
}

docs.title: 4.4 Global Exception Handling and Standardized API Responses
docs.text:
package com.deepcollege.fsd.unit3.exception;

import org.springframework.http.HttpHeaders;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatusCode;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.validation.FieldError;
import org.springframework.web.bind.MethodArgumentNotValidException;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ExceptionHandler;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestControllerAdvice;
import org.springframework.web.context.request.WebRequest;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.mvc.method.annotation.ResponseEntityExceptionHandler;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.*;

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {

    public static class ApiErrorResponse {
        private Instant timestamp;
        private int status;
        private String error;
        private String message;
        private String path;
        private Map<String, String> validationErrors;

        public ApiErrorResponse(int status, String error, String message, String path) {
            this.timestamp = Instant.now();
            this.status = status;
            this.error = error;
            this.message = message;
            this.path = path;
            this.validationErrors = new HashMap<>();
        }

        public Instant getTimestamp() { return timestamp; }
        public int getStatus() { return status; }
        public String getError() { return error; }
        public String getMessage() { return message; }
        public String getPath() { return path; }
        public Map<String, String> getValidationErrors() { return validationErrors; }
        public void setValidationErrors(Map<String, String> validationErrors) {
            this.validationErrors = validationErrors;
        }
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiErrorResponse> handleResourceNotFound(ResourceNotFoundException ex, WebRequest request) {
        String path = request.getDescription(false).replace("uri=", "");
        ApiErrorResponse error = new ApiErrorResponse(
                HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND.value(),
                HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND.getReasonPhrase(),
                ex.getMessage(),
                path
        );
        return new ResponseEntity<>(error, HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(InvalidOrderStateException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiErrorResponse> handleInvalidOrderState(InvalidOrderStateException ex, WebRequest request) {
        String path = request.getDescription(false).replace("uri=", "");
        ApiErrorResponse error = new ApiErrorResponse(
                HttpStatus.CONFLICT.value(),
                HttpStatus.CONFLICT.getReasonPhrase(),
                ex.getMessage(),
                path
        );
        return new ResponseEntity<>(error, HttpStatus.CONFLICT);
    }

    @Override
    protected ResponseEntity<Object> handleMethodArgumentNotValid(
            MethodArgumentNotValidException ex, HttpHeaders headers, HttpStatusCode status, WebRequest request) {

        String path = request.getDescription(false).replace("uri=", "");
        ApiErrorResponse error = new ApiErrorResponse(
                HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST.value(),
                "Validation Failed",
                "Input payload failed structural or semantic validation constraints",
                path
        );

        Map<String, String> errors = new HashMap<>();
        for (FieldError fieldError : ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors()) {
            errors.put(fieldError.getField(), fieldError.getDefaultMessage());
        }
        error.setValidationErrors(errors);

        return new ResponseEntity<>(error, HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiErrorResponse> handleGlobalException(Exception ex, WebRequest request) {
        String path = request.getDescription(false).replace("uri=", "");
        ApiErrorResponse error = new ApiErrorResponse(
                HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR.value(),
                HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR.getReasonPhrase(),
                "An unexpected internal server error occurred: " + ex.getMessage(),
                path
        );
        return new ResponseEntity<>(error, HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR);
    }
}

docs.title: 4.5 Web MVC Configuration with Content Negotiation and Interceptors
docs.text:
package com.deepcollege.fsd.unit3.config;

import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.HandlerInterceptor;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.ModelAndView;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.config.annotation.*;

@Configuration
@EnableWebMvc
public class WebMvcConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {

    public static class RequestLoggingInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {
        private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(RequestLoggingInterceptor.class);

        @Override
        public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response, Object handler) {
            request.setAttribute("startTime", System.currentTimeMillis());
            log.info(">> Incoming Request: [{} {}] from {}", request.getMethod(), request.getRequestURI(), request.getRemoteAddr());
            return true;
        }

        @Override
        public void postHandle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response, Object handler, ModelAndView modelAndView) {}

        @Override
        public void afterCompletion(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response, Object handler, Exception ex) {
            Long startTime = (Long) request.getAttribute("startTime");
            long duration = (startTime != null) ? (System.currentTimeMillis() - startTime) : 0;
            log.info("<< Completed Request: [{} {}] with Status [{}] in {} ms",
                    request.getMethod(), request.getRequestURI(), response.getStatus(), duration);
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry registry) {
        registry.addInterceptor(new RequestLoggingInterceptor())
                .addPathPatterns("/api/**");
    }

    @Override
    public void configureContentNegotiation(ContentNegotiationConfigurer configurer) {
        configurer
                .favorParameter(false)
                .ignoreAcceptHeader(false)
                .defaultContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .mediaType("json", MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .mediaType("xml", MediaType.APPLICATION_XML);
    }

    @Override
    public void addCorsMappings(CorsRegistry registry) {
        registry.addMapping("/api/**")
                .allowedOrigins("http://localhost:3000", "https://frontend.deepcollege.edu")
                .allowedMethods("GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "OPTIONS")
                .allowedHeaders("*")
                .allowCredentials(true)
                .maxAge(3600);
    }
}

docs.title: 4.6 Order REST Controller Implementation
docs.text:
package com.deepcollege.fsd.unit3.controller;

import com.deepcollege.fsd.unit3.dto.OrderDto.*;
import com.deepcollege.fsd.unit3.service.OrderService;
import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.support.ServletUriComponentsBuilder;

import java.net.URI;
import java.util.List;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/orders")
public class OrderRestController {

    private final OrderService orderService;

    @Autowired
    public OrderRestController(OrderService orderService) {
        this.orderService = orderService;
    }

    @PostMapping(
            consumes = {MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, MediaType.APPLICATION_XML_VALUE},
            produces = {MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, MediaType.APPLICATION_XML_VALUE}
    )
    public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> createOrder(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request) {
        OrderResponse createdOrder = orderService.createOrder(request);

        URI location = ServletUriComponentsBuilder
                .fromCurrentRequest()
                .path("/{id}")
                .buildAndExpand(createdOrder.getOrderId())
                .toUri();

        return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(createdOrder);
    }

    @GetMapping(
            produces = {MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, MediaType.APPLICATION_XML_VALUE}
    )
    public ResponseEntity<List<OrderResponse>> getAllOrders() {
        List<OrderResponse> orders = orderService.getAllOrders();
        return ResponseEntity.ok(orders);
    }

    @GetMapping(
            value = "/{id}",
            produces = {MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, MediaType.APPLICATION_XML_VALUE}
    )
    public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> getOrderById(@PathVariable("id") String orderId) {
        OrderResponse order = orderService.getOrderById(orderId);
        return ResponseEntity.ok(order);
    }

    @PutMapping(
            value = "/{id}/status",
            produces = {MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, MediaType.APPLICATION_XML_VALUE}
    )
    public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> updateStatus(
            @PathVariable("id") String orderId,
            @RequestParam("status") OrderStatus newStatus) {
        OrderResponse updated = orderService.updateOrderStatus(orderId, newStatus);
        return ResponseEntity.ok(updated);
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)
    public ResponseEntity<Void> deleteOrder(@PathVariable("id") String orderId) {
        orderService.deleteOrder(orderId);
        return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
    }
}

docs.title: 5. Node.js & Express.js Server Architecture
docs.text: Node.js represents an architectural paradigm shift in backend web servers, replacing dedicated thread-per-request models with an event-driven, single-threaded execution runtime backed by asynchronous non-blocking I/O multiplexers.

docs.title: 5.1 Event-Driven Asynchronous Non-Blocking I/O Model
docs.text:
Traditional multi-threaded servers (Apache, classic Tomcat) allocate a thread per connection, causing high context-switching and 1–2 MB RAM overhead per thread.

flowchart TD
    subgraph MultiThreaded["Traditional Multi-Threaded Model"]
        T1["Thread 1: DB Query -> SLEEP (Blocks 50ms)"]
        T2["Thread 2: File Read -> SLEEP (Blocks 20ms)"]
        TC["High Context-Switching (~1-2MB RAM per Thread Stack)"]
    end

    subgraph NodeModel["Node.js Event-Driven Architecture"]
        CallStack["Single JavaScript Thread\n(V8 Call Stack)"]
        EventLoop["libuv Event Loop\n(Orchestrator)"]
        KernelIO["OS Kernel Async I/O\n(epoll / kqueue / IOCP)"]
        WorkerPool["libuv Worker Pool\n(File I/O, Crypto, DNS)"]

        CallStack -->|"Delegate Async Task"| EventLoop
        EventLoop -->|"Non-blocking Sockets"| KernelIO
        EventLoop -->|"Blocking FS/Crypto"| WorkerPool
        KernelIO -.->|"Callback Ready"| EventLoop
        WorkerPool -.->|"Task Done"| EventLoop
        EventLoop -->|"Push Callback"| CallStack
    end

docs.title: 5.2 libuv Architecture and Event Loop Execution Phases
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["V8 Call Stack (Synchronous Code Execution)"] --> B{"Is Call Stack Empty?"}
    B -- No --> A
    B -- Yes --> Phase1["Phase 1: Timers\n(setTimeout, setInterval callbacks)"]
    Phase1 --> Micro1["Microtask Check\n(process.nextTick -> Promise reactions)"]
    Micro1 --> Phase2["Phase 2: Pending Callbacks\n(I/O callbacks deferred from previous loop)"]
    Phase2 --> Micro2["Microtask Check"]
    Micro2 --> Phase3["Phase 3: Idle, Prepare\n(Internal libuv housekeeping)"]
    Phase3 --> Micro3["Microtask Check"]
    Micro3 --> Phase4["Phase 4: Poll\n(Retrieve new I/O events, execute I/O callbacks)"]
    Phase4 --> Micro4["Microtask Check"]
    Micro4 --> Phase5["Phase 5: Check\n(setImmediate callbacks)"]
    Phase5 --> Micro5["Microtask Check"]
    Micro5 --> Phase6["Phase 6: Close Callbacks\n(socket.on('close') cleanup handlers)"]
    Phase6 --> Micro6["Microtask Check"]
    Micro6 --> B

docs.title: Detailed Event Loop Phases
docs.text:
1. Timers Phase: Executes callbacks scheduled by setTimeout() and setInterval().
  2. Pending Callbacks (I/O Callbacks): Executes deferred I/O callbacks (e.g., socket errors).
  3. Idle, Prepare: Internal libuv housekeeping.
  4. Poll Phase: Retrieves new I/O events and executes I/O callbacks. Blocks if poll queue is empty and no setImmediate is scheduled.
  5. Check Phase: Executes callbacks scheduled by setImmediate().
  6. Close Callbacks: Executes socket closure handlers (socket.on('close')).

docs.title: 5.3 Microtask Queues: process.nextTick() vs Promise Queue
docs.text:
Microtask queues execute immediately after synchronous code completes, before the event loop advances:

  1. process.nextTick() Queue: Highest priority. Drained before any event loop phase transitions.
  2. Promise Reactions Queue: Handles .then(), .catch(), and async/await. Drained immediately after process.nextTick().

docs.title: 5.4 Express.js Middleware Pipeline Architecture
docs.text:
Express.js implements the Chain of Responsibility Pattern: (req, res, next) => { ... }.

flowchart LR
    Req(["Inbound Request"]) --> M1["Middleware 1\nSecurity Headers"]
    M1 -->|"next()"| M2["Middleware 2\nBody Parser"]
    M2 -->|"next()"| M3["Middleware 3\nValidator"]
    M3 -->|"next()"| M4["Route Handler\nController Logic"]
    M3 -.->|"next(err)"| ErrM["Global Error Handler\n(err, req, res, next)"]
    M4 -->|"res.json()"| Res(["Response Sent"])
    ErrM -->|"res.status(500).json()"| Res

docs.title: Middleware Categories
docs.text:
1. Application-level: app.use(), app.get()
  2. Router-level: express.Router()
  3. Built-in: express.json(), express.static()
  4. Third-party: helmet, cors, morgan
  5. Error-handling: Exactly 4 parameters: (err, req, res, next)

docs.title: 6. Complete Production-Grade Node.js Express Server Implementation
6.1 Complete Runnable Server (server.js)
docs.text:
'use strict';

const express = require('express');
const crypto = require('crypto');
const http = require('http');

const app = express();
const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000;
const NODE_ENV = process.env.NODE_ENV || 'development';

// In-Memory Data Store
const productDatabase = new Map();
const initialSeedData = [
    {
        id: 'prod-001',
        title: 'Enterprise Mechanical Keyboard',
        description: 'Tactile hot-swappable mechanical switch keyboard with RGB backlighting',
        price: 149.99,
        category: 'Electronics',
        stock: 45,
        createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
        updatedAt: new Date().toISOString()
    },
    {
        id: 'prod-002',
        title: 'Ergonomic Vertical Mouse',
        description: 'Wireless optical vertical mouse designed to alleviate carpal tunnel strain',
        price: 79.50,
        category: 'Electronics',
        stock: 120,
        createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
        updatedAt: new Date().toISOString()
    }
];
initialSeedData.forEach(p => productDatabase.set(p.id, p));

// Security Headers Middleware
app.use((req, res, next) => {
    res.setHeader('X-Content-Type-Options', 'nosniff');
    res.setHeader('X-Frame-Options', 'DENY');
    res.setHeader('X-XSS-Protection', '1; mode=block');
    res.setHeader('Strict-Transport-Security', 'max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains');
    res.setHeader('Content-Security-Policy', "default-src 'self'");
    next();
});

// JSON Body Parser with strict payload limit
app.use(express.json({ limit: '10kb' }));

// Request Logging Middleware with High-Resolution Timing
app.use((req, res, next) => {
    const startTime = process.hrtime();
    const requestId = crypto.randomUUID();
    req.requestId = requestId;
    res.setHeader('X-Request-Id', requestId);

    res.on('finish', () => {
        const diff = process.hrtime(startTime);
        const durationInMs = (diff[0] * 1000 + diff[1] / 1e6).toFixed(2);
        console.log(`[${new Date().toISOString()}] [ID:${requestId}] ${req.method} ${req.originalUrl} | Status: ${res.statusCode} | Duration: ${durationInMs}ms`);
    });
    next();
});

// Input Validation Middleware
const validateProductPayload = (req, res, next) => {
    const { title, description, price, category, stock } = req.body;
    const errors = [];

    if (!title || typeof title !== 'string' || title.trim().length < 3 || title.trim().length > 100) {
        errors.push({ field: 'title', message: 'Title is required, must be between 3 and 100 characters' });
    }
    if (!description || typeof description !== 'string' || description.trim().length < 5 || description.trim().length > 500) {
        errors.push({ field: 'description', message: 'Description is required, must be between 5 and 500 characters' });
    }
    if (price === undefined || typeof price !== 'number' || price <= 0) {
        errors.push({ field: 'price', message: 'Price must be a positive number greater than 0' });
    }
    if (!category || typeof category !== 'string' || category.trim().length === 0) {
        errors.push({ field: 'category', message: 'Category must be a non-empty string' });
    }
    if (stock === undefined || !Number.isInteger(stock) || stock < 0) {
        errors.push({ field: 'stock', message: 'Stock must be a non-negative integer' });
    }

    if (errors.length > 0) {
        return res.status(400).json({
            status: 400,
            error: 'Bad Request',
            message: 'Input validation failed',
            validationErrors: errors,
            timestamp: new Date().toISOString()
        });
    }
    next();
};

// Modular Routing (/api/v1/products)
const productRouter = express.Router();

productRouter.get('/', (req, res) => {
    let results = Array.from(productDatabase.values());
    if (req.query.category) {
        const cat = req.query.category.toLowerCase();
        results = results.filter(p => p.category.toLowerCase() === cat);
    }
    const page = Math.max(1, parseInt(req.query.page, 10) || 1);
    const limit = Math.min(50, Math.max(1, parseInt(req.query.limit, 10) || 10));
    const startIndex = (page - 1) * limit;
    const paginatedResults = results.slice(startIndex, startIndex + limit);

    res.status(200).json({
        page,
        limit,
        totalItems: results.length,
        totalPages: Math.ceil(results.length / limit),
        data: paginatedResults
    });
});

productRouter.get('/:id', (req, res, next) => {
    const product = productDatabase.get(req.params.id);
    if (!product) {
        const err = new Error(`Product with ID '${req.params.id}' was not found`);
        err.statusCode = 404;
        return next(err);
    }
    res.status(200).json(product);
});

productRouter.post('/', validateProductPayload, (req, res) => {
    const { title, description, price, category, stock } = req.body;
    const newId = `prod-${crypto.randomBytes(4).toString('hex')}`;
    const timestamp = new Date().toISOString();

    const newProduct = {
        id: newId,
        title: title.trim(),
        description: description.trim(),
        price: parseFloat(price.toFixed(2)),
        category: category.trim(),
        stock: parseInt(stock, 10),
        createdAt: timestamp,
        updatedAt: timestamp
    };
    productDatabase.set(newId, newProduct);

    res.location(`/api/v1/products/${newId}`);
    res.status(201).json(newProduct);
});

productRouter.put('/:id', validateProductPayload, (req, res, next) => {
    const { id } = req.params;
    if (!productDatabase.has(id)) {
        const err = new Error(`Cannot update: Product with ID '${id}' does not exist`);
        err.statusCode = 404;
        return next(err);
    }
    const { title, description, price, category, stock } = req.body;
    const existing = productDatabase.get(id);

    const updatedProduct = {
        ...existing,
        title: title.trim(),
        description: description.trim(),
        price: parseFloat(price.toFixed(2)),
        category: category.trim(),
        stock: parseInt(stock, 10),
        updatedAt: new Date().toISOString()
    };
    productDatabase.set(id, updatedProduct);
    res.status(200).json(updatedProduct);
});

productRouter.delete('/:id', (req, res, next) => {
    const { id } = req.params;
    if (!productDatabase.has(id)) {
        const err = new Error(`Cannot delete: Product with ID '${id}' was not found`);
        err.statusCode = 404;
        return next(err);
    }
    productDatabase.delete(id);
    res.status(204).send();
});

app.use('/api/v1/products', productRouter);

// 404 Catch-All
app.use((req, res, next) => {
    const err = new Error(`Route '${req.originalUrl}' not found on this server`);
    err.statusCode = 404;
    next(err);
});

// Centralized 4-Argument Error Handler
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
    const statusCode = err.statusCode || 500;
    const errorResponse = {
        status: statusCode,
        error: http.STATUS_CODES[statusCode] || 'Internal Server Error',
        message: err.message || 'An unexpected internal error occurred',
        requestId: req.requestId || null,
        timestamp: new Date().toISOString()
    };
    if (NODE_ENV !== 'production') {
        errorResponse.stack = err.stack;
    }
    console.error(`[ERROR] [${req.requestId}] ${err.stack || err.message}`);
    res.status(statusCode).json(errorResponse);
});

// Server Initialization and Graceful Shutdown
const server = app.listen(PORT, () => {
    console.log(`[Express] Application running in ${NODE_ENV} mode on http://localhost:${PORT}`);
});

const handleGracefulShutdown = (signal) => {
    console.log(`\n[${signal}] Received. Shutting down gracefully...`);
    server.close(() => {
        console.log('[Express] HTTP socket listeners closed. Process terminated safely.');
        process.exit(0);
    });
    setTimeout(() => {
        console.error('[Express] Forcefully terminating process due to lingering connections.');
        process.exit(1);
    }, 10000).unref();
};

process.on('SIGTERM', () => handleGracefulShutdown('SIGTERM'));
process.on('SIGINT', () => handleGracefulShutdown('SIGINT'));

module.exports = app;

docs.title: 7.1 Roy Fielding's Six Core Architectural Constraints
docs.text:
1. Client-Server Architecture: Decouples user interface concerns from data persistence.
  2. Statelessness: No client context is retained on the server; each request contains all execution credentials.
  3. Cacheability: Responses must explicitly declare caching behavior (Cache-Control).
  4. Layered System: Clients cannot distinguish whether they connect directly to an origin server or an intermediary proxy.
  5. Code on Demand (Optional): Servers may extend client functionality with executable scripts.
  6. Uniform Interface: Governed by resource identification, manipulation via representations, self-descriptive messages, and hypermedia (HATEOAS).

docs.title: 7.2 The Richardson Maturity Model (RMM Levels 0 to 3)
docs.text: RMM Level Identifying Characteristics Typical Protocol / Pattern Example Request & Response Level 0: The Swamp of POX Uses HTTP strictly as a transport tunnel. Exactly one URI and one HTTP verb (POST) used for all operations. RPC-style actions embedded in payload. SOAP, XML-RPC, basic gRPC-Web tunneling. POST /api/service{"action": "cancelOrder", "orderId": 105}Always returns 200 OK. Level 1: Resources Introduces distinct resource-oriented URIs for individual entities, but still relies on a single verb (POST) to execute actions. RPC-over-HTTP with segmented paths. POST /api/orders/105/cancelPOST /api/orders/105/updateAddress Level 2: HTTP Verbs & Status Codes Employs the full standard set of HTTP Verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and standard HTTP Status Codes (200, 201, 204, 404). Standard REST APIs (Spring MVC, Express.js). DELETE /api/orders/105 -> 204 No ContentGET /api/orders/999 -> 404 Not Found. Level 3: Hypermedia Controls (HATEOAS) Incorporates hypermedia links (_links) directly inside response bodies. The client dynamically navigates allowable actions provided by the server. Fully compliant RESTful Hypermedia APIs (Spring HATEOAS). GET /api/orders/105{"id": 105, "status": "PENDING", "_links": {"cancel": {"href": "/api/orders/105/cancel"}}}

docs.title: 7.3 HTTP Verbs, Semantics, Safety, and Idempotency Matrix
docs.text: HTTP Verb Safe? Idempotent? Request Body Allowed? Cacheable? Primary Semantic Purpose Canonical Success Status Code GET Yes Yes No Yes Pure retrieval of resource representations. 200 OK HEAD Yes Yes No Yes Identical to GET, but server returns only headers, omitting response body. 200 OK OPTIONS Yes Yes No No Queries allowed HTTP methods on a URI (CORS preflight). 200 OK / 204 No Content POST No No Yes Only with explicit headers Submits data to create a new subordinate resource. 201 Created (with Location header) PUT No Yes Yes No Complete replacement of the target resource at specified URI. 200 OK / 204 No Content PATCH No No Yes No Partial update applying delta modifications to resource fields. 200 OK DELETE No Yes Optional (Rare) No Deletes the resource identified by the target URI. 204 No Content / 200 OK

docs.title: 7.4 HTTP Status Codes Master Hierarchy
docs.text:
• 1xx (Informational): 100 Continue, 101 Switching Protocols
  • 2xx (Success): 200 OK, 201 Created, 202 Accepted, 204 No Content, 206 Partial Content
  • 3xx (Redirection): 301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified, 307 Temporary Redirect, 308 Permanent Redirect
  • 4xx (Client Errors): 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 405 Method Not Allowed, 409 Conflict, 415 Unsupported Media Type, 422 Unprocessable Entity, 429 Too Many Requests
  • 5xx (Server Errors): 500 Internal Server Error, 501 Not Implemented, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout

docs.title: 7.5 URI Resource Modeling and Query Design Best Practices
docs.text:
• Nouns over verbs: GET /api/v1/orders (not /api/v1/getOrders)
  • Plural nouns for collections: /api/v1/customers
  • Clean hierarchical nesting: GET /api/v1/customers/{customerId}/orders/{orderId}/items
  • Query parameters for filtering, sorting, pagination: GET /api/v1/products?category=electronics&sort=-price&page=1&limit=20
  • Versioning: URI Path /v1/, Request Header X-API-Version, or Accept Header.

docs.title: 8. Spring MVC vs Node.js / Express.js Architectural Comparison
docs.text: Architectural Dimension Spring MVC (Java / Spring Boot) Node.js & Express.js Concurrency & Threading Model Multi-threaded (Thread-per-Request)Embedded Tomcat thread pool. Blocking I/O suspends worker thread. Single-Threaded Event Loop with libuvNon-blocking asynchronous I/O multiplexing via OS kernel (epoll). Execution Performance High CPU PerformanceJIT compiled; ideal for complex computations and enterprise transactions. High I/O ThroughputExcels at high-concurrency, lightweight I/O operations (streaming, chats, proxying). Type Safety & Tooling Static Type SystemCompile-time type checking, refactoring safety, mature IDE analyzers. Dynamic Typing (JavaScript)Rapid prototyping; requires TypeScript for enterprise compile-time safety. Memory Footprint Higher base memory overhead (\(250\text{ MB} - 1\text{ GB}\) JVM heap allocation). Minimal base memory footprint (\(30\text{ MB} - 100\text{ MB}\)). Rapid cold boot time. Best Suited Workloads Core enterprise backends, financial ledgers, distributed transactional services. Real-time web sockets, microservice API gateways, serverless functions (AWS Lambda).

docs.title: 9. Unit-3 Abbreviation Reference & Core Concepts Glossary
9.1 Consolidated Acronym & Abbreviation Table
docs.text: Abbr. Expanded Full Form Context / Architectural Meaning MVC Model-View-Controller Architectural pattern decoupling domain state, presentation, and routing. IoC Inversion of Control Design principle delegating control flow and object lifecycles to a framework. DI Dependency Injection Design pattern supplying dependent collaborating objects from an IoC container. AOP Aspect-Oriented Programming Programming paradigm modularizing cross-cutting concerns (logging, security). REST Representational State Transfer Architectural style for distributed hypermedia systems defined by Roy Fielding. RMM Richardson Maturity Model 4-tier grading scale (Levels 0–3) evaluating API compliance with REST principles. HATEOAS Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State Level 3 REST constraint embedding navigational links within resource payloads. DTO Data Transfer Object Plain object carrying data between processes to minimize serialization overhead. POJO Plain Old Java Object Java object unencumbered by framework-specific interface inheritance. DAO Data Access Object Architectural pattern abstracting and encapsulating database access logic. JPA Jakarta Persistence API Standard Java specification for Object-Relational Mapping (ORM). ORM Object-Relational Mapping Software technique mapping relational database tables to object-oriented classes. URI Uniform Resource Identifier Standard compact sequence of characters identifying an abstract or physical resource. URL Uniform Resource Locator Specific subset of URI specifying both resource identity and primary network access mechanism. URN Uniform Resource Name Specific subset of URI identifying a resource by name in a particular namespace. HTTP HyperText Transfer Protocol Application-layer protocol governing distributed hypermedia document exchange. HTTPS HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure HTTP communications encrypted over a Transport Layer Security (TLS) tunnel. TLS Transport Layer Security Cryptographic protocol providing communication privacy and data integrity over TCP. TCP Transmission Control Protocol Connection-oriented transport protocol guaranteeing ordered, error-checked packet delivery. RFC Request For Comments Formal publication of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) defining internet standards. JSON JavaScript Object Notation Lightweight, text-based, human-readable data interchange format. XML Extensible Markup Language Tag-based markup language defining a set of rules for encoding documents. CORS Cross-Origin Resource Sharing W3C mechanism allowing web applications to access resources from a different domain. CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery Web security attack tricking an authenticated user into executing unauthorized commands. JWT JSON Web Token Compact, URL-safe means of representing signed claims transmitted between parties. SSE Server-Sent Events Persistent HTTP connection enabling servers to push real-time event streams to clients. V8 Google V8 JavaScript Engine Open-source, high-performance WebAssembly and JavaScript engine written in C++. libuv Multi-platform Support Library C library powering Node.js event loops, thread pools, and non-blocking I/O. FIFO First In, First Out Queue scheduling discipline where oldest queued items are processed first. ACID Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability Four transaction properties guaranteeing reliability in database management systems. BASE Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency Data model philosophy of distributed NoSQL databases favoring availability over immediate consistency. RPC Remote Procedure Call Protocol allowing a program to execute a subroutine on a remote server as if it were local. SOAP Simple Object Access Protocol XML-based messaging protocol specification for exchanging structured information. OAS OpenAPI Specification Standard machine-readable interface description format for RESTful APIs. SoC Separation of Concerns Design principle separating a computer program into distinct, non-overlapping sections. SRP Single Responsibility Principle SOLID principle stating that every module or class should have only one reason to change.

docs.title: 9.2 Core Concepts Glossary
docs.text:
1. DispatcherServlet: The central Front Controller servlet in Spring MVC that intercepts all incoming requests, consults handler mappings, and coordinates controller execution, content negotiation, and response delivery.
  2. Inversion of Control (IoC) Container: The core runtime engine of the Spring Framework (ApplicationContext) that instantiates, configures, wires, and manages the complete lifecycle of Spring beans.
  3. ApplicationContext: The advanced Spring IoC container interface providing complete enterprise capabilities, including AOP proxy integration, message resource internationalization, event publication, and web application context wiring.
  4. Front Controller Pattern: An enterprise design pattern where a single centralized web handler routes, validates, and manages all incoming requests across an application.
  5. libuv Event Loop: The single-threaded execution coordination mechanism in Node.js that continuously processes six distinct phases (Timers, Pending Callbacks, Idle/Prepare, Poll, Check, Close) to dispatch asynchronous I/O callbacks.
  6. Microtask Queue: High-priority internal execution queues in Node.js (process.nextTick and Promise) that execute immediately after the current operation finishes, taking precedence over all macrotask event loop phases.
  7. Statelessness: The REST architectural constraint dictating that no client session context is retained on the server; every request must contain complete self-sufficient execution information.
  8. Idempotency: The mathematical property of an operation wherein executing it multiple times produces the exact same system state as executing it a single time (\(f(f(S)) = f(S)\)).
  9. Content Negotiation: The HTTP mechanism allowing clients and servers to agree on the payload format (application/json, application/xml) exchanged between them using Accept and Content-Type headers.
  10. HATEOAS: The Level-3 REST constraint wherein API responses contain embedded hypermedia links, allowing clients to dynamically discover and traverse valid application state transitions.

docs.title: Question 1: Explain the Model-View-Controller (MVC) architectural pattern with a neat component interaction diagram.
docs.text:
Marking Scheme:

  • Definition and primary purpose (1 Mark)
  • Clear explanation of Model, View, and Controller responsibilities (2 Marks)
  • Component interaction diagram / flowchart (1 Mark)
  • Benefits of Separation of Concerns (1 Mark)

Model Answer: The Model-View-Controller (MVC) architectural pattern decomposes an interactive application into three distinct layers to enforce the Separation of Concerns (SoC):

  1. Model: Encapsulates the application's business logic, domain entities, and data persistence state. It is entirely decoupled from the presentation format.
  2. View: Renders the model's state into a human-readable or machine-readable presentation format (HTML templates like Thymeleaf or serialized JSON/XML).
  3. Controller: Acts as the traffic coordinator. It intercepts incoming client HTTP requests, validates input parameters, delegates tasks to the Model layer, and selects the appropriate View for response rendering.
flowchart LR
    Client(["User / Client"]) -->|"1. HTTP Request"| C["Controller"]
    C -->|"2. Query / Update State"| M["Model (Business Logic)"]
    M -->|"3. Return Data"| C
    C -->|"4. Pass Data to View"| V["View (Renderer / JSON)"]
    V -->|"5. Return Response"| Client

Benefits: Decoupling ensures that user interfaces can be completely redesigned without modifying core business rules, multiple presentations (mobile apps, web browsers) can reuse the same model, and testability is significantly enhanced.

docs.title: Question 2: Differentiate between Inversion of Control (IoC) and Dependency Injection (DI). Why is Constructor Injection preferred over Field Injection?
docs.text:
Marking Scheme:

  • Distinction between IoC (principle) and DI (pattern) (2 Marks)
  • Architectural problems of Field Injection (1.5 Marks)
  • Concrete advantages of Constructor Injection (1.5 Marks)

Model Answer:

  • Inversion of Control (IoC): A high-level architectural principle wherein the framework controls program execution flow and object lifecycles ("Hollywood Principle").
  • Dependency Injection (DI): A concrete design pattern implementing IoC. Rather than an object instantiating collaborating dependencies via new ClassName(), dependencies are supplied ("injected") by an external container.

Why Constructor Injection is Preferred over Field Injection:

  1. Immutability & Thread Safety: Constructor injection allows injected fields to be declared final, guaranteeing that objects cannot be mutated or left in an inconsistent state after instantiation.
  2. Testability Without Frameworks: Classes with constructor injection can be directly instantiated in pure JUnit unit tests (new OrderService(mockRepo)) without initializing a heavy Spring ApplicationContext or relying on reflection.
  3. Prevention of NullPointerExceptions: Field injection permits objects to be instantiated with uninitialized dependencies if instantiated outside Spring, leading to runtime failures. Constructor injection enforces that all required dependencies must be provided at instantiation time.
  4. Code Smell Detection: A constructor with 7+ parameters immediately signals a violation of the Single Responsibility Principle, whereas field injection conceals bloated dependencies behind clean annotations.

docs.title: Question 3: Explain the Richardson Maturity Model (RMM) for REST APIs with practical examples for each level.
docs.text:
Marking Scheme:

  • Definition of RMM (1 Mark)
  • Level 0, Level 1, Level 2, Level 3 explanations with concrete URIs/payloads (1 Mark per Level = 4 Marks)

Model Answer: The Richardson Maturity Model (RMM) grades APIs across four evolutionary tiers of REST compliance:

  • Level 0 (The Swamp of POX): Uses HTTP strictly as a transport tunnel. All operations target a single endpoint URI using a single HTTP method (POST). Example: POST /api/service with payload {"action": "cancelOrder", "id": 101}. Always returns 200 OK.

  • Level 1 (Resources): Introduces distinct URIs for individual resources, but continues using a single verb (POST) for all operations. Example: POST /api/orders/101/cancel.

  • Level 2 (HTTP Verbs & Status Codes): Employs standard HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) according to their formal semantic definitions, returning standard HTTP status codes (200, 201, 204, 404). Example: DELETE /api/orders/101 returns 204 No Content.

  • Level 3 (Hypermedia Controls / HATEOAS): Responses contain navigable hypermedia controls (_links) informing clients of available state transitions dynamically. Example: 

    {
  "orderId": 101,
  "status": "PENDING",
  "_links": {
    "self": { "href": "/api/orders/101" },
    "cancel": { "href": "/api/orders/101/cancel" }
  }
}

docs.title: Question 4: Compare the concurrency and execution model of Spring Boot (Tomcat thread-per-request) and Node.js (libuv event loop).
docs.text:
Marking Scheme:

  • Detailed description of Spring Boot Tomcat thread pool model (2 Marks)
  • Detailed description of Node.js single-threaded event loop model (2 Marks)
  • Comparative workload suitability analysis (1 Mark)

Model Answer:

flowchart TD
    subgraph SpringBoot["Spring Boot (Tomcat Thread-Per-Request)"]
        Req1["Request 1"] --> Th1["Worker Thread 1 (Blocks on DB)"]
        Req2["Request 2"] --> Th2["Worker Thread 2 (Blocks on I/O)"]
        Mem["High Memory: ~1MB stack per thread\nLimited by pool size (~200 threads)"]
    end

    subgraph NodeJS["Node.js (libuv Event Loop)"]
        NReq["Thousands of Incoming Requests"] --> Loop["Single JS Thread (Event Loop)"]
        Loop -->|"Delegates I/O"| OS["OS Kernel (epoll/IOCP)"]
        Loop -->|"Delegates Crypto/FS"| Pool["libuv Worker Pool (4 Threads)"]
        NMem["Minimal Memory: Lightweight sockets\nHandles 50,000+ concurrent connections"]
    end
  • Spring Boot (Tomcat Thread-per-Request): Uses an operating system thread pool (default 200 worker threads). Each incoming HTTP request is assigned a dedicated thread that handles execution from start to finish. If the request executes a blocking SQL query, that thread remains idle in memory, consuming approximately 1 MB of stack memory. Thread context-switching creates CPU overhead under high concurrent connection loads.
  • Node.js (libuv Event Loop): Uses a single JavaScript execution thread backed by an asynchronous non-blocking event loop. When a database or network I/O call occurs, Node.js offloads the operation to the operating system kernel (epoll) and continues processing subsequent requests immediately. Once the I/O completes, its callback is placed in the event loop queue.
  • Workload Suitability: Spring Boot excels at computationally heavy, CPU-intensive, or multi-step transactional business logic. Node.js excels at high-concurrency, I/O-bound, real-time streaming operations with minimal CPU processing.

docs.title: Question 5: What is an idempotent HTTP method? Differentiate between PUT and PATCH with respect to request payloads and idempotency.
docs.text:
Marking Scheme:

  • Mathematical and architectural definition of idempotency (1.5 Marks)
  • Semantic definition of PUT (1.5 Marks)
  • Semantic definition of PATCH (1.5 Marks)
  • Comparison of payloads and idempotency guarantees (0.5 Marks)

Model Answer: An HTTP method is Idempotent if executing multiple identical requests produces the exact same system state as executing a single request (\(f(f(S)) = f(S)\)).

PUT vs. PATCH Comparison:

Feature PUT (RFC 7231) PATCH (RFC 5789) Semantic Meaning Complete Replacement of the target resource. Partial Modification applying delta changes to specific fields. Payload Requirement Must transmit the entire resource entity. Any omitted fields are typically overwritten with null or default values. Transmits only the specific fields requiring modification (or a JSON Patch sequence of operations). Idempotency Guaranteed Idempotent. Repeating the exact same PUT request 100 times results in the identical resource state on the server. Not Inherently Idempotent. While setting fixed fields is idempotent, delta operations like {"increment": 10} modify state on each execution. Example Request PUT /api/users/42{"name": "Alice", "email": "a@test.com", "role": "USER"} PATCH /api/users/42{"role": "ADMIN"}

docs.title: Question 6: Describe the complete 10-step request processing lifecycle of Spring MVC DispatcherServlet from the arrival of an HTTP request to the flushing of the response. Include a detailed sequence diagram.
docs.text:
Marking Scheme:

  • Comprehensive Front Controller Pattern explanation (1.5 Marks)
  • Detailed, accurate enumeration of all 10 canonical steps (5 Marks)
  • Clean, syntactically correct Sequence Diagram (2 Marks)
  • Detailed explanation of HandlerMapping, HandlerAdapter, and HttpMessageConverter roles (1.5 Marks)

Model Answer: Spring MVC organizes request handling around the Front Controller pattern implemented by DispatcherServlet. The detailed canonical 10-step request processing flow proceeds as follows:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Client as Client / Browser
    participant DS as DispatcherServlet
    participant HM as HandlerMapping
    participant HI as HandlerInterceptor
    participant HA as HandlerAdapter
    participant CTRL as Controller (@RestController)
    participant HMC as HttpMessageConverter (Jackson)

    Client->>DS: 1. Inbound HTTP Request
    DS->>HM: 2. Query HandlerMapping for Route
    HM-->>DS: 3. Return HandlerExecutionChain
    DS->>HI: 4. Invoke preHandle() (Interceptors)
    HI-->>DS: true (Proceed)
    DS->>HA: 5. Determine & Invoke HandlerAdapter
    HA->>CTRL: 6. Resolve Arguments & Execute Controller
    CTRL-->>HA: 7. Return Response DTO / Entity
    HA->>HMC: 8. Serialize Object to JSON/XML
    HMC-->>DS: Bytes Flushed to Response Stream
    DS->>HI: 9. Invoke postHandle() & afterCompletion()
    DS-->>Client: 10. HTTP 200 OK Response Delivered

Step-by-Step Technical Lifecycle:

  1. Step 1 — Arrival at Front Controller: The client initiates an HTTP transaction. The servlet container (Tomcat) routes the request matching / to DispatcherServlet.doService(), which initializes request attributes and passes execution to doDispatch().
  2. Step 2 — Handler Mapping Lookup: DispatcherServlet queries registered HandlerMapping beans (principally RequestMappingHandlerMapping). It inspects the request URI, HTTP method, and headers against controller metadata.
  3. Step 3 — Construction of HandlerExecutionChain: HandlerMapping returns a HandlerExecutionChain object containing the matched controller method reference along with an array of configured HandlerInterceptor instances.
  4. Step 4 — Interceptor Pre-Processing (preHandle): DispatcherServlet executes the preHandle() method of each interceptor in sequence. If any interceptor returns false, processing halts immediately, and the remaining pipeline is aborted.
  5. Step 5 — Handler Adapter Selection: DispatcherServlet selects an appropriate HandlerAdapter (typically RequestMappingHandlerAdapter) capable of invoking the controller method signature.
  6. Step 6 — Argument Resolution, Binding & Method Execution:
  7. The adapter uses HandlerMethodArgumentResolver to bind request bodies, path variables, and parameters to Java DTOs.
  8. It triggers validation via WebDataBinder (@Valid).
  9. It invokes the controller method via reflection.
  10. Step 7 — Return Value Handling: The controller executes business logic via services and returns a domain DTO or ResponseEntity<T>.
  11. Step 8 — Content Negotiation & Message Conversion: HandlerMethodReturnValueHandler inspects the client's Accept header. It selects a registered HttpMessageConverter (e.g., Jackson's MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter), serializes the Java object to JSON/XML, and writes the bytes to HttpServletResponse.getOutputStream().
  12. Step 9 — Post-Processing & View Resolution: For traditional SSR applications, a ViewResolver resolves the view name and renders HTML. For REST controllers, this step is bypassed.
  13. Step 10 — Completion and Cleanup (afterCompletion): DispatcherServlet calls afterCompletion() on all interceptors, allowing them to release resources, log execution duration, and clear ThreadLocal context variables. Finally, the HTTP response status code and headers are flushed to the client socket.

docs.title: Question 7: Design and implement a robust, production-grade Express.js application handling a RESTful resource (/api/v1/products). Your solution must include custom request logging, request body validation, modular routing, and a 4-argument centralized error-handling middleware. Explain how libuv manages asynchronous non-blocking I/O during database queries.
docs.text:
Marking Scheme:

  • Architectural explanation of libuv, event loop, and thread pool during async I/O (3 Marks)
  • Custom Request Logging Middleware with execution timing (1.5 Marks)
  • Robust Input Validation Middleware (1.5 Marks)
  • Modular Express Router implementation with proper HTTP verbs and status codes (2 Marks)
  • Centralized 4-argument Error Handling Middleware with stack sanitization (2 Marks)

Model Answer:

docs.title: Part 1: How libuv Manages Asynchronous Non-Blocking I/O
docs.text:
When an Express.js route executes an asynchronous database query or network call:

  1. The V8 call stack executes the query initiation function (e.g., db.query()).
  2. libuv checks the nature of the operation:
  3. For network socket operations (TCP connection to a database like PostgreSQL or MongoDB), libuv registers the file descriptor with the OS kernel's native event demultiplexer (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS, IOCP on Windows). No worker threads are blocked.
  4. For file system I/O or DNS lookups, libuv offloads the blocking system call to its internal Worker Thread Pool (default 4 threads, configurable via UV_THREAD_POOL_SIZE).
  5. The JavaScript thread immediately resumes execution and processes subsequent incoming HTTP requests without waiting.
  6. When the database server responds with query results over the TCP socket, the OS kernel notifies libuv during the Poll phase of the event loop.
  7. libuv enqueues the JavaScript callback onto the event loop queue, which is pushed onto the V8 Call Stack once all synchronous code finishes.

docs.title: Part 2: Complete Implementation Code
docs.text:
const express = require('express');
const crypto = require('crypto');
const app = express();

app.use(express.json());

// 1. Custom High-Resolution Logging Middleware
app.use((req, res, next) => {
    const start = process.hrtime();
    const reqId = crypto.randomUUID();
    req.id = reqId;

    res.on('finish', () => {
        const [sec, nano] = process.hrtime(start);
        const ms = (sec * 1000 + nano / 1e6).toFixed(2);
        console.log(`[${reqId}] ${req.method} ${req.originalUrl} -> ${res.statusCode} in ${ms}ms`);
    });
    next();
});

// 2. Custom Input Validation Middleware
const validateProduct = (req, res, next) => {
    const { name, price } = req.body;
    const errors = [];
    if (!name || typeof name !== 'string' || name.trim().length < 2) {
        errors.push('Field "name" is required and must be at least 2 characters');
    }
    if (price === undefined || typeof price !== 'number' || price <= 0) {
        errors.push('Field "price" is required and must be a number greater than 0');
    }
    if (errors.length > 0) {
        const err = new Error(errors.join('; '));
        err.statusCode = 400;
        return next(err);
    }
    next();
};

// 3. Modular Router
const router = express.Router();
const db = new Map();

router.get('/', (req, res) => {
    res.status(200).json(Array.from(db.values()));
});

router.post('/', validateProduct, (req, res) => {
    const id = crypto.randomUUID();
    const product = { id, name: req.body.name.trim(), price: req.body.price };
    db.set(id, product);
    res.location(`/api/v1/products/${id}`);
    res.status(201).json(product);
});

router.get('/:id', (req, res, next) => {
    const product = db.get(req.params.id);
    if (!product) {
        const err = new Error(`Product ${req.params.id} not found`);
        err.statusCode = 404;
        return next(err);
    }
    res.status(200).json(product);
});

app.use('/api/v1/products', router);

// 4. Centralized 4-Argument Error Handling Middleware
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
    const statusCode = err.statusCode || 500;
    const isProd = process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production';

    res.status(statusCode).json({
        status: statusCode,
        error: statusCode === 500 ? 'Internal Server Error' : 'Request Error',
        message: err.message,
        requestId: req.id,
        timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
        ...(isProd ? {} : { stack: err.stack })
    });
});

app.listen(3000, () => console.log('Server listening on port 3000'));

docs.title: Question 8: What are the core architectural constraints of REST? Explain why statelessness is critical for horizontal scalability. Detail how Content Negotiation works in Spring Boot and provide a complete implementation of a REST Controller supporting both JSON and XML responses with global exception handling.
docs.text:
Marking Scheme:

  • Detailed explanation of Fielding's 6 REST constraints (2 Marks)
  • In-depth architectural analysis of Statelessness and Horizontal Scalability (2 Marks)
  • Explanation of Content Negotiation mechanics (Accept, Content-Type, HttpMessageConverter) (2 Marks)
  • Complete Spring Boot Controller implementation supporting JSON/XML (2 Marks)
  • Global Exception Handler (@RestControllerAdvice) implementation (2 Marks)

Model Answer:

docs.title: Part 1: The Six Core Architectural Constraints of REST
docs.text:
1. Client-Server Architecture: Decouples user interface concerns from data persistence.
  2. Statelessness: Every request must contain all information required to complete execution; no session state is retained on the server.
  3. Cacheability: Responses must explicitly declare caching behavior (Cache-Control) to minimize redundant network round-trips.
  4. Layered System: The client cannot distinguish whether it connects directly to the end server or to intermediary proxies, load balancers, or gateways.
  5. Code on Demand (Optional): Servers may extend client functionality by transmitting executable scripts (e.g., JavaScript).
  6. Uniform Interface: Governed by unique resource identification (URIs), manipulation via representations, self-descriptive messages, and hypermedia (HATEOAS).

docs.title: Part 2: Why Statelessness is Critical for Horizontal Scalability
docs.text:
In a stateful architecture, user session state (e.g., shopping cart, authentication login) is stored in server memory (e.g., HttpSession). This introduces severe scalability constraints:

  • Sticky Sessions: Load balancers must route all subsequent requests from a specific client to the exact same physical server instance. If that instance crashes, the user's session data is lost.
  • Horizontal Auto-Scaling Failures: New server instances cannot handle traffic from existing users without complex distributed session replication mechanisms (e.g., Redis session clustering), which introduces network overhead and synchronization bottlenecks.

In a stateless architecture:

  • No session state is retained in server RAM. Authentication is verified through cryptographic tokens (JWTs) or stateless credentials provided in each request header (Authorization: Bearer <token>).
  • Any arbitrary server instance in an auto-scaling cluster can process any incoming request identically.
  • If a server instance fails, the load balancer routes traffic to a healthy instance with zero disruption to the user experience.
flowchart TD
    subgraph Stateful["Stateful Cluster (Sticky Sessions Required)"]
        ClientA["Client A"] --> LB1["Load Balancer"]
        LB1 -->|"Bound to Instance 1"| S1["Server 1 (Holds Session A in RAM)"]
        S1 -.->|"If Server 1 Dies"| Fail["Session Lost! User Logged Out"]
    end

    subgraph Stateless["Stateless Cluster (Seamless Auto-Scaling)"]
        ClientB["Client B (Passes JWT)"] --> LB2["Load Balancer"]
        LB2 --> S2["Server 1 (Stateless)"]
        LB2 --> S3["Server 2 (Stateless)"]
        LB2 --> S4["Server 3 (Stateless)"]
        S2 --- DB[(Shared Database)]
        S3 --- DB
        S4 --- DB
    end

docs.title: Part 3: Content Negotiation Mechanics
docs.text:
Content Negotiation allows a client and server to agree on the data representation exchanged over HTTP:

  • Accept Header (Client to Server): Specifies the MIME types the client can process (e.g., Accept: application/json, application/xml;q=0.9).
  • Content-Type Header: Informs the recipient of the media format contained in the request or response body.
  • Spring Boot Resolution: When a controller returns an object, Spring's ContentNegotiationManager inspects the request's Accept header. It iterates through registered HttpMessageConverter beans:
  • If application/json is requested, MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter serializes the object to JSON.
  • If application/xml is requested (and jackson-dataformat-xml is on the classpath), MappingJackson2XmlHttpMessageConverter serializes it to XML.

docs.title: Part 4: Implementation Code
docs.text:
// 1. Domain DTO Supporting Both Formats
package com.deepcollege.dto;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.dataformat.xml.annotation.JacksonXmlRootElement;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.*;

@JacksonXmlRootElement(localName = "Customer")
public class CustomerDto {
    @NotBlank(message = "Customer ID cannot be blank")
    private String customerId;

    @NotBlank(message = "Name cannot be blank")
    private String name;

    @Email(message = "Must be a valid email format")
    private String email;

    public CustomerDto() {}
    public CustomerDto(String customerId, String name, String email) {
        this.customerId = customerId;
        this.name = name;
        this.email = email;
    }

    public String getCustomerId() { return customerId; }
    public void setCustomerId(String customerId) { this.customerId = customerId; }
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public void setName(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public String getEmail() { return email; }
    public void setEmail(String email) { this.email = email; }
}

// 2. Controller Supporting JSON & XML Content Negotiation
package com.deepcollege.controller;

import com.deepcollege.dto.CustomerDto;
import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/customers")
public class CustomerRestController {

    @GetMapping(
            value = "/{id}",
            produces = {MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, MediaType.APPLICATION_XML_VALUE}
    )
    public ResponseEntity<CustomerDto> getCustomer(@PathVariable("id") String id) {
        if ("unknown".equalsIgnoreCase(id)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Customer with ID '" + id + "' was not found");
        }
        CustomerDto customer = new CustomerDto(id, "Engineering Student", "student@deepcollege.edu");
        return ResponseEntity.ok(customer);
    }

    @PostMapping(
            consumes = {MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, MediaType.APPLICATION_XML_VALUE},
            produces = {MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, MediaType.APPLICATION_XML_VALUE}
    )
    public ResponseEntity<CustomerDto> createCustomer(@Valid @RequestBody CustomerDto request) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(request);
    }
}

// 3. Global Exception Handler Supporting Standard Error Structures
package com.deepcollege.exception;

import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.MethodArgumentNotValidException;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ExceptionHandler;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestControllerAdvice;

import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    public record ErrorDetail(Instant timestamp, int status, String error, String message) {}

    @ExceptionHandler(IllegalArgumentException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ErrorDetail> handleNotFound(IllegalArgumentException ex) {
        ErrorDetail error = new ErrorDetail(
                Instant.now(),
                HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND.value(),
                HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND.getReasonPhrase(),
                ex.getMessage()
        );
        return new ResponseEntity<>(error, HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> handleValidation(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex) {
        Map<String, Object> body = new HashMap<>();
        body.put("timestamp", Instant.now());
        body.put("status", HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST.value());
        body.put("error", "Validation Error");

        Map<String, String> fieldErrors = new HashMap<>();
        ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().forEach(f -> fieldErrors.put(f.getField(), f.getDefaultMessage()));
        body.put("validationErrors", fieldErrors);

        return new ResponseEntity<>(body, HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST);
    }
}

docs.title: 1. Unit 4 Overview & Learning Objectives
docs.text:
Modern web applications require durable, highly available, and performant data persistence layers. In full-stack systems, application code rarely operates directly on raw disk storage; instead, it mediates data flow through Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMS) or Non-Relational (NoSQL) document stores.

This unit bridges the gap between software domain models and persistence tiers. We analyze the theoretical underpinnings of relational data modeling, database normalization, concurrency control, and transactions, followed by enterprise Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) and native driver integrations in Java and Node.js. Finally, we explore modern NoSQL architectures, aggregation pipelines, and distributed data theorems (CAP and PACELC).

flowchart LR
    subgraph Client_Tier ["Client Tier"]
        UI["Web / Mobile Browser"]
    end

    subgraph Application_Tier ["Application Tier"]
        Spring["Spring Boot API (JPA / Hibernate)"]
        NodeApp["Node.js Express API (MySQL2 / Mongo Native)"]
    end

    subgraph Persistence_Tier ["Persistence Tier"]
        RDBMS[("MySQL RDBMS (InnoDB ACID Storage)")]
        NoSQL[("MongoDB NoSQL (WiredTiger BSON Store)")]
    end

    UI -->|"HTTP / REST / JSON"| Spring
    UI -->|"HTTP / REST / JSON"| NodeApp
    Spring -->|"JDBC / TCP 3306"| RDBMS
    NodeApp -->|"MySQL Binary Protocol"| RDBMS
    NodeApp -->|"MongoDB Wire Protocol / TCP 27017"| NoSQL

docs.title: Figure 4.1: Enterprise Full-Stack Persistence Architecture
docs.text:
What it shows: The multi-tier architecture connecting client applications to backend execution runtimes (Java Virtual Machine and Node.js V8) and persistent storage engines across relational and non-relational boundaries.

Components:

  • Client Tier — Initiates HTTP/REST requests carrying JSON payloads.
  • Application Tier — Hosts business logic, validation, and object persistence frameworks (Spring Data JPA and Node.js drivers).
  • Persistence Tier — Guarantees durable storage using ACID-compliant relational engines (MySQL InnoDB) and horizontally scalable document databases (MongoDB WiredTiger).

Flow / Relationship: Client requests are processed by application services, which map domain entities to tabular relational structures or hierarchical BSON documents before executing wire-level database queries over persistent socket connections.

Key observations:

  • Relational integration relies on strongly typed schemas, relational keys, and ACID transactions.
  • NoSQL integration emphasizes polymorphic JSON-like documents, dynamic aggregation pipelines, and eventual consistency.

[Source: Unit 4 Course Specification, Module 4.1]

docs.title: 2. Relational Database Fundamentals & Architecture
docs.text: Relational Database Management Systems organize data based on the formal relational model pioneered by Edgar F. Codd in 1970. Before writing queries, developers must structure data into mathematical relations with strict key constraints and cardinalities.

docs.title: 2.1 The Relational Data Model & Formal Foundations
docs.text:
In relational theory, a database is a collection of relations. A relation corresponds to a table, a tuple corresponds to a row or record, and an attribute corresponds to a column header.

  • Relation Schema: Represented mathematically as \(R(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n)\), where \(R\) is the relation name and \(A_i\) are attributes defined over specific domains.
  • Domain: The set of atomic, indivisible values permitted for an attribute, denoted as \(\text{dom}(A_i)\).
  • Relation Instance: A finite set of tuples \(r(R) \subseteq \text{dom}(A_1) \times \text{dom}(A_2) \times \dots \times \text{dom}(A_n)\).
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Formal Relational Term       | SQL / Physical Implementation Equivalent                |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Relation                     | Table                                                  |
| Tuple                        | Row / Record                                           |
| Attribute                    | Column / Field                                         |
| Domain                       | Data Type & Constraints (e.g., VARCHAR(50), NOT NULL)  |
| Degree                       | Number of columns (Arity of the relation)             |
| Cardinality                  | Number of rows currently stored in the table           |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

💡 Core Principle: In a pure relation, tuples are unordered, attributes are unordered, and duplicate tuples are strictly prohibited. Every row must be uniquely identifiable.

docs.title: 2.2 Taxonomy of Relational Keys
docs.text:
Relational integrity requires keys to enforce entity identity and inter-table relationships. The relational model defines distinct key classifications:

[ Super Key ]  (Any attribute set guaranteeing tuple uniqueness)
      │
      ▼ (Minimal Super Key)
[ Candidate Key ]  (No extraneous attributes permitted)
   ├──► [ Primary Key ]    (Explicitly selected default table identifier; NOT NULL)
   └──► [ Alternate Key ]  (Remaining candidate keys not chosen as Primary Key)

[ Foreign Key ]    (Attribute referencing a Candidate/Primary Key in another relation)
[ Composite Key ]  (Key composed of two or more attributes)
[ Surrogate Key ]  (System-generated artificial identifier; e.g., AUTO_INCREMENT)
[ Natural Key ]    (Real-world business identifier with intrinsic domain meaning)
  • Super Key (\(SK\)): A set of one or more attributes that collectively identifies a unique tuple in a relation. Formally, if \(K\) is a super key of relation \(R\), then for any two distinct tuples \(t_1, t_2 \in r(R)\), \(t_1[K] \neq t_2[K]\).
  • Candidate Key (\(CK\)): A minimal super key. A super key \(K\) is a candidate key if no proper subset \(K' \subset K\) is also a super key.
  • Primary Key (\(PK\)): The specific candidate key chosen by the database architect as the principal identifier for the relation. It enforces entity integrity and cannot contain null values (NOT NULL constraint).
  • Alternate Key (\(AK\)): Any candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key. Implemented in SQL using the UNIQUE constraint.
  • Foreign Key (\(FK\)): An attribute or collection of attributes in a referencing relation whose values must match a candidate key or primary key in a referenced relation, or be null. Enforces referential integrity.
  • Composite Key: A primary or candidate key consisting of two or more attributes. Common in associative junction tables representing many-to-many relationships.
  • Surrogate Key: An artificially created value assigned to a record with no business meaning (e.g., auto-incrementing integers, UUIDs). It decouples the physical database key from volatile business attributes.
  • Natural Key: An attribute with real-world business meaning that already uniquely identifies the record (e.g., Social Security Number, International Standard Book Number, Vehicle Identification Number).

⚠️ Warning: While natural keys avoid additional surrogate columns, they introduce cascading updates across foreign keys whenever business identifiers change. Modern enterprise architectures strongly favor surrogate primary keys.

docs.text:
To illustrate relational architecture, we examine the standard Northwind enterprise ordering schema comprising Customers, Orders, Employees, Shippers, Products, Categories, and Suppliers.

docs.title: Figure 4.2: Northwind Relational Entity-Relationship Diagram
docs.text:
What it shows: The multi-table schema modeling enterprise order processing, demonstrating one-to-many (||--o{) relationships and many-to-many relationships resolved via an associative junction entity (ORDER_DETAILS).

Components:

  • Entity Tables: CUSTOMERS, ORDERS, PRODUCTS, EMPLOYEES, CATEGORIES, SUPPLIERS, SHIPPERS.
  • Associative Junction Table: ORDER_DETAILS, with composite primary key (order_id, product_id).
  • Referential Integrity Constraints: Foreign key references linking child records to parent records.

Flow / Relationship: A customer places zero or many orders. Each order is managed by an employee and fulfilled through a shipper. An order contains one or more line items (ORDER_DETAILS), each referencing a specific catalog product.

Key observations:

  • ORDER_DETAILS contains line-item level transaction pricing (unit_price) to insulate historical orders against future price changes in PRODUCTS.
  • Composite primary keys prevent duplicate product entries within a single order.

[Source: Unit 4 Course Specification, Module 4.1]

docs.title: 2.4 Cardinality, Modality & Referential Integrity Rules
docs.text:
Entity-Relationship relationships are governed by structural constraints:

  • Cardinality (Maximum Constraint): Defines the maximum number of entity instances in one entity set that can be associated with an entity instance in another entity set.
  • One-to-One (\(1:1\)) — e.g., User to UserProfile.
  • One-to-Many (\(1:N\)) — e.g., Customer to Orders.
  • Many-to-Many (\(M:N\)) — e.g., Orders to Products (resolved via junction table).
  • Modality (Minimum Constraint / Participation): Specifies whether the relationship is optional (\(0\)) or mandatory (\(1\)).
  • Optional participation (modality \(0\)): An entity can exist without participating in the relationship.
  • Mandatory participation (modality \(1\)): Every instance of the entity must participate in the relationship.
+-------------------+--------------------+-----------------------------------------------------+
| Crow's Foot Symbol| Notation           | Meaning                                             |
+-------------------+--------------------+-----------------------------------------------------+
| --||--            | Mandatory One (1,1)| Exactly one instance required                       |
| --o|--            | Optional One (0,1) | Zero or one instance permitted                      |
| --|<--            | Mandatory Many(1,N)| At least one instance required, up to unbounded     |
| --o<--            | Optional Many (0,N)| Zero or more instances permitted                    |
+-------------------+--------------------+-----------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: Referential Integrity Action Options
docs.text:
When a referenced tuple in a parent table is deleted or updated, the database engine enforces one of the following foreign key actions:

  1. ON DELETE RESTRICT / NO ACTION: Rejects the parent modification if matching child rows exist.
  2. ON DELETE CASCADE: Automatically deletes all corresponding child rows in the referencing table.
  3. ON DELETE SET NULL: Sets the foreign key columns in referencing child rows to NULL.
  4. ON DELETE SET DEFAULT: Replaces referencing child foreign keys with their declared default value.

📝 Exam Note: In financial systems, ON DELETE CASCADE is prohibited on transactional data like ORDERS or INVOICES. Architects must use ON DELETE RESTRICT or soft deletes (deleted_at TIMESTAMP) to prevent accidental destruction of audit records.

docs.title: 3. Database Normalization & Normal Forms
docs.text: Database normalization is a formal technique for organizing relational database tables to minimize data redundancy and prevent modification anomalies while preserving functional dependencies and lossless joins.

docs.title: 3.1 Functional Dependency Theory & Armstrong's Axioms
docs.text: Normalization relies on the mathematical concept of functional dependencies between attribute sets.

docs.title: Definition: Functional Dependency (FD)
docs.text:
Meaning: A functional dependency denotes a constraint between two sets of attributes in a relation.

Formal definition: Given relation schema \(R\) and subsets \(X \subseteq R\) and \(Y \subseteq R\), we say that \(X\) functionally determines \(Y\) (written as \(X \to Y\)) if and only if for every legal instance \(r(R)\), any two tuples \(t_1, t_2 \in r\) that agree on \(X\) must also agree on \(Y\):

\[ \forall t_1, t_2 \in r(R), \quad t_1[X] = t_2[X] \implies t_1[Y] = t_2[Y] \]

Here, \(X\) is called the determinant and \(Y\) is called the dependent.

docs.title: Armstrong's Axioms
docs.text:
William W. Armstrong established sound and complete inference rules for deriving all functional dependencies implied by a set \(F\):

  • Axiom of Reflexivity: If \(Y \subseteq X\), then \(X \to Y\). (Trivial dependency)
  • Axiom of Augmentation: If \(X \to Y\), then \(XZ \to YZ\) for any attribute set \(Z\).
  • Axiom of Transitivity: If \(X \to Y\) and \(Y \to Z\), then \(X \to Z\).

Secondary derived rules frequently used in schema analysis:

  • Union Rule: If \(X \to Y\) and \(X \to Z\), then \(X \to YZ\).
  • Decomposition Rule: If \(X \to YZ\), then \(X \to Y\) and \(X \to Z\).
  • Pseudotransitivity Rule: If \(X \to Y\) and \(WY \to Z\), then \(WX \to Z\).

docs.title: 3.2 Modification Anomalies: Insertion, Deletion, and Update
docs.text:
Unnormalized schemas exhibit three destructive anomalies:

Unnormalized Relation: EMP_PROJECT
+--------+---------------+------------+--------------+---------------+
| Emp_ID | Emp_Name      | Project_ID | Project_Name | Project_Budget|
+--------+---------------+------------+--------------+---------------+
| E101   | Alice Smith   | P01        | Apollo       | $500,000      |
| E101   | Alice Smith   | P02        | Artemis      | $300,000      |
| E102   | Bob Johnson   | P01        | Apollo       | $500,000      |
| E103   | Carol White   | P03        | Gemini       | $150,000      |
+--------+---------------+------------+--------------+---------------+
  • Insertion Anomaly: Cannot insert a newly created project (e.g., project P04, "Orion", budget $400,000) without assigning an employee, because Emp_ID is part of the primary key and cannot be NULL.
  • Deletion Anomaly: If employee E103 leaves the company and their record is deleted, all historical and budget information about project P03 ("Gemini") is permanently erased.
  • Update / Modification Anomaly: If the budget for project P01 ("Apollo") increases to $550,000, every matching record must be updated. If Alice's row is updated but Bob's row is missed, the database enters an inconsistent state.

docs.title: 3.3 Progressive Normalization: 1NF through BCNF
docs.text:
Normalization is progressive: each subsequent normal form satisfies all constraints of the preceding forms.

+──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
| BCNF (Every determinant is a super key)                  |
|   +──────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
|   | 3NF (No transitive dependencies on candidate keys)   |
|   |   +──────────────────────────────────────────────────+
|   |   | 2NF (No partial dependencies on composite keys)  |
|   |   |   +──────────────────────────────────────────────+
|   |   |   | 1NF (Atomic domain values; no repeating grps)|
+───┴───┴───┴──────────────────────────────────────────────+

docs.title: 3.3.1 First Normal Form (1NF)
docs.text: Rule: A relation is in 1NF if and only if all attribute values are atomic (indivisible) and there are no repeating groups or multivalued attributes.

docs.title: 1NF Violation Schema
docs.text:
-- VIOLATION: Non-atomic multivalued column 'skills'
CREATE TABLE employee_unnormalized (
    emp_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    emp_name VARCHAR(50),
    skills VARCHAR(200) -- Contains comma-separated values: 'Java, SQL, Docker'
);

docs.title: Resolved 1NF DDL
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE employees (
    emp_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    emp_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE employee_skills (
    emp_id INT NOT NULL,
    skill VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (emp_id, skill),
    FOREIGN KEY (emp_id) REFERENCES employees(emp_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

docs.title: 3.3.2 Second Normal Form (2NF)
docs.text: Rule: A relation is in 2NF if and only if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key (no partial functional dependencies).

docs.title: 2NF Violation Schema
docs.text:
Consider order_items_violation(order_id, product_id, product_name, quantity).

  • Primary Key: Composite key (order_id, product_id)
  • Functional Dependencies:
  • \((order\_id, product\_id) \to quantity\) (Full dependency)
  • \(product\_id \to product\_name\) (Partial dependency; product_name depends on a proper subset of the composite key)

docs.title: Resolved 2NF DDL
docs.text:
-- Table 1: Entity containing full dependency
CREATE TABLE order_items (
    order_id INT NOT NULL,
    product_id INT NOT NULL,
    quantity INT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES products(product_id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- Table 2: Entity isolating the partial dependency
CREATE TABLE products (
    product_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    product_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

docs.title: 3.3.3 Third Normal Form (3NF)
docs.text:
Rule: A relation is in 3NF if and only if it is in 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on any candidate key.

Formally, for every non-trivial functional dependency \(X \to Y\), at least one of the following must hold:

  1. \(X\) is a super key of \(R\), OR
  2. \(Y\) is a prime attribute (a member of some candidate key).

docs.title: 3NF Violation Schema
docs.text:
